title: UMSG recognizes three student organizations and announces new Presidential Space Committee
text:
The University of Maine Student Government (UMSG) met on Oct. 20 in the Bangor Room of the Memorial Union, where three clubs and student organizations were given recognition and a new Presidential Space Committee was announced.
Club maintenance
UMSG moved to grant recognition to the Debate Club, which club officers described as a way to connect students nationally through “critical thinking, public speaking and meaningful intellectual exchange.” The club already has 20 committed members and will meet in Room 402 of Neville Hall.
It’s On Us received final recognition, with 15 students regularly attending meetings in the Memorial Union and an email list of over 250 people. The organization focuses on sexual assault prevention and providing resources to those who may need them.
The Photography and Visual Media club also received final recognition, with more than 15 students regularly attending meetings in Shibles Hall and an email list of about 150 people. The club has hosted events such as light painting in the past and plans to increase outreach in order to give back to the community.
New business
The BPR student advisory board is having an open house Oct. 23 in the GEM multi-purpose room to help get students involved in on-campus student research.
UMSG introduced the first Presidential Space Committee, which will “make recommendations for the future portfolios of buildings on campus to either be built or torn down,” according to President Cynthia Shelmerdine. Buildings currently under review include Aubert Hall, Fogler Library and Hitchner Hall.
The University Volunteer Ambulance Corps (UVAC) has a new truck, and reported that all is going well within their organization.
UMaine Panhellenic is hosting self-defense classes through Alpha Omicron Pi, but is still waiting to be approved for funding by the Senate.
Executive reports
UMSG is looking for a new Director of Communications following the retirement of the position’s previous occupant.
The election for new senators from the College of Engineering and Technology and the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences will take place from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Nov. 18 in the Wade Center. Nomination forms become available Oct. 23, and the deadline for applications is Nov. 6. Candidates will campaign from Nov. 6 to Nov. 17, and the results of the election will be announced Nov. 19.
Special order announcement
There will be a UMaine UVote voter education event in the Bumps Room of the Memorial Union on Oct. 23 from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m.
There will be a Symphonic Band and Jazz Ensemble concert in the Memorial Union on Oct. 25 at 12 p.m. Tickets are free for students.
On Oct. 30, Alpha Tau Omega and Chi Omega will put on “Wicked for Wishes,” a haunted house charity event for the Make-A-Wish foundation.
On Nov. 1, Chi Omega will host a hockey tournament coached by players from both the men’s and women’s hockey teams. All proceeds will go toward the Make-A-Wish foundation.
With no further business to discuss, the 1,622nd UMSG meeting adjourned early just after 7 p.m.

title: Monster Mash Spins Halloween Hits Under The Versant Power Astronomy Center Dome In Orono
text:
Celebrate Halloween In “Spooktacular” Fashion With The Versant Power Astronomy Center’s “Monster Mash” Program
If you're looking for an alternative to the candy-centered chaos that often comes with celebrating Halloween, the folks at the Versant Power Astronomy Center on the campus of the University of Maine in Orono have another option for you: a music-filled sensory extravaganza inside the dome, in their newly installed comfy seats!
The show, "Monster Mash: A Halloween Spooktacular," will feature some of your favorite Halloween songs set to spooky visuals.

title: Study examines changes to Mount Katahdin's tree line
text:
Study examines changes to tree line on Katahdin, Maine's tallest mountain
The landscape atop Maine’s highest peak is changing through a process known as alpine greening, according to a new study.
Jonathan Chipman, the Dartmouth College researcher who commissioned the study, said notable changes have been observed on Mount Katahdin, as well as other mountains in Maine, New Hampshire and Quebec.
“This study uses satellite imagery from the past 40-plus years to look at long-term changes in the environment of the alpine zone on the summit of mountains across New England and eastern Canada, above tree line, where the climate is too harsh for trees to grow," Chipman told WMTW media partner WABI. "What we found is that over the past four decades, there’s been a gradual greening process above tree line on these mountains. In some cases, trees are starting to spread up into areas that were formerly above tree line. Climate warming is contributing to this."
Chipman went on to say that alpine zones — zones above the tree line where larger vegetation cannot grow — are likely to keep shrinking.
“What we will probably see is the alpine zones, especially the smaller ones, disappearing on these mountains,” Chipman said. "Many of the smaller alpine summits will basically be turning over into forest."
Baxter State Park natural resource director Nava Tabak said long-term data is key.
“It’s very hard to detect these changes year to year, and that’s why these studies like the ones that you’re asking about are so important, because they allow us to look over longer periods of time to see that, to actually be able to detect those changes,” Tabak said.
Tabak also said alpine sedge communities appear to be bearing the brunt of these long-term changes.
“Rare plants are, by their definition, somewhat more sensitive to these changes in population, sensitive to becoming extinct,” she said.
Operating as a public trust, Baxter State Park takes a hands-off wilderness approach, focusing on managing people, not plants, to let systems adapt naturally.
Tabak stressed that the most impactful thing people can do when they visit an alpine area is to stay on the marked trails.

title: Dunlap delivers closing congressional message ahead of Election Day
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, was in Bangor on Tuesday to deliver his closing message ahead of Election Day next week.
Dunlap, the current state auditor, was joined by several supporters. Maine AFL-CIO president Cynthia Phinney spoke about Dunlap’s union support. Erin Oberson, a registered nurse and co-president of the Maine State Nurses Union, spoke about the importance of implementing Medicare for All. Sportsmen Ed Pineau and Jeff McCabe spoke about Dunlap’s history with hunting and land protection.
Dunlap’s primary opponent, Jordan Wood, and former 2nd District U.S. Rep. Michael Michaud also supported him Tuesday. Both spoke about their lifelong ties to Maine, along with Dunlap’s. They said Dunlap would be available all year to constituents, referencing an admission by Dunlap’s Republican opponent, former Gov. Paul LePage, about spending winters in Florida.
Voting is already underway, and polls close Nov. 3.
Dunlap said he wanted to share one message before then.
“So here’s my promise. If you send me to Congress, I’ll never forget where I came from and I will never forget who sent me,” Dunlap said. “I’ll be your neighbor first and your congressman second. And I’ll come home every chance I get because home is where the work is.”
In a statement, King described Dunlap as “tough and smart and a strong advocate for his district.”

title: Judge extends court-ordered block on Trump’s renovation plans for public golf course in Washington
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge agreed Monday to extend an order blocking the Trump administration’s renovation plans for a century-old public golf course in the nation’s capital.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a preliminary injunction that temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the East Potomac Golf Course. The administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active.
“The Court earlier stated, ‘I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees.’ The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law,” Reyes wrote.
Reyes expressed astonishment that the government has asked her to “not to believe the sitting President” and disregard Trump’s statements about his plans for the golf course renovations.
“This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more,” Reyes wrote. “It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys.”
On Oct. 18, Trump announced plans on social media to close the golf course for 15 months, starting Nov. 15, and redevelop the 106-year-old park and course despite a court challenge by the D.C. Preservation League and two golfers. A day later, Trump posted that the work would start immediately.
Reyes, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Joe Biden, previously ordered the administration to suspend work on the project until at least Oct. 26.
Trump was asked about the case late Monday night as he arrived back at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland following a rally in Mississippi and indicated that work on the golf course will proceed as planned.
“It has the go-ahead. The judge feels that she would like to approve it as it goes along. And I didn’t know she was an architectural critic of golf courses,” Trump said sarcastically.
He added of the judge: “She knows nothing about that, so we’ll appeal that” while also calling his planned overhaul a “beautiful project for Washington, D.C.”
Trump later in a social media post reiterated a statement he made Oct. 18 that the course would close for 15 months. “We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons,” he wrote.
The plaintiffs challenging the project, DC Preservation League and two golfers, claim the work is inflicting irreversible damage. At a hearing, the judge excoriated the government after workers cut down at least 400 trees over a holiday weekend with little notice to the plaintiffs.
The course renovation project is part of the Republican president’s aggressive campaign to leave his personal imprint on Washington’s historic landscape. Those plans include construction of a huge ballroom at the White House, a massive arch and the creation of a National Garden of American Heroes in West Potomac Park. DC Preservation League is part of a coalition of organizations, including the Cultural Landscape Foundation and one D.C. resident, who have filed lawsuit challenging those plans.
Reyes rejected the administration’s request for her to recuse herself from the case. The government questioned her impartiality and accused her of engaging in “egregious” behavior from the bench during an emergency hearing in the case.
In Monday’s ruling Reyes stressed that she had hoped the parties could have resolved their dispute without judicial intervention. She noted that she had denied plaintiffs’ previous requests.
“The Court would much prefer not to have to resolve Lorax v. Once‑ler redux. Indeed, for months, the Court declined to intervene,” she wrote.
But she said the government forced her hand by bulldozing hundreds of trees without any notice, doing “what it assured all it would not do.”
Reyes quoted from a golf-related opinion written by the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, a conservative icon, in stressing the temporary nature of her own decision.
“Here, golf and government have again clashed,” Reyes wrote. “By issuing this preliminary injunction, the Court does not end the round: it simply marks the ball until the parties can fully and fairly litigate this case.
Democracy Forward President & CEO Skye Perryman, whose organization is co-counsel representing the plaintiffs, called the ruling “a big win that will rightly protect East Potomac Park from further irreparable harm.” She added, in an email, that the move will stop activities “while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court.”
___
An earlier version of this story incorrectly referred to Perryman as “he.” This version corrects her identity to “she.”
___
Associated Press reporters Gary Fields and Will Weissert contributed.

title: Maine teachers and students say school cellphone ban is working
text:
Jonathan Bisson walked through the double doors at Brunswick High School for his first day of the academic year in August. As a senior, the hallways felt familiar — except for a white, rectangular box by the door of his first class.
The box was knee height on small wheels and contained about 25 slots where students could insert their phones at the start of the day. The boxes are meant to help students comply with a new district policy spurred by recent state law prohibiting phone use in school.
Phone restrictions in class were nothing new, Bisson said. Many of his teachers last year required students to place their phones in small plastic pouches hung on the door or wall. His band teacher even used this as a way to gauge attendance: An empty pouch likely meant an absent student, he said.
But this year students in Brunswick and across Maine don’t get their phones back after each class. They cannot check social media on their phones in the hallways or at lunch. They can’t text their parents or friends at any point during the day.
A single paragraph on the 175th page of the state’s supplemental budget in April set a sweeping mandate for K-12 schools across the state: Ban cellphones and other electronic devices connected to the internet — with medical and other exceptions — from “starting bell to dismissal bell” by Aug. 1.
The new law, championed by Gov. Janet Mills, was meant to limit distractions and encourage real-life connections. It made Maine the 23rd state to enforce a statewide bell-to-bell cellphone ban, according to Emily Rapp, director of public policy for the Institute for Families and Technology, based in Washington, D.C.
Some Maine school districts said they braced for student pushback against the new restrictions.
But nearly three months into the new policy, school officials and teachers across Maine told The Maine Monitor they have been surprised by how understanding students have been, though they described some as begrudgingly compliant.
The clearcut policy and backing from the force of law has helped schools control phone use far better this academic year than in the past, said officials and teachers, who described the effects on students as overwhelmingly positive.
Teachers said students are more attentive in class, are more likely to stay on task and are completing more in-class work.
Students are connecting with each other more in the time between classes, staff across the state said. And during lunch, staff are hearing louder and more lively conversation in the cafeteria — a stark contrast from previous years when phone use stifled talking.
On his first day of school, Bisson placed his phone in the box, closed its glass door and sat at his desk. By force of habit he tried to retrieve his phone after class and felt a small surge of panic when the small door wouldn’t open.
But, as quickly as the feeling came, it faded.
“My phone left my mind, and I didn’t really think about not having it,” Bisson said. “In fact, I think I almost left it at school that day.”
Between school, jazz band, cross country and working as the editor in chief of the school’s student newspaper, The Dragon Gazette, which he revived last year from its last print in 1976, Bisson said he does not feel reliant on his phone. The ban did not change much about his daily routine, he said.
Many of Bisson’s classmates and friends were critical of the restrictions last year, he said, but they now support the ban as well.
‘Breath of fresh air’
Eric Hutchins teaches graphic arts at Bangor High School where he has worked for 24 years. He witnessed phones grow from a simple technology into a big distraction, which he felt he policed more than he taught his subject at times, he said.
Since the Bangor School Department set a stricter phone policy last year, which required students to place their phones in lockboxes at the start of each class, students have been much more attentive, Hutchins said.
Bangor’s shift this year was relatively small, Hutchins said. Teachers last year had to collect student phones and place them in a handheld lockbox at the start of every class. But now students go to their last class at the start of the day, place their phones in the lockbox, and then head to their first class. At the end of the day, their phones are waiting for them to pick up.
The shift in procedure saves five minutes each class, Hutchins said.
Students in Hutchins’ class work throughout the year on in-class projects that help different departments within the school — such as a poster for a school theater production. Since the stricter policy last year, he has seen a higher rate of completed projects, Hutchins said.
Andrew McCullough, an environmental science teacher at Brunswick High School, said the positive changes he has seen accompany the stricter phone policy are a “breath of fresh air.”
Students stay on task, he said. But the most dramatic changes can be seen in the interactions between students in the hallways and at the start and end of classes, he said.
Students would ordinarily “get their last fix” on their phones before his lessons started and be anxious to return to their phones once he stopped teaching, he said. Now they are more talkative with each other.
Looking back, McCullough said it was unfair to ask teenagers to monitor themselves between classes as social media connected them to the world and people around them.
“Even kids who are exceptional students, who are good kids struggle with that — in the same way that I struggle with it,” he said.
Powered off
Some kids still find ways to use their phones during school, but the new law has cut back on the number doing so and improved school life overall, students, administrators and teachers said.
Bisson said students routinely broke the rules last year in part because the punishment was less severe than it is now.
If a student was caught with a phone during class last academic year, it would be confiscated for the rest of class, he said. Now, the phone is taken for the rest of the day, and the rule is taken more seriously.
“The failure to adhere to the actual rules eroded people’s faith in them last year, and we’re getting some of that back now,” Bisson said.
Now the Brunswick School Department’s discipline for student cellphone use grows in severity from a warning to a meeting with parents for repeated offenses.
Teachers at Brunswick High School catch students on their phones every day, McCullough said, and, because of the strict rules, it is easier to spot. Phones are not supposed to be seen at all.
However, as of Oct. 15, no student had been required to meet with a school administrator and their parents, McCullough said.
At Bangor High School, teachers have been told to send students with phones or other prohibited electronic devices to school administrators where they will receive a detention, Hutchins said.
Bangor High School has had only two or three infractions as of Oct. 7, department spokesperson Raymond Phinney said. The department’s two middle schools have had none.
Other electronics, such as smart watches, which are also included in the state directive, are much more difficult for teachers to police and often go unrestricted so long as they are not distractions, teachers and students said.
Some students still circumvent the rules by keeping their phones in their backpacks or on their person. Then they leave class and use their phones in the bathroom or sneakily check them during lunch, students and staff said. But phones do not impede class instruction as much as before.
Jeff Lovejoy, principal of Belfast Area High School, said administrators knew they would “lose the fight” of some students using their phones in the bathroom when they enforced their new policy this year.
Due to a flexible student schedule, the school does not have lockboxes and instead requires students to have their phones powered off and out of sight in their backpacks or lockers for the school day.
Faculty at the midcoast high school catch students on their phones about once per week, he said.
And there are other technology challenges.
Earlier this school year students at Belfast Area High School used their school-issued Chromebooks to access an online game’s chatroom where they made anonymous posts that included bullying and racial slurs, Lovejoy said.
The incident showed administrators they needed more protocols around how students were using their laptops, he said.
Some parents were reluctant to forgo the easy connection to their child that they had grown accustomed to ahead of the passage of the law last year. But it appears that parents have still been able to reach their children — such as through school offices — when needed.
Annadene and Tom Fowler said the new process of getting in touch with their son, Eliot, is not worrisome and feels essentially the same as before. Eliot, a sophomore at Belfast Area High School, leaves his phone in his backpack everyday. In an emergency, he can get it quickly.
If Eliot’s parents need to reach him during the school day, they often email him.
Andy Badeaux, a father of two students at Brunswick High School, said he has trouble getting in touch with his children through their phones anyway because the cell signal at the school is like a “black hole.”
“My default position is supporting whatever needs to happen so the classroom can be effective at what it’s supposed to do,” Badeaux said.
This story appears as part of a collaboration to strengthen investigative journalism in Maine between the BDN and The Maine Monitor. Read more about the partnership.

title: These Portland food workers see the bright side of the dark before the dawn
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For those of us on standard day shifts, there’s a certain mystery and exoticism to people who work before dawn.
In the food world, bakers are known for starting their days in the dark, which is also famously when it’s time to make the doughnuts. We recently clocked in on the early shift to observe the routines of two other food producers: a barbecue pitmaster, and a small-batch coffee roaster.
They enjoy the solitude that affords them peaceful yet highly productive mornings. They’re partnered with their equipment, a customized, reverse-flow smoker and a RoasTronix S9X coffee roaster. They know the strengths and quirks of these quiet co-workers inside out.
When the clocks fall back to standard time on Sunday, they gain a little extra morning light for several weeks. But — except maybe during the deepest gloom of winter — it seems their passion for their work transcends the darkness altogether.
KEEPER OF THE FLAME
Low and slow is barbecue’s mantra. To render tough, primal cuts of meat into smoke-seasoned, juicy and meltingly tender treasures, you need to cook them at low temperatures, very slowly.
The beloved brisket at Terlingua in Portland spends at least 12 hours in the smoker, mostly at about 250 degrees, for instance. The restaurant has a gas-assisted, overnight smoker inside the kitchen to help augment its supply. But the bulk of their smoked meats — including pork shoulder, ribs, chicken, turkey and specialty cuts like beef cheeks — start cooking every day before dawn in the smokehouse, an attached shed just behind the kitchen.
Terlingua pitmaster Ben Bellevue starts his day there at 5 a.m. It helps that his commute is just 15 seconds, door-to-door; he lives with his wife and young son directly above the Washington Avenue restaurant’s dining room.
First order of business: Start the fire. Bellevue steps down into the smokehouse and makes for the custom-built, reverse-flow smoker. Terlingua co-owner Pliny Reynolds and his metalworker friend crafted the vaguely steampunk unit from a 500-gallon water tank and a Warner wood stove.
Bellevue lights grease-soaked butcher paper and kindling in the firebox. Its flat, cast-iron top gets so hot, he’ll sometimes cook his breakfast on it. Once the ember base is ready, he starts feeding the box with kiln-dried red oak. Reynolds and Bellevue swear by their Phippsburg-sourced hardwood, because it burns long, hot and clean.
In early summer, it’s light out at the start of Bellevue’s shift, which is nice. But he’s so used to starting in the dark, it makes him feel like he’s running behind, even at 5 a.m.
Turning the clocks back has that same disorienting effect, though the extra morning light slowly dwindles, then disappears in the dead of winter. “I like starting the day a little bit in the dark,” he said. “Don’t really like January, when it’s like 8:30 and it’s still kind of dark in here.”
‘ZEN AND THE ART OF BARBECUE’
This time of year, after peak season, Bellevue could start a little later, say 6 a.m. But that also makes him feel rushed. And there’s plenty to do still. Terlingua goes through as much as 200 pounds of brisket and 100 pounds of pork shoulder on a busy fall day.
Bellevue coats prime-grade, trimmed briskets first with a blend of mustard and pickle juice, then dry seasonings. He lets them sit for a few minutes so the rub can reliably stick and form the bark, barbecue’s prized, delectable dark crust. Then he sets the briskets and the day’s other meats on the smoker’s racks, arranging them strategically on and around the hot spots.
The smokehouse has no clock, and Bellevue doesn’t often check his phone for the time. “I’ve got a little bit of time blindness,” he said. “I go by the flow of the day.” He gauges the progress of the morning by the the staggered arrivals of day shift cooks, or the shafts of light that stream through cracks in the smokehouse roof.
There’s a distinctly meditative element to his early morning work. He’s focused, on task, but fully present and aware of his surroundings. “I’m trimming brisket by myself at 6 in the morning, and I’ll hear the first planes take off at the airport,” he said. Or he hears the sudden psssh of a truck’s airbrakes out on Washington Avenue, and the metal clang of its gate, and knows it’s time for a food or wood delivery.
Bellevue isn’t monkish about the quietude. The smokehouse has a TV screen, and he sometimes puts on a replay of an NFL game he missed over the weekend. Or he’ll listen to food or fantasy football podcasts. Or maybe some Sturgill Simpson or outlaw country, a taste he acquired about eight years ago in the smokehouse at Lewis Barbecue in Charleston, S.C., his barbecue boot camp.
He worked the 3 a.m.-1 p.m. shift at Lewis for 18 months, and his commute was 20 minutes without traffic. The smokehouse was in a separate building from the kitchen, and he estimates he walked about six miles during each 10-hour shift.
Temps inside the Lewis smokehouse averaged around 95 degrees, and grew much hotter in the summer, when it was already 85 degrees outside with 90 percent humidity at 3 a.m. Between work and his regular jogging routine, Bellevue thinks he lost 45 pounds in six months. Still, it was a chance to work under Texas-style barbecue guru John Lewis, and the experience was formative.
Bellevue has cooked in other types of restaurants — Duckfat, The East Ender and the former Grace, where he met his wife. But barbecue suits him best.
“With line cooking, you’re a machine. Making this dish for one minute, and then you’re done and on to the next thing,” he said. “In the smokehouse, I’ve got 30 minutes before I have to check the smoker again, so I’ve got 15 minutes to do this, 15 minutes to do that. And that’s a little better for the way my brain works.
“I tell everybody I have a perfect job. I don’t commute, I get to be outside. And as the guy I used to work with says, ‘I get paid to play with fire.'”
Reynolds worked the early morning shift himself for Terlingua’s first six years. He was happy to hand off the predawn pitmaster duty, but still vouches for its genuine pleasures.
“You get here first thing in the morning, you light up the smoker, make a pot of coffee, and you’re just in your own world and zone and pace for three to four hours. It’s a pretty great way to start every day,” Reynolds said. “Zen and the art of barbecue.”
ROASTING IN THE DARK
When you work at a small-batch coffee company, good coffee is a built-in perk.
Rwanda Bean head roaster Kyle Mitchell typically arrives at the Thompson’s Point roastery around 5 a.m., three hours before it opens, and makes himself a pour-over blonde roast while the roasting machine warms up.
Mitchell roasts as many as 1,000 pounds of beans in a busy week, maybe 700 pounds a week in the off-season. In nearly two years since he’s been on the job, he’s roasted 78,676 pounds of Rwandan coffee — the equivalent of a fully loaded 18-wheeler, or 10 African elephants.
Small roasting companies need to start early in the day to stay on track with orders, and Mitchell is also Rwanda Bean’s head of production and order fulfillment. As a wholesaler, the company supplies beans and ground coffee to nearly every Whole Foods in New England, for example, along with about 10 cafés in Greater Portland. They also have retail and subscription customers both locally and around the country.
The roasted coffee Mitchell already has on hand on a given morning will be packaged and shipped out by the end of that day, so he needs a fresh supply. “What’s being roasted today might be bagged later today,” he said. On a recent Wednesday morning, he was roasting 300 pounds of beans, in roughly 17-pound batches.
Mitchell lives in Portland, and gets up for work around 4:15 or 4:30 a.m., depending when his cat wakes him up. He’s a naturally early riser.
“I was always the kid in school who wanted to get to school an hour early,” Mitchell said. “As a skier, I love the dawn patrol. You get the best tracks.”
It’s still dark out when Mitchell begins scooping and weighing 17.7-pound batches of beans. He pours a batch into the hopper of the pre-programmed RoasTronix S9X roaster, which looks like a trio of shiny, conjoined water heaters. The roaster drum whirls and whooshes as it gently stirs and heats the beans. Mitchell monitors multiple temperatures on the unit’s digital display — radiant heat from a halogen bulb; conductive heat on the surface of the stainless steel drum; and convection airflow.
When Mitchell first started roasting at Rwanda Bean, they didn’t yet have the fancy electric RoasTronix.
“The gas roaster I learned on, I had to sit there all day, every day, to manually adjust throughout the roast,” he said. “I’m turning the gas knob to make micro-adjustments to the temperature. I had to give it my full attention. I still pay attention to it (now), and it still fluctuates a little bit, so I have to make sure it’s meeting our quality. But I can multitask.”
Around 6:15 a.m., he glances out one of the large front windows in the lofty space. The horizon glows with dawn’s first light.
“The sunlight here at the Point is really nice in the mornings. The sun comes up right over the highway. It’s a beautiful place to work. At one point in the day, it’s blinding, but besides that, it’s really nice.”
FALLING BACK IS A MIXED BLESSING
All of Rwanda Bean’s raw green beans are single-origin, sourced from one farming cooperative in Rwanda. Rwandan coffee has a subtle inherent sweetness, with citrus and cherry notes. Blonde roast lets the light citrus flavor come through; dark roast delivers more robust, nutty chocolate flavor.
On this Wednesday, Mitchell is making medium roast beans, taking them past “first crack” stage where they shed their outer chaff layer. Each batch takes about 16 minutes, including a cooldown cycle. He’s careful to inspect the cooldown tray for any beans that might have stuck in the roaster and burned.
“One burned bean will ruin a cup of coffee, for sure,” he said.
The air in the roastery isn’t as thickly perfumed with coffee as you might imagine, but it wafts seductively from the freshly roasted beans as they twirl in the cooling tray. Open the lid of a 50-gallon barrel full of their dark roast beans, and the heady aroma envelops you.
Mitchell sees the fall clock change as a mixed blessing. “Having that sun come up a little earlier makes the day feel like it goes by a little faster,” he said, and helps him ward off any seasonal depression. But he also likes to go for long afternoon runs and bike rides, which are harder to pull off after work during standard time.
Regardless of when dawn breaks, Mitchell loves the serenity of early mornings at work. “The peace is the beauty of it,” he said. “I appreciate being able to come in and have things quiet.”
Mitchell has worked in the service industry, and likes interacting with people. Some customers will stop by the roastery after they open at 8 a.m. to buy a bag or two, and Mitchell still gets several people a day coming in for a cup of coffee, even though the space hasn’t been a café since 2023.
At the end of his workday, Mitchell tends to find himself as equally fulfilled as Rwanda’s orders.
“I enjoy coming in here every day knowing that what I’m doing is what a lot of people need to start their day.”

title: Beloved high school football player hit, killed by allegedly drunken driver after game
text:
FEDERAL WAY, Wash. (KING) - Friends, family and teammates are mourning a 16-year-old Washington state student-athlete who was hit and killed by an allegedly drunken driver after a Friday night football game.
Deejay Tuiasosopo, 16, came from a family of standout athletes, including an all-star University of Washington quarterback – but his family says he was building his own legacy. The Federal Way High School junior played multiple sports, valued his education and cared about the people around him.
“He was always there for you. He always had a big smile on his face, no matter what was going on,” said Tuiasosopo’s friend, Stormie Corey. “He was lighting up every single room.”
After a Friday night football game, Tuiasosopo was standing on the sidewalk around 10:45 p.m. when two cars collided on Pacific Highway South in Federal Way. The crash sent one of the cars onto the sidewalk, hitting and killing the 16-year-old.
Police arrested the 29-year-old man driving the car that hit Tuiasosopo on suspicion of vehicular homicide. Investigators suspect he was driving under the influence.
“It didn’t feel real. It felt like I was stuck in a nightmare. Nothing can prepare you for that kind of moment,” Corey said. “He had so much life to live.”
Now, Tuiasosopo’s family, friends and teammates are left mourning his death, a loss that still doesn’t feel real.
“He wasn’t just a friend. He was a brother to me, and I just feel like all of us football players are going to remember this night,” said Chester Maletala, one of his football teammates. “We’re still going to have him spiritually in our hearts and in our head. We told ourselves already we’re going to make it to state for him.”
Tuiasosopo’s family said in a statement in part that “his energy, light and infectious presence reached far beyond what we, as his family, even realized.”
The suspect’s next court appearance is expected Wednesday. The investigation into the incident is ongoing.

title: Annual loon count finds the population in Maine is down, but not concerning
text:
Annual loon count finds the population in Maine is down, but not concerning
Maine Audubon says the annual loon count found the population in Maine is down in 2026 compared to 2025, but there is no cause for concern right now.
The loon count results released on Tuesday found an estimated Common Loon population of 2,770 adults and 276 chicks in southern Maine (the area south of the 45th parallel). The 2025 count estimated 3,174 adults and 568 chicks in southern Maine.
In 2024, the loon count for southern Maine estimated a population of 3,146 adults and 420 chicks. Those figures are more than double the inaugural loon count in 1983, when Maine Audubon estimated a population of 1,417 adults and 176 chicks.
Maine has one of the largest populations of Common Loons in the country. Alaska has the most, followed by Minnesota and then Maine and Wisconsin, which have similar populations of loons.
The 43rd annual loon count was held in July, with a record 1,861 volunteers helping count loons on 438 lakes and ponds in Maine.
The Audubon said its focus is on long-term trends, not just year-to-year comparisons.
Officials said there were several factors that could have depressed the numbers during this year's count.
Many counters reported fog and windy conditions during the survey window this window and there was also smoke from Canadian wildfires over parts of the state at the time. These conditions can make it harder to actually see and observe loons, especially chicks.
Many volunteer counters also reported seeing loons still on the nest at the time of the July count, with chicks not expected to hatch until the coming weeks.
Maine Audubon's Loon Pair Monitoring project also saw instances of delayed nesting or loons over-incubating the eggs in their first nest. While some loon pairs might successfully raise chicks each year, other pairs will only fledge chicks every other year or every few years, which still allows for maintaining a healthy statewide population.
"With high estimates the last two years and lower estimates this year," said Maine Audubon Community Science Manager Mady Eori, "the next few years will allow us to truly understand what trends we're seeing in the adult and chick populations. We still believe the loon population is healthy in Maine and it's important to remember that the population does not need to grow each year to be a stable, healthy population. However, a year like this highlights the importance of supporting long-term monitoring efforts. Without historical data to compare estimates to, we wouldn't be able to track population trends as closely, and get ahead of any potential threats to the loon population."
Maine Audubon said there is not enough data collected on lakes in northern Maine to provide population estimates for the whole state. However, this year volunteers counted on 125 northern lakes, a number that grows each year, and observed 515 adults and 40 chicks.
A handful of "extended duration" volunteers also participated, for the second year in a row, in a new project that allows them a week-long window to survey remote lakes that lack easy boat access. They observed 53 adult loons and 3 chicks.
Anyone who is in northern Maine and is interested in participating next year should contact conserve@maineaudubon.org.
Maine Audubon is the oldest and largest conservation organization in the state with eight public centers and sanctuaries and seven chapters. The organization is independent of the National Audubon Society, but Maine Audubon said it has a collaborative relationship with the national organization and they share conservation goals.

title: Lynne G. Bradford | Obituaries
text:
Lynne G. Bradford, 76, passed away on Oct. 17, 2026, under the compassionate care of the staff of Birch Bay Village’s Safe Harbor in Bar Harbor. Nee Lynne Shelley Gardner, she was born on Oct. 18, 1949, in Houlton, Maine to Clyde “Holmes” and Elizabeth “Bette” (Gentle) Gardner.
Her early years were spent in Houlton near extended family, but the family soon relocated to Presque Isle, where Holmes opened Gardner’s Studio, House of Photography, on Academy Street. Younger brother Leslie Holmes Gardner joined the family in 1955. The family enjoyed an active family life, especially camp life at East Grand Lake and Drew’s Lake. Lynne attended Presque Isle High School, graduating in 1967. She fondly recalled being a “Rainbow Girl” and was named “Best Dressed” in her high school yearbook, a trend she’d carry forward through life. She attended Westbrook Junior College and graduated in 1969. Shortly thereafter, she married David John Dow, son of John and Helen Culberson Dow of Cedar Street at the Presque Isle Congregational Church. The couple started married life in Bangor, where Lynne worked briefly as secretary to William S. Cohen, subsequently Maine representative, senator, and Secretary of Defense. Lynne and David had two children, Melissa “Missy” and Jonathan “Jad” Dow and settled on Mount Desert Island before divorcing in 1974.

title: Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly rallies Maine Democrats for Troy Jackson in Freeport
text:
FREEPORT — U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona and possible 2028 presidential candidate, rallied support for local Democrats, including U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson, one week before the midterm elections.
Kelly leaned heavily into a populist message Tuesday evening at Maine Beer Company, saying that a Democratic Senate majority is needed to stand up to President Donald Trump and to help working-class families who are falling further behind, while the rich get richer.
“The system is still working — it’s just not working for you,” Kelly told a crowd of nearly 400 people while standing on a countertop. “You know what it’s working for? The people writing the rules, the rich, the powerful, the predators in the Epstein files. And the people who kissed Donald Trump’s ass. That’s who it works for.”
The event comes one week before the midterm elections. Jackson is locked in a tight battle against five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins in Maine’s closely watched Senate race. The seat is viewed as a prime pickup opportunity for Democrats, but Collins has proved resilient in the past.
In addition to Jackson, Kelly also rallied support for Rep. Chellie Pingree, who is running for reelection in the 1st District; and Hannah Pingree, who is running for governor.
Kelly’s visit comes a week after former Sen. Joe Manchin, a longtime Democrat turned independent from West Virginia, campaigned with Collins.
At campaign stops in Lewiston and Norway, Manchin, who left the Democratic Party in 2024, called Collins the “soul of the Senate” and applauded her bipartisan credentials — something increasingly rare in the age of Trump.
During his brief remarks, Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president, talked about how political elites often look down on working-class people like him. He referenced a new Collins ad featuring former TV personality Bill Green.
After praising Collins, Green said he knows Jackson and that “we’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here. We’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective.”
Jackson said the spot shows how people in power are working to keep ordinary working people down, claiming things like healthcare, child care, reproductive care and affordable prescription drugs and other needs are impossible to achieve.
“They want to make us feel like we’re something less,” Jackson said. “I just had that today with Bill Green. Yeah, I know what a cord would cost. I sure do. And a lot of people right now are trying to figure out how they’re going to heat their homes. … But we’re going to build something different that is actually going to stand up for people. And I’m excited about that.”
Kelly’s appearance is a big departure from the other national surrogates who came to Maine to campaign for Jackson. In recent weeks, Jackson has rallied Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. — all of whom are progressive stalwarts. Both Warren and Ocasio-Cortez held events geared toward college students.
Kelly, however, is more moderate. But he found common cause with Jackson in his messages about making corporations pay their fair share, helping working-class families and opposing Trump, who he said “isn’t even trying to do the job anymore.”
Kelly talked about how he came under fire from Trump over the summer when he released a video message urging troops to only follow legal orders. After that, Trump focused the power of the federal government against him, he said.
“In response, Donald Trump said I should be hanged, executed, prosecuted,” Kelly said. “He couldn’t even get the order right. Then he tried to indict me and throw me in jail. But that wasn’t about me. It’s actually about silencing veterans, retired service members. Really, it’s about silencing all of us.”
Kelly frequently referred to his wife, former congresswoman Gabby Giffords, who was shot by a gunman. He also discussed his personal background — being raised by two police officers, attending public school, serving in the Navy, becoming an astronaut and a U.S. senator.
“And president,” someone from the crowd shouted.
“We’ll see,” Kelly replied to cheers.

title: Aroostook potato farm brings spooky spuds to Halloween
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Last Halloween, Aroostook County kids got to dig through buried eyeballs, bones and brains in a faux graveyard to unearth bags of potato chips.
This year, they’ll get to do it again during Houlton’s All Shire’s Eve.
It’s part of a growing “Trick or Tater” national trend. Daniel J. Corey Farms of Monticello rolled a large green tractor and the graveyard experience into historic Market Square in 2025 for the innovative spooky spuds adventure. The immersive event really took off.
Working alongside the town’s Community Impact Alliance, Ben Corey and Chloe Wheeler helped kids capture almost 900 bags of potato chips for their Halloween treat.
The increasingly popular Trick-or-Tater, which involves handing out potatoes alongside the usual fun-size candy, started five years ago on social media, according to Kayla Vogel, manager of community engagement and influencer partnerships for Potatoes USA, the national marketing and research organization for potato farmers.
The spooky spuds movement is booming around the country and in some communities it’s now a tradition with a “potato house” on every block, Vogel said.
“People get really excited when they find the potatoes that were out there,” she said. “It’s been a really fun way for us to highlight potatoes not only as a nutrient dense vegetable but offer a fun way to be part of Halloween.”
The County couple decided, instead of offering the traditional All Shire’s Eve trunk or treat fun, they would bring the biggest green tractor for a hayride and then set up the graveyard in a trough with soil so the kids could have a fun, spooky experience, said Wheeler, who handles community engagement for the seed potato farm.
“Prior to Halloween we purchased 1,000 bags of Lay’s potato chips, and their treat is a bag of Lay’s potato chips grown from our seed potatoes,” she said. “It’s important for Ben to talk about farming to future generations, and when you plant a big green tractor downtown kids naturally ask questions and that’s a gateway for Ben to talk about it.”
Frito Lay breeds their own proprietary potato variety for taste, quality and crispness, Dan Corey said from their potato farm in Florida.
“So it’s always the same to make sure the golden Lay’s taste exactly the same as when you were 3 years old to today,” he said.
Dan Corey Farms in Maine and Florida provide seed potatoes that are planted and grown from Florida to Canada and then harvested for the snack food company.
“Our seeds reach a lot of acres,” Corey said. “We’re supplying the Florida growers, North Carolina, South Carolina, Delaware, Indiana.”
During the school year, Wheeler travels to local schools to teach the students a farm to table lesson.
“I like to take every opportunity I can to bring Ben and his family and the farm into the community and share with everybody the reality that there are small families who work together to put the food on your table,” she said. “So impressive to represent farm families and a good opportunity for our community to see that these big farmers are real people and real families that take pride in what they do.”
Whether in school or during the Halloween event, the kids are naturally very curious and have all kinds of questions about farming.
“What color are the tractors?”
“What’s the biggest potato you’ve ever grown?”
When Wheeler visits a school she often has a lesson where the students cook something from a potato.
“The last time I went, we made french fries,” Wheeler said. “The kids used vegetable cutters and cut their potatoes and turned them right into french fries. They could really see what harvest to table looks like and they took vegetable cutters home.”
Families are still reaching out to Wheeler to share that they now use the vegetable cutters and make the fries all the time, she said.
According to Dan Corey, the Caribou Russet is a bigger potato and makes an excellent french fry because of its length.
For Halloween this year they are bringing a tractor back downtown, but a bigger one this time, Wheeler said.
“This year we will dive into the barnyard theme and instead of Lay’s Classic potato chips we actually purchased Lay’s Ruffles, which come in a red bag, so that’s even more fitting,” she said.
Potatoes USA’s chefs cooked up a new lineup of spooky spud recipes for the season. They include Spooky Spud Skulls, crispy skull-shaped potatoes that become a “frightful” appetizer with cheese and pepperoni; Monster Mash, green mashed potatoes; and Mashed Potato Mummy Meatloaf Cupcakes, which the council said are perfect for a Halloween-inspired family dinner or a savory cupcake-decorating station at any spooky celebration.
The Halloween event is next Saturday in downtown Houlton starting at 3 p.m.

title: Judge extends court-ordered block on Trump’s renovation plans for public golf course in Washington
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge agreed Monday to extend an order blocking the Trump administration’s renovation plans for a century-old public golf course in the nation’s capital.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a preliminary injunction that temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the East Potomac Golf Course. The administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active.
“The Court earlier stated, ‘I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees.’ The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law,” Reyes wrote.
Reyes expressed astonishment that the government has asked her to “not to believe the sitting President” and disregard Trump’s statements about his plans for the golf course renovations.
“This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more,” Reyes wrote. “It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys.”
On Oct. 18, Trump announced plans on social media to close the golf course for 15 months, starting Nov. 15, and redevelop the 106-year-old park and course despite a court challenge by the D.C. Preservation League and two golfers. A day later, Trump posted that the work would start immediately.
Reyes, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Joe Biden, previously ordered the administration to suspend work on the project until at least Oct. 26.
Trump was asked about the case late Monday night as he arrived back at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland following a rally in Mississippi and indicated that work on the golf course will proceed as planned.
“It has the go-ahead. The judge feels that she would like to approve it as it goes along. And I didn’t know she was an architectural critic of golf courses,” Trump said sarcastically.
He added of the judge: “She knows nothing about that, so we’ll appeal that” while also calling his planned overhaul a “beautiful project for Washington, D.C.”
Trump later in a social media post reiterated a statement he made Oct. 18 that the course would close for 15 months. “We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons,” he wrote.
The plaintiffs challenging the project, DC Preservation League and two golfers, claim the work is inflicting irreversible damage. At a hearing, the judge excoriated the government after workers cut down at least 400 trees over a holiday weekend with little notice to the plaintiffs.
The course renovation project is part of the Republican president’s aggressive campaign to leave his personal imprint on Washington’s historic landscape. Those plans include construction of a huge ballroom at the White House, a massive arch and the creation of a National Garden of American Heroes in West Potomac Park. DC Preservation League is part of a coalition of organizations, including the Cultural Landscape Foundation and one D.C. resident, who have filed lawsuit challenging those plans.
Reyes rejected the administration’s request for her to recuse herself from the case. The government questioned her impartiality and accused her of engaging in “egregious” behavior from the bench during an emergency hearing in the case.
In Monday’s ruling Reyes stressed that she had hoped the parties could have resolved their dispute without judicial intervention. She noted that she had denied plaintiffs’ previous requests.
“The Court would much prefer not to have to resolve Lorax v. Once‑ler redux. Indeed, for months, the Court declined to intervene,” she wrote.
But she said the government forced her hand by bulldozing hundreds of trees without any notice, doing “what it assured all it would not do.”
Reyes quoted from a golf-related opinion written by the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, a conservative icon, in stressing the temporary nature of her own decision.
“Here, golf and government have again clashed,” Reyes wrote. “By issuing this preliminary injunction, the Court does not end the round: it simply marks the ball until the parties can fully and fairly litigate this case.
Democracy Forward President & CEO Skye Perryman, whose organization is co-counsel representing the plaintiffs, called the ruling “a big win that will rightly protect East Potomac Park from further irreparable harm.” She added, in an email, that the move will stop activities “while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court.”
___
An earlier version of this story incorrectly referred to Perryman as “he.” This version corrects her identity to “she.”
___
Associated Press reporters Gary Fields and Will Weissert contributed.

title: 'Kate & Allie' and 'McMillan & Wife' star Susan Saint James dies at 80
text:
Susan Saint James, 'Kate & Allie' and 'McMillan & Wife' star, dies at 80
Susan Saint James, best known for her roles on the TV series "Kate & Allie" and "McMillan & Wife," has died at the age of 80.
People Magazine reported the actress died on Oct. 26 after being diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.
She was "generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up," family members shared in a statement with People Magazine. "She taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people."
The Hollywood Reporter, which confirmed James' passing via family, said the actress was 20 years old when she scored a part alongside Franciosa in the 1966 NBC/Universal TV movie "Fame Is the Name of the Game."
Directed by Stuart Rosenberg, who would soon helm "Cool Hand Luke," it served as the pilot for "The Name of the Game."
Six months after "The Name of the Game's" final episode, she became a part of the 90-minute drama series "McMillan & Wife."
James was a part of several other productions, notably in 1984 for her role on the CBS sitcom "Kate & Allie," where two childhood friends raised their kids in a Greenwich Village brownstone they shared.
When the series was canceled in 1989 after the sixth season — it was nominated three times for the Emmy for outstanding comedy series — James decided to pretty much shut down her acting career, The Hollywood Reporter said.
"She never met a stranger," her family said in a statement following her passing. "Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story. Her defining act: weeks after losing her youngest son, Teddy, in the November 28, 2004, plane crash, she delivered his eulogy as a note to each of her other children and her husband, giving them words to heal. Even in the deepest grief of her life, she put everyone else first. Days after the crash, she sat with Tim Russert to thank the people who had reached out and to tell them the family was okay.”
Survivors include her third husband, Dick Ebersol, the former Saturday Night Live executive producer and head of NBC Sports, whom she married in November 1981.

title: All those end-of-season gardening tasks? Don’t bother
text:
We had the first frost of the season a week or so ago, which is about the time I expect it every year in Cape Elizabeth. In my early years of gardening it would have meant the start of a vast list of garden chores.
But a half century of experience, including mine and that of more knowledgeable people, has declared many of those chores unnecessary.
What to do with all those leaves
The largest of those chores is raking the lawn. Early on, I would rake several times a year. When we got a lawn mower with a grass catcher, I would mow the lawn every couple of weeks and clear the leaves when mowing.
This year I have mowed just twice and will mow again sometime closer to when the ground freezes, so the lawn will be free of leaves when the first heavy snow falls — if it does. Leaves trapped under snow could smother the lawn plants, which at our house includes lawn grasses, some clover, violets and other plants.
We have a large shaded area that I used to mow as recently as 10 years ago. It is next to a wooded area of our property and where we keep the wood we burn in our fireplace. It was there that we first decided to leave the leaves — permanently. The first year a few wildflowers sprouted, mostly native asters, which have smaller blossoms than the named hybrids, along with daisies, brown-eyed Susans and other flowers.
The leaves that we do remove from our lawn and gardens never leave the property. I rake them onto a tarpaulin and haul them to where I have set up bins made from pallets that were left at the town transfer station. I grind the leaves using an electric leaf mulcher. Several companies manufacture them, and they all seem to last about five years.
My recommendation for a rake is a True Temper clog-free model that prevents leaves getting stuck between the tines.
The cut-up leaves decompose a little over the winter, and by springtime we spread the chopped leaves between the rows in the vegetable garden. The chopped leaves keep the weeds down, make decent paths and eventually will be worked into the soil of our vegetable garden as we plant and weed. A decade ago I created five bins of chopped leaf mulch, but this year I am planning on only two.
What about the rest of the garden?
This is even more about personal preferences. It will do no harm at all to your garden soil or future plants to leave the leaves where they are. It would actually be harmful to some wildlife and even your garden to remove the plants.
Flowering plants also produce seeds, which have two benefits. Many birds eat those seeds. Here, a wide variety of birds including jays, cardinals, goldfinches, sparrows, chickadees and more will feed on the seeds. The second benefit to letting seed heads remain in gardens is that some seeds fall onto your soil and make new plants.
Ornamental grasses look good blowing in the breeze above the snow, so we usually leave those up. And flower heads such as coneflowers stand up to snow and look interesting in the winter. Any plants with hollow stems serve as homes for beneficial insects.
The plants I do remove are the ones that get soggy and flop to the ground as soon as they freeze or, in some cases even frosted. These include hosta, most annual plants, tomatoes, cucumbers and squash. I generally leave the roots in the soil, where they will decompose over the next year.
It won’t do any damage to next year’s growth or to your soil if you leave these plants in your gardens over the winter. But during the recent too frequent years in which we have no snow cover, they just look ugly.
Other things to do
Plant spring-flowering bulbs. They are available everywhere now.
Also, if you want blossoms over the holiday season, it is time to start amaryllis, paperwhite narcissus and other bulbs.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens won’t open its Gardens Aglow exhibit until Nov. 14, but tickets are on sale already, so make your reservations now if you want to go on a specific date.
From The Garden is published in partnership with Eat Drink Lucky and sponsored by Skillins Greenhouses.

title: Grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, who testified about Trump and Jan. 6, sources say
text:
Grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, who testified about Trump and Jan. 6, sources say
Justice Department prosecutors on Tuesday tried and failed to secure a grand jury indictment of former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, who had testified about President Donald Trump's role in the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol riot, according to two people familiar with the matter.
Video above: Cassidy Hutchinson's Jan. 6 testimony on weapons
Hutchinson was a key witness for the special House committee that investigated the events of Jan. 6. Her explosive 2022 testimony implicated the president in the violence of the day, saying that Trump was aware of the potential for violence on Jan. 6, but still chose to move ahead with his speech directing people to the Capitol building.
The long-running case has become a point of controversy between lawmakers and employees of the Justice Department, sources familiar with the matter have told CNN. Some inside the department believed that there was not enough evidence to bring a viable criminal case against her, and worried that it would be seen as a problematic way to target another of Trump's perceived enemies.
Lawmakers across the aisle have also called on the department to abandon its investigation, including Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, who called the matter an act of "lawfare" directed by the president.
Hutchinson, a former aide to White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, told the committee that Trump grew angry upon hearing supporters that day were seen with weapons including guns and knives and had been stopped at security checkpoints. Hutchinson said she heard Trump say something similar to, "I don't effing care that they have weapons. They're not here to hurt me. Take the effing mags away. Let my people in."
She also detailed what she heard were Trump's efforts to force his motorcade toward the Capitol — an account that has been disputed by others who were with the president that day.
Former special counsel Jack Smith, who investigated the Jan. 6 attack, told members of Congress in a closed-door interview earlier this year that Hutchinson wasn't a powerful witness in the investigation, in part because many of her stories were secondhand.
Hutchinson also claimed then-White House deputy chief of staff Tony Ornato told her Trump lunged at a Secret Service member when he was told he couldn't go to the Capitol following his speech that day.
Ornato and others have denied this account.
This story is developing and will be updated.

title: Maine Sure Loves Its Beer, and These 2025 Numbers Prove It

text:
Maine Sure Loves Its Beer, and These 2025 Numbers Prove It
Well, Gen Z must not have much of a presence here in Maine, because if 2025 proved anything, it’s that Mainers still love drinkin' beer.
And boy, did we drink plenty of it.
Whether it was a local craft brew, an ice-cold domestic, or something imported from overseas, Mainers certainly did their part to keep the beer industry thriving.
And judging by the latest numbers, it looks like Vacationland more than held its own when it came to knocking back a few cold ones.
How Much Beer Did Maine Drink Last Year?
Mainers drank a ton of brewdogs last year. How much, you ask? According to the latest data from beerinfo.com, the average Mainer consumed over 31 gallons of beer in 2025. That was good enough to rank Maine as the 11th highest state for beer consumption.
Congratulations?
That's a ton of suds. It basically means the average Mainer drank nearly six pints a week. That's a solid number, and considering many Mainers don't drink, some of those weekly averages must be pretty alarming for certain individuals. Like, there's definitely a few dudes out there who are taking down numbers we can't even perceive.
What State Drank the Most Beer Last Year?
As impressive (?) as that is, it's nothing compared to our brethren across the border in New Hampshire. The Granite Staters actually came in first for beer consumption, with an average of 43 gallons per year. Apparently, their new motto is: "Live Free, Drink a Ton, or Die."
Vermont also finished ahead of Maine, ranking 7th overall. The Green Mountain folks averaged a respectable 34 gallons of beer per year.
As for the driest state? I'll give you one guess. Yep, it's Utah, with an average of just 12 gallons. Lowly or healthy, depending on your perspective.

title: Former Ellsworth PTA treasurer accused of stealing $37K arrested after skipping court
text:
A former Ellsworth school group treasurer accused of stealing more than $37,000 was arrested Tuesday morning.
Judge Terrence Harrigan issued an arrest warrant for Joshua Dudeck, who served as treasurer of Ellsworth Elementary Middle School Parent, Teacher and Friends, after he failed to appear in court Monday to enter into a plea agreement.
Dudeck, 46, was arrested before 8:30 a.m. Tuesday by the intersection of State and North streets in Ellsworth. He was transported to Hancock County Jail, according to Corey Bagley, an Ellsworth Police Department detective.
Dudeck’s attorney, Will Ashe, said he missed court Monday due to a family emergency, according to the Ellsworth American. Harrigan issued the arrest warrant after learning from Ellsworth Schools Superintendent Amy Boles that Dudeck had dropped off his kids at school Monday morning, the American reported.
Dudeck’s bail was set at $10,000, though he has not yet made bail because he is still being processed at Hancock County Jail, Bagley said, adding that he was still incarcerated as of 1 p.m.
The former school board candidate faced a plea agreement that would have sentenced him to four years in prison with all but seven months suspended and three years of probation, according to Ashe. He was also expected to agree to pay more than $34,000 in restitution.
It was not immediately clear whether the plea agreement still stands, Ashe said, adding the decision would be made by District Attorney Bob Granger.
“We have been to Court three times for him to enter his plea and he showed up twice without money, and then failed to show up at all yesterday,” Granger stated. “The State sought an arrest warrant because all indicators suggested that he did not have the funds to make restitution and therefore possibly faced a more serious sentence. I think his non-appearance yesterday was the classic ostrich approach to problem solving.”
After skipping court and failing to pay the full restitution, Dudeck could now face a more serious sentence than the previous plea agreement, Granger said, adding Dudeck could proceed to a trial if he wished, but that he has already admitted to much of the conduct alleged in the charges.
“Mr. Dudeck has made multiple court appearances, he’s been following all his bail conditions and we had a possible plea agreement yesterday,” Ashe said. “We’ve been trying to resolve this case and it’s just unfortunate that a warrant was issued after he was unable to appear in court.”
Dudeck, who placed third in a 2021 three-way race for Ellsworth school board, was indicted over the summer by a Hancock County grand jury on one county of felony theft by unauthorized taking.
He is accused of stealing the school group’s funds between October 2022 and April 2025, during which time he served as the group’s treasurer, according to the indictment.
Following a police investigation into the missing funds, Dudeck allegedly admitted to cashing the group’s checks into his personal accounts. Court documents indicate the treasurer was struggling with addiction at the time.
Dudeck, a former New York lawyer, allegedly lied to the school group’s members about having purchased specialized playground equipment for children with disabilities, according to court documents. He had not purchased the equipment and had instead emptied the accounts for personal use.
Granger said he could not “think of a more vulnerable group of victims.”
Boles said the parent teacher group is focused on supporting students and staff and trusts that local police and the District Attorney’s office will bring Dudeck to justice.
“The impact of this situation has extended far beyond the financial loss. Our Parent Teacher Friend organization is made up of dedicated volunteers who work tirelessly to provide meaningful opportunities and support for our students and staff,” Boles stated. “The loss of more than $37,000 created significant uncertainty and stress for our school community, adding an undue burden to staff who are already working hard every day to meet the needs of our students.”

title: UMaine unions question budget shortfall, looming layoffs in emergency town hall
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
University of Maine faculty and staff at a town hall Monday night argued that the impacts of the university’s $19 million budget shortfall should not fall on employees or students.
The emergency event on the campus in Orono, attended by more than 100 people, was hosted by a coalition of the university’s faculty, staff and graduate worker unions, as well as some student organizations, known together as UMaine United. Speakers, including state lawmakers, professors, staff members and students, said the university cannot afford to lose more of its workforce, and that cuts would weaken the quality of the institution.
“We cannot cut our way to excellence,” said Sara Abronze, president of the systemwide professional staff union.
Speakers also asked the administration for greater transparency in the budget decision-making process.
The university announced last month that it would need to pursue staff and faculty layoffs, among other strategies, in response to an expected $19 million budget deficit.
The initial letter addressed plans to reduce the gap by about $10 million through reductions in academic affairs, including by eliminating a fifth of vacant positions. Then an announcement last week laid out a plan to reduce the shortfall by another $6 million through nonacademic cuts, including workforce reductions, relying less on external vendors and other means to bring the deficit to $3 million.
The school has not yet released details on who will be laid off, although the latest plan called for the elimination of vacant positions from athletics, student life and the president’s office.
Enrollment rates at the flagship university, which include its regional campus in Machias, have declined by 7% over the past five years, even as student numbers across the entire system have gone up.
The proposal to close the budget gap includes a goal of increasing enrollment by 1% across several categories, including first-years, transfers, graduate students and adult degree completers, and improving undergraduate retention by 1%.
Speakers at Monday’s town hall said it will be harder to attract more students if the university cuts faculty and programs.
They also criticized the Maine Legislature, saying it has underfunded public higher education in the state, and called on the incoming incoming governor and legislators to support increased state appropriations that keep up with inflation.
Rep. Amy Roeder, a Democratic lawmaker from Bangor and a part-time lecturer at the university, said students and the institution will suffer from the loss of staff and faculty. Roeder said that during her time as the House chair of the labor committee, she heard lots of arguments from employers.
“The workers always seem to get the lecture about being realistic. Well, let’s be realistic,” Roeder said. “You cannot reduce the people available to students and promise the students the same education.”
Faculty Senate President Brian McGill said the latest proposed cuts come on the heels of a 7% reduction across the board and a 17% reduction in faculty following postpandemic retirement incentives.
“What are the students going to have left when that’s done?” McGill said.
The Faculty Senate passed an emergency resolution in September asking the administration for clarity on the origins of the budget crisis and how the university would make decisions about cuts. It also requested a role in reviewing proposals and offering recommendations.
McGill said Monday that the administration’s response was unsatisfying and it questioned why faculty wanted the information it sought.
“How about because we’re on the chopping block?” he said. “How about because some of us have worked here for decades and we care about this place and we have a stake in what it looks like in three years, in five years, and we care about the students that are here?”
Graduate worker Andrii Obertas, a master’s student in the mathematics and statistics department, said the quality of the university has already been undermined by the faculty and staff anxieties. He criticized the University of Maine System’s polarizing recent $1.4 million contract with OpenAI to get ChatGPT Edu for every student and employee across the system.
“Firing teachers and buying AI for our students: This is truly the message that Maine’s flagship university wants to stand behind,” Obertas said, to boos from the crowd.
The unions are circulating a petition against layoffs, which organizers said had more than 350 signatures as of Monday.
The university will present its full budget proposal to the system’s board of trustees in January.

title: Cheerios teams up with Ziploc to create resealable bags inside cereal boxes (finally)
text:
(Gray News) — It’s been a long time coming: General Mills is introducing the first cereal box that includes a resealable bag.
Say goodbye to folding, rolling or clipping the bag, or even transferring the cereal to an airtight container.
Cheerios and Honey Nut Cheerios will be available with new packaging that includes a Ziploc PantrySeal™ bag.
General Mills said this marks the first resealable bag inside a traditional cereal box, making it easier to pour and reseal while helping keep cereal fresh longer.
“General Mills has received letters, emails and DMs asking for an easier way to reseal a cereal box, and we decided it was time to partner with the ultimate freshness brand: Ziploc®,” said Emilie Knox, Vice President and Business Unit Director for Cheerios at General Mills. “Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ takes a small, everyday cereal frustration and finally gives consumers the simple solution they’ve been asking for, making the whole routine easier and more enjoyable.”
The new boxes will be available exclusively at Walmart.com beginning Oct. 27 and will be available at retailers nationwide in the coming months.

title: ‘Ugh, they are black’: Couple sue broker who allegedly sent racist text before showing
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A New York couple have filed a housing discrimination lawsuit after they say a real estate broker sent a racist text message while they were looking for an apartment to rent.
Lisa Renee Olaso and her fiancé, Cyril Christopher, were excited to relocate from Delaware to Queens in June after the former got a new job. A broker from Douglas Elliman Realty was scheduled to show them an apartment for rent.
The couple, who are both Black, say the broker never met them in person and instead saw them from a distance as they arrived for the showing. That’s when they say they got a racist text message from the broker that was meant for the property owner.
“As we were getting out of the car, I received a text message that said, “Ugh, they are black,” Olaso said.
Olaso told her fiancé to get back in the car. She then explained to the broker why.
“When she looked at her phone, she started to explain that there were previous Black tenants in the neighborhood and that they had caused a lot of trouble,” Olaso said.
The couple are now suing Douglas Elliman Realty, the broker and several people listed as owners of the property. Their attorney, Kenneth Mollins, argues that the text message did not occur in isolation.
“Unless the person receiving the text gets it in some context to know why she’s sending that. So, we believe the homeowner was in some way responsible here,” Mollins said.
A Douglas Elliman spokesperson said in a statement last Wednesday that the broker was fired from the company, which has “a zero-tolerance policy for discrimination of any kind.”
Olaso says the broker apologized, but the hurt remains.
“All of us get up as Americans and we work hard and we all should be treated fairly,” she said through tears.
Christopher says the experience was painful.
“It’s like judging a book by its cover. You haven’t even read the book, and you already made a judgment call,” he said.
Following the incident, the couple moved to Long Island.
