title: Israel’s polls close as Netanyahu seeks another term in office. Here’s what exit polls are showing
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli voters delivered a rebuke Tuesday to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with exit polls indicating voters gave his opponents a solid majority in the next parliament. Whether those disparate parties can form a government is uncertain and will likely take weeks of haggling.
The easiest path would involve Netanyahu’s main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, partnering with Arab-led parties, but that could prove politically difficult and potentially alienate other opposition factions.
Exit polls released early Wednesday by major Israeli TV stations suggested that Netanyahu’s bloc and Eisenkot’s each won about 51 seats, and Arab parties won about 18. That would set the stage for weeks of political jockeying before a prime minister is declared — or another round of elections is called.
Eisenkot said the exit polls show a “lack of confidence” in Netanyahu and he vowed to form a new government. Arab voters celebrated the exit polls while supporters of far-right parties aligned with Netanyahu expressed disappointment.
Netanyahu had yet to make a public statement early Wednesday, hours after the exit polls were released.
Like all surveys, exit polls are subject to potential error. Preliminary results are expected in the coming hours. Final results are expected in the coming days and may vary from the exit polls.
An inconclusive result would leave Israel in political limbo after the country’s first national election since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
The race was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s nearly unbroken 17-year rule, which had left Israelis bitterly divided on a host of issues even before the deadliest attack in the country’s history. The resulting wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, along with settler violence in the occupied West Bank, have stoked worldwide outrage, straining ties with Israel’s closest allies and fueling a rise in antisemitism.
Among Israelis, the election was broadly viewed as a struggle over the character of the state, pitting Netanyahu and his ultranationalist and religious allies against those seeking to preserve its liberal and secular foundations. The opposition may soon have to grapple with the social divisions — between right and left, and between Jews and Arabs — that have widened during Netanyahu’s long and polarizing rule.
The process of coalition building will begin
Voter turnout was the highest since 1999, with more than 77% of eligible voters casting ballots, according to the Central Elections Committee. Over 7 million people were eligible to vote, and tens of thousands reportedly arrived from overseas.
Israel’s president will be tasked with asking the party leader with the best prospect of forming a government, usually one with the most seats, to cobble together a coalition. If Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud emerges as the largest party, he could claim that right.
Meanwhile, there will be heavy pressure on Eisenkot to reach a deal with the Arab parties, while Netanyahu and his allies are likely to cast any such alliance as illegitimate and even treasonous.
Netanyahu had warned earlier that Arab parties could make or break the election, saying they were receiving “truly massive support” and heading to the polls in “unprecedented numbers.”
If no one can cobble together a majority coalition, new elections could be held early next year. Israel held five elections between April 2019 and November 2022 because of a similar stalemate.
No single party has ever won an outright majority in the country’s 120-seat parliament, forcing political leaders to forge coalitions. Minority governments are also possible, but they must rely on support or cooperation from parties outside the government to pass legislation.
Netanyahu’s current coalition peaked at 68 members before it began to disintegrate over the past year.
Eisenkot says exit polls point to ‘lack of confidence’ in Netanyahu
As the exit polls were broadcast, supporters at Eisenkot’s party headquarters jumped for joy, chanting his name.
In a speech early Wednesday that focused on national unity, he pledged to form a government and promised “a new era — an era of hope” for Israelis.
“Today, Israel went out to a referendum over the leadership that will lead Israel in the coming years,” Eisenkot said to cheers from supporters. “The people decided in favor of change.”
Eisenkot warned Netanyahu not to “dare use Israel’s security for your political needs” while he is a caretaker prime minister, an apparent reference to reports that the Israeli leader considered an attack against Iran in the sensitive days leading up the election.
At Netanyahu’s party headquarters, filled mainly with media, the few supporters present chanted Netanyahu’s name, draping themselves in flags with his face on them and kissing posters.
Netanyahu’s supporters see him as a steady hand and a consummate statesman who has led Israel through a war of redemption after the country’s darkest hour. They think he is protecting Israel’s security and Jewish identity in the face of international pressure and liberal elites at home.
His detractors see him as a polarizing leader who, beset by an ongoing corruption trial, dragged out the war in Gaza and its hostage crisis for political reasons. They say he is undermining Israel’s independent judiciary and weakening its democratic underpinnings. And they accuse him of abetting the system that has allowed ultra-Orthodox religious Jews to avoid military conscription.
“The present government is driving the country into the ground,” voter Angela Bengur said in Jerusalem.
Eisenkot is viewed by supporters as a capable leader with sterling security credentials who, along with his likely governing partners, could act as a bulwark against creeping illiberalism. As someone personally touched by the conflict — his son and two nephews were killed in Gaza — his backers believe that he feels deeply the pain that still courses through Israel.
Parties that likely would support Eisenkot have vowed to improve Israel’s international standing and work to conscript ultra-Orthodox men while bolstering the independence of the judiciary.
The elections are about “who serves and who evades service — who takes an active part in building this country and who doesn’t,” said voter Nisso Shitrit in Tel Aviv’s Jaffa neighborhood.
Oct. 7 and its aftermath were a major focus of the election
The election is Israel’s first national vote since the Oct. 7 attack that sparked the war in Gaza and related conflicts. In Tel Aviv, families of some killed on Oct. 7 or former hostages held a moment of silence during the vote.
“Remember all those whose voices are no more,” said Yona Adam, whose daughter Mapal Adam was killed.
Israel has found itself increasingly isolated over its conduct in Gaza and the West Bank. Public support among Americans has plummeted, and partners in Europe and elsewhere have slapped sanctions on Israel. Netanyahu faces an international arrest warrant over alleged crimes against humanity in Gaza, allegations he denies.
Also hanging over the election were lingering tensions with Iran. Netanyahu ramped up threats ahead of the vote, warning Tehran it would face “a devastating blow” if it attacked Israel.
___
Associated Press writers across Israel contributed to this report.

title: Special needs teacher accused of pouring hot sauce on student’s tongue as a punishment
text:
HOUSTON COUNTY, Ala. (WTVY/Gray News) - An Alabama special needs teacher is facing child abuse charges after deputies say she poured hot sauce on a student’s tongue.
Heather Varner Hunter, a 46-year-old special needs teacher at Cottonwood Elementary School, allegedly used hot sauce to punish a student for sticking out their tongue in September. A Houston County Sheriff’s Office investigation followed.
Jail records show Hunter was arrested Monday afternoon. She is no longer employed by the Houston County School System, according to Superintendent Brandy White.
White said the school system cooperated fully with authorities, and all information has been turned over to the Alabama Department of Human Resources.
Hunter was named Teacher of the Month in March, according to 95.5 WTVY-FM. She said she had taught at Cottonwood for eight years and spent 18 years as an educator.
Hunter was released after posting a $2,500 bond.

title: Washington County Commission advised to hold confirmatory vote Wednesday on budget estimate
text:
MACHIAS, Maine (THE MAINE MONITOR) - Members of the Washington County Budget Advisory Committee have dropped a request for legal representation after Sheriff Barry Curtis removed Vice Chairman Ben Edwards from a sweeping public records request.
Committee members voted to ask the Washington County Commission for legal representation last week after Edwards was named in a Freedom of Access Act request for three years worth of emails, texts and other communications.
The same request was made of commissioners David Burns, Billy Howard and Courtney Hammond, and members of the county treasurer’s office. Edwards was the only budget committee member named in the records request, but other committee members believed they would be named in shared communications and wanted to have legal representation.
On Tuesday, Committee Chairman Brian Schuth said Curtis reached out after learning budget committee members had this concern and notified him that Edwards “has been dropped from the FOAA request.”
Schuth said that he and Curtis discussed how they were both acting to protect the institutions they are leading, and while Schuth said he disagreed with the “need to target the Budget Advisory Committee, we are serving in a public capacity and every record we produce is a public record.”
Schuth said he has confidence that committee members and the Sheriff’s Office will be “able to treat each other with respect going forward. There is no longer need to ask for formal representation from lawyers.”
On Oct. 13, attorney David Joyce of Brann & Isaacson filed a FOAA request on behalf of the Sheriff’s Office seeking records for all Sheriff’s Office expenditures, personnel and official vehicle information the county used in its budget process for 2025, 2026 and 2027. The request covers all patrol and investigative units within the Sheriff’s Office, the Washington County Jail, the Regional Communications Center and any personnel under the sheriff’s command.
The same day, attorney Michael Carey from the same firm sent a letter to commissioners, Schuth and budget committee members asserting that commissioners failed to follow state law when they forwarded a draft budget to the advisory committee without first voting on their own budget estimate. According to Carey, the budget committee’s work since Sept. 15 is “only preliminary because the Washington County Commission has not yet fulfilled its legal responsibility to begin the budget development process.”
According to Washington County Chief Deputy Michael Crabtree, legal fees for the Sheriff’s Office are being paid by the Maine Sheriff’s Association.
In response to Carey’s letter, the commission’s attorney, Jonathan Pottle, who was hired in September to help reorganize county government and sort out growing disagreements among county employees, sent a letter to the commissioners on Monday advising them to hold a confirmatory vote on the budget estimate to satisfy the budget committee’s concerns.
According to Pottle, “from a review of county records, it is clear on September 10, 2026, the commissioners provided the 2027 budget estimate to the Budget Advisory Committee,” noting commissioners held budget workshops leading to an advertised public hearing on Sept. 10, and the minutes of that meeting “plainly state all three commissioners were present, along with the Budget Advisory Committee members listed, and that the 2027 budget estimate, referred to as the 2027 budget proposal, was being turned over to the Budget Advisory Committee to conduct its process.”
Pottle also noted that members of the budget committee were each given three-ring notebooks containing the budget estimate at that meeting, so even “in the absence of a distinct recorded submission vote,” taken together “this all demonstrates the commissioners submitted a 2027 budget estimate to the Budget Advisory Committee” on Sept. 10. Further, he notes, the budget document is “not described as a staff draft or someone else’s draft,” and should be considered the commissioners’ draft.
But there is a note on the top right of the summary page that reads, “8/19/2026 – DRAFT budget,” and commissioners have said several times that the document reflects department head requests in full since no cuts were approved by commissioners.
Burns had expressed frustration in August when he couldn’t convince Howard or Hammond to support what he called “nickel-and-dime” cuts to the budget, “but without that I guess we have to send the budget through.”
Following the Sept. 10 public hearing and meeting with budget committee members, Burns and Howard sent individual memos to the budget committee with suggested cuts, most of which were aimed at the Sheriff’s Office and some of which had been discussed but not approved by the full commission.
These memos are one of the key points in Carey’s letter asserting improper procedure, writing that the memos “do not replace the county commission’s statutory duty to take action to start the budget process.”
The untouched draft budget represents $17.1 million in spending, a $3.7 million, or 27.6 percent, increase over last year’s final budget.
Without cuts, property taxes must cover $15 million of that total, which is $3.4 million more than last year.
Pottle’s letter acknowledges that Sheriff Curtis and others have questioned whether the budget committee actually has a submitted budget estimate for 2027, and has recommended commissioners conduct a confirmatory vote when they meet on Wednesday, Oct. 28, “to resolve any uncertainty that may exist.”
That vote, Pottle advises, should identify the 2027 budget estimate notebook and confirm that it was given to budget committee members on Sept. 10 as commissioners’ 2027 budget estimate. He further advised Wednesday’s minutes should reflect the confirmatory vote, and a copy of the budget estimate notebook should be attached to those minutes.
Pottle also noted in his letter that he was aware of concerns raised about whether the commissioners must “approve” the 2027 budget estimate when submitting it for review by the budget committee. “The answer is ‘no,’” he wrote, “because all the statute requires is submission of a budget estimate” for the coming year no later than 90 days before the end of the county’s fiscal year.
The budget committee must then review the estimate and submit its recommendations back to commissioners at least 45 days before year-end, which is Nov. 16.
Commissioners and budget committee members will then hold an informational meeting with the county’s legislative delegation, and commissioners must act on the budget at least 15 days before the end of the fiscal year. If they want to make any changes to the budget committee’s recommendations, they must hold a joint meeting with the budget committee to negotiate those changes.
If commissioners fail to approve the negotiated budget, state law authorizes the budget committee to adopt a final budget. If a budget is not approved by Jan. 1, the county will run on an interim budget capped at 80 percent of the 2026 budget until adopting a new one.
The budget committee will next meet on Tuesday, which is Election Day, and some members questioned whether they could start making recommendations since the budget process has been challenged.
“Well, presumably, if we have a budget we would begin making decisions at that meeting,” Schuth said, provided the commission takes a confirmatory vote as advised.
He said the committee could, if members wanted, “dig in our heels on this and try to compel behavior, but we don’t do so by ceasing to do our job. You see that?”
He suggested the committee continue its work, acknowledging “it’ll be messy at first, but let’s try to put it all together and then we can hold the final recommendation at that point, if we want to. Let’s do the work.”
On Tuesday, the committee completed its review of the last of the department requests, including a $1.9 million estimated increase in employee benefits, which includes increases in health insurance, paid family leave and the county’s match share of federal insurance contributions, or FICA, and employee IRAs.
The FICA increase is estimated at $620,795, or $301,996 year over year, which Finance Director Jenny Windsor explained is tied to salaries, including overtime. “When you increase overtime FICA is going to increase,” she said.
The budget committee also reviewed increased liability and Workers Compensation insurance, both of which the county purchases through the Maine Municipal Association, which are estimated to climb to $413,168, or 35.46 percent more than the current year.
Windsor pointed out that many of the line items the committee has reviewed have changed since the work began on Sept. 15, including a projected $400,000 savings in health insurance, bringing that cost down to $2.2 million. There have been changes elsewhere, which she has kept note of during the committee’s six meetings to date.
Committee member Martha Howell, who is a selectperson in Lubec, asked whether the committee should expect to see a revised budget with those updated figures for each of their notebooks.
“I’ve asked for that,” Schuth said, but if they don’t get that he said he would ask Windsor to be prepared to provide updates, including updated year-to-date expenditures since the budget was drafted in August and notes spending as of Aug. 19.
Schuth said he’d like to see a new version of the budget, incorporating any changes and updates from the finance department, by Monday at the latest.
“Should the commissioners choose to adopt a significantly different budget” when they meet Wednesday, Schuth said, “of course we hope that those necessary changes will be incorporated in whatever they provide.”

title: Woman dies after being hit by car in McDonald’s parking lot
text:
WHITE OAK, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A woman died after being hit by a vehicle in the parking lot of a fast-food restaurant, authorities said.
White Oak police responded to the fatal crash around 4:35 p.m. Oct. 21 in the McDonald’s parking lot in the 600 block of East U.S. Highway 80.
During the investigation, officers determined a woman walked out of the building, crouched in the driveway and began looking in her purse when a vehicle drove around the building and hit her, authorities said.
Officers determined the woman was not visible to the driver due to rounding a blind corner and the woman being so low to the ground, according to a release.
Paramedics took the woman to a hospital, where she later died, according to the release.
Police determined the crash was an accident, and no criminal charges will be filed, according to the release.
“Any incident involving the loss of life is a tragedy,” a department spokesperson wrote. “Our thoughts are with the family of the victim.”

Schuth said he has confidence that committee members and the Sheriff’s Office will be “able to treat each other with respect going forward. There is no longer need to ask for formal representation from lawyers.”
On Oct. 13, attorney David Joyce of Brann & Isaacson filed a FOAA request on behalf of the Sheriff’s Office seeking records for all Sheriff’s Office expenditures, personnel and official vehicle information the county used in its budget process for 2025, 2026 and 2027. The request covers all patrol and investigative units within the Sheriff’s Office, the Washington County Jail, the Regional Communications Center and any personnel under the sheriff’s command.
The same day, attorney Michael Carey from the same firm sent a letter to commissioners, Schuth and budget committee members asserting that commissioners failed to follow state law when they forwarded a draft budget to the advisory committee without first voting on their own budget estimate. According to Carey, the budget committee’s work since Sept. 15 is “only preliminary because the Washington County Commission has not yet fulfilled its legal responsibility to begin the budget development process.”
According to Washington County Chief Deputy Michael Crabtree, legal fees for the Sheriff’s Office are being paid by the Maine Sheriff’s Association.
In response to Carey’s letter, the commission’s attorney, Jonathan Pottle, who was hired in September to help reorganize county government and sort out growing disagreements among county employees, sent a letter to the commissioners on Monday advising them to hold a confirmatory vote on the budget estimate to satisfy the budget committee’s concerns.
According to Pottle, “from a review of county records, it is clear on September 10, 2026, the commissioners provided the 2027 budget estimate to the Budget Advisory Committee,” noting commissioners held budget workshops leading to an advertised public hearing on Sept. 10, and the minutes of that meeting “plainly state all three commissioners were present, along with the Budget Advisory Committee members listed, and that the 2027 budget estimate, referred to as the 2027 budget proposal, was being turned over to the Budget Advisory Committee to conduct its process.”
Pottle also noted that members of the budget committee were each given three-ring notebooks containing the budget estimate at that meeting, so even “in the absence of a distinct recorded submission vote,” taken together “this all demonstrates the commissioners submitted a 2027 budget estimate to the Budget Advisory Committee” on Sept. 10. Further, he notes, the budget document is “not described as a staff draft or someone else’s draft,” and should be considered the commissioners’ draft.
But there is a note on the top right of the summary page that reads, “8/19/2026 – DRAFT budget,” and commissioners have said several times that the document reflects department head requests in full since no cuts were approved by commissioners.
Burns had expressed frustration in August when he couldn’t convince Howard or Hammond to support what he called “nickel-and-dime” cuts to the budget, “but without that I guess we have to send the budget through.”
Following the Sept. 10 public hearing and meeting with budget committee members, Burns and Howard sent individual memos to the budget committee with suggested cuts, most of which were aimed at the Sheriff’s Office and some of which had been discussed but not approved by the full commission.
These memos are one of the key points in Carey’s letter asserting improper procedure, writing that the memos “do not replace the county commission’s statutory duty to take action to start the budget process.”
The untouched draft budget represents $17.1 million in spending, a $3.7 million, or 27.6 percent, increase over last year’s final budget.
Without cuts, property taxes must cover $15 million of that total, which is $3.4 million more than last year.
Pottle’s letter acknowledges that Sheriff Curtis and others have questioned whether the budget committee actually has a submitted budget estimate for 2027, and has recommended commissioners conduct a confirmatory vote when they meet on Wednesday, Oct. 28, “to resolve any uncertainty that may exist.”
That vote, Pottle advises, should identify the 2027 budget estimate notebook and confirm that it was given to budget committee members on Sept. 10 as commissioners’ 2027 budget estimate. He further advised Wednesday’s minutes should reflect the confirmatory vote, and a copy of the budget estimate notebook should be attached to those minutes.
Pottle also noted in his letter that he was aware of concerns raised about whether the commissioners must “approve” the 2027 budget estimate when submitting it for review by the budget committee. “The answer is ‘no,’” he wrote, “because all the statute requires is submission of a budget estimate” for the coming year no later than 90 days before the end of the county’s fiscal year.
The budget committee must then review the estimate and submit its recommendations back to commissioners at least 45 days before year-end, which is Nov. 16.
Commissioners and budget committee members will then hold an informational meeting with the county’s legislative delegation, and commissioners must act on the budget at least 15 days before the end of the fiscal year. If they want to make any changes to the budget committee’s recommendations, they must hold a joint meeting with the budget committee to negotiate those changes.
If commissioners fail to approve the negotiated budget, state law authorizes the budget committee to adopt a final budget. If a budget is not approved by Jan. 1, the county will run on an interim budget capped at 80 percent of the 2026 budget until adopting a new one.
The budget committee will next meet on Tuesday, which is Election Day, and some members questioned whether they could start making recommendations since the budget process has been challenged.
“Well, presumably, if we have a budget we would begin making decisions at that meeting,” Schuth said, provided the commission takes a confirmatory vote as advised.
He said the committee could, if members wanted, “dig in our heels on this and try to compel behavior, but we don’t do so by ceasing to do our job. You see that?”
He suggested the committee continue its work, acknowledging “it’ll be messy at first, but let’s try to put it all together and then we can hold the final recommendation at that point, if we want to. Let’s do the work.”
On Tuesday, the committee completed its review of the last of the department requests, including a $1.9 million estimated increase in employee benefits, which includes increases in health insurance, paid family leave and the county’s match share of federal insurance contributions, or FICA, and employee IRAs.
The FICA increase is estimated at $620,795, or $301,996 year over year, which Finance Director Jenny Windsor explained is tied to salaries, including overtime. “When you increase overtime FICA is going to increase,” she said.
The budget committee also reviewed increased liability and Workers Compensation insurance, both of which the county purchases through the Maine Municipal Association, which are estimated to climb to $413,168, or 35.46 percent more than the current year.
Windsor pointed out that many of the line items the committee has reviewed have changed since the work began on Sept. 15, including a projected $400,000 savings in health insurance, bringing that cost down to $2.2 million. There have been changes elsewhere, which she has kept note of during the committee’s six meetings to date.
Committee member Martha Howell, who is a selectperson in Lubec, asked whether the committee should expect to see a revised budget with those updated figures for each of their notebooks.
“I’ve asked for that,” Schuth said, but if they don’t get that he said he would ask Windsor to be prepared to provide updates, including updated year-to-date expenditures since the budget was drafted in August and notes spending as of Aug. 19.
Schuth said he’d like to see a new version of the budget, incorporating any changes and updates from the finance department, by Monday at the latest.
“Should the commissioners choose to adopt a significantly different budget” when they meet Wednesday, Schuth said, “of course we hope that those necessary changes will be incorporated in whatever they provide.”

title: DOJ to send election monitors to South Portland, Maine secretary of state says
text:
READFIELD, Maine (WABI) - Maine’s secretary of state says the Justice Department will now send election monitors to South Portland as well as Portland and Lewiston.
Reason for added location
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the Justice Department did not give Maine a specific reason for sending monitors to an additional location. She said the department cited federal voting rights and election laws.
Monitors in other states
Bellows said she does not see Maine’s monitoring as connected to its litigation with the Trump administration. She said Justice Department monitors were sent to most states during the primaries and will be sent to all 50 states, including red states.
Bellows said, “Most voters had no idea that they were there. They were seated in the same place that any other observer at the polls is seated. They were plain clothes. They’re not in uniform of any sort. So for voters, the experience is the same: a safe, secure election free from any interference or intimidation.”
Rules for monitors
Bellows said Justice Department monitors cannot enter the voting area, handle ballots or equipment, or interact with voters. She said Maine election officials will enforce those rules.

title: Dollar General sued for allegedly charging customers at register more than advertised
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) - The Federal Trade Commission has sued the bargain chain Dollar General for what it characterized as “long-running deceptive pricing practices” by charging customers more once they reach the register than the prices that are displayed on shelves and in advertisements.
Twenty states joined in the complaint, filed by the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee. It said that Dollar General failed to correct the issue despite what it said was “extensive corporate knowledge of the problem.”
“Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” wrote Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection.
Dollar General, based in Goodlettsville, Tennessee, just outside of Nashville, did not immediately return a request for comment from The Associated Press.
The states joining the FTC lawsuit include: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin, according to the FTC.
Americans have become frustrated with higher prices, and also what they perceive to be new methods used by restaurant chains and major retailers in setting prices including the use of artificial intelligence tools.

title: Cause of fire that destroyed rural Penobscot County home undetermined
text:
Investigators have not determined what caused the Saturday night fire that destroyed a Greenfield Township home.
The residents awoke around 9 p.m. to find fire spreading through the Cross Road home, which consisted of two structures connected by a passageway, according to Shannon Moss, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
By the time firefighters arrived, about 10:28 p.m., the home was already engulfed in flames.
Everyone inside, along with pets, safely escaped from the home.
The home was a total loss.
Investigators have identified several possible causes, including a pellet stove, smoking materials, extension cords and battery-operated tools, Moss said.
The origin of the fire is currently considered undetermined.
Greenfield Township is northeast of Old Town and on the Penobscot-Hancock county line.

title: Cornell faces questions over dorm assignment for student disciplined in sexual assault case
text:
One of the seven Cornell University students disciplined in connection with an alleged 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house returned to campus this fall after a three-semester suspension and was placed in a co-ed dorm with a roommate who had no idea about his past, according to a professor familiar with the housing arrangement.
University housing officials then left the accused student in that shared room for two weeks after the woman who made the allegation filed a lawsuit in September publicly accusing him of rape, psychology professor Corinna Loeckenhoff said at a Faculty Senate meeting. Meanwhile, Cornell students shared the accused student’s name and dorm location on social media.
“This was a clear security risk,” Loeckenhoff told Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff at the Oct. 14 meeting, according to a recording obtained by The Associated Press.
“Cornell’s own records show that, at the very least, he admitted to taking drugs and having sex with an intoxicated person,” Loeckenhoff said. “Why was Housing Services not aware of this? They had no clue until the shocked roommate contacted them and asked them for a room change,” she said.
Kotlikoff faces a possible no-confidence vote from faculty this week. Debate on the issue resumes Wednesday. In response to questions from the AP, Cornell said it would examine how the dorm room situation was handled.
“The university will review whether concerns were raised with housing or other offices and, if so, whether appropriate accommodations were provided,” the university said.
Cornell explains decision to allow student’s return
The woman, identified in court papers by the pseudonym Jane Doe, sued Cornell and seven men last month, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in 2024.
All those men have denied her allegations, saying either the sex was consensual or they weren’t involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter, and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York’s attorney general.
Cornell disciplined several members of the Chi Phi fraternity following a monthslong Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write “reflection” papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times.
One of the expelled students later enrolled at Nova Southeastern University in Florida. The university said it was unaware of the allegations when it admitted him and acted immediately after learning of them. It declined to say what action it took or whether he remains enrolled, citing federal student privacy laws.
The student who returned to Cornell this fall had been suspended for three semesters.
Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney representing the student, said his client maintains the encounter was consensual. He cautioned against treating all seven accused students as equally responsible.
“These are seven different people, with different circumstances, and each deserves to be judged on the evidence concerning him,” Miltenberg said.
In her lawsuit, Jane Doe accused the student of having sex with her without her consent alongside another fraternity member and later joining other men in snorting ketamine from her body.
Details of the allegations remained largely out of public view until Jane Doe filed her lawsuit, rattling students and faculty.
Cornell anthropology professor Noah Tamarkin said students in one of his classes didn’t think accused students should be back on campus.
“The other students in the class are uncomfortable with it,” Tamarkin told the AP.
Cornell’s media relations office said in a statement that students who complete a suspension and fulfill other sanctions “regain the same rights and responsibilities as their classmates, including eligibility for housing.”
Cornell president says disciplinary committee decided punishment
Loeckenhoff raised her concerns during a Faculty Senate meeting at which professors were debating whether to pass a resolution expressing no confidence in Kotlikoff’s leadership.
She declined to elaborate on her remarks, citing student privacy concerns. The roommate declined an interview request made through an intermediary.
Kotlikoff replied at the meeting that the decision to allow the student to return to campus was made by the university’s disciplinary panel, not him.
“It’s something you might disagree with — I may disagree — but we didn’t hear the evidence,” Kotlikoff said.
However, Kotlikoff acknowledged the university’s duty to respond to concerns about the student’s presence on campus.
“If we didn’t do that, I pledge to look into what happened there,” he said.
Kotlikoff was serving as interim president when the woman reported the assault in 2024. He suspended the fraternity, publicly condemned the behavior of the men involved and convened a task force on sexual assault. But he’s faced criticism for not following up with the woman or doing more to push for a criminal investigation or harsher discipline.
Privacy rules limit sharing info on discipline
Federal privacy law does not categorically prohibit universities from sharing a student’s disciplinary history with housing officials.
The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act allows universities to share student records with school officials who need the information to carry out their responsibilities, according to U.S. Department of Education guidance.
The law allows colleges to disclose some information when a student has been found responsible for violating school rules involving violence, including forcible sexual assault, or a nonforcible sex offense.
Kristi Patrickus, an attorney and board member of the Association for Student Conduct Administration, said universities have leeway to restrict campus housing access for students returning from suspension, even if they are allowed to resume classes. But federal privacy protections generally prevent universities from warning roommates about another student’s disciplinary history.
“There are not really any exceptions that allow us to tell a roommate, like, ‘Hey, this person is returning from suspension. Be careful,’” Patrickus said.
David Karp, director of the Center for Restorative Justice at the University of San Diego, has studied how colleges handle students returning from suspensions for sexual misconduct. He said universities often focus on disciplinary sanctions without adequately addressing the needs of those involved or the broader campus community.
“I don’t think it meets people’s needs very well, even if it meets university compliance needs,” Karp said.
___
Associated Press writer Michael Biesecker in Pittsburgh contributed.

title: Maine Averaged 21 Deer Crashes Per Day in 2025
text:
Most drivers in Maine will tell you that there is enough to worry about when behind the wheel without adding wildlife into the mix.
From excessive speeders to distracted drivers and beyond, keeping an eye out for a moose or a deer often times seems like an afterthought.
But according to driving data released by AAA for 2025, thinking about collisions with deer specifically shouldn't be an afterthought at all because it's happened about once-per-hour every single day last year.
There Were 7,672 Deer involved Vehicle Crashes in Maine For 2025
Over the last several years, there have been more than 32,000 vehicle accidents in Maine that have involved deer. In 2025 alone, there were 7,672 deer crashes averaging out to more than 21 per day.
Maine ranks number 9 in the nation in odds of having a deer-related vehicle crash and those odds are set to increase over the next few months.
That's because deer mating season has arrived in Maine and during the peak of rutting season in November, deer crashes around the state typically spike. Roughly 20% of the deer crashes in 2025 took place in November.
The Cost From Deer-Related Crashes in Maine Can Be Expensive
While frightening, deer crashes in Maine rarely prove to be fatal for drivers. What they can be is incredibly expensive.
Depending on the severity of the impact, repair costs on vehicles average anywhere from $3,000 to $6,000 per accident.
Injuries and damage costs rise when drivers attempt to swerve and avoid a deer, often causing motorists to hit guardrails, trees or other vehicles.
Deer activity during mating season is most prominent in the early morning hours and around the evening commute.

title: US military says 5 were killed by a strike on an alleged drug boat in the eastern Pacific
text:
US military says 5 were killed by a strike on an alleged drug boat in the eastern Pacific
The U.S. military said it attacked a boat it accused of smuggling drugs in the eastern Pacific Ocean on Tuesday, killing five people, as the Trump administration continues its campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America.
The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed by the U.S. military's boat strikes to at least 240 in more than 70 strikes. The Trump administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” in September 2025.
As with most of the military’s statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes and that “intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narcotrafficking.”
The military did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. A video posted on X showed a small boat in the water before it was enveloped by an explosion.
President Donald Trump has said the U.S. is in “armed conflict” with cartels in Latin America and he has sought to justify the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing “narcoterrorists.”
Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the U.S. over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India.
The attacks have drawn intense scrutiny from some Democratic lawmakers and military legal scholars. The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the U.S. military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the lethal operations, which includes a military commander’s intent, target development and execution. But the evaluation will not probe the legality of the strikes.
Tuesday's strike is among a few that have followed Secretary of State Marco Rubio's pledge in September to seek the approval of U.S. allies in the region for carrying out such attacks. Rubio told reporters that while the U.S. has “the capacity to act unilaterally,” it would rather work with its allies because that is “the most effective way to do it.”
Rubio's statements in Peru last month appeared to signal a shift in strategy. However, Rubio also said the U.S. military would “still blow up ships if need be” and the approach would be “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination.”

title: Teenager charged in hit-and-run that killed 6-year-old getting off the bus
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A 17-year-old was charged in connection with a hit-and-run that killed a 6-year-old girl in Charlotte last week, according to authorities.
Charlotte police announced Monday that Lachevis Finnie, 17, was arrested in the hit-and-run death of 6-year-old Mariana Espinoza. He was charged with felony hit-and-run resulting in death.
Espinoza was hit by a car while crossing at the intersection last Friday in east Charlotte. Espinoza, a student at Devonshire Elementary School, had just gotten off the school bus.
Police said Espinoza was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries and died there the following day.
Doorbell camera footage obtained by WBTV on Monday shows the moments before Espinoza was hit.
Court documents filed Monday allege that Finnie was driving the Mercedes-Benz that hit and killed Espinoza.
Police had released a photo of the gray Mercedes-Benz, believed to be the car involved in the hit-and-run, Monday morning. By Monday evening, police said they identified Finnie as a suspect in the case after “conducting a traffic stop on the suspect vehicle.” The car had been seized as evidence.
An affidavit alleged Finnie did not stop after the collision and did not call 911. The document said he claimed he fled “due to being scared.” The affidavit also said Finnie “confessed to striking the child,” and has since been cooperative with the investigation.
Finnie appeared in Mecklenburg County court on Tuesday. During that appearance, he was appointed a public defender and had his bond set at $2.5 million. He was also ordered to complete a mental health evaluation.

title: Political candidate charged with child molestation days before election
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — A Republican candidate in Georgia running for the state House of Representatives has been arrested on charges of public indecency.
According to Cobb County authorities, Andre Stafford is accused of public indecency and child molestation, a felony charge, in connection with an Oct. 15 incident in Smyrna.
The arrest warrant said a girl walking to her bus stop was approached by a gray 2024 Kia Forte whose driver exposed himself. Police said Flock surveillance cameras tracked the car to Stafford, whom the victim identified in a photo lineup.
Stafford is running for house district 42 in Smyrna, a seat held by Democrat Gabriel Sanchez.
Stafford has been photographed with a number of prominent GOP officials, including state Sen. Greg Dolezal, who is running for lieutenant governor; U.S. Rep. Barry Loundermilk; and state Rep. Houston Gaines, who is running for a congressional seat now held by U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, seeking to unseat U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia’s nationally watched 2026 midterms.
“Mr. Stafford has volunteered on many campaigns across the state this year, including ours,” Collins said. “The charges are sickening, and if they’re true, then he belongs on a list and behind bars.”

title: 2-time ‘Jeopardy!’ winner arrested for 2nd time in less than a year
text:
RALEIGH, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) — A two-time “Jeopardy!” winner from North Carolina was arrested again, records show.
Court records show 44-year-old Philip Joseph “Joey” DeSena was arrested on Oct. 23 in Wake County.
Charges and arrest details
DeSena was charged with 10 counts of second-degree sexual exploitation of a minor. An arrest warrant indicated the charges stemmed from DeSena’s alleged possession of sexually explicit pictures and videos that showed children.
He was booked into the Wake County Jail and was denied bond during an initial court hearing Monday.
Previous case
DeSena’s latest arrest came almost a year after his first one on Dec. 1, 2025. He was charged with two counts of felony secret peeping following his first arrest. Those charges stemmed from the alleged recording of a female in a bedroom and bathroom.
DeSena pleaded guilty to the peeping charges on July 27, 2026. He was subsequently sentenced to 60 months of probation. He was also ordered to complete 100 hours of community service and to obtain a mental health assessment or evaluation.
Records showed the court recommended the assessment or evaluation be completed by a psychiatrist or psychologist who specializes in psychosexual treatment.
He is scheduled to be back in court on the new sexual exploitation charges on Nov. 16.
‘Jeopardy!’ background
DeSena, who lives in Raleigh, won two episodes of “Jeopardy!” in November 2024, and participated in the show’s “Winter 2025 Champions Wildcard” tournament in January.
Between his two wins, the engineer raked in $44,698.

title: Judge to consider whether California should count 20,000 ballots disputed by Trump administration
text:
Los Angeles (AP) — A federal judge in Los Angeles will hear arguments Tuesday afternoon over whether the Department of Justice can bar California from counting the ballots of of some 20,000 people until it can confirm they are U.S. citizens.
The hearing before U.S. District Judge David O. Carter comes as voting is underway statewide with a week left before the midterm election concludes Nov. 3. Noncitizen voting has been a key focus of President Donald Trump’s administration as U.S. voters decide which party will control Congress for the rest of his term, though available data indicates the illicit practice is exceedingly rare.
The Republican administration sued election officials in the heavily Democratic state in mid-October, accusing them of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 names it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. The federal government is asking Carter to block the state from counting those ballots until the voters’ immigration status can be verified.
The federal government had sought an emergency appeals court ruling before Tuesday’s hearing but was rebuffed by a divided panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
California officials say the lawsuit came too late
California officials warned in court filings that any effort to heed the Trump administration’s requests would potentially “disenfranchise legitimate voters,” delay certification of the election and “cause general uncertainty in the election results.”
Two of the three appeals panel judges echoed those concerns after hearing oral arguments Sunday. While the ruling mainly called it premature for an appeals court to get involved before the district court could hear the case, the two judges wrote separate concurrences making it clear they wouldn’t support setting aside the ballots.
The dissenting judge argued, however, that both state and federal law bar noncitizens from voting and that compels California to vet potentially illegal ballots before they are counted. The failure to do so, he wrote, would cause irreparable harm to the election.
California mails ballots to all active registered voters among the state’s roughly 23 million electorate. More than 3 million voters statewide have already cast ballots.
At least one county registrar, Clinton Curtis in Shasta County, testified in a sworn declaration submitted by the federal government that setting apart ballots flagged by the Justice Department would be feasible.
“In my experience, locating and segregating challenged ballots is entirely possible and not catastrophic,” Curtis wrote.
But local elections officials offered conflicting testimony in which they described serious obstacles.
Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores argued in court filings that it would be impossible to set apart votes for immigration status verification once they’ve been counted.
Voting information is confidential, she said in the filing, noting that once a ballot is mailed in, it is separated from its envelope with its individual voter identification markings, making it impossible to verify based on information provided by the federal government.
State and federal government battle over accuracy of list
At the heart of the dispute is whether the Justice Department’s list is accurate in the first place.
Flores also wrote that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration’s list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, individuals with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the U.S., which the filing notes “is strong evidence of citizenship.”
Nicolas Bartell, the associate director of the federal Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate, said his department re-checked those 200 records and found that only four likely had citizenship and one person was dead. The directorate is a specialized division within U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Elsewhere in the filing, Bartell said the investigation was “ongoing” and noted that at least 189 records have “minor data discrepancies” — but he didn’t say whether those records overlapped with Los Angeles’ sample.
Bartell in a separate filing gave the most detailed account yet into its methodology for developing the 20,000 names in a court filing on Monday. Notably, the federal government is not using the SAVE database, which judges elsewhere have ruled illegally aggregates sensitive personal data and risks purging eligible voters from the rolls.
Bartell wrote that the agency cross referenced publicly available voter registration data with a combination of data from a third-party data collection site, Department of State records and Social Security Administration records. Then, an individual agent combs through the list of registered voters whose citizenship could not be verified using government data.

title: Island police week of Oct. 29
text:
Bar Harbor
A fuel pump hose was found on the side of the road and returned to the owning gas station.
Officer Payson removed a traffic hazard from the roadway on Route 3.
A small black bag was found and turned in to the police department for safekeeping.
Someone turned in a found credit card to the police department.
While conducting a traffic stop, David Jellison, 39, of Harrington, was arrested on an outstanding warrant.
The police department received a report of someone finding a loose dog. The dog was later reunited with its owner.
Officer Cake assisted the Bar Harbor Fire Department at the scene of a medical call.
After a traffic stop, Lloyd Taylor, 34, of Mount Desert, was arrested and charged with operating under the influence.
A United States passport was turned in to the police department by a whale watch company.
Officer Frost spoke to a business about trespassing concerns.
After a traffic stop, Robert Huneken, 40, of Sag Harbor, N.Y., was arrested and charged with operating under the influence.
On Friday, Oct. 23, Joris Korstanje, 22, of Bar Harbor, was arrested and charged with operating under the influence and possession of schedule W and X drugs after a traffic stop.
Officers received a complaint of a vehicle running another vehicle into a ditch. Officer Cake checked the area and found no vehicles in the ditch and the Southwest Harbor Police Department located and stopped the suspect vehicle.
Officers provided traffic control for the Connors Emerson Elementary School Halloween parade.
A decorative or costume ring was found and turned in to the department.
A lost wallet was turned in to the department.
Officer Harrington took a report of potential animal abuse in Bar Harbor. Upon investigation it was determined that the dog was fine and being supervised by their owner while they were working.
Danielle Kersey, 25, of Bangor, was arrested and charged with violating conditions of release.
After a traffic stop and investigation, Ivan Porter, 56, of Amherst, was arrested and charged with violating conditions of release.
Several reports were made of fireworks coming from West Street. Officer Kline made contact with the business that had a permit for the fireworks.
The police department received a report of people camping on town property. The subjects were located and advised of the ordinance against camping in public.
Someone called to report a trespassing issue. The suspect was located and verbally warned for trespassing.
A 911 call regarding a possible missing person was made on Sunday, Oct 25. The missing subject was found and reunited with their family.
Mount Desert
Officer Cake spoke to a resident who asked about having a vehicle towed from their property. The person was advised he could have the vehicle towed at the owner’s expense.
The police department took two calls reporting a drone being operated in Northeast Harbor. The drone was being used to survey property and did not appear to be violating any laws.
Officer Dickens took a report of vehicles speeding in the Somesville School zone. The area will be added to the roster for additional enforcement patrols.
Sgt. Brundrett responded to a residence in reference to a family dispute. After investigation, the incident was determined to be verbal only and no crimes had been committed.
Southwest Harbor
On Oct. 18, officers assisted with the MDI Marathon.
The department received multiple accidental 911 calls throughout the week.
Someone reported that a camper van was illegally parked on Herrick Road.

title: Trump offers $1 million for voter fraud tips as midterms loom
text:
Trump offers $1 million for voter fraud tips as midterms loom
President Donald Trump is offering a $1 million reward for anyone who reports voter fraud that leads to a conviction.
With the midterms quickly approaching, Trump posted to his social media accounts Monday, offering big money for voter fraud tips in previous or upcoming elections.
Related video above | Trump announces announce $25 million whistleblower program for alleged government fraud
"Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud," Trump wrote.
It is unclear where that money would come from.
There is no evidence of widespread voter fraud in U.S. elections, though Trump has spent years claiming that there is and that it cost him the 2020 election he lost.
The offer is higher than a whistleblower program unveiled last week.
The Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, or WHIP for short, was launched by President Trump and Vice President JD Vance during an Oval Office event Tuesday. The $25 million program, administered by the Department of Justice, promises rewards of up to $30,000 for actionable information.

title: Man accused of firing gun before hourslong standoff in New Hampshire
text:
New Hampshire man accused of firing gun before hourslong standoff in Pittsburg
A New Hampshire man faces multiple charges after authorities said he was involved in a standoff with law enforcement for hours after firing a gun at a Pittsburg property.
Derrick Chase, 32, of Pittsburg, has been charged with felony reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon and misdemeanor counts of endangering the welfare of a child, simple assault and obstructing the report of a crime or injury in connection with the incident.
New Hampshire State Police officials said that troopers received a report of a domestic violence assault happening in Pittsburg shortly after 10:45 p.m. Monday.
While troopers responded to the scene, they asked members of the U.S. Border Patrol to help secure the scene. State police said that Border Patrol agents heard a gunshot when they arrived at the scene, so additional help was requested, including from the State Police SWAT Unit and the Colebrook Police Department.
Officers learned that the person who fired the gun, later identified as Chase, was barricaded inside a garage on the property, and that a woman and several children were in a nearby home.
State police said coordinated efforts were made to safely evacuate the woman and children from the scene as additional law enforcement personnel arrived, and that officers also worked to secure the area and temporarily closed nearby roads while waiting for specialized resources.
Chase peacefully surrendered at about 4:13 a.m. Tuesday and was taken into custody without further incident, according to authorities.
State police said no injuries were reported during the incident.
According to officials, Chase refused the services of a bail commissioner and was taken to the Coos County Department of Corrections. Chase was scheduled to be arraigned Tuesday.
Authorities are asking anyone who has information regarding the incident to contact Trooper Jeremy Brann by calling 603-846-3333 or sending an email to Jeremy.C.Brann@dos.nh.gov.

title: Boys, girls soccer seasons wrap up with first-round playoff exits
text:
BAR HARBOR — The 2026 fall season came to an end for both the MDI girls and boys soccer teams on Friday, Oct. 23, after both teams came tantalizingly close to upsetting higher-seeded teams, but ultimately failed to advance past the preliminary round of the Class B playoffs.
The MDI boys, entering the playoffs as a No. 11 seed, suffered a heart-breaking 1-0 defeat against rival Ellsworth, the No. 6 seed in the tournament. This was the third meeting between the two teams this fall, with MDI improving its standing in each of the matchups.
While Ellsworth looked like the better team in the first meeting between the rivals, earning a 2-0 victory at home in September, the Trojans played them to a 1-1 draw in the final regular season match of 2026 — and this playoff contest was somehow even closer. The game was one of the more riveting 0-0 draws a fan is likely to see, with both teams moving the ball, generating scoring chances, and playing strong defense. The 75 minutes of scoreless soccer played were a testament to the strong performances by both goalkeepers, Benny Baldridge for MDI and Brayden Pooler for Ellsworth, who kept their respective teams in the game with their decisive and athletic play in net.
Unfortunately for Baldridge, his clean sheet was sullied very late in the contest when Ellsworth’s Hunter Winslow uncorked a long throw-in from the far sideline, with around four minutes left in the game, that took an unfortunate bounce.
“When I throw the ball in on our side, our attacking side of the field, I’ve just got to put it in the box,” Winslow said when going back over the goal, “and that one just happened to skip off the defender and go into the back of the net.”
MDI tried its best in the remaining minutes to generate an equalizer, but Pooler and Ellsworth’s defense held strong, even as the temperature continued to drop as the night wore on. Isaac Ellis came achingly close to finding the back of the net several times before and after the Ellsworth goal. Wyatt Ford had a shot miss just wide. Owen Dwyer gave the Eagles all they could handle in the box on corner kicks. But the Trojans could not find the goal they needed before the final whistle blew on their season.
The girls team, seeded at No. 9, came perhaps even closer to pulling off an upset after taking their road game against No. 8 Erskine Academy into double overtime before falling 3-2 on penalty kicks.
The Trojans managed to keep the game deadlocked at 2-2 through two full overtime periods, thanks to goals by Rosie Ellis and Cedar Nobel Brown. But after five penalty kicks, Erskine came out on top and advanced to play the top-seeded John Bapst.
“This season was incredibly special for our program,” said girls head coach, Justin Harding, after the match.
“Obviously, the loss to Erskine was a difficult way for it to end, and I know our players wanted an opportunity to keep playing. But I don’t think that one result should define this team or take anything away from what they accomplished. For the first time in several years, MDI Girls Soccer made it back to the playoffs, and considering everything this group had to overcome to get there, I couldn’t be prouder of them.”
A common challenge for both the boys and girls soccer programs this season was injuries, something that both coaches have acknowledged are part of any high school soccer season. The injury bug hit MDI hard in 2026, however, and with both team’s fielding a smaller roster to begin with due to the smaller class size at MDIHS, it made it a much more difficult challenge for them to overcome.
“There were stretches where it felt like we had a different starting lineup every day. We constantly had players changing positions, taking on new responsibilities, and even had to adjust our formation based simply on who was healthy enough to play. At one point, we had more than 10 players dealing with injuries. Considering that our entire program consists of only about 24 athletes gives some perspective on what this group was facing. Yet they continued to compete,” Harding pointed out.
“They showed up every day and figured it out. Players stepped into positions they weren’t accustomed to playing. Younger players were asked to take on responsibilities much earlier than we anticipated. Veteran players accepted whatever role we needed them to take on a particular day. We changed lineups, positions and formations, sometimes from one game to the next, and nobody used any of it as an excuse.
And through all of that, we weren’t simply trying to survive games. We remained competitive. We won games. Ultimately, we earned our way back into the postseason.
I think that says more about the character of this team than any individual win or loss ever could.”
Harding gave a tremendous amount of the credit to the team’s nine seniors: Gabriella Joy, Claire Dow, Katie Dow, Morgan Culshaw, Matilda Hanley, Maeve Hurley, Aoife McLoughlin, Gwen Stager and Delilah Damon-Dong.
“Many of these players have been part of this program through some very difficult seasons. They have experienced the frustration that comes with losing, injuries, low numbers, and rebuilding a program when success doesn’t happen immediately. They could have allowed those experiences to define their careers. Instead, they decided to help change the direction of the program,” said Harding.
“That’s why making the playoffs this season meant so much more than simply qualifying for another game. For this senior class, I think it represented something tangible. After everything they had invested and experienced, they left this program knowing they had helped get MDI Girls Soccer back into the postseason.”
Losing nine seniors from a program of roughly 24 athletes is significant, Harding added, with more than a third of the entire program walking across the graduation stage this spring. But the coach expects to return roughly 15 players in 2027, along with 5-10 incoming freshmen to add to that 15. And what was a hardship this season could turn into a blessing in the future as some of the younger players on the team gained valuable experience filling in when needed this season.
“Because of the injuries and adversity we experienced this year, many of those returning players were forced into meaningful situations earlier than we might have anticipated. They played important minutes. They learned different positions. They experienced the pressure of meaningful games. Most importantly, they spent a season watching this senior class demonstrate what commitment to a program looks like. Now it becomes their program,” said Harding.
“The wins mattered. Getting back to the playoffs mattered tremendously. But what matters even more is that this group, and particularly these nine seniors, helped change the direction of MDI Girls Soccer.”

title: Voters to weigh Trump’s record on 2024 campaign promises
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump won a second term by making many promises to voters. Nearly two years after he was sworn in, those voters can judge whether he kept them, and they will decide in days how he has done.
When Trump campaigned for president in 2024, he told voters he would turn around the U.S. economy and close America’s borders.
Trump often speaks about his record on illegal immigration on the campaign trail.
“Two years ago, we inherited the worst border in American history, and we turned it into the safest border, the best border by far in the history of our country,” Trump said at a rally in Arizona October 14.
Voters give the president high marks on closing the southern border. However, his immigration policies have been met with criticism.
Also, Trump has consistently received low approval ratings on his management of the U.S. economy, in part due to the ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs.
Trump fulfilled promises to eliminate taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security. He also frequently made another pledge during the 2024 campaign.
“We will target everything from car affordability to housing affordability to insurance costs to supply chain issues … to the price of prescription drugs,” Trump said in a campaign speech in Asheville, N.C., on August 14, 2024.
Gas prices are up 40% since Trump was sworn in. The increase is driven primarily by disruptions to global oil supplies related to the conflict in Iran.
Trump repeatedly promised “no new wars” during his 2024 presidential campaign and said he would keep the U.S. out of foreign conflicts.
The war in Iran is continuing, as is the Ukraine-Russia war. Trump promised to end the Ukraine-Russia war on his first day in office.
Trump is now promising to deal with Cuba on the way home from Iran.

title: Cherryfield dam removal opens path for Atlantic salmon
text:
CHERRYFIELD, Maine (WABI) - Crews removed the Cherryfield Ice Dam this summer, allowing Atlantic salmon to swim farther upstream.
The Downeast Salmon Federation (DSF) partnered with the town, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on the project.
One of the key goals of the improvement project is to increase fish passage. Years ago, hundreds of fish passed through the river. In recent years, that number has dropped significantly.
Ellie Mason, habitat restoration project manager for the Downeast Salmon Federation, said the dam was known to block fish.
“There was video footage from the top of the dam where you could see salmon jumping, but they weren’t getting to the other side,” Mason said. “And so everyone knew, okay, this is something that’s blocking fish passage.”
Mason joined the federation in 2024 and oversaw the design, permitting and construction.
Cable Pool Park upgrades
The project also includes upgrades to the adjacent Cable Pool Park. Crews are finishing a play area and expanding public access.
Crews also are repurposing old concrete from the dam to build an amphitheater.
Construction is almost complete. Final improvements are set to be done next year.
Community tour
The Downeast Salmon Federation is hosting a community open tour of the project Friday, October 30 from 4 to 5:30 p.m.

title: Tennessee inmate serving life for murder stole a truck after slipping through the prison fence
text:
A convicted murderer who escaped from a Tennessee prison and stole a truck from a nearby farm remained free on Tuesday, authorities said.
Jacob Morley, who was serving a life sentence for killing a co-worker four years ago, was found to be missing from the Northwest Correctional Complex late on Sunday.
The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation released surveillance video from the farm, which is near Tiptonville and about a 2-mile (3-kilometer) walk through fields from the prison, showing Morley open the truck’s unlocked driver’s side door and drive off at around 1 a.m. Monday.
Firefighters in Hornbeak, about 12 miles (19 kilometers) east of the farm, said on social media that investigators confirmed their cameras captured footage of the truck driving by their station about 15 minutes later.
Authorities said Morley, 28, slipped through a fence in his prison clothes, but they haven’t released additional details, including whether they think anyone helped him.
Morley is 5 feet 11 inches (1.8 meters) tall and weighs 240 pounds (109 kilograms). He has brown hair and green eyes.
Morley is serving a life sentence for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s home after he had been missing for a few weeks. The two lived in Carter County, in eastern Tennessee.
Along with first-degree murder, Morley was convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest. When Morley saw deputies at his home, he led officers on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said.
Prison officials have offered a reward of up to $2,500 for Morley’s arrest. They said law enforcement agencies have searched buildings and other structures near the prison, which is about 90 miles (145 kilometers) north of Memphis in flat farmland near a bend in the Mississippi River.
Several violent attacks between inmates and by employees have been reported in recent years at Northwest Correctional Complex. A grand jury in July returned dozens of indictments for five inmate killings and other violent acts.
Northwest Correctional Complex can house 1,776 men and can house minors who have been convicted as adults, according to the Department of Correction.

title: Bangor council approves $100,000 for warming shelter funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Bangor city councilors voted Monday to direct a total of $100,000 to local nonprofits to support two city warming shelters.
$10,000 will go to The Well Warming Center, a daytime shelter that councilors said served roughly 70 to 80 people a day last winter.
Up to $90,000 will go to the Together Place Peer Run Recovery Center for its as-needed nighttime warming shelter.
The two shelters were selected because of the services they provided last winter.
The funding comes from money the city already had for heating assistance, general assistance and a community development block grant.
Together Place board President Shea Mullaney said at Monday’s meeting that the allocation is a maximum expenditure for services as delivered. He said that means the organization will not receive the money upfront.
Mullaney said the funds will help support operations at the state average of $44 a bed per night. He said the funds will also allow Together Place to pay its staff.
The city’s advisory committee on homelessness will develop requirements and policies for the shelters’ operations.
The funding passed unanimously, though Councilor Wayne Mallar was reluctant in his approval. Councilor Michael Beck recused himself from the vote because of a conflict of interest. Councilor Daniel Carson was not present for the meeting.

title: FBI raids mansion as part of an investigation into former Rep. Eric Swalwell
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal law enforcement agents searched a Beverly Hills home early Tuesday as part of an investigation into Eric Swalwell, who resigned from Congress amid a wave of sexual misconduct allegations, two people familiar with the investigation told The Associated Press.
Agents searched the home of wealthy developer and Swalwell donor Stephen Cloobeck, where the ex-Congressman spent time before resigning from office in April, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation.
Swalwell, D-Calif., has denied criminal wrongdoing.
Messages seeking comment were left for Swalwell’s lawyer and for a lawyer who represented Cloobeck in another matter.
Cloobeck, who founded the Diamond Resorts International timeshare company and ran last year for California governor, contributed more than $23,000 to Swalwell’s congressional campaigns since 2017, federal campaign finance records show.
He told the New York Post in April that he cut ties with Swalwell as accusations against him mounted.
“I am no longer associated with a man that takes advantage of women,” Cloobeck told the newspaper. “I support women’s rights.”
In May, Cloobeck was charged with witness intimidation in an unrelated case. He has pleaded not guilty. In August, the online prediction market platform Kalshi temporarily banned him after it said he bought $10,000 worth of contracts on his short-lived gubernatorial candidacy.
Tuesday’s search is the latest escalation in the federal investigation of Swalwell — one of several probes begun after a woman came forward with allegations that he sexually assaulted her twice, including when she worked for him.
The San Francisco Chronicle, followed by CNN, first reported the allegations. CNN also reported that three other women alleged various kinds of sexual misconduct by Swalwell, including sending them unsolicited explicit messages or nude photos.
Around the same time, another woman came forward with allegations that Swalwell raped her at a Southern California hotel in 2018. She said she had one glass of wine and believes that Swalwell drugged her. She said she planned to make a report to law enforcement.
Asked about the search at Cloobeck’s address, FBI spokesperson Lourdes Arocho said: “Early this morning the FBI conducted an operation in the Los Angeles region related to an ongoing criminal investigation. We have no further comment.”
In August, federal agents seized electronic devices from Swalwell at the San Francisco airport and searched his Washington home.
Swalwell, an Iowa native, was elected in 2012 and represented a House district east of San Francisco. He launched a presidential run in April 2019 but ended it a few months later after failing to catch on with voters.
The seven-term lawmaker had been seen as one of the leading candidates in California’s gubernatorial race before dropping out after the allegations surfaced.
The office of Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg has said it is also investigating Swalwell after a former staffer told CNN and the Chronicle that Swalwell raped her at a hotel while he was in New York City for a charity gala in 2024.
In a statement, Bragg’s office encouraged “survivors and anyone with knowledge of these allegations to contact our Special Victims Division.”
Los Angeles prosecutors were also said to be weighing charges.
Swalwell was one of Republican President Donald Trump’s top Democratic antagonists in Congress. He was a prominent member of the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees during Trump’s first term and served as one of several Democratic prosecutors for Trump’s second impeachment after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.
Swalwell was removed from the Intelligence Committee by then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., in 2023 based on Swalwell’s contact with a suspected Chinese spy, Christine Fang.
Fang was reported to have come into contact with Swalwell’s campaign as he was first running for Congress in 2012 and to have participated in fundraising for his 2014 campaign.
Federal investigators alerted Swalwell to their concerns and briefed Congress about Fang in 2015, at which point Swalwell says he cut off contact with her. He was not accused of wrongdoing and a House Ethics Committee investigation that was opened in 2021 closed two years later without any action.
