title: The Exoneree Band: How a group of wrongfully convicted men found their voice through music
text:
(Aging Untold)— They don’t have the fame of The Beatles or the fortune of The Rolling Stones, but the members of The Exoneree band share something far more profound.
Now, as free men, they are using the power of music to heal, to tell their stories, and to build a brotherhood unlike any other.
The band was born out of the Innocence Network’s annual conference, a gathering that brings together wrongfully convicted people from across the country.
In 2011, this group of musically inclined exonerees found each other, and what started as a jam session quickly turned into something more.
“It turned into a really nice brotherhood of guys who were not only musicians but had went through the same thing of being wrongfully convicted,” one band member recalls.
Living in different parts of the country, they come together to create a sound that is both a celebration of their freedom and a testament to their resilience. Their music is a form of therapy, a way to process the unimaginable trauma of being stripped of their lives and liberty.
“For me, it’s kind of like a therapy thing,” says one member. “Getting to share my story through music.”
Each member carries the weight of a story that would break most people.
Ted Bradford and his bandmate Eddie Lowry were both wrongly convicted of rape.
“I just couldn’t believe that they were accusing me of this, something that I could never do,” Bradford says.
Donovan Allen was convicted of murdering his own mother, a crime that stole his youth and his freedom.
“My mother was killed exactly one week before my 19th birthday,” he shares. “And from the age of 19 to almost 35, I was inside.”
Collectively, they lost decades of their lives before DNA evidence finally cleared their names. While they are grateful for their freedom, the scars of their time in prison run deep.
“No one deserves to see the things that I’ve been forced to see,” says one member.
It’s a burden that could understandably make them want to leave the past behind. But instead, they choose to amplify their stories, to turn their pain into a powerful message of hope and resilience.
“It’s an emotional release for us, and it’s healing,” they say. “When we’re up on the stage, it’s a healing for us and for our community.”
Their setlist is a mix of cover songs, often with a twist to reflect their unique journey, and deeply personal original music.
Fellow exoneree Amanda Knox has joined them on stage for a special rendition of “I Will Survive,” a song that takes on a whole new meaning when sung by those who have truly overcome the impossible.
But it’s their original songs that carry the most weight.
One member wrote a song called “My Cell,” a raw and honest account of life in a small prison cell. He recalls listening to music on headphones in his cell, dreaming of being on stage.
“And it’s finally happening,” he says with a smile.
At a recent performance for a packed house of Innocence Network members, Ted Bradford debuted a new song, “Innocent Man.”
It’s a powerful and emotional plea for justice, with a chorus that cries out, “Lord, why don’t you shine your light on me? Reveal the truth and help them see, for you know the truth will set you free.”
The Exonerated may never achieve mainstream fame, but that’s not their goal.
They have found something far more valuable.
Brotherhood. Purpose. Voice.

title: ‘Ugh, they are black’: Couple sue broker who allegedly sent racist text before showing
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A New York couple have filed a housing discrimination lawsuit after they say a real estate broker sent a racist text message while they were looking for an apartment to rent.
Lisa Renee Olaso and her fiancé, Cyril Christopher, were excited to relocate from Delaware to Queens in June after the former got a new job. A broker from Douglas Elliman Realty was scheduled to show them an apartment for rent.
The couple, who are both Black, say the broker never met them in person and instead saw them from a distance as they arrived for the showing. That’s when they say they got a racist text message from the broker that was meant for the property owner.
“As we were getting out of the car, I received a text message that said, “Ugh, they are black,” Olaso said.
Olaso told her fiancé to get back in the car. She then explained to the broker why.
“When she looked at her phone, she started to explain that there were previous Black tenants in the neighborhood and that they had caused a lot of trouble,” Olaso said.
The couple are now suing Douglas Elliman Realty, the broker and several people listed as owners of the property. Their attorney, Kenneth Mollins, argues that the text message did not occur in isolation.
“Unless the person receiving the text gets it in some context to know why she’s sending that. So, we believe the homeowner was in some way responsible here,” Mollins said.
A Douglas Elliman spokesperson said in a statement last Wednesday that the broker was fired from the company, which has “a zero-tolerance policy for discrimination of any kind.”
Olaso says the broker apologized, but the hurt remains.
“All of us get up as Americans and we work hard and we all should be treated fairly,” she said through tears.
Christopher says the experience was painful.
“It’s like judging a book by its cover. You haven’t even read the book, and you already made a judgment call,” he said.
Following the incident, the couple moved to Long Island.

title: Colorado's glaciers thinned dramatically due to record low snow and heat in 2026
text:
DENVER (AP) — The most prominent glaciers in Colorado thinned dramatically over the past year due to record low mountain snow and record warm temperatures, according to new research.
Their shrinking is on par with recent observations of glacier loss across the planet as warmer temperatures accelerate melting and less snow falls to replenish their ice, threatening water sources, increasing mountain hazards and contributing to sea level rise.
While glaciologists typically measure changes over longer intervals, glaciologist Dan McGrath at Colorado State University sought to find out what happened over 2026 since it was such an exceptional year. The state’s worst snowpack on record, followed by record summer heat, left the year-round ice masses in the Rocky Mountains exposed.
The Andrews Glacier thinned by more than 12 feet (3.7 meters) in this single year, the Arapaho Glacier lost nearly 10 feet (3 meters), and the Isabelle Glacier lost about 6.5 feet (2 meters) — doubling their rate of thinning from the prior five years, McGrath said. In the decade before that, the thinning measured a foot or less per year.
St. Mary’s Glacier, a perennial snowfield popular among hikers and skiers, melted completely in September.
“What we’re witnessing is the loss of that part of Colorado’s identity. And it’s not just Colorado,” said McGrath, who specializes in glacier dynamics. “Obviously we see it in the Alps and we’re seeing it in other mountain ranges in the western U.S., the European Alps and globally. There are very clear, consistent patterns across these ranges.”
Climate change is shrinking glaciers faster than ever
More than 7 trillion tons of ice (6.5 trillion metric tons) has been lost worldwide since 2000, according to research, a slow-motion disaster that sometimes provokes sudden devastation: More than 1,300 people were killed in August after a massive section of rock and overlying glacier collapsed near Nepal’s border with China.
Glaciers in Switzerland lost 5.5% of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record, due to heat waves and low winter snowfall. The GLAMOS Swiss glacier monitoring service and Swiss Academy of Sciences said this month that alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving long-term under such conditions. Switzerland is home to the most glaciers in the Alps.
In Washington state, researchers with the North Cascade Glacier Climate Project have surveyed six glaciers on Mount Baker during an annual summer trip. Director Mauri Pelto said this year’s survey shows the fastest average retreat since 1950 with the collapse of several large ice caves, which form as warm air circulates in retreating glaciers.
Mountain glaciers in the contiguous United States average just 0.16 square miles (0.41 square kilometers), or about 100 acres (about 40 hectares), and are widely distributed at high elevations. Since the mid-1900s, about one-quarter of them have disappeared and the remnants have lost a third of their area and volume, according to a new study co-authored by Brian Menounos, an earth sciences professor at the University of Northern British Columbia.
The runoff supplies water to high alpine and downstream ecosystems across the western United States, and eventually these areas may become more vulnerable to extreme drought as the glaciers disappear, he added.
And in a “one-two punch,” wildfires also are hastening the melting by darkening the surfaces of glaciers with soot and dust, Menounos said, making them more vulnerable to absorbing sunlight.
Glaciers could re-form if carbon pollution declines substantially and temperatures drop enough to enable snowfall to build year-round, eventually compressing again into glacial ice, but that may take several hundred years, Menounos added.
Colorado’s glaciers may not have much time left
Looking at how much ice Colorado’s remaining glaciers have lost, McGrath thinks they could soon disappear. The Andrews Glacier has already lost half of its ice since 2017, he said.
“This past decade has showed us that these glaciers are out of balance with the climate here in Colorado, in the western U.S., and they’re thinning at a rate that could lead to their demise in the next 20 years,” he said.
Harlan Ulmer, 20, is a student at Colorado State University who has photographed the glaciers annually since 2022 and volunteers with McGrath’s research project. He said it’s sad to see their decline, but important to record.
“Being Gen Z, I came in too late to ever see the glaciers at their largest,” he said. “But I think we have the opportunity, I have the opportunity, to sort of document the changes that are taking place in my time to preserve them for future generations and for posterity.”
___
McDermott reported from Providence, Rhode Island.

title: Political candidate charged with child molestation days before election
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — A Republican candidate in Georgia running for the state House of Representatives has been arrested on charges of public indecency.
According to Cobb County authorities, Andre Stafford is accused of public indecency and child molestation, a felony charge, in connection with an Oct. 15 incident in Smyrna.
The arrest warrant said a girl walking to her bus stop was approached by a gray 2024 Kia Forte whose driver exposed himself. Police said Flock surveillance cameras tracked the car to Stafford, whom the victim identified in a photo lineup.
Stafford is running for house district 42 in Smyrna, a seat held by Democrat Gabriel Sanchez.
Stafford has been photographed with a number of prominent GOP officials, including state Sen. Greg Dolezal, who is running for lieutenant governor; U.S. Rep. Barry Loundermilk; and state Rep. Houston Gaines, who is running for a congressional seat now held by U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, seeking to unseat U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia’s nationally watched 2026 midterms.
“Mr. Stafford has volunteered on many campaigns across the state this year, including ours,” Collins said. “The charges are sickening, and if they’re true, then he belongs on a list and behind bars.”
Jackson’s campaign has said Stafford has no connection to their campaign.
Stafford’s representatives did not immediately comment regarding the situation.
Georgia’s general election is on Nov. 3.

title: A stealth ship is ghosting the Portland boatyard where it’s stored
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Portland boatyard has filed a lawsuit against the owners of a military prototype vessel known as Ghost as the ship racks up more than $1,000 a day in fees from overstaying its storage contract.
The suit, filed Monday in U.S. District Court in Portland, says Ghost’s New Hampshire-based owner, Juliet Marine Systems, owes Portland Yacht Services more than $30,000 after a storage agreement expired on Sept. 30 and notices regarding the outstanding balance have gone unanswered.
Portland Yacht Services, based on West Commercial Street, is asking the court to issue a process of maritime arrest, under which a ship is detained until debts are paid, a settlement is reached or the court takes other action.
Once a judge signs the warrant, anyone claiming an interest in the vessel has 14 days to announce themselves. They then have 21 days to respond to the claim. If the owners of Ghost fail to file a statement of interest, the vessel may be sold to satisfy the Portland Yacht Services claim.
Gregory Sancoff, who designed Ghost, said Tuesday that Juliet Marine Systems has dissolved as a corporation and that he resigned as president of the company months ago. He declined to comment further.
Grayson Szczepaniak, an attorney at Archipelago Law who is representing Portland Yacht Services, also declined to comment on the suit Tuesday.
Ghost, a 38-foot-long prototype built in 2009, is not your everyday vessel.
It has what’s known as a super-cavitating hull that allows it to run at top speed through rough seas by lifting out of the water. It was designed for military use, and it’s made of aluminum and stainless steel, making it difficult to find with sonar.
According to the suit, Ghost was first brought to Portland Yacht Services three years ago and has been stored there since under several agreements. The most recent agreement was effective from July 1 through Sept. 30, and it stipulated that if the two sides didn’t execute a new agreement by Sept. 30, Ghost would incur additional storage fees of $1,087 per day.
According to a 2014 article in Bloomberg Businessweek, Ghost was built in a hangar at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery. Sancoff, who previously made millions from building and selling medical technology companies, designed the vessel after being inspired to dive into marine technology and weaponry.
The article said Juliet Marine Systems began as an 18-person startup with $15 million invested in the project.
Ghost was originally designed as a manned vessel for covert insertion or extraction missions, but efforts by the startup to get a U.S. military contract were unsuccessful.
At the time, Sancoff said Ghost could “get into denied-access ocean areas and loiter for 30 days with the fuel on board,” listen to cellphone conversations, and “launch operations and leave, and no one knows you’re there.”
In early 2025, General Dynamics partnered with Juliet Marine Systems to test using Ghost as an unmanned or optionally manned vessel. At the time, Matt McGonigle at General Dynamics Mission Systems told Defense News that they were running tests in Portland. Attempts to reach General Dynamics were not immediately successful Tuesday.

title: Portland postpones vote on allocating $900,000 for winter warming shelter
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland postpones vote on allocating $900,000 for winter warming shelter
The Portland City Council voted Monday night to postpone a decision on whether to allocate $900,000 from the city’s Opioid Settlement Fund for a winter warming shelter.
Portland postpones vote on allocating $900,000 for winter warming shelter
The Portland City Council voted Monday night to postpone a decision on whether to allocate $900,000 from the city’s Opioid Settlement Fund for a winter warming shelter.
The Portland City Council voted Monday night to postpone a decision on whether to allocate $900,000 from the city's Opioid Settlement Fund for a winter warming shelter.
The proposed funding would help operate an emergency shelter at 166 Riverside Industrial Parkway during the 2026-2027 winter season, supplementing funding from the Maine State Housing Authority.
The city estimates total operating costs at Riverside to be about $1.2 million, which is about $500,000 more than the downtown shelter option, including rent, utilities, insurance and property taxes. A transportation plan to shuttle shelter guests to and from the downtown area would also be needed.
The vote to postpone was taken after city leaders went into a closed-door executive session to discuss alternative options.
"I think as a matter of transparency it should be something that is discussed in public," Portland resident Michael Hayes said during public comment on the motion to go into executive session. "When you talk about what ideas did not pan out, we could probably hear about that now and why."
The shelter plan has changed in recent weeks. The city said Seeds of Hope is no longer willing to operate a shelter at Elena's Way because of community resistance and regulatory challenges. Preble Street also declined to operate a shelter at that location, according to the city update.
While no public comment was taken, Preble Street called on councilors ahead of the vote to approve a warming shelter plan, ideally one that is on the peninsula for easier access.
"Temperatures are already dropping below freezing at night, and the Portland City Council has yet to approve a winter warming shelter," wrote Preble Street on Facebook. "We cannot let our unhoused neighbors suffer outside."

title: Maine program seeks donated deer, moose and bear meat for people in need
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry is accepting donations for its Hunters for the Hungry program, which could put deer or moose meat on the tables of families in need this winter.
The program supplies wild game meat to food pantries, soup kitchens and homeless shelters across Maine.
“This program allows hunters to give back in a meaningful way, turning their harvest into life-saving meals for neighbors in need,” said Gus Nelson, Director of The Emergency Food Assistance Program (TEFAP) in Maine.
The department is accepting donations of bear, deer and moose meat.
Hunters will not pay to have their donated meat processed.
Hunters who want to keep some of their game can do so and donate the rest.
Hunters, landowners and meat processors with questions can call 287-7513. They also can email H-4-H@maine.gov to sign up.
If you would like to become an approved processor for the Hunters for the Hungry program, you will need to submit an application.

title: Maine Senate race is close, while Pingree and Charles are tied in governor's race, poll finds
text:
Maine Senate race is close, while Pingree and Charles are tied in governor's race, poll finds
Democrat Troy Jackson holds a 49% to 47% lead over Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins among likely voters in Maine, while Democrat Hannah Pingree and Republican Bobby Charles are tied at 44% support in the governor's race, according to a new Marist poll released Tuesday.
Maine Senate race is close, while Pingree and Charles are tied in governor's race, poll finds
Democrat Troy Jackson holds a 49% to 47% lead over Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins among likely voters in Maine, while Democrat Hannah Pingree and Republican Bobby Charles are tied at 44% support in the governor's race, according to a new Marist poll released Tuesday.
Independent Rick Bennett received 6% in the governor's contest, and 6% of likely voters were undecided.
The likely voter results are within the poll's margin of error of 6.6 percentage points.
While Charles and Pingree are tied among likely voters, among registered voters, Pingree has an 11-point advantage.
In the Senate race polling, Jackson leads Collins by 9 percentage points among registered voters, up from a 4-point lead earlier in October.
Despite Jackson's narrow lead among likely voters, 58% said they expect Collins to be reelected. In the governor's race, 63% said they believe Pingree will win.
Democrats also lead on the generic congressional ballot. Among likely voters, 52% said they would support the Democratic candidate in their district, compared with 47% for the Republican. The Democratic advantage was 11 points among registered voters, according to the poll.
Views of President Donald Trump and personal finances were also featured in the survey. Forty-two percent of likely voters said Trump was not much of a factor in their congressional vote, while 41% said their vote was against him and 16% said it was in support of him. Overall, 42% of likely voters approved of Trump's job performance and 58% disapproved.
Asked about their household finances, 46% of likely voters said they had gotten worse over the past year, 15% said they had improved, and 38% said they had stayed about the same.
The Marist Poll surveyed 1,449 Maine registered voters from Oct. 22-25, 2026, using live telephone interviews, text messages and online surveys. The margin of error was 4.1 percentage points for registered voters and 6.6 percentage points for likely voters.

title: Maine Sure Loves Its Beer, and These 2025 Numbers Prove It
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Sure Loves Its Beer, and These 2025 Numbers Prove It
Well, Gen Z must not have much of a presence here in Maine, because if 2025 proved anything, it’s that Mainers still love drinkin' beer.
And boy, did we drink plenty of it.
Whether it was a local craft brew, an ice-cold domestic, or something imported from overseas, Mainers certainly did their part to keep the beer industry thriving.
And judging by the latest numbers, it looks like Vacationland more than held its own when it came to knocking back a few cold ones.
How Much Beer Did Maine Drink Last Year?
Mainers drank a ton of brewdogs last year. How much, you ask? According to the latest data from beerinfo.com, the average Mainer consumed over 31 gallons of beer in 2025. That was good enough to rank Maine as the 11th highest state for beer consumption.
Congratulations?
That's a ton of suds. It basically means the average Mainer drank nearly six pints a week. That's a solid number, and considering many Mainers don't drink, some of those weekly averages must be pretty alarming for certain individuals. Like, there's definitely a few dudes out there who are taking down numbers we can't even perceive.
What State Drank the Most Beer Last Year?
As impressive (?) as that is, it's nothing compared to our brethren across the border in New Hampshire. The Granite Staters actually came in first for beer consumption, with an average of 43 gallons per year. Apparently, their new motto is: "Live Free, Drink a Ton, or Die."
Vermont also finished ahead of Maine, ranking 7th overall. The Green Mountain folks averaged a respectable 34 gallons of beer per year.
As for the driest state? I'll give you one guess. Yep, it's Utah, with an average of just 12 gallons. Lowly or healthy, depending on your perspective.

title: South Portland girls soccer makes program history with playoff win
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SOUTH PORTLAND — It took an extra 21 minutes and 41 seconds of tense overtime action for the South Portland High girls soccer team to make program history.
Charlie Savage headed in a corner kick from Maci Rauscher with 7:19 remaining in the second overtime to give the fourth-seeded Red Riots a 1-0 win against equally gritty and competitive Bonny Eagle in a Class A South quarterfinal Tuesday night.
It was the first regional quarterfinal win in South Portland girls soccer history, dating back to the inaugural 1987 season.
“It was definitely something we were working for and we knew this was a winnable game and we would make school history doing it,” said Savage, whose triplet sisters, Maizie (goalkeeper) and Reese (right back), are also in the starting 11.
The Red Riots (11-2-2) advance to play No. 1 Scarborough (14-0-1), the four-time defending regional champion. Scarborough won the regular-season meeting, 2-1.
Bonny Eagle (9-4-3), the No. 5 seed, and South Portland played to a 0-0 tie over 90 minutes in the regular season, meaning the clubs had gone 192 minutes, 41 seconds without a goal against each other before Savage scored.
“Both teams were incredible tonight. My girls gave me everything and that’s all I could ask for,” said Bonny Eagle coach Michelle Riesbeck.
RUN OF PLAY
In the first half, both teams had bids that went off target. In the second half, Maizie Savage (five saves) and Bonny Eagle keeper Keona Ingram (eight saves) made solid stops, including one especially alert play by Ingram to come off her mark and smother a potential bid by speedy sophomore South Portland striker Sasha Neff. Bonny Eagle’s defense did well to contain Neff, with center back Hayleigh Sawyer showing close attention.
In the final 15 minutes of regulation, Bonny Eagle gained a slight edge, playing a cleaner style and finding feet with its passes on the rough grass field that had extreme slope along the sidelines.
South Portland changed the dynamic in the first overtime. Led by left wing Violet Wedick’s runs, the Red Riots cranked up seven shots and forced Ingram to make four saves, with another shot blocked by defender Charlotte Beaulieu.
Bonny Eagle’s Taytum Lauziere nearly won the match in the final seconds of the first 15-minute overtime, striking a left-footed corner kick that curled toward goal and glanced just off the top of the crossbar.
WINNING SEQUENCE
Just before the winning goal, Ingram tipped a direct kick by Wedick up and over the net. Rauscher delivered the corner kick to the near post.
“In that instant, with seven minutes left in the second overtime, we knew we didn’t want to go into (penalty kicks),” Charlie Savage said. “We were putting everything on the line. It was whoever gets to it.”
Savage is a two-way midfielder, not one of South Portland’s primary offensive threats, but she does have a knack for the big moment, said first-year South Portland coach Jarrod Carnrick.
“She does so much work at both ends of the field, defensively breaking up plays and starting counterattacks, (and) keeping possession in the attacking third,” Carnrick said. “It really doesn’t surprise me that she pops in and bags the goal in the last moment.”
TURNAROUNDS
A consistent playoff team since 2015, Bonny Eagle improved by four wins this season, including a 1-0 preliminary-round win against No. 12 Portland. South Portland’s rise has been dramatic. The Red Riots tied the 2004 team for most wins in a season after going 3-9-2 and finishing 14th in 2025.

President Donald Trump is focusing on traditionally Republican states, including Texas and Mississippi, as part of his final push ahead of the midterm elections.

title: Magician encourages kids to 'just keep going' when things are tough
text:
Using sleight of hand and illusions that provoke double-takes, a North Carolina man is on a mission to help kids persevere through adversity.
Magician and motivational speaker Caleb Morgan visited Aroostook County schools last week with his wife, Maria, to bring his message to Maine for the first time.
Nearly a fifth of Maine children from 3 to 17 suffer from anxiety, one of the highest rates in the country, according to the John T. Gorman Foundation. Schools around the state have upped their efforts to bolster students’ mental health by hiring counselors or instituting new programming aimed at helping kids cope. Morgan hopes sharing his own story of perseverance combined with fun tricks will help instill positive messages that kids will remember.
“My family dealt with an abusive situation. We had somebody tell us, ‘Someday, this is going to be a story that can help somebody,’” Morgan said Friday in Van Buren. “The pain has a purpose now.”
Morgan’s act intersperses motivational tips with illusions that engage his audience, including card tricks.
A speaker can give great insight, but a visual example can help bring a point home in a different way, he said. For instance, people who’ve seen magicians often recall things years later that made their mouths drop, and he hopes his presentations do that for kids.
Morgan was a teacher at one time, and discovered a lot of students were dealing with challenges that affected their performance and how they felt about life in general.
“The thing I saw back then, and the thing that I see a lot of educators dealing with today is students giving up — apathy, just not pushing through new things and not trying new experiences,” he said. “And so we teach them, essentially, ‘Don’t give up. Keep going.’”
Morgan entertained the students with card tricks, interactive activities where objects seemed to disappear and then reappear somewhere else, and even an illusion using newspapers, where torn-up pieces of a paper were seemingly restored in front of everyone.
He and his wife have recently been to Iowa and Minnesota, and last week also visited schools in Bangor, Presque Isle and Washburn. Van Buren was one of their last stops before the holiday season, he said.
Kylie LaPierre, who served as Van Buren principal last year, booked Morgan’s visit several months ago, Principal Ralph Fantasia said. The students knew the assembly would feature an illusionist, but beyond that they didn’t know what to expect.
“Once he came in and started doing his stuff, they were caught. They were pulled in,” Fantasia said. “You could see them leaning in [going], ‘No way. No way.”
Besides messages of “don’t stop believing” and “just keep going,” Morgan shared that every problem has a solution if approached step by step, Fantasia said.
High school student Ethan Morin liked the magic tricks, but more than that, the life lessons.
“You can see a very good connection between what he’s demonstrating and how it connects with his real life,” Morin said. “Don’t think of everything in life as the big picture. Look at it as one tiny picture that builds up into bigger pictures.”
After an assembly for the entire student body, Morgan also presented sessions for student leaders and teachers.
Sometimes after an assembly, students will come up and share their own difficulties with him. That takes bravery, Morgan said, adding he hopes he can serve as an example of someone who’s pushed through adversity.
He loves it when students appreciate the illusions and the bigger message.
“There’s something special about being able to see students’ eyes light up and be able to share a different perspective with them, show them that there’s hope,” he said. “They can say, ‘Whatever I might be struggling through, I can keep that smile on my face because I can see that there’s a way through this.”

title: A one-city ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine brokered by First Lady Melania Trump is in effect
text:
MYKOLAIV, Ukraine (AP) — A localized ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia took effect early Tuesday ahead of a humanitarian mission led by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, as missile attacks resumed in Kyiv.
Meanwhile, Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister spoke on the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, officials said, in their first-known direct contact since shortly after Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
After the conversation with Putin, the two Nordic leaders had a telephone conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, according to Zelenskyy’s office.
Russia and Ukraine began observing a localized ceasefire in a devastated southern Ukrainian city Tuesday, before a planned humanitarian mission brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, but Moscow kept up its deadly missile attacks on other cities in the meantime.
The local pause in fighting started at 3 a.m. to allow an aid mission into the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky later this week. The situation in Oleshky is desperate, with food and medical supplies running perilously low for the up to 2,000 people still there, as drones and land mines restrict movement.
Deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine, as Moscow’s full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark in February, has undermined previous attempts at limited ceasefires, which quickly unraveled or never took hold.
The humanitarian truce was a high-stakes operation for both Moscow and Kyiv, with both sides keen to win U.S. President Donald Trump’s favor.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators as well as the militaries of the two countries confirmed in separate statements that the Oleshky ceasefire had begun.
Nordic leaders speak by phone to Putin and Zelenskyy, officials say
The call, confirmed by the offices of Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, followed an Oct. 20 meeting in Oslo between the two Nordic leaders, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff.
The call was held in consultation with Ukraine, according to the official statements by the two Nordic countries. Stubb and Støre initiated the call to discuss the war and upcoming trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States that are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in November.
The two European leaders spoke on behalf of their own countries and not the whole of Europe, the statements said.
“The discussion was frank and substantive,” Stubb said. “We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions.”
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs,” Støre said. “The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation.”
Melania Trump and Pope Leo worked for a truce in Oleshky
According to her office, Melania Trump led talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine after meeting with U.N. officials who briefed the American first lady on the situation in Oleshky.
Up to 2,000 people are stranded in the city, unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the U.N. The partly occupied Kherson region of Ukraine where Oleshky is located is notorious for the dangers of Russian drone attacks on soldiers and civilians.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that “so far there have been no reports of violations.”
Pope Leo XIV spoke earlier this month with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging them to allow humanitarian aid into Oleshky and the safe evacuation of civilians, the Vatican said.
Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened.
The Kremlin said at the time that Putin voiced support for the Vatican’s plea, and an agreement was reached to coordinate efforts in this regard.
Moscow and Kyiv have blamed each other for the humanitarian crisis.
Russia, as the occupying power, must under international law ensure that civilians under its occupation live safely. Ukraine has repeatedly tried to negotiate a humanitarian corridor for evacuations and aid delivery with Moscow.
The aid mission is planned ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered talks between delegations from Russia and Ukraine expected next month that will seek to lay the groundwork for detailed peace negotiations later.
Lull in Oleshky uneasy, a Ukrainian official tells The AP
The local ceasefire is due to last through Saturday, or longer if needed. Its geographical scope was unclear, though it was centered on Oleshky and other nearby parts of the Kherson region.
Oleshky is about 550 kilometers (340 miles) southeast of Kyiv, where the Dnipro River separates Russian and Ukrainian forces. Oleshky sits across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, the region’s administrative capital. Russian forces seized Kherson in the early stages of the 2022 full-scale invasion, but retreated across the river several months later.
The Ukrainian-held side of the Kherson region was quiet Tuesday. Only Russian reconnaissance drones were in the sky, local authorities said, though they cautioned it was too early to draw any conclusions and that they didn’t trust Russia.
“It’s too early to say. Let’s wait and see, because you can’t trust the enemy, especially the Russians,” Yaroslav Shanko, head of the Kherson city administration, told The Associated Press.
“There have been previously announced ceasefires more than once, and they had no effect on Kherson … and, let’s say, a lull like this is sometimes even frightening.”
Shanko acknowledged the situation was unusual. He typically travels with a portable drone detector that constantly picks up drones overhead, but it had gone silent. He said he still kept glancing at it, but it showed nothing.
The quiet stands in contrast to daily life in the city, where people are wounded or killed nearly every day, he said.
City services plan to use the pause to carry out utility work that is usually too dangerous because of constant drone activity.
Russian missiles kill at least 3 civilians in Ukraine, officials say
Minutes after 3 a.m., multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded in multiple parts of the country.
Late Monday, the capital also came under attack, when Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 10 injured, city officials said. In Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.
“It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post shortly afterward.
___
Susie Blann and Derek Gatopoulos contributed to this report from Kyiv.

title: Former true-crime producer accused of posing as aircraft heiress added to FBI most-wanted list
text:
(Gray News) - A 75-year-old woman who allegedly posed as an heiress to steal more than $14 million has been added to the FBI’s Most Wanted list.
According to the FBI, Mary Carole McDonnell is accused of posing as the heiress to the McDonnell Aircraft family with an $80 million secret trust.
The McDonnell Aircraft Corporation was an aerospace manufacturer best known for its military aircrafts.
The FBI said the alleged scheme began in July 2017 and lasted until May 2018.
McDonnell allegedly obtained $14.7 million from Banc of California, as well as an additional $15 million from other financial institutions.
On Dec. 12, 2018, a federal arrest warrant was issued for McDonnell. She faces charges of bank fraud and aggravated identity theft.
McDonnell is described as 5-foot-7 with blond hair and blue eyes. She weighs about 145 pounds and has a scar on her right knee.
Mary Carole McDonnell was the chief executive officer of Bellum Entertainment, LLC, a company based in Burbank, Calif., that produced and distributed several television shows, including true-crime programs like “It Takes a Killer” and “I Married a Murderer.”
McDonnell has used several aliases, including Mary Carole Carroll, Mary Carol McDonnell, Mary Carroll McDonnell, Mary C. Carroll and Mary Carroll McDonald.
McDonnell is believed to be in Dubai, but she has ties to Los Angeles and Montgomery, Alabama.

title: At the heart of a debate over a new jail in Penobscot County is a question of who should be incarcerated
text:
Prisoners’ medical and behavioral health needs are at the center of a debate over plans to build a new jail in Penobscot County.
County officials say a new, larger jail is necessary to meet the needs of the people in their custody, the majority of whom struggle with mental illness, addiction or both. The proposal follows previous efforts by the county to build a new jail in Bangor, and a group of concerned citizens is fighting against the latest plan, arguing that the money should instead be directed at preventing incarceration.
The issue will go to Penobscot County residents on Nov. 3 when they vote on a referendum question about whether to authorize relocating the jail from Bangor to a site outside the county seat. If approved, the county will be a step forward in a plan that has been in motion since 2018 to replace the more than 150-year-old jail and build a new correctional facility that could cost upwards of $80 million. Next Tuesday’s vote is only on whether the county can move the jail to a new location, not on specific plans for a facility.
The question voters will see on their ballot is: “Do you favor authorizing the Penobscot County Commissioners, as required under Title 30‑A, §122, to relocate the county correctional facility and any related buildings to a site outside of the county seat?”
The county has proposed building a 109,000-square-foot, 258-bed facility, most likely on a parcel in Hampden where the county negotiated an option-to-buy contract with the owner. Previous proposals, including one to build an eight-story jail in downtown Bangor on the site of a former YMCA, fell apart after public outcry or for logistical reasons.
If voters approve the move next week, the county then plans to ask residents in next November’s election to approve a 30-year bond to finance the project. The bond is expected to be between $72 and $84 million, with county taxpayers paying about $5 million in annual debt service, though the numbers could change as design plans and construction pricing are finalized, Penobscot County Commissioner Andre Cushing said.
The county’s goal is to open a new jail in about five years. The request comes at a time when the county is under scrutiny for budget shortfalls and rising tax rates. The jail budget, which accounts for about a third of the county’s total spending, has in particular been a point of contention: Officials for several years drained county reserves so the county could fund the jail without raising taxes, leaving its bank accounts in the red, audits found.
That’s now catching up with officials. Last week, the commissioners recommended a nearly 28% increase in next year’s budget, which comes a year after they approved a more than 15% hike in property taxes.
For the group fighting against the new jail, these budget concerns also highlight questions over who is being incarcerated and whether the county could do more to address the number of people making their way through the system.
Space concerns
County officials have said the move is necessary because the current facility, last renovated nearly four decades ago, is dilapidated and overcrowded. The jail has a maximum capacity of 157 people. For the past several years, its average daily population has exceeded that, forcing the jail to board prisoners out at other county jails for $100 per person per day.
On average last year, 66 prisoners a day were boarded out to other facilities, according to data The Maine Monitor obtained in a records request. This year, the jail expects to spend about $2.1 million on boarding, per the current county budget. A 2019 report projected the jail’s average daily population could grow to 300 by 2033 based on growth since the mid 1990s.
“This is not about building a new correctional facility, it’s about replacing the current facility that is in disrepair,” Penobscot County Sheriff Troy Morton said in an emailed statement. “It’s not about locking up more people, it’s about reducing the extreme cost to board out individuals.”
A group called No Penobscot County Jail Expansion is encouraging voters to reject the proposal. The group’s position is that the county and the district attorney’s office should focus on reducing the jail population rather than building a new jail.
“It doesn’t take a lot to clean up the space, to put more coats of paint on the wall, to buy new mats, to change the shower curtains more often, to train your people better,” said Doug Dunbar, one of the group’s members and the founder of Penobscot Community Cares, a nonprofit serving people experiencing substance use disorder and homelessness.
“But this is about much more than a building to me and others. This is about a moment in time where we have the opportunity to bring about changes to the system,” he said.
After a string of drunk driving arrests nearly a decade ago, Dunbar was incarcerated at the Penobscot County Jail and later boarded out to Two Bridges Jail in Wiscasset. The Bangor jail, he said, was overpopulated and filthy. At one point he lived in a converted classroom where he and five to six other men slept on cots lined up head to toe.
The group is also concerned that a larger facility will lead to more people getting thrown in jail. Cushing and Chelsea Lynds, the Democratic candidate for district attorney in Penobscot County, said the size of the facility will not influence the number of people being charged with crimes that result in jail time.
But it’s not a concern outside the realm of possibility, said Algeria Wilson, the associate policy director at Wayne State University’s Center for Behavioral Health and Justice.
“Sometimes when you build a new jail, there is a need to use it and use it to its full capacity,” she said. “I couldn’t imagine that if you’re building a 200-bed facility that 100 of those beds were just not going to be used.”
Treatment needs
County officials have argued one reason to build a new facility is to add a medical wing and create space to address substance use and mental health issues among prisoners.
Precise data on the number of people in county jails with a substance use disorder is difficult to come by, but, according to some estimates, three-quarters of the population in Maine jails are struggling with an addiction.
County jails are spending millions of dollars a year on medical and behavioral health care for prisoners, including more than $9 million on medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder.
In facilities that lack the space and staff to provide a higher level of health care, such as the Penobscot County Jail, prisoners are often shuttled off site to get medical attention, adding to jails’ transportation and overtime spending. Cushing said the jail lacks the space to provide even basic medical attention, such as dental cleanings or routine check-ups.
The new facility would have a nearly 4,000-square-foot medical wing with a nurses station, offices and 16 beds, according to county plans. It would also have a multipurpose space for education, substance use and re-entry programming.
It’s not a solution that satisfies Dunbar and others who oppose the new facility.
Dunbar was released from the Penobscot County Jail in 2018 after 136 days to finish his sentence through a drug treatment program. At the time, there were only a half dozen such programs statewide.
“I know that if I had just served my time in jail, particularly after what I witnessed and experienced in Penobscot County Jail,” Dunbar said, “I would have been drinking again as soon as I got to a store and could have purchased more alcohol.”
Instead he was given an alternative that saved his life, he said, something too few other people are offered.
Jail alternatives
There are currently 15 specialty courts statewide, including nine Adult Treatment and Recovery Courts, the latest of which opened in Aroostook County in July. Through these courts, people who meet certain criteria can avoid jail time if they complete specialized programs aimed at addressing the underlying substance use or mental health factors that may have led to criminal conduct.
The courts’ reach, however, remains limited. Nearly 500 people participated in one of the state’s treatment courts last year, including 32 from Penobscot County. More than 25,000 people, meanwhile, were booked in county jails.
Working with the Portland-based justice reform organization Society Impact, No Penobscot County Jail Expansion put together a proposal to increase diversion opportunities.
The proposal calls for implementing diversion programs at three stages –– before arrest, after arraignment and after release –– to expand the number of opportunities when someone’s eligibility for a diversion program can be assessed. The groups have also proposed different diversion tracks corresponding to different levels of offenses.
The majority of people incarcerated in Maine jails have not been sentenced. Maine’s indigent defense system has for years been dealing with what Lynds, who is currently an assistant district attorney, called a “crippling” defense lawyer shortage. The system is moving so slowly that, although state law caps jail sentences at less than a year, jail officials estimated that some people are stuck there for up to two years waiting for their day in court. Last year, 86% of the prisoners at the Penobscot County Jail were awaiting sentencing on an average day, according to data obtained by The Monitor.
But building a new jail and expanding diversion programs are not mutually exclusive, said Lynds, who is running unopposed.
“We need more avenues that are not incarceration to send people to, for sure,” she said. “But even if we had the best diversion programs in the world, we still have to have a jail.”
The current facility is unsafe, she said. The layout is dysfunctional; there isn’t enough storage space; and there are constant plumbing issues, among other concerns. It would cost the county $1.22 billion over 35 years to repair, maintain and operate the current jail, versus $850 million to build a new jail, pay back the bond and run annual operations over the same time period, according to an analysis done by consulting firm Dirigo Strategic Advisors for the Board of Commissioners.
Lynds said she agrees that it would be ideal to get people the help they need before they end up in the criminal justice system but that it is not always feasible. Regardless, she added, the jail still has a responsibility to care for the people in its custody in a facility that is safe and well equipped.
Wilson, from Wayne State, warned that jails should not be thought of as the “first stop for mental health treatment or substance use disorder treatment,” adding that jails can be mentally destabilizing for many people. While public safety is a priority, so, too, is ensuring that people have access to treatment outside of jails.
There’s a balance to strike when it comes to building new jail facilities, said Wanda Bertram, a spokesperson for the nonprofit Prison Policy Initiative. While they should not be dirty and dysfunctional, they are ultimately institutions built for surveillance and should not be thought of as a substitute for a treatment center.
Bertram said that’s why increasing community-based programs should be a part of the conversation. Diversion programs can help. But addressing “crimes of poverty” –– camping bans, unpaid fines and other nonviolent, minor offenses –– would go a long way.
“People who are being brought to jail for these reasons often have serious unmet needs in the way of housing or in the way of health care,” Bertram said. “Are you really building something that you know is going to be better maintained, or is it really just kind of like we’re recycling the same kind of solutions and ideas that we’ve always had?”
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: Down East deaths of grandmother, grandchildren ruled accidental drownings
text:
The grandmother and two grandchildren found in a vehicle in the ocean at Roque Bluffs last month died due to an accidental drowning, officials announced Tuesday.
Sharon Bukulmez, 61, of Mount Desert, was last seen the night of Sept. 19 leaving a family wedding in Jonesboro with her granddaughter Kinsley Grubb, 5, and grandson Sawyer Grubb, 3, both of Bar Harbor, according to Maine State Police.
They did not arrive in Machias as expected, police said, and location information obtained from Bukulmez’s cellphone led officials to a boat ramp at the end of Schoppee Point Road in Roque Bluffs.
Bukulmez’s vehicle was located submerged in Pond Cove at about 7 a.m. Sept. 20, police said, and the three bodies were recovered that morning.
The Maine Office of the Chief Medical Examiner determined their official causes of death to be accidental drownings, Maine State Police announced in a news release Tuesday.
The incident is still under investigation, the news release said.

title: Maine Chief Medical Examiner Released New Information About 3 Deaths in Roque Bluffs Pond
text:
More information has been released about a Maine grandmother and her two grandchildren found deceased in a vehicle in Roque Bluffs.
More Details Released About the Deaths of a Grandmother and 2 Grandchildren
The bodies of 61-year-old Sharon Bukulmez of Mount Desert, 5-year-old Kinsley Grubb, and 3-year-old Sawyer Grubb, both of Bar Harbor, were discovered in Sharon's vehicle on Sunday morning, September 20th.
After an examination by the Chief Medical Examiner, it was determined that all three people died of drowning and their deaths were accidental.
Maine Woman and 2 Grandkids Found Deceased in a Submerged Vehicle in Roque Bluffs
The trio was last seen at approximately 8:30 pm on Saturday, September 19th, 2026, leaving a family function in Jonesboro.
They were traveling to Machias and were reported missing after failing to arrive.
As law enforcement launched a search, the Bar Harbor Police Department obtained location information from Bukulmez's cellphone, which indicated a location in the water near the boat ramp at the end of Schoppee Road in Roque Bluffs.
Maine State Police were notified, and troopers responded to the scene, including divers who located the vehicle at approximately 7 am., submerged in Pond Cove
Two Women in 2013 Also Died in a Submerged Vehicle in Roque Bluffs, Maine
In 2013, two women died when their vehicle became submerged in Roque Bluffs.
Local authorities took Amy Stiner of Machias and Melissa Moyer of Pennsylvania, who was five months pregnant, to their vehicle after they got lost while hiking.
After a short time, the women called to say they had driven their vehicle into the water, and then the phone went dead.
According to CBS News, the women had driven into the ocean after traveling the wrong way down a road.
They were found deceased in their submerged vehicle sometime later.
We'll update this story as more details become available.

title: Historic downtown Bangor building to be turned into 14 studio apartments
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
More than a dozen new apartments are coming to a previously vacant historic building in downtown Bangor.
Pike Project Development bought the Pearl Building on the corner of State and Harlow streets this past spring and began renovating the second through fifth floors into 14 studio-style apartments, according to Zack Pike, one of the company’s developers.
The Bangor-based company hopes to have the units completed next summer but doesn’t yet know how much they’ll be rented for. Each is designed to have an open floorplan and one full bathroom, Pike said.
Once online, the units will help improve a local and statewide housing shortage that has contributed to home prices staying high after spiking years ago. The project is also an example of how housing can be created in existing buildings rather than built from scratch and can revive historically significant properties.
“It’s really rewarding to give these buildings new life, and the upper floors are often neglected for commercial uses, especially in a five-story building,” Pike said. “The whole idea is to take these buildings, breathe new life into them and make them as wonderful as they had been in the past.”
The Pearl Building was constructed soon after the Great Fire of 1911 swept through that section of the city, leaving a path of destruction. The building served as office space with the Pearl & Dennett Co., a large insurance and real estate company, occupying the ground floor, according to a 1915 Maine Chamber of Commerce Journal.
“We’ve been doing work downtown for quite a few years and I can’t remember ever seeing any activity on the upper floors,” Pike said. “It feels like it was abandoned office space.”
Today, two commercial spaces are available on the ground floor. One holds Log Jam Vintage, which opened in May 2025 and sells a variety of men’s and women’s clothing and accessories made during and before the 1990s. The other is empty.
While the building’s lower floor was in good condition, the upper floors needed a significant amount of demolition and repair work due to years of neglect. Most immediately, the roof needed to be replaced, as a leak had caused water damage, and masonry needed to be repaired, Pike said.
The company, which specializes in restoring historic buildings in Bangor and beyond, previously helped renovate 33 State St., located diagonally across the intersection, as well as 24 State St. next door, which holds Orono Brewing Company, among other buildings.
With any restoration project, Pike said workers try to keep as many original features in a building as possible. For this project, the building’s original windows will be repaired and remain in place.
“We’re reglazing them and fixing the broken glass,” Pike said. “One of the unique features of the building are the curved windows on the corner of State and Harlow Streets. We’re repairing those curved windows and putting them back into place.”
Aside from providing more housing options in Maine’s third-largest city, Pike said the new units will benefit local businesses eager for employees and patrons who live nearby.
“More people in the downtown area are going to inevitably help the downtown businesses as well the overall atmosphere and spirit of the downtown,” Pike said. “More people here means a more thriving community.”

title: Former true-crime producer accused of posing as aircraft heiress added to FBI most-wanted list
text:
(Gray News) - A 75-year-old woman who allegedly posed as an heiress to steal more than $14 million has been added to the FBI’s Most Wanted list.
According to the FBI, Mary Carole McDonnell is accused of posing as the heiress to the McDonnell Aircraft family with an $80 million secret trust.
The McDonnell Aircraft Corporation was an aerospace manufacturer best known for its military aircrafts.
The FBI said the alleged scheme began in July 2017 and lasted until May 2018.
McDonnell allegedly obtained $14.7 million from Banc of California, as well as an additional $15 million from other financial institutions.
On Dec. 12, 2018, a federal arrest warrant was issued for McDonnell. She faces charges of bank fraud and aggravated identity theft.
McDonnell is described as 5-foot-7 with blond hair and blue eyes. She weighs about 145 pounds and has a scar on her right knee.
Mary Carole McDonnell was the chief executive officer of Bellum Entertainment, LLC, a company based in Burbank, Calif., that produced and distributed several television shows, including true-crime programs like “It Takes a Killer” and “I Married a Murderer.”
McDonnell has used several aliases, including Mary Carole Carroll, Mary Carol McDonnell, Mary Carroll McDonnell, Mary C. Carroll and Mary Carroll McDonald.
McDonnell is believed to be in Dubai, but she has ties to Los Angeles and Montgomery, Alabama.
Anyone with information is asked to contact their local FBI office or a U.S. embassy or consulate.

title: A Deering parent for Kate Snyder
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
My two sons went to Ocean Avenue Elementary School, and my younger is now a junior at Deering High School. For personal reasons, I care about how the Portland City Council attends to the schools.
But even more, I care because strong schools are fundamental to a city’s full potential. In Portland, families and property owners directly impact our schools’ ability to operate. State aid follows each child, and property taxes cover about three-quarters of the school budget. When families can’t afford to stay, the aid shrinks and the tax bill grows.
Kate Snyder knows our schools need kids to fill the halls. Her focus on housing is how we keep them here. Her budget expertise will keep our schools whole and protect resources where they’re needed most.
On Nov. 3, I’m ranking Kate Snyder first for City Council at-large. I hope other school families will too.
Emily Bruce Plumb
Portland

title: Maine farm surplus turned into ready-to-heat meals for the hungry
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Two local nonprofits and a regional supermarket have launched a pilot program to get 100,000 frozen, scratch-made meals to Mainers at risk of going hungry over the next year to offset high grocery prices and federal benefit cuts.
By connecting commercial funding, surplus farm crops and nonprofit logistics, the Harvest to Home initiative attempts to establish a statewide distribution network specifically dedicated to prepared, frozen meals.
“At the end of the day, everyone deserves a good, comforting meal,” said Colin Freeman of Preble Street, one of the nonprofits behind Harvest to Home. “Hundreds more individuals and families across Maine will have access to nutritious, delicious food every single week.”
The number of Mainers facing hunger continues to rise. A Feeding America report released in July says more than 203,000 people in Maine are at risk of going hungry, the highest that it’s been in a decade, according to 2024 data.
Preble Street will cook and package the meals at its Food Security Hub in South Portland using produce donated from Maine farms. Staff and volunteers will use blanchers, blast chillers and dehydrators to turn farm surplus that would otherwise spoil into shelf-stable frozen food.
Good Shepherd Food Bank will collect the frozen meals weekly and deliver them to its 380 food pantry partners across Maine. Distribution started Tuesday with a batch of 2,000 meals, including dishes like miso chicken, pork and corn stew and beef bolognese.
A $150,000 grant from Hannaford Supermarkets kickstarted the pilot, which will cost an estimated $530,000, according to project leaders. The rest will be absorbed by Preble Street and Good Shepherd through donations and general operating funds.
Each scratch-made meal will cost about $5.30 to make, accounting for packaging, labor and utilities.
The program targets Maine residents struggling to cook for physical, geographic or financial reasons, including low-income seniors, rural residents, working families or the unhoused. The prepared meals eliminate the need for complex cooking equipment or home kitchen storage.
“We are especially focused on our senior population, who are especially vulnerable as oil prices have gone up,” said Heather Paquette, president of Good Shepherd Food Bank. “Some of them are going to the food pantry for the first time.”
While 100,000 meals expand access across rural and urban centers, it represents a fraction of Maine’s broad hunger relief needs. Preble Street alone serves about 700,000 meals annually in the Portland region.
Thousands of Mainers have lost access to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program because of sweeping changes that began rolling out last fall. Organizers hope the pilot creates a lasting model for hunger relief.
“Ensuring hungry Mainers have the food they need is part of our mission, it’s part of our DNA,” said Ali Lovejoy, vice president of mission advancement at Preble Street. “We have confidence … we can work with our partners, community members, and supporters to meet that need.”

title: Families of ironworkers killed during ballpark construction get free tickets to World Series
text:
Families of ironworkers killed during ballpark construction get free tickets to World Series
The roar of thousands of fans filled American Family Field for Game 2 of the World Series on Saturday.
Among the crowd were RJ, Betsy, Sawyer and Hazel Wischer.
Through the dance breaks and rally towel cheers, the memories of what and who helped make it all possible rounded home plate.
"Probably nobody that was on that job site before or after the accident ever really thought that the World Series was going to be played there," RJ said.
On July 14, 1999, the then-under-construction Miller Park was the site of a heartbreaking tragedy. The crane being used in the construction of the retractable roof collapsed. Three ironworkers — Jerome Starr, William DeGrave and RJ's father, Jeffrey Wischer — were all killed.
"He was the person that wanted to teach you and show you and tell you how to do things the right way or a better way," RJ said while talking about his father.
Multiple memorials outside the stadium are in place to help honor the three men's lives.
"I like walking over to the statues and the plaques where 'Jeffrey Wischer' was engraved," Sawyer said. "I have to say, he looks a lot like my dad."
RJ said every time he walks into the stadium, he can't help but think of his father.
"I'm always looking around at the structure because I am an ironworker now. So, like, knowing what goes into it, I actually point out at one point in time to Sawyer, like, look at how many bolts are in that connection," RJ said. "It's just one connection out of the many connections in this entire stadium. Like, look at how many bolts are in there. And then, of course, you had to sit there and count every single one, like, there's 38 in that one connection. And I was like, yeah, you don't know how long that takes for one person to make that connection. It's a lot, so you just appreciate it a little bit more."
RJ was only 8 years old when his father died. Now, 27 years later, thanks to the Brewers and the Ironworkers Union, he got to witness history in the stadium his dad helped build.
"I felt that my old man was having a Miller High Life next to me, and Bob Uecker was probably having a High Life next to him," RJ said.
"Being able to sit in the stands and watch him watching the game through our kids' eyes and experience that all together like it was something special," Betsy Wischer said.
The Brewers and Ironworkers Union offered free tickets to the Wischers and the other families whose loved ones were killed in 1999.
It's a moment RJ and Betsy said they'll never forget.
"Grateful of what my father helped build, grateful of the Brewers, grateful of the Ironworkers. Grateful for all of it," RJ said.

title: Sen. Angus King endorses Matt Dunlap in Maine CD2 race
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A major endorsement in the race for Maine’s Second Congressional District came in Tuesday morning.
“I think Matt will make a great member of Congress, and I look forward to working with him,“ said Independent Senator Angus King, who is officially endorsing Democrat Matt Dunlap.
Dunlap will square off against former Governor Paul LePage at the polls on November 3rd.
King says Dunlap made a strong impression on him when they worked together in the State House when King was governor and Dunlap was a lawmaker.
“When you serve as governor, you get to know a lot of legislators, but one I particularly remember is Matt Dunlap because he was tough and smart and a strong advocate for his district,” King said in a video message. “He also has been a great advocate for the sportsmen and women of Maine. In fact, he has a hunting license. He can represent the whole second district in Congress, and that’s what we need.”
“When Senator King was Governor, we worked closely on major issues for Maine sportsmen. I’m honored to have his support and endorsement, and look forward to the chance to work with him to lower prices if elected,” Dunlap said. “Mainers are frustrated by high prices on home heating oil, groceries, hockey sticks, and pretty much everything else under the sun. We’ve got to end the war that’s keeping gas prices high and end the tariff taxes that are keeping grocery prices high.”
King has also endorsed Hannah Pingree for governor.
LePage senior campaign adviser Brent Littlefield commented on the endorsement, saying: “The last time Angus King endorsed in a race Governor LePage was in he endorsed Eliot Cutler. Matt Dunlap is now in the same company as Eliot Cutler.”

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: More Sunshine Ahead this Week, with Chilly Temperatures Tuesday Night
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Quiet and dry weather continues across Northern Maine this week, but temperatures will be anything but steady. After a cool Tuesday, temperatures tumble into the teens and lower 20s Tuesday night before rebounding sharply later in the week. By Thursday, many communities could climb close to 60 degrees.
Skies continue to clear tonight as colder air settles into Northern Maine. Most of Aroostook County will fall into the upper 20s, including around 29 degrees in Caribou and Houlton and 28 in Presque Isle. Northwest winds will remain around 5 to 10 mph, with some gusts up to 25 mph early.
Tuesday will be sunny but noticeably cooler. Temperatures in Caribou will start around 29 degrees during the morning and only climb into the lower 40s during the afternoon. Despite the chill, no rain is expected and sunshine will dominate throughout the day. Northwest winds will generally run around 10 to 15 mph, with gusts up to 25 mph possible across Northeast Aroostook.
The coldest part of this stretch arrives Tuesday night. Clear skies and lighter winds will allow temperatures to fall into the teens and lower 20s across much of Northern Maine. Presque Isle and Houlton could fall to around 19 degrees, while Caribou drops to around 21. Several colder locations across the North Woods and Saint John Valley could fall into the upper teens.
Sunshine continues Wednesday, with highs recovering into the mid to upper 40s. Temperatures then rise substantially Thursday as southwest flow develops ahead of the next cold front. Highs should reach the upper 50s across Northwest Aroostook and around 60 degrees from Caribou and Presque Isle south toward Houlton. Thursday will feature partly to mostly sunny skies for much of the day.
Thursday will be the standout mild day of the week. Caribou and Houlton are forecast to reach around 60 degrees, while Presque Isle could reach the lower 60s. That would put temperatures roughly 10 degrees or more above average in several locations. A cold front approaches Thursday night into Friday morning. A few showers remain possible across northern areas, but rainfall amounts are expected to be very light and localized, generally less than one tenth of an inch. Beyond that front, the dry pattern continues through the weekend. For the latest forecast details, check out the First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Trump to hold Ohio rally amid governor’s race controversy
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With Election Day less than a week away, President Donald Trump is expected to make another campaign stop in Ohio, where two competitive races could have national implications.
The president’s visit comes amid growing controversy surrounding Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, whose campaign released a viral attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton.
In the ad, Acton’s mother calls her daughter a liar. But critics say the video omits crucial context about Acton’s childhood.
Acton and her brother were removed from their mother’s custody after Acton’s stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her.
“My opponent has chosen to exploit my childhood to save his struggling campaign, but it’s not going to work,” Acton said at recent campaign even.
The ad has drawn criticism from lawmakers in both parties, including Ohio’s Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.
Ramaswamy, however, has defended the commercial, and argued that voters should be allowed to hear the allegations and make their own decisions.
Trump has also repeatedly defended the ad.
“The mother said terrible things,” Trump said. “Anybody seeing that would say, no way I’m voting for her.”
The controversy comes as recent polls suggests Democrats are gaining ground in Ohio, raising the stakes for Trump’s latest campaign stop.
Wednesday’s scheduled rally in Chillicothe will also put a spotlight on Ohio’s competitive U.S. Senate race, which could help determine which party controls the chamber.
Republican Sen. Jon Husted is facing a challenge from Democrat Sherrod Brown, who is attempting a political comeback after losing his Senate seat in 2024 to Trump-endorsed candidate Sen. Bernie Moreno.
