title: Jayson Tatum rescues Celtics with OT buzzer-beater
text:
BOSTON — Jayson Tatum buried a 17-foot jumper at the overtime buzzer to cap a 40-point night, and the Boston Celtics beat the Brooklyn Nets 125-124 on Tuesday night for their third straight victory.
Tatum finished 10 of 20 from the field and 18 of 22 from the free-throw line. Paul George added 20 points and Derrick White scored 16 for the Celtics, who have not lost since they blew a 22-point lead in their season opener at Detroit.
Michael Porter Jr. had 27 points and 12 rebounds for Brooklyn (0-4), and Julius Randle scored 24 points.
Nets rookie Mikel Brown Jr. made a tying 3-pointer with 0.2 seconds remaining in regulation, but in OT, he missed a layup with 2.3 seconds left to set up Tatum for the winning basket. Brown, the sixth pick in the NBA draft out of Louisville, finished with 17 points.
Boston’s Mitchell Robinson missed two free throws with 3 seconds left in regulation, giving Brooklyn a chance at the tying 3. Robinson, a career 50.7% free-throw shooter, went 1 of 4 from the line and is 2 of 8 this season.
With 33.7 seconds remaining in regulation, White slipped behind the defense and Tatum found him for a tiebreaking dunk. White was fouled on the play and converted the free throw for a 114-111 lead.
Neither team led by more than eight points. The Nets went ahead 109-104 on a basket by Randle with 2:57 left before the Celtics rallied.
The Celtics made 2 of 16 3-point attempts in the first half but trailed just 61-56. They fared a bit better from long range in the second half, going 9 of 22.
Up next
Nets: Host Detroit on Friday night
Celtics: Host Chicago on Friday night

title: 115 Maine schools host mock elections
text:
115 Maine schools host mock elections
115 Maine schools host mock elections
Maranacook Community High School was one of more than 100 Maine schools to host mock elections a week ahead of the midterms.
For the Readfield school, the students voted in the U.S. Senate, gubernatorial and CD2 races.
It's a program organized by the Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, who says that those who take part in mock elections as students are more likely to become lifelong voters.
"We think that this is a great way for students to get introduced to the idea of voting and to recognize it's pretty easy, that it doesn't take a lot of time," said Bellows. "It's not terribly complicated."
Maranacook students who did vote said they did so to better prepare for the real thing, once they turn 18. The students also added it's a good opportunity to share their opinions.
Some of the students said they went into the mock election with some background on the candidates, including what they've seen on television.
"Probably what has been done with each of these people and what they say that they are going to do, because I believe it's very important and we have a lot of problems in society," said sophomore Serenity Longfellow.
"Along with the commercials on TV, there's like some of them are like, don't vote for this person, bad person. But then there's also a lot of this stuff on the other sides as well," added sophomore Madelyn Begin.
The students also stated an intention to involve themselves more in the world of politics following Tuesday's mock election experience.
"I want to know about what's going on in the world and not just based off what my dad says or like my parents are saying or what teachers are saying," added sophomore Rorie Sage.
Maranacook principal Michele LaForge said that during her five years with the school, this is the largest student involvement she's seen.
LaForge mentioned that while mock elections always bring an increase in political discussion throughout the school, this year, it's been incredibly respectful.
"I get fewer people telling me that their vote doesn't matter," stated LaForge. "I think that it is an opportunity for them to share what is always there. There's a heightened political atmosphere in schools today than there was 25 years ago when I started."
According to Bellows, the statewide mock election results are expected to be announced on Wednesday.

title: US and Cuban officials get in a shouting match during UN debate over economic embargo
text:
US and Cuban officials get in a shouting match during UN debate over economic embargo
U.S. and Cuban officials engaged in a stunning shouting match on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, the latest in a series of public spats between the longtime adversaries over Washington's escalating economic campaign against Havana.
Video from August above: Driving through Havana, Cuba, during another blackout
The interaction began shortly after U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz took the podium to argue against supporting the annual resolution this week condemning the U.S.' decades-long economic embargo against the island country.
As Waltz was detailing years of alleged corruption by the socialist government, members of the Cuban delegation, including Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez, began to slam on their designated table and yell for a point of order.
Then, as U.N. officials sought to tone down the outbursts, Rodríguez walked down the aisle to the head of the General Assembly and yelled to Waltz, “You are a liar!"
Waltz responded, “You understand who you’re dealing with? This is America. Back up.”
While the moment represented a shocking break from diplomatic decorum traditional to the U.N., it perfectly captured the heightened tensions between Cuba and the U.S. as President Donald Trump's administration seeks to force changes to Cuba’s political system by increasing its already punishing economic campaign.
The Caribbean country — already facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles — is now being pushed to a breaking point after Trump, a Republican, announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba. The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that affect basic activities such as cooking, the water supply and internet and telephone services.
Cuban officials have also repeatedly stressed that as U.S. officials demand that Cuba open up to private investment, Washington keeps piling on sanctions that get in the way of the very economic opening it has sought for decades.
The outbursts Tuesday come a week after a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behavior of the island’s government.
Waltz and other U.S. officials have been using these public events and gatherings at the world body to try to persuade U.N. member states to vote on Wednesday against the annual resolution, which is aimed at calling out the U.S. government’s “maximum pressure policy” against Cuba.
For the past 34 years, the resolution has received overwhelming support. Last year, the vote was 165-7, with 12 abstentions. Argentina, Ukraine and Hungary opposed the measure for the first time.
While such resolutions are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion.

title: In its second year, Maine’s Bagel-Off showcases the best local dough
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WISCASSETT — It wasn’t until bagel 13 that I started to struggle.
Until then, my friends/co-tasters and I had been going strong in our effort to cast an informed vote for Maine’s best bagel. We, along with about 300 others, mingled at the Maine Tasting Center on a sunny Saturday morning, taking thoughtful bites of dough that hailed from Naples to Northport.
Stomachs full and palates exhausted, we tried our 14th and final bagel. It was pretty good.
It was my second year attending the event organized by the Maine Grain Alliance, focused on highlighting local flours and craftsmanship in one of America’s favorite baked goods. I could not have had a more different experience to last year’s.
Last August, my friends and I arrived hungry at the farmers’ market in Brunswick only to discover a line for the first Maine Bagel Bake-Off wrapping around the whole market.
We were not to sample any bagels that day. After we’d waited in line for more than two hours, organizers sold us half-price tickets because they were running low on stock. Despite a guarantee that there would still be some bagels left by the time we reached the end of the second line, they had run out and our tickets were refunded.
It’s become something of a mythic event among my friends: how we waited for so long, discovered there would be no cream cheese, then we wouldn’t get any bagels; how we made friends with the couple standing next to us in line, how we all went to nearby Dutchman’s afterward to make up for it, met our new friends’ puppy, created a group chat.
Maine Grain Alliance Executive Director Tristan Noyes mentioned last year’s event before I even brought it up.
“Admittedly, I don’t think we were prepared for…” Noyes trailed off with a laugh, describing how the 2025 event went awry.
In Noyes’s retelling, the Bagel-Off (then called the Bagel Bake-Off, since renamed) was planned as a way to show off the great local grain innovations among the state’s bagel makers.
The goal was to crown two winners, one judged by a group of bagel-tasting professionals, and one by public opinion. Noyes knew Sam Silverman, a Bowdoin graduate and the founder of New York BagelFest, who served as a judge, and other bagel professionals involved with the Alliance’s annual Kneading Conference.
But anticipation for the event went unexpectedly viral (the announcement on Instagram garnered 950 likes and more than 1,500 shares). It was too much for the organizers, the parking lot, or the bagel supply to handle. “Never has something gone so viral so quickly,” Noyes said. “The demand was just out of this world.”
So he and the other organizers took extra care in arranging this year’s edition. The event moved to the Maine Tasting Center in Wiscasset. Tickets were sold in advance. The bagels would be served farmers’ market-style, with each baker at their own booth. And there would be cream cheese.
That effort paid off. Saturday’s event was delightfully well-organized. Participants received a bagel passport with all of the vendors (perfect for detailed note-taking), a tray to hold samples and a ticket to cast their vote. The event offered regular and whipped cream cheese, alongside coffee and apple cider samples. Nobody ran out of bagels — in fact, bagel makers were generous with additional flavors or specialty schmears to sample. The lines for each booth moved quickly and the bakers were eager to talk about their submission, the flours and techniques they employed.
In all, 14 bakers offered up their bagel for consideration, ranging from some of Maine’s best-known bakeries, like Scratch in South Portland and Dutchman’s in Brunswick, to home bakers and microbakeries. There was no requirement to use local grains, but bakers received a bonus from the judges if at least 10% of the flour in their recipe was local. Noyes said 10 of this year’s bakers did.
Most bagel makers tried to stand out with unique flavors: three featured rosemary, two brought pretzel bagels and two included caramelized onion, while others offered pumpernickel, french toast, jalapeno cheddar and za’atar. The styles ranged from Montreal to New York, wood-fired to sourdough.
My group found plenty of common ground — Spark’s flavorful salt and fennel bagel and the Dutchman’s za’atar bagel were both crowd-pleasers — and were split on others, like the pumpernickel from La Tartine in Belfast.
One of the most memorable samples was from Knead & Knosh (last year’s judge’s winner, an award that prompted home baker Jeff Mao to open a brick and mortar store in Topsham). Mao submitted a Malay curry and sultana bagel this time around, a grown-up cinnamon raisin bagel with warm spices like turmeric, cumin and coriander, and bits of golden raisin. I loved it (even as a cinnamon raisin skeptic) but we agreed it was perhaps better as a fun bite than a whole bagel.
In the end, I cast my vote for Scratch’s rosemary honey bagel, a chewy — almost puffy — and perfectly salty sourdough creation with a cornmeal crust. Two of my friends’ votes went to Spark, while another cast her ballot for Blue House’s rosemary onion (which came with a charred scallion cream cheese, the standout spread of the morning.)
When the winners were announced in the early afternoon, the people’s choice award went to Blue House, a small-batch Portland home bakery, while the judge’s award went to Scratch. Both of the winners used Maine-grown grains in their bagels.
“We had an incredible, incredible, close competition in a million ways,” Noyes said before presenting the Golden Bagel awards to the winners. He also gave delayed trophies to last year’s awardees, including people’s choice winner Orchard Ridge.
While I’m taking a very short break from bagels, I’m confident I’ll have space for more by next year.

title: Shipwreck found in Gulf of Maine more than 80 years after WWII sinking
text:
The SS Cornwallis was simply in the wrong place at the wrong time when it was sunk by a German U-boat in the Gulf of Maine in December 1944, claiming 43 lives.
As for the shipwreck’s discovery off Mount Desert Rock this summer, the timing was impeccable.
Eight divers based in Portsmouth, New Hampshire — the Nomad Exploration Team — located the Canadian vessel nearly 400 feet below the surface in July and announced their find Tuesday.
The team began its search for the Cornwallis in 2019, seeking to locate one of the largest unfound shipwrecks left in New England and bring renewed attention to an eight-decade-old tragedy.
They were moments away from missing it completely.
It’s not the team’s first major discovery — it found the William H. Machen off the coast of Portsmouth in 2017 and the USS Eagle 56 off Cape Elizabeth a year later — but members told the Portland Press Herald this month that locating the Cornwallis required some of their most daunting dives to date.
And equally as compelling as the New Brunswick-bound vessel’s story, the divers said, is that of the submarine that sank it, which is also forever tied to Maine.
DEC. 3, 1944
The 1944 sinking of the Cornwallis was actually the ship’s second encounter with a U-boat’s torpedo: It had been hit off the coast of Barbados two years prior.
Refloated, the 400-foot freighter — originally built in 1921 — was on its way from Barbados to St. John, New Brunswick, before its fateful encounter with the U-1230 on Dec. 3, 1944.
The steam merchant ship was carrying sugar, molasses and 48 people, including seven armed guards, when it was struck by a torpedo at about 6 a.m.
It sank in minutes, according to contemporaneous newspaper reports, and the five survivors were rescued by the Portland fishing trawler Notre Dame and taken to Rockland.
More than one-third of the 43 who perished were from Nova Scotia. For dive team member Danny Allan, that made the mission personal.
“One of the crew members grew up 10 miles from the house I grew up in,” he said.
But the Cornwallis was not the prime objective of the U-1230.
“The U-boat wasn’t looking for them,” said Don Ferrara, another member of the team. “They were just there.”
Operation Elster (or “Magpie” in English) is a story some Mainers may be more familiar with.
Days before sinking the Cornwallis, the U-1230 was at the crux of a Nazi intelligence operation when it dropped off two spies in the town of Hancock. The precise location — a beach on Crabtree Neck — was recognized by the National Register of Historic Places in 2003, dubbed the “Nazi Spy Landing Site.”
The two spies took a taxi to Bangor, caught a train to Portland and made their way to New York City. Their mission (to gain information about American industry and technology) was ultimately unfruitful.
While the spies headed south, the U-1230 stayed off the Maine coast until they got clear, said dive team member Jeff Goodreau.
“Here comes the Cornwallis, and fate is made,” he said.
THE SEARCH
Between the beginning of its quest in 2019 and the climactic moment this July, the dive team undertook several expeditions looking for the Cornwallis. For every hour spent on the water, Allan said, there were at least 10 hours of groundwork.
Along with Allan, Ferrara and Goodreau, the other members of the discovery team are Mark Bowers, Josh Cummings, Bob Foster, Nate Garrett and Ryan King; the crew also enlisted the help of Ross Baxter, an experienced boat captain.
They knew its approximate location — roughly 10 miles southwest of Mount Desert Rock — but that still leaves a lot of ocean to scan.
One of the first steps was to gather as much knowledge as possible on the vessel and determine where it was most likely to have been at the moment it sank. That included digging into the history, pulling the ship’s archived blueprints, and talking with authors and historians.
The team also came to lean on the knowledge of local fishermen. In wrecks as violent as those caused by a torpedo, there tends to be a lot of evidence left behind, and conversations with fishermen can reveal some clues.
Allan explained there were three potential locations: where the survivors were found, where debris was located, and where a mariner claimed to have pulled up the Cornwallis’ compass housing.
Then, there’s the Gulf of Maine to grapple with, which includes research into its topography, tide charts and weather reports.
“There are big tides up off of the Mount Desert area,” Goodreau said. “A lot of weather, a lot of fog. … Any way you look at it, the challenge is just getting there, whether it’s a five-hour run from Portsmouth or trailering a boat up there.”
JULY 11, 2026
The Nomad crew located the Cornwallis early on the second day of its July expedition and almost missed it — twice.
As the team began to scan the first grid of the ocean planned for July 11, it passed the Cornwallis on the boat’s port side, Allan said.
“We’re looking at the side-scan sonar, and it was within 300 feet of our boat, and we did not recognize it,” Allan said.
Then came the second pass.
“We were in the last 100 yards of the last track,” Goodreau said. “We were reprogramming the GPS when it popped up.”
And there it was, prompting a rush of excitement — and some expletives, the team members admitted.
“We were over the moon,” Ferrara said.
Then, they realized how close they came to missing it.
“We would’ve written off that whole section as ‘we already looked there’ and wouldn’t have found it,” Allan said.
“We’d still be up there burning fuel and wasting time,” added Goodreau.
But a sonar scan matching the vessel’s design still leaves a little room for doubt. To be 100% certain, Allan said, “you go down, and you actually touch it.”
400 FEET TO GO
Along with the jubilation of finding a shipwreck comes solemnity, the team members said, and both grow stronger the closer you get.
“You’re the first person to see and touch this wreck literally in 80 years, so you’re ecstatic,” Allan said. “But it’s also extremely sobering because this is a grave. Forty-three souls lost their lives on this wreck.”
Though they have decades of experience diving off New England’s coast, the Down East descents pushed them to their limits.
“It’s very deep, it’s very cold, a lot of current,” Goodreau said. “Pretty much the worst-case scenario as far as diving goes.”
The first dive was the worst, Ferrara said, because his light died. He was essentially diving blind.
“It’s possibly the scariest dive I’ve ever done,” Ferrara said.
The maximum depth for recreational diving is 130 feet below the surface. Despite his experience as a technical diver, Allan said the nearly 400-foot dives to the Cornwallis tested his comfort zone.
“I’ve been stuck inside a U-boat while diving; I’ve been stuck in the back of caves. These were by far the hardest dives I’ve ever done,” Allan said, adding, “It’s at the limit, quite honestly, of what I am willing to do.”
And they’ll do it again: Allan said the team plans to explore the wreck at least once a year to document the Cornwallis’ state and rate of deterioration.
But the major payoff has already come, the team said.
“There are 43 families that lost brothers and sons and husbands. … It’s closure for their families,” Allan said.

title: Charles proposes $207 million emergency plan for gas, heating costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles outlined a $207 million emergency plan on Maine gas and heating oil costs one week before the election.
Charles and a crowd of supporters gathered outside the Dysart’s in Bangor to announce several steps he would take if elected governor.
Charles said while he cannot change oil markets or stop the war in Iran, there are changes that can be made here in Maine to limit the impacts on residents. He said on day one in office, he would put into action the $207 million emergency plan—proposing taking $207 million out of the state’s rainy day fund.
Charles said he would suspend Maine’s gas tax for 90 days. He would use roughly $60 million from the rainy day fund to backfill the money lost to the Highway Fund.
He also said he would use $100 million from the rainy day fund to support heating for schools to reduce tax burdens.
Charles also advocated for doubling LIHEAP assistance to $42 million and advocated for allocating an additional $5 million for the crisis intervention program for families in need.
“This is the exact reason a rainy day fund is set up. When people have a one-time need,” Charles said. “I am trying to get the gas tax suspended for 90 days so that everybody in the state doesn’t have to worry.”
Charles said a 12-step plan would be unveiled after inauguration. He also urged Gov. Janet Mills to adopt his plan for the end of her tenure.

title: A US cruise ship ends a global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs and 200 passengers lose their homes
text:
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — A U.S. cruise ship on a residential world voyage suspended its operations in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to abandon their floating homes.
The Odyssey set sail two years ago on a three-year voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel.
The Florida-based company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 has recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia during the war in Iran. Villa Vie Residences said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surge in fuel costs.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” it said. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
Sihanoukville Autonomous Port said in a statement last week that the ship docked on Oct. 23 for a five-day visit. It was to head to Vietnam but remained in the port Wednesday.
The ship carried 203 passengers with 15 nationalities, mostly Americans, and 156 crew members. It had a capacity of 650 residents.
Passengers have been told to leave the ship, but the crew’s status was unclear.
The Odyssey had a confirmed itinerary into November 2027. The company planned for a second residential cruise ship to enter service in early 2029, but the statement on the suspension of the Odyssey’s voyage did not address the second ship.
___
This version has corrected the date when the voyage was expected to end from 2030 to 2027.

title: Where the candidates in Maine stand on healthcare
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: Where the candidates for office in Maine stand on healthcare
Maine's Total Coverage asked viewers what issues they are most interested in learning more about heading into the midterm election.
After hundreds of submissions, one of the top issues on voters' minds is healthcare. Maine's Total Coverage asked all the candidates for governor and congressional office about their stance on the issue.
Gubernatorial candidates
The race for the Blaine House began with two crowded primaries. Republican Bobby Charles was the winner of a seven-way ranked-choice voting primary and Democrat Hannah Pingree won in a five-way race. Independent Rick Bennett, who left the Republican Party last year, was the only independent who got the required number of signatures to get on the November ballot.
Earlier this month, almost 1,000 Mainers lost healthcare because of changes that went into effect on Oct. 1.
The next legislature will have to decide if the state will allocate more funding for MaineCare when lawmakers return to the state capitol in January. There will also be a new governor in the Blaine House.
Bennett said MaineCare reimbursements to healthcare providers need to be paid.
"As governor, the top thing I can do is pay our providers on time and fairly," he said. "The state has a very healthy cash balance. But we've seen time and again that we've delayed payments to providers, hospitals, behavioral health centers."
Charles also said that hospitals need to be reimbursed on time, but said it's not just healthcare facilities the next governor will need to be looking at.
"People now have to travel, because of [Gov. Janet] Mills and Pingree, an hour in some places to get a prescription," Charles said. "What if you need an immediate antibiotic because your child, you know, stepped on a rusty nail? You need access quickly."
Pingree campaigned over the summer with moms in Lincoln County who were trying to keep the labor and delivery unit there open. She said she wants to bring experts to the table to try to keep these facilities open, but also support other rural facilities.
"I think we're going to have to use things like the Rural Health Transformation Grant to ensure that we keep rural hospitals open," she said. "A lot of these folks are worried about not being able to recruit the workforce they need, and so focusing on programs like how we recruit rural primary care doctors and how we provide the incentives to ensure that people go to northern Maine and Washington County."
Senate candidates
The midterms are high stakes for both parties. Democrats are hoping to take the majority in Congress, heading into President Trump's final two years in office. Republicans, who hold the majority in both chambers, want to keep it.
The highly anticipated Senate race has been closely watched for months. Senator Susan Collins is seeking a historic sixth term in Washington. Democrat Troy Jackson replaced Graham Platner as the party's nominee in late July after Platner dropped out following a sexual assault allegation he denies. Jackson, seeking to help Democrats flip the U.S. Senate.
Collins said rural hospitals are near and dear to her as an Aroostook County native. She says she's used her position in the Senate to secure funding for most Maine hospitals.
Collins also said she did not vote in favor of the final passage of the one big beautiful bill because of cuts to Medicaid.
"I grew up in rural Maine, so I know how important our rural hospitals are, and there is no one who has secured more funding for rural hospitals than I have," Collins said. "That included putting a $50 billion rural health care fund into the big beautiful bill. Even though I voted against the bill, I was responsible for that funding."
Jackson, the Senate hopeful, says hospitals are at risk of closing down because of the One Big Beautiful Bill, criticizing Collins for taking a vote to advance the bill.
Jackson says his top priority if elected is securing Medicare for all. He says he will try to make sure everyone nationwide has affordable, quality health care.
“People keep this narrative that we can't do Medicare for all because it won't be as good of a system, that it’s a problem,” Jackson said. “I haven't had a Canadian tell me that they don't like their healthcare system, and I've worked with them for years.”
Candidates for Congress in Maine's 1st District
The race for Maine's 1st Congressional District is a rematch. Army veteran Ron Russell is challenging Congresswoman Chellie Pingree for her seat in Washington.
Pingree has held the congressional seat for nearly two decades. Russell ran against her back in 2024, but lost.
Russell secured the Republican nomination back in June, defeating newcomer Joshua James Pietrowicz.
Russell says hospital closures and lack of access are tragic, adding health care needs to be fixed. The Army veteran says he wants to commercialize medicine and avoid Medicare for all, calling it socialist.
“The worst of it is the government does not do anything well when it runs a particular program, and we have so many examples of that happening,” Russell said. “To put them in charge of everyone's healthcare, I think, would be disastrous.”
On the contrary, Congresswoman Pingree says she's a big supporter of Medicare for all. She also warns of funding cuts to Medicaid starting in the new year, pointing to people losing coverage.
"People, I think, including a lot of doctors, would rather be under a single payer kind of system," Pingree said. "We could do that by slowly dropping the age, you know, working it out over time."
Candidates for Congress in Maine's 2nd District
The race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District began when Congressman Jared Golden still planned to run for his seat.
Former two-time Republican Governor Paul LePage got in the race to take on Golden. LePage was uncontested in the primary. Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap filed paperwork to primary Golden.
Golden eventually left the race, and three other candidates got in to primary Dunlap.
Dunlap won in a four-way ranked-choice voting primary in June to take on LePage.
He said he hears from people worried about being able to afford healthcare all the time and supports a universal system.
"It's really to negotiate a price for a knee replacement, and then you pay the full freight. And that way they get paid," Dunlap said. "They know what they're going to get paid in advance and they can plan for that. And the patient doesn't have to worry about a co-pay or, or, you know, paying 40% of a $100,000 bill that they don't have."
LePage said universal healthcare would be problematic and would lead to more closures of facilities.
"Free is expensive to somebody," he said. "And guess who's paying this one? The hospitals. That's one issue. MaineCare is a big issue. The other major issue hospitals are having is recruitment and retention of physicians, of medical personnel. You can't get specialists to move to Presque Isle, Maine, or Calais, Maine, and that's a major issue."

title: Jay-Z chooses himself to perform at 2027 Super Bowl halftime show
text:
Jay-Z chooses himself to perform at 2027 Super Bowl halftime show
Rapper Jay-Z has selected himself to perform the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show.
Video above: Pastor describes how he officiated a wedding during Bad Bunny's halftime show
The "99 Problems" rapper has been in charge of choosing the halftime performer for each Super Bowl since 2019 after his entertainment company, Roc Nation, signed a partnership deal with the NFL.
Miley Cyrus and Justin Bieber were previously considered front-runners to perform at Super Bowl LXI.
The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation officially announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his “Jay-Z 30” concerts over the weekend. The run began with three shows at Yankee Stadium in New York, continued in London and ended in Southern California.
Jay-Z’s Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league’s entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, “If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now.”
Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.
Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog includes the albums “Reasonable Doubt,” “The Blueprint” and “The Black Album,” and hit songs such as “Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem),” “99 Problems” and “Empire State of Mind,” his collaboration with Alicia Keys.
His 1996 debut, “Reasonable Doubt,” was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame last year.
Jay-Z's career has extended into music publishing, artist management and sports. He co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.
Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.
Bad Bunny performed at last season's Super Bowl in February. His songs had sharp gains across streaming charts, playlists and music discovery platforms in the hours following the show.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Here’s how to keep your pet safe during Halloween
text:
(CNN) - Halloween brings hazards for pets, according to the American Veterinary Medical Association, which says emergency animal clinics see a spike in cases during October.
Dr. Jen Quammen, president of the American Veterinary Medical Association, said the biggest hazard may not be candy.
“I think sometimes the biggest Halloween hazard isn’t exactly the candy; it might be the front door. The doors opening over and over. There are strangers in costumes,” Quammen said.
Keep pets secure
Quammen said pet owners should make sure pets are microchipped and have ID tags and collars in case they slip out an open door. She said owners should also consider this before taking pets trick-or-treating.
“I would always encourage folks to know their pet,” Quammen said. “I think I would just consider that the pet gets a vote in this conversation.”
Candy dangers
Unattended candy can be dangerous for pets. Chocolate is not the only concern. Treats made with a sugar-free sweetener called xylitol can also be harmful.
Quammen said pet owners should contact their veterinarian or poison control if pets get into either type of candy.
“And the other thing about candy is our pets don’t really usually unwrap it. They also eat the wrappers, and those can be an issue as well if they get swallowed,” Quammen said.
Costume tips
Best Friends Animal Society recommends the following when dressing up pets:
- Keep costumes comfortable
- Don’t put pets in anything that restricts movement
- Make sure pets can see clearly
- Remove any small parts that can be chewed off and swallowed
- If pets show signs of distress, opt for a festive bandana instead
Quammen said preparation is the top tip for a safe Halloween: “A little bit of preparation can really keep Halloween super fun and keep your pet out of the ER.”

title: Maine Senate race is close, while Pingree and Charles are tied in governor’s race, poll finds
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Democrat Troy Jackson holds a 49% to 47% lead over Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins among likely voters in Maine, while Democrat Hannah Pingree and Republican Bobby Charles are tied at 44% support in the governor’s race, according to a new Marist poll released Tuesday.
Independent Rick Bennett received 6% in the governor’s contest, and 6% of likely voters were undecided.
The likely voter results are within the poll’s margin of error of 6.6 percentage points.
While Charles and Pingree are tied among likely voters, among registered voters, Pingree has an 11-point advantage.
In the Senate race polling, Jackson leads Collins by 9 percentage points among registered voters, up from a 4-point lead earlier in October.
Despite Jackson’s narrow lead among likely voters, 58% said they expect Collins to be reelected. In the governor’s race, 63% said they believe Pingree will win.
Democrats also lead on the generic congressional ballot. Among likely voters, 52% said they would support the Democratic candidate in their district, compared with 47% for the Republican. The Democratic advantage was 11 points among registered voters, according to the poll.
Views of President Donald Trump and personal finances were also featured in the survey. Forty-two percent of likely voters said Trump was not much of a factor in their congressional vote, while 41% said their vote was against him and 16% said it was in support of him. Overall, 42% of likely voters approved of Trump’s job performance and 58% disapproved.
Asked about their household finances, 46% of likely voters said they had gotten worse over the past year, 15% said they had improved, and 38% said they had stayed about the same.
The Marist Poll surveyed 1,449 Maine registered voters from Oct. 22-25, 2026, using live telephone interviews, text messages and online surveys. The margin of error was 4.1 percentage points for registered voters and 6.6 percentage points for likely voters.

title: Mark Kelly brings 2028 buzz to Maine rally for Troy Jackson
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
FREEPORT, Maine — U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona told supporters of Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson on Tuesday that next week’s election “is not going to be about Donald Trump,” then built most of his pitch around stopping the president.
Kelly, a retired Navy fighter pilot often named among Democratic contenders for president in 2028, spoke to a packed crowd at Maine Beer Co. a week before Jackson faces Republican Sen. Susan Collins. He argued Republicans in office had failed to check a “wannabe dictator” in Trump, though he never named the centrist Maine senator.
The two-day swing makes Kelly the latest national Democrat to campaign for Jackson, following Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. Collins has gone the other way, campaigning last week with former independent Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia in a bid to keep a toss-up race that could decide Senate control focused on Maine and her independence.
Kelly hit on core themes of Jackson’s campaign. He said a Democratic majority would force the wealthy to pay higher taxes, repeal health care cuts, end corruption by Trump and his family, regulate artificial intelligence and stop stock trading by lawmakers.
“The election here in a week is not going to be about Donald Trump,” he said. “It’s about you. You know better than anybody what it’s like to worry about your kids, your future, your health care, your budget, your freedom.”
The health care pledge goes to the most disputed vote of the race. Last year, Collins voted to bring Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act to the Senate floor. She was then one of three Republicans who voted against its final passage, citing an estimated $5.9 billion hit to Maine’s Medicaid program over a decade.
Jackson and his allies have focused on the first vote in debates and a volley of ads. Collins said she let the bill advance so she could write a $50 billion rural health care fund into it. Maine is set to receive $190 million from that fund in its first year, including some used to bail out a struggling Bangor-area provider. Democrats say the fund doesn’t come close to covering the cuts.
The visiting Democrats have each pitched Jackson to a different audience. Sanders has called him a working-class voice “taking on the oligarchs” and fighting for Medicare for All. Ocasio-Cortez appealed to Maine women last week over health care cuts and Collins’ vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
In Lewiston last week, Manchin called Collins “the soul of the Senate,” pointed to their bipartisan work on infrastructure and health care and said “she’s not a Trump senator.”
Kelly told the crowd that elections are “not rocket science” and urged supporters to knock on doors and make calls. He said that despite Jackson’s steep spending gap with Republicans in the Maine race, “the odds are on our side.”
Polls of the toss-up race have shown Jackson slightly ahead but Collins running well among older and swing-voting Mainers. Jackson needs some former Collins voters to cross over, and the crowd included at least one.
Vanessa Smith, a 56-year-old artist from Raymond, said she once voted for Collins but is now “completely appalled at the state of our country.” She cited what she called attacks under Trump on religious freedom and minorities.
“Mr. Trump is a bit of a bully and disgusting if things don’t go his way,” she said. “I’m just looking for a more happy, joyous, honest America.”
Jackson, addressing the crowd standing on a bar, said Americans know “the country is broken” under the second Trump administration, but turnout is crucial. Kelly and Jackson also urged votes for Hannah Pingree, the Democratic nominee for governor, and her mother, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree of the 1st District.
The younger Pingree told the crowd many had already voted early but said Democrats still had to reach voters turned off by negative ads.
“Every single day matters,” she said.

title: Sen. King endorses Dunlap in Maine's 2nd Congressional District race
text:
Sen. Angus King endorses Matt Dunlap in Maine's 2nd Congressional District race
State Auditor Matt Dunlap, the Democratic candidate for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat, has received an endorsement from independent U.S. Sen. Angus King.
Dunlap's campaign shared a video on Tuesday in which King, who caucuses with Democrats in the Senate, mentioned Dunlap's advocacy for Maine's sportsmen and sportswomen.
King and Dunlap have worked together in state government. Dunlap represented the 121st District in the Maine House from December 1996 to January 2005, a tenure that coincided with most of King's two terms as Maine governor (January 1995 to January 2003).
"When you serve as governor, you get to know a lot of legislators. But one I particularly remember is Matt Dunlap. Why? Because he was tough and smart, and a strong advocate for his district," King said in the video shared by the Dunlap campaign. "He has also been a great advocate for the sportsmen and women of Maine. ... He can represent the whole 2nd District in Congress, and that's what we need. I think Matt will be a great member of Congress and I look forward to working with him."
"When Senator King was governor, we worked closely on major issues for Maine sportsmen. I'm honored to have his support and endorsement, and look forward to the chance to work with him to lower prices if elected," Dunlap said in a statement. "Mainers are frustrated by high prices on home heating oil, groceries, hockey sticks, and pretty much everything else under the sun. We've got to end the war that's keeping gas prices high and end the tariff taxes that are keeping grocery prices high."
Dunlap and his Republican opponent, former Gov. Paul LePage, are looking to succeed Congressman Jared Golden, who announced in November 2025 that he would not seek reelection to the U.S. House of Representatives.
House Speaker Mike Johnson recently visited Maine to campaign for LePage, who was elected to two terms as Maine governor (2011-19) after serving seven years as mayor of Waterville (2004-11).

title: Serial killer Ted Bundy linked to another 1970s homicide
text:
PARK CITY, Utah (AP) — DNA connects serial killer Ted Bundy to the death of another Utah teenager, authorities announced Tuesday, exactly 52 years after her body was discovered in the woods by a hunter.
Bundy has been dead since 1989, but the tally of his confirmed victims continues to grow due to advances in DNA testing. He killed at least 30 women and girls in multiple states in the 1970s, and many more escaped or survived with injuries.
Investigators are satisfied that Bundy was responsible for killing 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith in 1974, a death that had long been listed as a cold case, Summit County Attorney Margaret Olson said at a news conference.
They were able to close the case by making crucial connections with DNA found on Smith and Laura Aime, another Bundy victim whose case was resolved last April in Utah County. Bundy’s DNA was on file in Florida, where he was convicted and ultimately executed.
Besides that evidence, Smith’s death showed hallmarks of Bundy’s “pattern, motive, means and opportunity,” Olson said.
Decades-old evidence was key to the case
Utah’s state crime lab got new technology in 2023 that extracts DNA from samples even if they are small, degraded from age or contain DNA from multiple people.
“This case demonstrates the importance of preserving evidence,” said Salt Lake County Sheriff Rosie Rivera, whose department has also investigated homicides linked to Bundy.
“We have to solve these cases to the best of our ability,” she said, explaining the importance of tapping science, even so many years later. “Nobody is just going to walk away and just blame everything on Ted Bundy, even though many cases have been that way. Here in the state of Utah, we take it very seriously.”
Smith’s relatives were contacted about the findings but declined to attend the news conference and declined to speak to reporters, the Summit County Sheriff’s Office said. Her parents are deceased.
Smith’s father was police chief in Midvale, south of Salt Lake City. She was at a pizza parlor and a restaurant before she disappeared on Oct. 18, 1974, The Salt Lake Tribune reported at the time. Nine days later, her body was found in Summit County.
“With every case closure, may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out,” Utah County Sgt. Mike Reynolds said.
Bundy investigations are not finished
Bundy was executed by electric chair in Florida in 1989 after being convicted of three murders, including the killing of two women at the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University.
He gave a series of confessions in his final days, including to some crimes that were previously unknown to police. Not all of those cases have been confirmed.
Besides Florida and Utah, authorities said Bundy had victims in Colorado, Idaho and Washington state. They said they’re especially working to solve the 1974 death of 16-year-old Nancy Wilcox of Utah.
Solving the Smith homicide “does not close the book on Ted Bundy,” said Det. Ben Pender of the Salt Lake County Sheriff’s Office, which has the Wilcox investigation. “Information kind of leads to Ted Bundy but again we’re not for certain on Nancy Wilcox. We’re going to continue to work that case.”

title: AP sources: Federal agents search Beverly Hills mansion in investigation of ex-Rep. Eric Swalwell
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal law enforcement agents searched a Beverly Hills home early Tuesday as part of an investigation into Eric Swalwell, who resigned from Congress amid a wave of sexual misconduct allegations, a law enforcement official and two people familiar with the investigation told The Associated Press.
Agents searched the home of wealthy developer and Swalwell donor Stephen Cloobeck, where the ex-Congressman spent time before resigning from office in April, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation.
Swalwell, D-Calif., has denied criminal wrongdoing.
Messages seeking comment were left for Swalwell’s lawyer and for a lawyer who represented Cloobeck in another matter.
Cloobeck, the founder of the Diamond Resorts International timeshare company, told the New York Post in April that he cut ties with Swalwell as accusations against him mounted.
“I am no longer associated with a man that takes advantage of women,” Cloobeck told the newspaper. “I support women’s rights.”
Tuesday’s search is the latest escalation in the federal investigation of Swalwell — one of several probes begun after a woman came forward with allegations that he sexually assaulted her twice, including when she worked for him.
The San Francisco Chronicle, followed by CNN, first reported the allegations. CNN also reported that three other women alleged various kinds of sexual misconduct by Swalwell, including sending them unsolicited explicit messages or nude photos.
Asked about the search at Cloobeck’s address, FBI spokesperson Lourdes Arocho said: “Early this morning the FBI conducted an operation in the Los Angeles region related to an ongoing criminal investigation. We have no further comment.”
In August, federal agents seized electronic devices from Swalwell at the San Francisco airport and searched his Washington home.
Swalwell, an Iowa native, was elected in 2012 and represented a House district east of San Francisco. He launched a presidential run in April 2019 but ended it a few months later after failing to catch on with voters.
The seven-term lawmaker had been seen as one of the leading candidates in California’s gubernatorial race before dropping out after the allegations surfaced.
The office of Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg has said it is also investigating Swalwell after a former staffer told CNN and the Chronicle that Swalwell raped her at a hotel while he was in New York City for a charity gala in 2024.
In a statement, Bragg’s office encouraged “survivors and anyone with knowledge of these allegations to contact our Special Victims Division.”
Los Angeles prosecutors were also said to be weighing charges.
Swalwell was one of Republican President Donald Trump’s top Democratic antagonists in Congress. He was a prominent member of the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees during Trump’s first term and served as one of several Democratic prosecutors for Trump’s second impeachment after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.
Swalwell was removed from the Intelligence Committee by then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., in 2023 based on Swalwell’s contact with a suspected Chinese spy, Christine Fang.
Fang was reported to have come into contact with Swalwell’s campaign as he was first running for Congress in 2012 and to have participated in fundraising for his 2014 campaign.
Federal investigators alerted Swalwell to their concerns and briefed Congress about Fang in 2015, at which point Swalwell says he cut off contact with her. He was not accused of wrongdoing and a House Ethics Committee investigation that was opened in 2021 closed two years later without any action.

title: Breast cancer survivor faced hair loss during chemotherapy and reclaimed her identity
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (Aging Untold) — Hair loss is often the most common and visually striking side effect of chemotherapy, especially for women.
Lisa Steinhauser, a breast cancer survivor, said she lost her hair and part of her identity during chemotherapy. Now she inspires patients to find strength during their own battle.
Hair as part of her identity
“So when I knew I was going to lose my hair, that was pretty hard because I had a lot of it,” she said.
Hair has always been Steinhauser’s craft, artistry and expression.
Diagnosis and treatment
In December 2021, Steinhauser went in for a routine mammogram, and she said doctors found a spot they were concerned about.
“I really was not expecting it to be anything at all, but it was,” she said.
She was diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive, invasive type of breast cancer. Treatment is intense.
“It was not fun,” Steinhauser said. “I went every three weeks.”
Shaving her head
Steinhauser’s hair began to fall out during treatment.
“Being in the shower and washing my hair and having those handfuls come out,” she said.
Steinhauser decided to shave off the remaining hair.
“I decided that that was not going to define me,” she said.
Her grandchildren shaved her hair off for her.
“I am going to still be that fun, spunky person that I’ve always been,” she said. “I just rocked the bald.”
Message to others
Steinhauser said she is now clear of the disease, “NED — no evidence of disease.”
She said she wants people to know there is hope.
“No matter what’s happening, you don’t know. There is going to be hope and just keep fighting,” she said.
Dr. Rhea Rogers shares her story
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said she identifies with Steinhauser. The same thing happened to her during cancer treatment. When Rogers’ hair was falling out, she shaved her head.
“I identify with her. You know, just depends on how people view their identity. And, you know, some people are just tied to their hair and all that, but really it’s your heart,” Rogers said.
Rogers shared a similar message of hope that Steinhauser did.
“Just don’t give up,” she said.

title: Elizabeth Warren, Troy Jackson hold town hall in Waterville
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) -Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren held a town hall Monday afternoon at the Playhouse at Waterville Station.
They took questions on education, student loan debt, artificial intelligence and the economy.
Warren and Jackson said Republicans must lose control of the Senate for Democrats to challenge President Trump’s agenda.
Warren said a change in the Senate majority would determine whether Democrats could use their constitutional authority to investigate the administration and influence what legislation reaches the floor.
“We are here to deliver on our constitutional responsibilities,” Warren said. “I truly believe that is the kind of difference. That is the difference between the path America takes that just says handed over to a handful of rich insiders or pull this government back to make it work for the rest of us who are trying to make it work for ourselves, our families, our neighbors.”
Jackson echoed Warren’s criticism of Republicans in Congress, saying they have failed to hold Trump accountable on issues including health care, tariffs and government spending.

title: Suspect arrested in Instagram sextortion investigation 3 years after teen’s death
text:
Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988 to connect with the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.
STREETSBORO, Ohio. (WOIO/Gray News) - An arrest has been made in connection to the death of an Ohio high school student who died by suicide after becoming a victim of sextortion.
James, 17, died Nov. 19, 2022, after being targeted on Instagram.
Streetsboro police, along with the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force and Homeland Security Investigations, said a man in his early 20s is now in jail.
In 2022, the 17-year-old thought he was exchanging photos with a 19-year-old girl who reached out to him on Instagram.
James’ mother Tamia says after the encounter, in less than 24 hours her son received more than 200 text messages and dozens of calls from what she believes was a group of people saying they were going to ruin his life if he didn’t pay them thousands of dollars.
Through the investigation, they tracked the IP address and were eventually able to connect him to the crime.
Police said the suspect will stand trial and could face more than 10 years in prison.

title: 'That '70s show' actor Danny Masterson's rape convictions upheld by California appeals court
text:
California appeals court upholds 'That '70s show' actor Danny Masterson's rape convictions
A California appeals court on Tuesday upheld actor Danny Masterson's convictions and long prison sentence for raping two women at his home in 2003.
In an 89-page ruling, the three-judge panel unanimously found that the “That '70s Show” actor had failed to demonstrate that the lower court made errors that would warrant granting him a new trial. The panel also rejected a petition filed by Masterson that claimed ineffective assistance of counsel.
Masterson's first trial ended with a deadlocked jury in 2022, but at his retrial the following year, he was convicted of raping two women. He was sentenced to 30 years to life in prison.
His attorneys said in an emailed statement Tuesday that they would seek review at the California Supreme Court.
Among the claims that the court rejected were that Masterson's convictions violated the 10-year statute of limitations for forcible rape, as the statute does not apply where there are multiple victims; that the trial court excluded evidence in his favor; and that the trial court exhibited bias against his religion.
Masterson is a prominent member of the Church of Scientology, and his accusers are former members who said they grew disillusioned with the institution after they were assaulted. They said church officials told them what had happened to them was not rape, and that its policies prevented them from going to police. The church vehemently denied having any such policy.
Masterson, 50, has been serving his sentence at the California Men’s Colony in San Luis Obispo. He will not be eligible for parole for more than 20 years.
Masterson starred with Ashton Kutcher, Mila Kunis and Topher Grace in “That ’70s Show” from 1998 until 2006. He had reunited with Kutcher on the 2016 Netflix comedy “The Ranch,” but he was written off the show after the allegations surfaced.

title: The Latest: Israelis vote in a tense election seen as a referendum on Netanyahu
text:
No clear winner in Israeli election, exit polls suggest, as Netanyahu’s fate hangs in the balance
Israelis appear to have handed a rebuke to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in national elections, exit polls indicated. But what’s next is uncertain as there's no clear winner and no obvious path to a governing majority.
The election was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving prime minister.
Related video: Are electronic voting machines "flipping" votes? Experts say no.
His party, Likud, appears to have gotten the most votes. But the exit polls by major Israeli TV stations indicate that support for his religious-national coalition dropped significantly.
The exit polls suggested his opponents could secure a solid majority in the next parliament. But whether those disparate parties, including Arab-led parties, can form a government is uncertain, and will likely take weeks of haggling.
Here are some key points to know as the polls closed in Israel on Tuesday night.
Exit polls suggest no clear winner, complex power-jockeying ahead
In Israel, voters choose not individuals but parties. Since no party has ever captured a parliamentary majority on its own, party leaders must agree to come together in a governing coalition.
Exit polls indicated that Netanyahu's bloc of supporters won about 50-51 seats in parliament, while the bloc led by his main challenger, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, won 51-52. That would leave each side well below the 61 seats needed to form a government with a parliamentary majority.
The exit polls suggested that Arab-led parties captured the remaining 18 seats.
Arab parties could play a key role in next coalition
Official results aren't expected until later this week.
If the Arab parties do as well as the exit polls suggest, they could play a decisive role in selecting Israel's next prime minister.
Both Netanyahu and some of Eisenkot's partners have said they will not join a government with Arab parties. Eisenkot has signaled he is ready to work with them under certain conditions, but this could risk alienating some of his partners.
Like all surveys, exit polls are subject to potential error and final results, expected in the coming days, may vary from the exit polls.
Campaigns gave short shrift to Palestinian issues
Israelis are largely opposed to a Palestinian state. No major candidate advocated a return to the long-moribund peace process.
Even Mansour Abbas, a Palestinian Arab politician who leads Ra’am, the first Arab-led party to join a governing coalition in 2021, centered his campaign on concerns about crime in Arab communities.
As exit polls were shown on a screen at an Abbas election night event in Sakhnin, an Arab city in northern Israel, supporters of the small Arab-led party Ra’am erupted in celebration.
Enduring impact of Oct. 7 attacks reflected in election
This election was held against the background of the enduring trauma of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, when militants killed 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and abducted 251 others, and the ensuing wars in Gaza and beyond.
The deadliest day in Israel’s history featured prominently in the campaigns. Israelis have focused on the security failures surrounding Oct. 7 and the enormous burden on their society, rather than on the humanitarian situation in war-devastated Gaza.
Netanyahu has rejected an investigation into Oct. 7 and blamed the army for the failures that day. His supporters say he led the country back from that difficult day and scored important achievements in wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Netanyahu’s opponents said he should be held accountable for the security failures that occurred on his watch and have demanded a commission of inquiry, and their strong showing signaled in the exit polls indicates the lingering deep divide.
Among Jewish Israelis, there’s a religious divide over military service
The country has also been deeply divided by exemptions from military service granted to ultra-Orthodox males. These exemptions are especially contentious after three years of wars.
Netanyahu’s governing coalitions have long relied on ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties that have demanded these exemptions remain in place.
Netanyahu’s rival Eisenkot — who lost his son and two nephews to combat in Gaza — has vowed to end the de facto exemptions. He repeated that promise speaking to supporters in Tel Aviv early on Wednesday morning.
The exit polls, which also indicated a drop in support for ultra-Orthodox parties, signaled voter unhappiness over these exemptions.
High voter turnout throughout the day and across the country
The final update from Israel’s Central Elections Committee put voter turnout at 77.7% of eligible voters by the time polls closed.
That’s the highest turnout at that hour since 1999, and just over seven percentage points higher than at the same time in the previous election in 2022. The elections saw high turnout all day, reflecting the high stakes of the election.

title: US woman convicted of getting Islamic State training after becoming teen bride to a fighter
text:
US woman convicted of getting Islamic State training after becoming teen bride to a fighter
A New York woman whose father took her to Syria as a teenager and arranged her marriage to an Islamic State fighter was convicted Tuesday.
US woman convicted of getting Islamic State training after becoming teen bride to a fighter
A New York woman whose father took her to Syria as a teenager and arranged her marriage to an Islamic State fighter was convicted Tuesday.
A New York woman whose father took her to Syria as a teenager and arranged her marriage to an Islamic State fighter was convicted Tuesday of receiving weapons training from the militant group.
Prosecutors said Halima Salman, a U.S. citizen, pledged loyalty to the extremist group and willingly participated in its activities. Jurors were shown a video of her holding an assault rifle, a photo of her with the group's flag, and loving text messages she sent her husband.
Brooklyn-based U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said in a statement that the verdict held Salman “accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization.”
Related video above: Federal officials in Minnesota announce arrest of teen allegedly planning terror attack
The defense sought to portray Salman, now 27, as a teenager who was unwittingly trapped in Syria's civil war, first by her father and later by an extremist husband whose orders she had to follow.
“You try to leave, it is death,” Salman testified. She said she refused to be “married off” at age 18 and repeatedly tried to get a divorce.
Salman, her mother and even her defense attorneys wept after hearing the verdict. Still in tears, Salman and her mother later hugged each other across the railing between the audience and the courtroom well.
Jurors, who began deliberating Thursday, had repeatedly indicated Monday that they were struggling to reach a unanimous decision. The members declined to comment as they left court after the verdict.
Salman's lawyers also declined to comment. They are asking the judge to set aside the verdict and acquit her, as federal law allows if a judge finds the evidence presented at a trial doesn't legally support a conviction. Such requests are often made but rarely granted.
Salman’s conviction carries the potential for up to 10 years in prison. Sentencing currently is set for Feb. 2.
The Islamic State group, which the U.S. government designates as a terror group, seized large parts of Iraq and Syria in 2014 and declared the territory to be a caliphate. Despite its defeat in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria two years later, the group still has sleeper cells that carry out deadly attacks in both countries.
Born in Brooklyn, Salman was 17 when her father took the family on what she thought was a trip to visit relatives in Turkey in 2017. Instead, the van crossed into Syria, where masked gunmen surrounded them. Salman said she was frightened and confused, and had no idea where her father was taking them.
“I do blame my father for a lot of things that happened,” she testified.
She said she spent three months in housing run by the Islamic State group before reuniting with her family. They moved twice because their homes were hit by airstrikes.
On the first day of her marriage, Salman recalled, her husband told her: “Get up, stupid wife, it’s time for you to be a wife.”
She spent much of the marriage doing domestic labor for her husband and mother-in-law. Her father died after being injured in an airstrike in 2018.
Prosecutors insisted Salman was dishonest and had more agency in Syria than she claimed. They got her to concede during cross-examination that she once sent a religious song about Osama bin Laden to her husband. Prosecutors also disputed Salman’s account of a poor marriage, citing two loving text messages she sent to her husband.
“The evidence shows that the defendant received military training from a violent, brutal, terrorist organization — an organization that is responsible for attacks across the world,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda Shami told the jury in a closing argument last week.
Salman's husband took a video of her holding an assault rifle, which prosecutors said she had been trained to use. When she testified, Salman said she was only complying with her husband’s request to carry the rifle.
She recalled that her last year of marriage was particularly harrowing, as constant bombings sometimes forced them to live in the streets, where she recalled seeing “dead bodies everywhere.”
The couple eventually fled with other refugees in a truck, where she told her husband they were going to separate, and Salman testified that she never saw him again.
She was detained in Baghouz, Syria, in 2019 by forces opposed to the Islamic State group. She was arrested by U.S. authorities when she returned to New York in 2024.

title: Magician delivers message about perseverance to Van Buren students
text:
VAN BUREN, Maine (WAGM) - A magician brought a message about perseverance and believing in yourself to students in Van Buren on Friday.
Caleb Morgan said his interest in magic started with a gift from his mother when he was 8 years old. He now combines that interest with his background in education.
“And so my background as a magician, combining those two to show them something they’ve never seen before and then get them to realize they can keep pushing through and achieve whatever goals they’re trying to achieve,” Morgan said.
Message tied to his own experiences
Morgan said his message about overcoming obstacles comes from more than his work as a magician. He said his experiences growing up helped shape the message he shares with students.
“So my message partially being about fear is because fear was something that kind of racked my life as a student. I came from kind of a broken home and I’m very blessed to be pulled out of that situation, but I had to learn how to overcome that fear and really attack my goals and that’s what we’re showing students,” Morgan said.
Performing on national television
Morgan has faced fear himself, including by performing on national television. He said the experience pushed him to trust his preparation and keep moving forward, even when he was not sure what would happen.
“When I got the opportunity to be on national TV on the Penn and Teller: Fool Us show, I was terrified that something was going to go wrong in front of over a million people. But I just had to keep going like we’re telling the students today, just keep going and you’ll see your goals,” Morgan said.
Failure as part of the process
Morgan said failure does not have to mean giving up for students who are afraid to try something new. He said it can be part of learning how to succeed.
“What I would say if somebody’s trying to pursue a dream but they’re worried they’re going to fail is that you are going to fail. And that’s okay. Failure is a part of the process. So you just have to keep going and realize just because I failed at something doesn’t mean I’m a failure. It means I can get back up, dust myself off, and go again,” Morgan said.
Morgan said he hopes students leave with the confidence to pursue their goals, regardless of the challenges they face.

title: More young adults are living with their parents, according to survey
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - The high cost of living and a challenging job market are keeping more young Americans at home.
Nearly half of adults under the age of 30 now live with a parent, according to the Federal Reserve’s latest survey of household economics and decision-making.
That’s up 6 percentage points since 2022 and 12 percentage points since 2019.
The cost of housing, high mortgage rates and everyday expenses like groceries and gas are the main reasons behind the trend.
According to AAA data, U.S. diesel futures have also surged above $5 a gallon, for the first time since April 2022.
Americans are feeling a little better about the economy after consumer confidence hit a 12-year low in September.
According to the Conference Board’s latest report, the consumer confidence index jumped 7.5 points in October to 91.7.
However, confidence remains well below recent historical levels, and persistent inflation continues to squeeze household budgets.

title: Angus King endorses Matt Dunlap in his race against Paul LePage
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Independent U.S. Sen. Angus King on Tuesday endorsed Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap in his 2nd Congressional District bid against Republican former Gov. Paul LePage.
King, who caucuses with Democrats and is now in his third Senate term, made an endorsement video crediting Dunlap, a former state representative from Old Town, for his strong advocacy for his district while their time in Augusta overlapped.
“When you serve as governor, you get to know a lot of legislators, but one I particularly remember is Matt Dunlap … because he was tough and smart,” the former independent governor said.
The announcement marked a boost for Dunlap from one of the few political voices left on the sidelines in the 2026 election. Forecasters see the Democrat as an underdog but still competitive in the district won three times by President Donald Trump. Centrist Rep. Jared Golden is leaving his seat after four terms.
The latest polls from Democratic pollsters and the University of New Hampshire showed Dunlap with a narrow lead, but LePage is still narrowly favored to take the seat back for Republicans, according to Decision Desk HQ, the Bangor Daily News’ election results partner.
In his endorsement video, King appealed to the 2nd District’s gun owners, referencing Dunlap’s time leading the Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine.
“He also has been a strong advocate for the sportsmen and women of Maine,” King said. “In fact, he has a hunting license. He can represent the whole Second District. I think Matt will be a great member of Congress, and I look forward to working with him.”
On top of endorsements from President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who said the race was in the “top five” nationwide, the National Rifle Association endorsed LePage this summer. The sportsman’s alliance issued A+ ratings to both without endorsing.
The endorsement from King, now in his third term on Capitol Hill, is a rare one. He endorsed Democratic nominee for governor Hannah Pingree, the former Maine House speaker, in September. He backed Republican Sen. Susan Collins for reelection in 2014.
But their relationship has been frostier of late. He did not pick a side in Collins’ 2020 race with Democrat Sara Gideon, but his wife, Mary Herman, appeared in a Gideon ad. King’s 2024 challenger, Demi Kouzounas, said she chose to run after getting a supportive call from Collins, who did not formally endorse in the race.
Asked about the lack of an endorsement in Collins’ race with Democrat Troy Jackson, King’s office said Monday it’s in keeping with his longstanding practice to not weigh in on races that involve his colleagues across the political spectrum. The senator believes it could undercut progress with whomever wins come next year if he was previously pushing against them.
Dunlap in a statement said he worked closely with King on sportsmen issues in particular. He said he was honored to have the senator’s support and looked forward to working with him in Washington if elected, particularly on lowering prices.
“Mainers are frustrated by high prices on home heating oil, groceries, hockey sticks, and pretty much everything else under the sun,” he said. “We’ve got to end the war that’s keeping gas prices high and end the tariff taxes that are keeping grocery prices high.”

title: Maine needs to rein in government spending
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sen. Scott Cyrway represents Senate District 16, comprising Albion, Oakland, Fairfield, Waterville and Winslow. He serves as the Senate Republican lead on the Legislature’s Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee.
I grew up on a farm and started my working life in agriculture. There was always something that needed money, but that did not mean you could afford it all. You had to decide what came first and what could wait. I believe state government should handle taxpayers’ money with that same care.
Maine’s latest budget forecast shows why that matters. The Maine Bureau of the Budget projects a $1.085 billion General Fund gap for the 2028-29 budget cycle. It also projects a separate Highway Fund gap of $256.7 million. Together, that means expected spending is roughly $1.3 billion more than expected revenue.
Those numbers may change, but they tell us we have a problem to address. The next governor and Legislature will have to bring spending and revenue into balance. We should start by looking at what the state spends and what it can afford.
Democrats have controlled the governor’s office and the Legislature for eight years. They wrote the budgets and decided how to pay for them. They are responsible for those decisions and should explain why the state faces another large gap after raising taxes and fees.
Republicans warned that spending was growing too fast. Yet the legislative majority continued to approve more spending and ask Maine people to pay more. Those tax and fee increases have not kept us from facing another round of difficult budget decisions.
The current General Fund budget exceeds $12 billion. This year’s supplemental budget also took nearly $300 million from the Budget Stabilization Fund, the state’s emergency reserve. Before asking taxpayers for more, lawmakers need to explain where that money is going and whether it is being used well.
Earlier this year, I raised concerns about funding for agricultural and forestry programs. Those programs were not adequately funded in the budget, while lawmakers considered borrowing money to pay for them. I introduced an amendment to fund them directly through the supplemental budget.
I support our farmers and loggers. I also believe we should make room for those needs in the budget before asking taxpayers to take on debt and pay interest. With a budget this large, lawmakers should be willing to choose which spending comes first.
We need to take the same close look at MaineCare. The program has needed more than half a billion dollars in additional funding over the last two years. We need clear answers about why costs are rising and whether payments are being made properly.
Independent audits would help us get those answers. People who depend on MaineCare need a program they can count on, and taxpayers need to know their money is being spent properly. Both deserve better than repeated requests to cover another shortfall.
Audits alone will not close the gap. We also need to review programs, change those that are not working and stop spending money on things we cannot afford. Departments should explain what they spend, what people receive in return and how they plan to control costs.
I will oppose new taxes or fees to keep paying for spending the state cannot sustain. Maine families already have bills to pay. They should not have to keep finding more money because lawmakers will not make hard choices.
The next budget needs to put necessary services first and keep spending within what Maine can afford. That will mean saying no to some requests and changing how some programs operate. Making those decisions is part of our job, and we owe it to taxpayers to do it.
