title: Rep. Pingree talks federal support, sustainability with Maine fiber farmers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON, Maine (WABI) — Maine Congresswoman Chellie Pingree met with farmers in Knox County to address the growing hurdles facing local fiber producers and discuss the future of the state’s textile industry.
During a visit to Meadowcroft Farm, owner Nanne Kennedy highlighted how a lack of infrastructure and cuts to federal grant programs complicate the post-production process.
“Trying to turn your commodity into a saleable product — we don’t have a lot of infrastructure manufacturing options, certainly not locally,” Kennedy said. “Everything I do is within a five-hour radius. That’s really important to me.”
Kennedy pointed out the economic and energy disparities between natural fibers and fossil-fuel-based synthetics, noting how local natural fiber growers lack comparable support.
“[It is] much cheaper to take something soft and fluffy to make something soft and fluffy, but we don’t have the support to do that,” said Kennedy.
Following a tour of Meadowcroft Farm, a roundtable took place with area farmers to discuss additions to a draft of the Farm to Fabric Act.
The proposed legislation aims to expand federal agriculture funding, including both food and fiber production. The roundtable follows Pingree’s introduction of the Textile Waste Reduction Act last month.
“This administration has cut back on a lot of the programs that are important to farmers, so it’s good to see where those cuts are hurting farmers,” Pingree said.
Roundtable discussions centered on high entry costs for new producers, utilization of waste wool, and the broader environmental toll of synthetic textiles.
“70% of our clothing is made from fossil fuels, polyesters, and synthetics,” Pingree said. “Not only does it add a lot of questions for what people are wearing, but it ends up in our waste stream. There’s a lot of fast fashion now, and clothing is thrown away very quickly.”
Pingree emphasized that boosting domestic fiber processing creates both economic opportunities for growers and sustainable alternatives for consumers.
“We want to support more clothing that is sustainable, lasts longer, but also gives more opportunities to our American farmers — whether it’s cotton, linen, flax, or wool,” Pingree said. “And wool is a product that we make a lot of in Maine, so we want to support that.”

title: InvestigateTV+: Giving people their voice back
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A deadly disease takes a Vermont man’s ability to speak until technology gives him a new voice. InvestigateTV+ explores a partnership using artificial intelligence to improve patients’ lives.
Plus, after a disability payment error puts a father’s home in jeopardy, we examine how the issue was resolved and tips to help if you’re falling behind on payments.
Giving ALS patients their voice back
ALS, often called Lou Gehrig’s disease, is a cruel illness. There is no cure, it’s always fatal, and Vermont has the highest rate per capita in the country with around 27 people living with it now in the state.
To help those losing independence and their, a nonprofit is working to restore the ability to communicate with loved ones and doctors.
A disability payment error
Henry Adams almost lost his house after a disability payment error caused a mortgage trial payment to bounce, kicking him out of a loan program that he entered while trying to take care of his wife through her cancer battle.
Falling behind on mortgage payments, Henry Adams enrolled in an FHA loan modification program through U.S. Bank. The program paused the mortgage for several months, then required three consecutive on-time trial payments to qualify for final approval of the loan modification.
Affirmations & exercise
Research from the National Library of Medicine shows more than 30% of the world’s population suffers from chronic pain.
That’s 2.4 billion people who might feel hope after hearing Allyn Minton’s story.
The Nashville-based licensed physical therapist has been pain-free for a full year, thanks to a breakthrough she says has changed her mind.
Intergeneration duo creating cards
Riley Haughey sits at her kitchen table with a tackle box of tools, drawing her newest critter with markers.
The 11-year-old fifth grader creates colorful animal drawings she calls Riley’s Critters. Each critter ends up on a greeting card.
“This is like top notch printing I feel like,” Riley said.
The printer is 85-year-old Tony Klain.

title: Raising school-aged grandkids: how to handle homework and school in a digital age
text:
(Aging Untold) — For some older adults, this chapter of life was supposed to mean retirement. Instead, they are raising school-age kids again, navigating online portals, teacher apps and school meetings that look nothing like the school they remember.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing how older caregivers can manage the digital side of modern schooling — and why their experience still matters.
“You’re not probably the most confused”
When the day-to-day of supporting a child’s education starts to feel overwhelming, older adults should know they are not alone.
“I think it might be important to know that you may be the oldest member in the PTA, but you’re not probably the most confused,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said. “There are many younger parents that are still trying to learn to navigate the online portals and the tablets that their kids have, not having textbooks.”
Cradduck pointed out that school itself has changed for everyone, not just older caregivers.
“School isn’t what it once was, and math doesn’t math anymore. There’s this new math thing,” Cradduck said. “There’s a lot of things that have changed. But for our older community that are managing and helping school-age children, there’s a lot of help for you.”
Cradduck said the most important step is figuring out what resources are available. (See below for resources.)
“I think that’s the most important thing to find out is what resources are available to you, and how can you tap into it and make sure that you find a tutor that can help with some of the things you’re not maybe the best at,” Cradduck said.
Leaning on what’s worked before
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said older adults should remember that they have been through this before.
“It might look different, but the younger parents — they haven’t helped kids go all the way through school,” Ambrose said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke encouraged older caregivers to draw on past experience and to ask for help.
“Think of all the difficult things you’ve been through, and look at what did you do then that made that successful,” O’Rourke said. “So one of them is asking for help. I love the library — the librarians will help with the Wi-Fi and the app and give you other resources.”
O’Rourke also pointed to school staff as a resource.
“If you go into the school counselors, the guidance counselors, the parent liaison people, just stop and then know your weak spot,” O’Rourke said.
Board-certified physician Dr. Rhea Rogers recommended that older adults also talk to the teachers so they understand the situation.
Consistency matters more than perfection
She noted the added weight older caregivers carry when they take on this role.
“Because as an older adult who thought they were going to retire, you’re doing two jobs,” Rogers said. “You’re still trying to navigate your own health, your own decisions and things that pertain to you. Then you’ve got to also look at this other person.”
Rogers said children don’t need a perfect caregiver — they need steadiness.
“Really, for a child, they just need consistency. You don’t have to be a perfect caregiver. They just need to know that they matter,” Rogers said.
Reframing the role as mentorship
Cradduck said older caregivers often have more time and presence to offer than younger, working parents.
“If you’re at that retirement age and you’ve retired, most of the moms and dads are both working, and you do have that better quality time to be able to sew into the children,” Cradduck said. “Mentorship is what we’re to do when we age.”
O’Rourke added that older caregivers don’t need new credentials to contribute.
“What do you need to learn? You’ve already learned. You’ve already gotten educated. So use that — use what you have,” O’Rourke said. “Think about the other parents being exposed to you, like your generation, and what you can give just by being there.”
Ambrose agreed that the impact goes beyond the day-to-day logistics.
“Just that love, consistency, willingness — and these kids will remember that. That’s quite a legacy,” she said. “Grandparents have a big impact on kids anyway.”
Ambrose closed with a reframe for caregivers who feel stretched thin.
“It might sometimes seem like an interruption, but it could be disguised as your greatest legacy,” Ambrose said.
Resources
- Librarians
- Teachers
- Tutors
- School counselors
- Parent liaisons
Key takeaways
- You’re not alone in feeling lost. Many younger parents are also struggling to navigate school portals, apps and tablets — it’s not just an older-generation problem.
- Find out what resources exist first. Libraries, tutors, school counselors and parent liaisons can help fill in the gaps older caregivers may feel around technology or coursework.
- Draw on what already worked. Past experience solving hard problems — including asking for help — is a skill older caregivers already have.
- Reframe the role as mentorship. Older caregivers often have more unhurried time than dual-working parents, and that presence is valuable on its own.
- This can be a legacy, not just a burden. What feels like an interruption to retirement may be remembered by kids as a defining relationship.

title: Tours offer Halloween enthusiasts visits to former psychiatric hospital and funeral home
text:
WESTLAND, Mich. (AP) — It’s not enough these days for some Halloween enthusiasts to be scared by actors dressed up in spooky getups at makeshift haunted houses: They want the “real” thing.
At a former psychiatric hospital in suburban Detroit and a former funeral home in Toledo, Ohio, visitors can embark on guided paranormal investigations or even set out on their own with rented equipment, such as a handheld electromagnetic field (EMF) meter.
“Guests that come here on our paranormal tours, they get touched, they get grabbed, handprints on clothing, whistled at,” said Justin Cox, founder of Michighost Paranormal, which leads paranormal investigation tours of the Eloise Asylum attraction’s upper floors, where patients were treated. “Everything that you can imagine has happened here, and we’ve heard it all.”
The facility began as a 19th-century poorhouse and operated under various names as it expanded into a complex with dozens of buildings. By the late 1920s, it was one of the nation’s largest public health facilities.
“In the paranormal field, we believe that trauma leaves energy, which creates hauntings. This place had a lot of tragedy, a lot of trauma, so we believe it’s super haunted,” Cox said.
Family members of patients and others with ties to Eloise have argued against offering for-profit amusement at a site where vulnerable people suffered.
The upper floors of the asylum feel alive
Most of the complex’s buildings were razed in the 1980s, but a five-story, red-brick structure that came to be known as the Kay Beard Building still stands and is home to Eloise Asylum.
It’s there that Cox and his team lead guests on tours of the upper floors, including a room with a bathtub used in hydrotherapy sessions. It’s not uncommon for guests to get in the tub.
And if you “think you can handle the night here, we offer that as well,” Cox said about their overnight stays.
Eloise Asylum haunted attraction’s lead makeup artist and scare actor, Lexi Carter, has gone on the paranormal investigation tour. She said the upper floors feel alive.
Paranormal investigators use spirit boxes to scan radio frequencies for sounds they believe could be messages from spirits. They also use EMF readers to measure changes in electromagnetic fields that some associate with paranormal activity.
Carter said it was wild “watching those go off.”
“Oh, my God. It blew me away. I was like, ‘No way. This is real,'” she said. “‘This is so cool.'”
Tours include visits to embalming and autopsy rooms
Fifty miles (80 kilometers) south sits the former Urbanski Funeral Home, which hosted thousands of viewings and services from 1926 until its sale last year. Now called Mortuary Manor, the 60,000-square-foot (5,580-square-meter) building serves as a funeral home museum and much more.
Paranormal investigators can check out the embalming and autopsy rooms, as well as a morgue where it is standard practice for guests to take pictures of themselves lying on a slab that juts out from a basement wall.
Mortuary Manor will host its first wedding in November on Friday the 13th, of course. And guests who pony up $200 can spend the night in a five-room suite. Operations manager Cory Leibenguth lives in a neighboring upstairs apartment.
He said the building has modern amenities like indoor plumbing, heating, air conditioning and Wi-Fi. That “sets us apart from some of these other abandoned locations that don’t have any of that. And then there’s not a lot of funeral homes you can go investigate, either.”
Mortuary Manor visitors can also watch a horror movie projected onto the wall of the main sitting room while surrounded by caskets.
It’s all part of elevating the Halloween experience for hard-core fright fans.
“In today’s world where everybody is so stressed out … Halloween is a time that everybody can just relax and just enjoy the time with their friends and their family, maybe get scared along the way,” Cox said.

title: Brewer bans syringe services
text:
Brewer, a city with no syringe services, has banned the needle exchange programs from opening in the city.
The Brewer City Council voted unanimously Tuesday to ban the programs from physical and mobile locations in the city by changing the city’s land use ordinance. The vote followed comments from 10 Brewer residents who said they didn’t want needle exchange programs or discarded syringes in the city.
Councilors did not discuss the code change before or after voting.
Syringe programs and exchanges are contentious in Bangor, where a six-month ban was proposed earlier this year, but this is the first time a ban has been passed in a neighboring community. The programs, which have been proven to lower disease exchange rates, allow people to exchange used needles for sterilized ones.
Residents at Bangor City Council meetings have said the programs are causing needles to be discarded in open community areas, causing safety issues.
Brewer residents who spoke at the meeting said the biggest fear they had about a syringe program opening in the city was that Brewer would not be as safe or clean as it currently is. Many speakers drew comparisons to Bangor, saying that the Queen City did not have the level of public safety Brewer did, at least partially because of the needle exchange programs.
“Bangor is having huge problems, and Brewer’s already experiencing problems. I think a service location could attract increased foot traffic, loitering and public drug use. We’ve seen it all in Bangor,” Kathleen Kramer, a City Council candidate, said during public comment.
Residents did not point out any specific problems Bangor was facing, other than saying that discarded needles were being found in public spaces.
Public Safety Direct Chris Martin said needles, and an encampment, have been found in Brewer this year.
Brewer Public Works employees cleaned an encampment under a railroad overpass tunnel last week, Martin said. Brewer police officers filled a gallon bucket with used needles found at the site, Martin said.
Other syringes have been found along Wilson Street and the Brewer Riverwalk, Martin said.
Every time needles have been found, one of the city’s departments has been dispatched to clean them up. Having a syringe exchange program in the city could create more waste and put more strain on city services, Martin said.
The waste would not only take up city staff time, but could put “hazardous waste” in public spaces, Martin said.
“Their presence creates legitimate concerns for residents, family, children, pets and the municipal employees responsible for maintaining our community,” Martin said.
Brewer is one of multiple Greater Bangor communities that said needles were being found along the Penobscot River. One syringe found along the Brewer Riverwalk earlier this year poked a 3-year-old child.
The ban does not make it impossible for residents to buy sterilized needles.
Brewer police officers checked at every pharmacy in the city Monday to ensure needles can be bought, Martin said. Some locations were selling 100 syringes for roughly 14 cents each, which Martin said should make them affordable.
“How can people not afford to get a clean syringe?” Martin said at the meeting. “Because you’re paying $110, $120 a gram for the drugs, and if you’ve got a loaded syringe, you probably have about $20 worth of dope in that loaded syringe.”
Although Martin has spent roughly a year and a half working toward getting this ordinance changed, he said the exchange programs now banned in the city have positive effects, but aren’t being held accountable.
“Maine’s [syringe service program] framework is intended to advance public health, including reducing the transmission of infectious diseases. Those objectives deserve recognition. At the same time, the framework must also provide meaningful accountability for syringe distribution, collection, safe disposal, and impacts on surrounding communities,” Martin said.

title: Truck stolen by escaped Tennessee inmate is found abandoned in Illinois, authorities say
text:
Truck stolen by escaped Tennessee inmate is found abandoned in Illinois, authorities say
An escaped Tennessee inmate convicted of murdering a co-worker stole a truck from a nearby farm and apparently made it to southern Illinois before abandoning it, authorities said Tuesday.
Jacob Morley, who was serving a life sentence for killing a co-worker four years ago, was found to be missing from the Northwest Correctional Complex late on Sunday.
The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation released surveillance video from the farm, which is near Tiptonville and about a 2-mile walk through fields from the prison, showing Morley open the truck's unlocked driver's side door and drive off at about 1 a.m. Monday.
Firefighters in Hornbeak, about 12 miles east of the farm, said on social media that investigators confirmed their cameras captured footage of the truck driving by their station about 15 minutes later.
Related video above: Maine man who drove over his wife with a truck dies a year into murder sentence
The truck was found abandoned Tuesday in Marion, Illinois, about 120 miles north of the prison and roughly 90 miles southeast of St. Louis.
Marion Police Chief David Fitts said the truck appeared to have be left neatly parked behind a shopping center at 4 a.m. Tuesday, according to surveillance video. Someone reported it to police at about 11 a.m. Tennessee investigators said Morley still hasn’t been found.
“He has vanished,” Fitts said. “We haven't had any reports of stolen vehicles or anything else suspicious around here.”
Authorities said Morley, 28, slipped through a fence in his prison clothes, but they haven't released additional details, including whether they think anyone helped him.
Morley is white, 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 240 pounds. He has brown hair and green eyes.
Morley is serving a life sentence for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s home after he had been missing for a few weeks. The two lived in Carter County, in eastern Tennessee.
Along with first-degree murder, Morley was convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest. When Morley saw deputies at his home, he led officers on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said.
Prison officials have offered a reward of up to $2,500 for Morley's arrest. They said law enforcement agencies have searched buildings and other structures near the prison, which is about 90 miles north of Memphis in flat farmland near a bend in the Mississippi River.
The escape is the latest of a string of problems in Tennessee prisons.
Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada announced his resignation after less than three years on the job following the failed execution of Christa Pike on Sept. 30.
Pike remained alive after being given two massive doses of pentobarbital, the drug Tennessee uses in lethal injections. Her lawyers said it appears the IVs in her arms were never properly inserted into her veins or blew out quickly, keeping the drugs from entering her bloodstream. The state is conducting an independent investigation into its death penalty system and what happened to Pike.
Meanwhile, several violent attacks between inmates and by employees have been reported in recent years at Northwest Correctional Complex. A grand jury in July returned dozens of indictments for five inmate killings and other violent acts.
In a hearing before a Tennessee Senate subcommittee last month, prison officials said they had 470 open jobs among their 6,000-person workforce. They also warned a 2022 law requiring inmates to serve more of their sentences was increasing prison populations and could lead to overcrowding.

title: Maine Chief Medical Examiner Released New Information About 3 Deaths in Roque Bluffs Pond
text:
More information has been released about a Maine grandmother and her two grandchildren found deceased in a vehicle in Roque Bluffs.
More Details Released About the Deaths of a Grandmother and 2 Grandchildren
The bodies of 61-year-old Sharon Bukulmez of Mount Desert, 5-year-old Kinsley Grubb, and 3-year-old Sawyer Grubb, both of Bar Harbor, were discovered in Sharon's vehicle on Sunday morning, September 20th.
After an examination by the Chief Medical Examiner, it was determined that all three people died of drowning and their deaths were accidental.
Maine Woman and 2 Grandkids Found Deceased in a Submerged Vehicle in Roque Bluffs
The trio was last seen at approximately 8:30 pm on Saturday, September 19th, 2026, leaving a family function in Jonesboro.
They were traveling to Machias and were reported missing after failing to arrive.
As law enforcement launched a search, the Bar Harbor Police Department obtained location information from Bukulmez's cellphone, which indicated a location in the water near the boat ramp at the end of Schoppee Road in Roque Bluffs.
Maine State Police were notified, and troopers responded to the scene, including divers who located the vehicle at approximately 7 am., submerged in Pond Cove
Two Women in 2013 Also Died in a Submerged Vehicle in Roque Bluffs, Maine
In 2013, two women died when their vehicle became submerged in Roque Bluffs.
Local authorities took Amy Stiner of Machias and Melissa Moyer of Pennsylvania, who was five months pregnant, to their vehicle after they got lost while hiking.
After a short time, the women called to say they had driven their vehicle into the water, and then the phone went dead.
According to CBS News, the women had driven into the ocean after traveling the wrong way down a road.
They were found deceased in their submerged vehicle sometime later.
We'll update this story as more details become available.

title: Hunter Biden laptop issue resurfaces as judge scolds prosecutors over case against ex-FBI officials
text:
Hunter Biden laptop issue resurfaces as judge scolds prosecutors over case against ex-FBI officials
A federal judge on Tuesday scolded the Justice Department for its unorthodox handling of a criminal case against two former FBI officials accused of making false statements to Congress about their knowledge of a laptop the Justice Department says belonged to Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden.
U.S. Magistrate Zia Faruqui struck from the record an amended criminal complaint filed overnight by the Justice Department that added a new obstruction charge against the two former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, after concluding that it was improperly submitted. Such charging documents require sign-off from a judge that probable cause exists to believe a crime was committed by a defendant, but this complaint was filed straight to the docket with no court approval.
The ruling came during a dramatic, hours-long hearing in which an agent who worked the case conceded under defense lawyer questioning that the investigation into the former officials was launched after a July speech from President Donald Trump on election interference and that the inquiry was mandated by FBI Director Kash Patel. The Kansas City-based agent, Bryan Witt, said he had been assigned to the investigation and regarded it as a “huge distraction” from other casework.
“I had concerns that this would be political,” he said.
The developments were setbacks for a Justice Department that has employed unusual maneuvers during a series of splashy and politically charged investigative actions before next week’s midterm elections. Newly unsealed documents in a separate case, for instance, revealed that prosecutors are attempting to again prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, an outspoken Trump critic, in a manner that Comey's lawyers say is legally invalid.
Faruqui said he had never before seen a prosecutor file an unsigned criminal complaint, describing it as “inappropriate” given defendants’ presumption of innocence. He ticked off several atypical aspects of the case, including the decision to file charges via criminal complaint, which the judge noted is more often used when the government has disrupted an active crime or needs to take a defendant into custody immediately because of a potential danger to society.
“Everything is a little sideshow on top of a sideshow,” the judge said, saying prosecutors appeared to be throwing “gas” on defendants’ assertions that there is nothing typical about this case.
The case has political undertones
Witt testified under questioning from Margaret Donovan, a lawyer for Floris, that Patel had mandated the investigation immediately after a Trump primetime address in July in which he amplified debunked theories about the 2020 election he lost and elevated his yearslong push to raise doubts about the legitimacy of U.S. elections.
Among the grievances the White House raised at the time was a disputed FBI memo about a potential effort by China to influence the election through manufactured fraudulent drivers' licenses.
Floris, then a senior official based at FBI headquarters, has long been a magnet for congressional Republican criticism for her role in having ordered the document to be recalled because of concerns about the reliability of the memo.
Trump and some allies have cited that memo to support their narrative that China sought to interfere on behalf of his Democratic challenger, Joe Biden, during the 2020 election — even though that perspective was the minority viewpoint within the U.S. intelligence community.
Witt said the basis for the investigation was Trump administration concerns that the FBI had suppressed in the heat of the 2020 campaign information that could have been harmful to the Bidens. He said he understood that the timing of the investigation and the direct ties to the White House would be regarded as inherently political.
Even before that testimony was elicited, Mary Dohrmann, another lawyer for Floris, broached what she called the “elephant in the room,” saying "evidence is mounting that this prosecution is about some political football.”
Defense lawyers disputed the crux of the allegations
The case, announced Friday, accuses the former officials of falsely playing down their knowledge about a laptop the Justice Department says Hunter Biden abandoned at a computer repair shop in 2019.
Prosecutors say they claimed to have no independent insight into the FBI's recovery of the laptop while being interviewed in 2023 in a separate congressional Republican investigation into the Biden family. In reality, according to the criminal complaint, the two participated in numerous discussions about the laptop in their capacity as leaders of the since-disbanded FBI Foreign Influence Task Force that was set up to monitor foreign influence.
The Justice Department contends that the defendants' professed lack of knowledge misled the congressional investigation and impeded their efforts to scrutinize Biden family business dealings.
But Ronald Safer, a lawyer for Benavides, challenged that assertion during the hearing Tuesday as he questioned an FBI agent who investigated the case against the former officials. He also pointed out that Benavides, in 2023, was asked about events that occurred several years earlier, casting doubt on whether anything his client said was intentionally false.
“What evidence have you uncovered that in September of 2023, Mr. Benavides remembered the correct answers, in your view, to the questions asked about Hunter Biden but gave knowingly incorrect answers?” Safer asked.
It is a very intricate saga
The prosecution, a rare Justice Department criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race after the New York Post revealed the existence of a laptop it said had been dropped off by the younger Biden at a Delaware computer repair shop about a year earlier.
The Post said it had obtained a hard drive of the laptop from Rudy Giuliani, a close ally of President Donald Trump, and reported on some of the contents of the computer, including emails that appeared to show some of Hunter Biden's foreign business dealings.
The curious circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian involvement, particularly when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community had assessed that Moscow was attempting to undermine the candidacy of Democratic nominee Joe Biden, who went on to defeat Trump in 2020, and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens.
But Trump's then-national intelligence director, John Ratcliffe, quickly sought to quell speculation about the laptop's provenance by saying there were no signs it had anything to do with Russian actors. The FBI said it had nothing to add to Ratcliffe's statement and investigated the younger Biden on gun and tax charges that later resulted in felony convictions. President Joe Biden pardoned his son in late 2024.

title: Stillwater River Trail Of Lights Returns To Orono. Free Holiday Tradition Draws Thousands To The Area
text:
Folks In Orono Are Gearing Up For Their 7th Season Of Lights And Whimsy As They Set Up The Stillwater River Trail Of Lights
While it may still be a few months away, folks in Orono are prepping for this year's holiday season early...
...Because it takes a lot of time and effort to put something this dazzling together!
If you haven't yet made the trek out 92 Bennoch Road, off of Brownie's Park (or Brownie's Beach as the locals call it) along the Stillwater River to check out the Stillwater River Trail of Lights, you should add it to your Christmas bucket-list for this year.
Read More: Halloween Events In Orono Bring Trick-or-treating And Adult Fun
What started as a fun little light display 7 years ago has turned into a must-see holiday tradition for many, with picture-worthy pop ups along the way.
According to one of the event organizers, Anthony Francis, while they may not know the exact total number of who makes it through the path each year, it's well into the thousands.
"It is difficult to estimate attendance because the Trail is free and does not require tickets, but we received roughly 200,000 requests for directions last season. It has become a tradition for many families, with multiple generations returning year after year. We have celebrated engagements, weddings, and countless family milestones along the Trail. The event also brings meaningful activity to Orono and its local businesses during the holiday season."
As is the case in many situations, something this fabulous doesn't just come together overnight. It takes many hands many months to make this magic happen.
"We are incredibly grateful for the support of our sponsors, including presenting sponsor University Credit Union, Harvest Moon for Santa’s List, Harvey RV & Marine for the main photo area, the Town of Orono and Sunbelt Rentals for lift support, Sargent’s Construction, and Northeast Paving."
"Several sponsors have also provided volunteers who have worked alongside our small core group. The exact number of people involved changes throughout the setup as different businesses and volunteers join us."
Set up for this year's display started at the beginning of September.
"The trail is growing, the lights are going up, and Christmas will be here before we know it!"
With help from a team of community members, volunteers and local businesses, this year's display is slowly starting to take shape.
"We are happy to share that all of the overhead lighting is complete, including new sweeping teal sections and red-and-green zigzag lights. We are now working on the trees, displays, photo areas, and pathway markers."
"Section five is officially in the air! A big shout-out to Andrew and Ryan from A.M. Smart construction LLC for braving the rain and spending the past two days hanging lights with me. We added a canopy of red-and-green zigzag lights over the trail. We may be working backward through the sections, but the Stillwater River Trail of Lights is moving forward and reaching new heights!"
"The Trail is located largely on private property and is generously shared with the public. We ask visitors to stay on the marked trail, respect all signs and barriers, keep pets leashed, and clean up after them. Visitors should also dress for winter conditions and be prepared for snow, ice, mud, and uneven ground."
Organizers say they should be up and running and ready for visitors for the first weekend in December.
"The Stillwater River Trail of Lights will open as planned on Friday, December 4, 2026. The lights will be on nightly from 4 to 9 p.m., weather permitting."
And they say they've got something really fun in the works for one special night this season.
"December 18 will be an especially exciting night. The Town of Orono is planning to coordinate fireworks with the lights, and the trolley will also return."
There is a small parking lot area at the beginning of the trail that can fill up quickly. It's recommended that you pay attention to the traffic signs and watch out for pedestrians walking to and from the area when you do make it into the lot. And at times, it can get a little slick, so appropriate footwear is important.

title: How a disability payment error nearly cost this father his home
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
STONE MOUNTAIN, Ga. (InvestigateTV) — Henry Adams almost lost his house after a disability payment error caused a mortgage trial payment to bounce, kicking him out of a loan program that he entered while trying to take care of his wife through her cancer battle.
Adams held up a photo of his wife, Ellen Adams, and their daughter, Caitlin, on the back deck of their family home.
“This is us in the house when we first got here. Caitlin was so little,” he said. “She’s 21 now.”
The Adams lived in the home for almost two decades, during years in which the couple served as pastors in Atlanta. Their homeless outreach ministry was even featured in a local media outlet.
Adams said he survived cancer years earlier but was left with a disability. “I went through chemo and they was able to kill it but it left me with a disability,” he said, describing swelling in his leg.
He receives disability income from his previous employer, AT&T, and later found at-home work in cybersecurity, but Ellen Adams’ condition worsened after a years-long battle with breast cancer.
“I needed to watch her,” Adams said, describing frequent medical appointments and treatment.
As health costs mounted, Adams said finances tightened. “Things were getting really tough.”
Falling behind on mortgage payments, Henry Adams enrolled in an FHA loan modification program through U.S. Bank. The program paused the mortgage for several months, then required three consecutive on-time trial payments to qualify for final approval of the loan modification.
Hours after Adams admitted his wife to the ICU for what would be the final time on April 1, he received a call from the bank.
The scheduled disability direct deposit did not arrive, the mortgage payment bounced, and he was immediately removed from the loan program trial.
“If you miss that trial payment, there is no do-over,” Adams said. “There is no grace.”
AT&T’s disability provider later acknowledged what it described as a “systemic issue” that delayed payments by two days. Recipients were notified in a letter dated April 8.
“They had a glitch in their system,” Adams said. “They didn’t alert the thousands of people that they were servicing, so none of us knew that our direct deposits would not be in the bank by the last day of the month.”
Adams said the bank told him he owed nearly $10,000 in back payments and faced immediate foreclosure. “I never thought I’d be facing foreclosure in the house we celebrated in,” he said. “We had our baby here. We grew her up here.”
When asked who should be held accountable, Adams said, “I hate to blame the long-term disability department... but now we could possibly be homeless.”
Hours before Atlanta News First Investigates met with Henry Adams, Ellen Adams died at the hospital.
In a recording from one of Ellen Adams’ sermons before she became ill, she preached: “Jesus got it... He said, ‘I got something for you, I’m not gonna leave you like this, I’m not gonna leave you in sorrow.’”
They were words that would ring true for her husband years later.
We contacted AT&T, U.S. Bank and the federal loan provider to inquire about the payment delay and whether an exception was possible.
Within days, U.S. Bank worked out a policy exemption with the FHA program allowing Adams to restart the trial period in July.
“When [the bank] called me, I could not stop crying on the phone,” Adams said. “God rescued us and he used you all to rescue us, to help us, to support us.
“You came and sat down, and you listened, when a lot of other people wouldn’t listen,” Adams, who is now focusing on raising money for his wife’s funeral in early June, said.
Tips to avoid issues from payment delays:
- Try to pay loan payments early when possible
- Check your bank accounts often to verify deposits arrived
- Ask your lender about hardship exceptions if payment issues occur
“The client’s mortgage is an FHA loan, and we are required to follow their servicing guidelines which include a number of automatic actions if the requirements are not met,” a US Bank spokesperson said. “That said, we value our longstanding relationship with Mr. Adams and acknowledge the unfortunate circumstances involved, and we have worked directly with the FHA on a policy exception and will be in a position to offer reinstatement to the trial plan.”
“This unfortunate incident stemmed from a system error at our third-party benefits provider and affected a small number of people who receive long-term disability payments from us,” said an AT&T spokesperson. “We have apologized to Mr. Adams for the disruption this caused and are working closely with our vendor to help ensure this does not happen again.”
We reached out to AT&T’s third-party benefits provider for comment and did not receive a response.

title: Trump to hold Ohio rally amid governor’s race controversy
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With Election Day less than a week away, President Donald Trump is expected to make another campaign stop in Ohio, where two competitive races could have national implications.
The president’s visit comes amid growing controversy surrounding Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, whose campaign released a viral attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton.
In the ad, Acton’s mother calls her daughter a liar. But critics say the video omits crucial context about Acton’s childhood.
Acton and her brother were removed from their mother’s custody after Acton’s stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her.
“My opponent has chosen to exploit my childhood to save his struggling campaign, but it’s not going to work,” Acton said at recent campaign even.
The ad has drawn criticism from lawmakers in both parties, including Ohio’s Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.
Ramaswamy, however, has defended the commercial, and argued that voters should be allowed to hear the allegations and make their own decisions.
Trump has also repeatedly defended the ad.
“The mother said terrible things,” Trump said. “Anybody seeing that would say, no way I’m voting for her.”
The controversy comes as recent polls suggests Democrats are gaining ground in Ohio, raising the stakes for Trump’s latest campaign stop.
Wednesday’s scheduled rally in Chillicothe will also put a spotlight on Ohio’s competitive U.S. Senate race, which could help determine which party controls the chamber.
Republican Sen. Jon Husted is facing a challenge from Democrat Sherrod Brown, who is attempting a political comeback after losing his Senate seat in 2024 to Trump-endorsed candidate Sen. Bernie Moreno.

title: Lewiston house known for Halloween spirit lights up again after owner comes back from ‘dark place’
text:
LEWISTON — Every fall, the Jellison family’s Sabattus Street house becomes Maniac Manor, making it a go-to place for lovers of extravagant Halloween decorations.
That seemed in jeopardy earlier this year for the first time since 2017 due to a fire last December caused by some outdoor Christmas decorations and then debilitating knee pain that resulted in major surgery just three weeks ago for Aaron Jellison.
“I was in a really dark place this summer (because of the pain),” said Jellison, who found himself weeks behind in creating his usual scary scene. The setting includes three 12-foot skeletons, a giant grim reaper, rooftop creatures and eerie lighting among more than $100,000 worth of decorations.
Ultimately, Jellison didn’t want to let anyone down, or miss out on the friendly competition that occurs with nearby homeowners who also go a little overboard at Halloween. So with some encouragement from his wife, Shannon, he and his family got going.
“I want to give back to the community, especially the doctors who helped fix my knee,” Jellison said. “I can’t give anybody any monetary gain, but I can at least give them my time and open my home to everyone.”
A FIRE, THEN SURGERY
The problems started just before last Christmas, for which, Jellison admits, he also goes a little overboard. On Dec. 20, Jellison was putting up neon lights around the home and replacing old electrical cords as he went.
But he missed one, he says, and the apparently overloaded cord started a fire that night. No one was hurt, but it damaged a corner of the home and made Jellison even more aware of the need to decorate safely.
Then came the debilitating knee pain.
Jellison was diagnosed in 2001 with bone cancer in his knee. Over the past few years, he said, the pain increased to the point he had trouble walking, eventually keeping him from working in the months preceding surgery.
Three weeks ago he had his knee replaced, putting him on the road to recovery.
“The pain I was in was unimaginable,” he said. “When I got my surgery, I got my life back.”
After surgery, Jellison spent a total of 11 days on and off in the hospital. It didn’t look like the decorations would get up.
Typically, the Jellisons start Halloween preparations in August by bringing their decorations outside. By mid-September, they have everything in place outdoors and inflated, and by the first week of October they’re able to transform the inside of their home too.
With his debilitating knee pain and then the surgery, it didn’t seem possible this year.
But Shannon’s encouragement helped him feel rejuvenated and carry on the tradition, he said. Since his surgery, Aaron and his five children turned their property into Maniac Manor.
“There was a lot of skepticism whether I was going to, whether I should,” said Jellison. “But I decided if I could do it, I’m going to do it. It was a depressing time for the family.”
And do it he did. His daughter Alexis Jennison said that after her father got his new knee, he did triple the work in one week than he did in three months last year.
“I’m not going to let my knee stop me from doing what I love,” said Jellison. “The community loves it, my family loves it, and it’s my favorite season.”
‘MAGIC IN THE AIR’
Jellison also got inspiration from other Halloween lovers in the area, including well-decorated homes on Farwell Street and East Avenue that annually draw a lot of onlookers.
“I call them my OGs, my original ghouls,” said Jellison. “We got some new contenders in the area, but you got to bow down to royalty.”
With their Halloween display up this year despite the odds, the Jellisons want to inspire, and give people something to enjoy.
“There’s magic in the air around this time of the year,” Jellison said. “A lot of people say autumn is their favorite time, but for me it’s more than that. You can’t burn up the Halloween spirit. It’s a hard thing to kill, even with a chain saw.”
Once Halloween is done, Aaron said he will train his sights on Christmas. Although the home had the fire last year, he said he’s upgraded the electrical around the home so this year all will be merry and bright.

title: Medicare open enrollment underway, deadline is Dec. 7
text:
Maine (WABI) - Medicare open enrollment is underway, and people covered by Medicare have until Dec. 7 to review their coverage for next year. Nearly 400,000 Mainers rely on Medicare.
Experts say people should review their coverage even if they are satisfied with their current plan. Premiums, out-of-pocket costs and covered services can change from year to year.
Medicare Part D plans cover prescription drugs picked up at the pharmacy. AARP says those plans can get complicated.
Leigh Purvis, prescription drug policy principal at the AARP Public Policy Institute, said enrollees can see changes in several areas.
“You can see changes in your deductible. You can see changes in your premium. There’s also an increase in the maximum out-of-pocket spending cap, which is now $2,400, so there are a lot of different things for you to take a look at, but what’s most important is that plan covers the drugs you need at a cost you can afford,” Purvis said.
AARP is available to help with questions about Medicare open enrollment. More information is available at aarp.org/medicare or medicare.gov.

title: The Exoneree Band: How a group of wrongfully convicted men found their voice through music
text:
(Aging Untold)— They don’t have the fame of The Beatles or the fortune of The Rolling Stones, but the members of The Exoneree band share something far more profound.
Now, as free men, they are using the power of music to heal, to tell their stories, and to build a brotherhood unlike any other.
The band was born out of the Innocence Network’s annual conference, a gathering that brings together wrongfully convicted people from across the country.
In 2011, this group of musically inclined exonerees found each other, and what started as a jam session quickly turned into something more.
“It turned into a really nice brotherhood of guys who were not only musicians but had went through the same thing of being wrongfully convicted,” one band member recalls.
Living in different parts of the country, they come together to create a sound that is both a celebration of their freedom and a testament to their resilience. Their music is a form of therapy, a way to process the unimaginable trauma of being stripped of their lives and liberty.
“For me, it’s kind of like a therapy thing,” says one member. “Getting to share my story through music.”
Each member carries the weight of a story that would break most people.
Ted Bradford and his bandmate Eddie Lowry were both wrongly convicted of rape.
“I just couldn’t believe that they were accusing me of this, something that I could never do,” Bradford says.
Donovan Allen was convicted of murdering his own mother, a crime that stole his youth and his freedom.
“My mother was killed exactly one week before my 19th birthday,” he shares. “And from the age of 19 to almost 35, I was inside.”
Collectively, they lost decades of their lives before DNA evidence finally cleared their names. While they are grateful for their freedom, the scars of their time in prison run deep.
“No one deserves to see the things that I’ve been forced to see,” says one member.
It’s a burden that could understandably make them want to leave the past behind. But instead, they choose to amplify their stories, to turn their pain into a powerful message of hope and resilience.
“It’s an emotional release for us, and it’s healing,” they say. “When we’re up on the stage, it’s a healing for us and for our community.”
Their setlist is a mix of cover songs, often with a twist to reflect their unique journey, and deeply personal original music.
Fellow exoneree Amanda Knox has joined them on stage for a special rendition of “I Will Survive,” a song that takes on a whole new meaning when sung by those who have truly overcome the impossible.
But it’s their original songs that carry the most weight.
One member wrote a song called “My Cell,” a raw and honest account of life in a small prison cell. He recalls listening to music on headphones in his cell, dreaming of being on stage.
“And it’s finally happening,” he says with a smile.
At a recent performance for a packed house of Innocence Network members, Ted Bradford debuted a new song, “Innocent Man.”
It’s a powerful and emotional plea for justice, with a chorus that cries out, “Lord, why don’t you shine your light on me? Reveal the truth and help them see, for you know the truth will set you free.”
The Exonerated may never achieve mainstream fame, but that’s not their goal.
They have found something far more valuable.
Brotherhood. Purpose. Voice.

title: Missing woman reportedly found alive in Mexico, but her family has doubts
text:
PHOENIX (KPHO/Gray News) — Mexican authorities said a missing Arizona woman was believed to have been found in Tijuana, but family members say they have doubts.
Shayna Feinman, 35, was reported missing in March 2024.
A Tijuana security force said Feinman was found on Oct. 23 after reports of a woman matching her description in an Encino neighborhood.
The security force said the woman was confirmed to be Feinman, but Yavapai County Sheriff’s Office officials initially said they couldn’t independently confirm her identity because of “insufficient evidence.”
Feinman’s sister Kara added that she did not recognize the person in Mexico and didn’t have hard evidence that the person was indeed her sister.
Kara said this wasn’t the first time Feinman was reported to have been spotted.
Feinman’s sister called these types of reports with little evidence from law enforcement agencies disheartening to the family.
Tijuana officials said they took the woman in question to a safe location to await contact with the Feinman family and U.S. authorities.
Details were not immediately shared about how Feinman may have ended up in Mexico.
Yavapai County Sheriff’s deputies said Feinman vanished without a trace on March 9, 2024, while walking to a friend’s house.
Two men were arrested in connection with her disappearance in 2024. Loved ones said they have been holding onto hope of her return.
The Yavapai County Sheriff’s Office updated its investigation, stating that the woman in Tijuana was indeed believed to not be the missing woman.

title: Canadian steamship torpedoed by Nazi U-boat discovered off MDI
text:
In mid-July, off the coast of Mount Desert Island, a group of volunteer divers made a historic discovery: the final resting place of a Canadian merchant ship torpedoed by a German U-boat that had just landed two Nazi spies in Maine.
The self-funded group of New England divers had spent the past seven years searching for the sunken World War II vessel, whose demise made headlines after the U-boat that sank it dropped off two Nazi saboteurs near Hancock.
For decades, the SS Cornwallis’ final resting place sparked curiosity among locals, fishermen and history buffs. It’s also one of roughly 150 shipwrecks that have been documented in the waters around MDI.
Now, roughly 82 years after the fatal sinking — which killed 43 crew members, most of whom were Canadian — nine divers hope to provide long overdue closure to the victims’ surviving family members.
Danny Allan, a member of the Nomad Exploration dive team, who discovered the ship, described the exhilaration of finding a vessel they’d spent years trying to track down.
“You’re the first person to touch this wreck in literally 80 years: no one has seen it [or] touched it,” Allan said. “[It’s] also a sobering realization that there’s 43 people on this wreck, and it’s their final resting place. It’s a weird yin and yang between so excited but very sobering that it’s essentially a grave for these sailors.”
Just days before the Canadian ship loaded with sugar and molasses was wrecked by the fatal torpedo, the German submarine that fired at it had dropped off two Nazi spies near Hancock Point. Two residents who were later interviewed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation said they spotted a pair of underclad men carrying suitcases along a snowy road on the Hancock Point peninsula.
The men — William C. Colepaugh and Erich Gimpel — were equipped with, among other spy gadgets, radio gear, security ink, $60,000 in cash and 99 small diamonds. The pair, one of whom was a Connecticut native, were sent to eavesdrop on American servicemen to learn about the country’s advancements in developing an atomic bomb.
The Nazi spies reached New York City after hailing a cab to Bangor and train to Portland. After the American saboteur turned himself in, the pair were sentenced to death by hanging, a sentence that was eventually commuted to life in prison by President Harry Truman after the war’s end.
At the time of its sinking, the SS Cornwallis was carrying 48 people, including seven armed guards, Allan said. The wreck’s five sole survivors reached life rafts and were later spotted by aircraft and retrieved by fishing boats. They were transferred to a U.S. Navy rescue vessel and brought to Rockland.
Stéphane Ouellette, president and CEO of the Merchant Navy Commemorative Theme Project, a Canadian initiative aimed at preserving merchant mariners’ history, said the ship’s discovery helps honor the sacrifices of Canadian and American lives lost during the Battle of the Atlantic, a six-year military campaign that killed 72,200 Allied naval and merchant seafarers and 30,000 German sailors, according to the U.S. Navy.
“The Cornwallis reminds us of the tremendous price paid by merchant mariners to sustain the Allied war effort,” Oullette said. “Their legacy continues through today’s seafarers, whose work remains essential to global security, national defense and the world economy. We owe it to those who never came home, and to the families who have kept their memories alive, to ensure their sacrifices are never forgotten.”
The divers, who spent hours reviewing historical tide charts and weather data, believed the ship would be found somewhere near three general locations: the area where the survivors were picked up, the spot where debris was found and the place the Coast Guard estimated the ship was.
Throughout the group’s five trips looking for the SS Cornwallis, which weighed 5,485 tons and measured 400 feet long, the divers spent days scanning more than 50 square miles of search grids, Allan said.
They finally found the ship on July 11 with the help of side-scan sonar, an underwater imaging system. After identifying the ship with sonar equipment, the group of technical divers dove nearly 400 feet — longer than a football field — underwater to reach the wreck.
But once underwater, the divers were met with exceedingly low visibility — the poorest they’d come across of any wreck — because of the ship’s depth and the water’s siltiness, they said. Most of their dives lasted well over two to three hours.
The divers used the ship’s blueprints to confirm they’d discovered the correct vessel.
The shipwreck was found roughly 10 miles west southwest of Mount Desert Rock, a remote island about 25 miles from MDI. The wreck is in federal waters and doesn’t belong to the state, Allan said, adding that the U.S. Navy also can’t claim it because the ship never belonged to the military branch.
“If you’re in federal waters and you’re not a Navy ship, then it belongs to everyone and no one,” Allan said. “We could file paperwork to take ownership of it, [but] we’re not planning to do that. For us, the real reward is to find the wreck, put a place on the map [and] give closure to the families.”
Now, the team of nine are busy documenting various parts of the shipwreck, and hope to land a remotely operated vehicle on the ship by next year, Allan said.
“One of my goals, personally, is to find something small to bring back to give to the families,” Allan said, noting that such a task would be difficult given the ship’s depth.
The dive team included Allan, Ross Baxter, Mark Bowers, Josh Cummings, Don Ferrara, Bob Foster, Nate Garrettt, Jeff Goodreau and Ryan King, according to the group.
The SS Cornwallis was not the first historic shipwreck the team has found. In previous years, the group discovered the SS William H. Machen, which sank in 1942 after colliding with a cargo freighter, and the USS Eagle 56, a Navy ship torpedoed by a German U-boat off Cape Elizabeth just two weeks before World War II ended.
Allan said three factors drove the team’s interest in this particular shipwreck. First, the SS Cornwallis is the largest shipwreck in New England waters that, up until July, had not been found.
Its storied past also elevated the fascination: Not only was it destroyed by a German submarine with links to Nazi spies, but it’s one of only five wrecks in history that was torpedoed and sank twice, Allan said.
Two years before its fatal sinking on Dec. 3, 1944, the New Brunswick-bound steamship was torpedoed in Barbados by another German U-boat. The ship sank but was later refloated, fixed and returned to service in 1944, the diver said.
Allan noted the ship’s discovery underscores “just how close the war came to the shores of Maine.”
“One of the things that the public often doesn’t realize is the military connection to this,” Allan said. “There were seven armed guards on the ship and machine guns and various sized guns. The military connection to these ships can’t be understated.”
The shipwreck’s discovery was also personal to some of the divers: 19 of the crew members hailed from Nova Scotia. Allan, also a Nova Scotian, said one of the crew grew up just 10 miles from his childhood home.
“The discovery of the SS Cornwallis, more than 80 years after its sinking off the coast of Maine, brings history home to the families of the 43 people who never returned,” Oullette said. “For their descendants, this is more than the discovery of a shipwreck — it is a deeply personal connection to loved ones lost and sacrifices carried across generations.”
Correction: An earlier version of this report misspelled Jeff Goodreau’s name.

title: Bruins’ streak ends with loss to Hurricanes
text:
RALEIGH, N.C. — Sebastian Aho’s third-period goal gave the Carolina Hurricanes a 2-1 win over the Boston Bruins in a matchup of early leaders in the Eastern Conference on Tuesday night.
Pyotr Kochetkov made 14 saves to improve his record to 8-0-0, matching the longest season-opening winning streak by a goalie in franchise history. He tied former teammate Frederik Andersen, who set the mark five years ago.
Jackson Blake also scored for the Hurricanes, who were in their first home game in two weeks following a 3-1-1 road trip.
Carolina killed two power plays in the final five minutes, helping it halt Boston’s eight-game points streak.
Pavel Zacha scored for the Bruins. Jeremy Swayman made 28 saves.
Aho’s eighth goal of the season came with 9:41 remaining, shortly after Boston’s Matthew Poitras hit the post with a backhanded attempt on an open net. Aho has a team-high 19 points for the team with the best record in the league.
Zacha scored 1:31 into the game on a power play, but the Bruins failed to convert the rest of the game.
Blake tied the score with 52 seconds left in the first period.
The Hurricanes were scoreless on four power plays.
Carolina entered the game as the first NHL team to reach 20 points, marking a first-time accomplishment for the franchise.
Up next
Bruins: visit St. Louis on Thursday
Hurricanes: host Columbus on Thursday

also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Hunters Are Helping Feed Families in Need
If you love to hunt but don't need/want the meat for yourself, the Hunters for the Hungry program can help you donate it to Maine's food-insecure.
Maine Wild Game Hunters Can Donate Their Harvest to Feed the Needy
My husband enjoys hunting, and he typically gets one or two deer each year. But it's just the two of us, so we end up with venison in our freezer when the next season rolls around.
READ MORE: Still No Proof of Bigfoot in Maine
Bow hunters have been in the woods for weeks, and firearms season starts this weekend, so venison will soon fill freezers all over the state.
And some hunters will have venison they don't want or need.
Maine Hunters for the Hungry Program Provides Game Meat to the Food Insecure
The Maine Hunters for the Hungry program provides places to donate the meat to people in need.
Hunters for the Hungry is a collaboration between the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, state biologists, Maine State Troopers, and hunters.
It supplies lean, high-protein game meat to food pantries, soup kitchens, and homeless shelters, providing thousands of nutritious meals for Maine's most vulnerable populations.
How to Donate Game Meat to Maine's Hunters for the Hungry Program
And the process is pretty easy.
If you have bear, deer, or moose meat to donate, contact an approved meat processor.
The Department of Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry will cover processing costs.
Game must be legally harvested, tagged, and field-dressed, and kept cold, before arriving at the processing facility.
You don't have to donate the entire animal, either. If you want to donate a few pounds of meat, the program will happily accept it.
One warning: Hunters for the Hungry cannot accept donations from animals harvested in the 'Do Not Eat' advisory area.
It will make the hunt even sweeter knowing your donation will give food-insecure families a delicious Maine meal.

title: Alex Pretti’s family says they have no answers nine months after federal agents killed him
text:
Alex Pretti’s family says feds are still stonewalling efforts for justice
The parents of Alex Pretti, a U.S. citizen shot and killed by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, are accusing the Department of Justice of violating their rights under a federal victims’ rights law, as they demand transparency and justice in their son’s death.
In a July letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche — obtained exclusively by CNN — an attorney representing Michael and Susan Pretti wrote they have not received any substantive updates from the DOJ regarding an investigation into their son’s death, and called the department’s attitude toward the case “cruel.”
“The government’s pattern of conduct is not only unconscionable, but unlawful,” the letter states.
Pretti’s parents on Tuesday accused the federal government of “shielding Alex’s killers” by not turning over the entire federal case file to state investigators.
Video below: Video shows Alex Pretti scuffle with federal officers in Minneapolis 11 days before his death
“We will no longer stay silent about the actions of the Department of Justice in the 275 days since Alex’s murder,” Pretti’s father, Michael, said in the family’s first news conference since the 37-year-old ICU nurse’s death.
The Pretti family met with U.S. Attorney for the District of Minnesota Dan Rosen on July 13, the letter explains, the same day Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced in a news conference federal officials had handed over volumes of evidence from Pretti’s shooting.
However, the letter goes on to say that, despite a public acknowledgment from local officials of an evidence-sharing agreement, Rosen refused to provide any information and would not even confirm the arrangement.
“It is impossible to convey how the government’s refusal to engage in transparent communication with the Pretti family has compounded their heartbreak,” the missive says.
“Further, with each such refusal, U.S. Attorney Rosen even refused to explain the basis for his position, instead stating only that ‘I can’t tell you for all kinds of reasons,’ without providing a single one,” according to the letter.
Federal investigators who briefly agreed to share their evidence with state law enforcement have since stopped cooperating, said Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, who is leading a lawsuit against the Department of Justice.
“We are in litigation with the federal government right now to secure the rest of the remaining file, which they could give us this morning if they were inclined to do so, but it looks like we’re going to need a court order. I’m sorry that it comes to that,” Ellison told CNN’s Sara Sidner Tuesday morning. “Any prosecutor can tell you, you can’t go forward with half a file. You need the whole thing.”
CNN has reached out to the DOJ and the US Attorney for Minnesota.
In its response to Minnesota’s lawsuit, the Department of Justice said it is not required to turn over evidence to a state agency before an active court case is underway.
The Pretti family’s attorney, Steve Schleicher, says they have heard nothing from the DOJ since sending their letter.
“I’ve never seen a family treated with such cruelty and disrespect,” he said.
Pretti’s death was captured in its entirety on video. Like some other incidents that occurred as a result of the Trump administration’s ongoing immigration crackdown, the footage from Pretti’s shooting differed from the version of events provided by the Department of Homeland Security.
Kristi Noem, then-DHS secretary, initially described Pretti as a “terrorist” who “attacked” officers after “brandishing” a weapon, though the video disputed those claims. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller referred to Pretti as an “assassin” who tried to murder federal agents.
“No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex,” Michael Pretti said Tuesday.
During the incident, Pretti was pepper-sprayed in the face. One of the officers can be heard in the footage shouting: “Gun! Gun! Gun!” as Pretti is on his knees and bent forward. An agent removed Pretti’s gun from his waistband and can be seen exiting the skirmish. At about the same time, one agent drew his service weapon.
About a second after the agent holding Pretti’s weapon moved away, the officer who drew his own weapon appeared to fire several shots at Pretti before another agent drew his weapon and a shot rang out. The other officer then raised his gun and fired more shots. At least 10 gunshots can be heard on the video.
The DHS report on its initial investigation into Pretti’s death says an officer yelled, “He’s got a gun” multiple times before the officers fired.
“It’s difficult to get up every day, to function, to be a parent, knowing that your child’s never coming home,” Susan Pretti told CNN’s Jake Tapper after Tuesday’s news conference. “No parent should have to live what we’re living. No daughter should have to wake up and know that her only sibling is no longer here.”
“What the federal government has taken away from us, from his friends, his family, his colleagues, from his patients, from the patients’ families. They’ve taken away all of that — and it’s reprehensible,” he told Tapper.
Susan Pretti said she knew Alex as her son, but the outpouring of support they’ve received from his friends and coworkers has helped her see another side of him.
“Every letter and card that we received from his colleagues, telling us who he was, at work … not only helping his patients but his colleagues,” Susan Pretti said, choking up. “You know what that’s like for a parent to hear? It is probably the kindest thing a parent can ever hear about their child.”
Michael Pretti said his trust in the government is fading.
Pretti’s death followed the fatal shooting of Renee Good on Jan. 7 and the non-fatal shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis on Jan. 14 by immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge. Those incidents prompted significant protests in Minneapolis and across the country for weeks.
Hennepin County prosecutors have fought the DOJ for key evidence in Pretti’s death for months, after federal law enforcement repeatedly threw up blockades to their access.
On the day Pretti was killed, the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension attempted to access the scene to launch an investigation but was banned by federal authorities. CNN was on scene the next day when the BCA first accessed the scene on a court order from a state judge.
State and local investigators sued the Trump administration in federal court to obtain evidence in Pretti’s killing. After an evidence-sharing agreement between the DOJ and Minnesota investigators was finalized in June, Hennepin County prosecutors received volumes of evidence in Pretti’s shooting.
Weeks later, the DOJ abruptly changed course and stopped sharing information, leaving Hennepin County prosecutors unable to access crucial evidence such as the weapons used to shoot Pretti and the firearm Pretti was carrying in his waistband at the time of the altercation, according to court records filed October 13.
The letter from Pretti’s parents asks the DOJ to identify the federal employees who shot and killed Pretti, commit to sharing information with state and local investigators, confirm whether the FBI is continuing to investigate Pretti’s murder, and return any items of Pretti’s personal property no longer needed for evidentiary purposes.
“No family should have to beg the U.S. government to do its job,” the letter says. “And no government should act with such caprice.”
The Pretti family’s attorney declined to say Tuesday whether they would file a suit of their own against the Department of Justice.
“The family will avail itself to any and all remedies in its pursuit of justice for Alex,” Schleicher said.
Until they find justice, the family is comforted by shared memories of their son. Michael Pretti recalled a specific camping trip when Alex was about 6 years old. Just as they were wrapping up the weekend and preparing to leave, Alex rode his new bike off a small bridge and into a creek.
“He comes back and he’s soaked,” Michael Pretti said with a grin, prompting a chuckle from his wife. “That was a good memory, that was a good weekend that stands out,” he said, adding “that’s probably where his love for hiking and biking started.”

title: Physical therapist takes simple approach to end her chronic pain
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Research from the National Library of Medicine shows more than 30% of the world’s population suffers from chronic pain.
That’s 2.4 billion people who might feel hope after hearing Allyn Minton’s story.
The Nashville-based licensed physical therapist has been pain-free for a full year, thanks to a breakthrough she says has changed her mind.
Minton opened Swell Studio after turning to the low-impact exercise in her 20s.
She had injured her back while transferring a patient. She learned to manage her pain with daily, core-strengthening exercise and physical therapy. That is, until debilitating pain returned every year, on a certain day.
“Over the years, as I would get stressed through times in my life, my dad getting cancer and passing away, my back would start to just go out on me,” Minton said. “I went to the doctor, and he said, ‘Allyn, you were here last year to the day.’”
The debilitating pattern repeated itself, until one year ago.
Mind-body connection
“As I started calming the nervous system and looking at those thoughts, slowly with the repetition of affirmations — it’s that repetition that’s key — my thoughts started to change. And my back pain disappeared,” Minton said.
A 2022 review of multiple studies in the Harvard Gazette explains how adding psychological therapies with physical ones, including reframing negative thoughts, can change how the body feels pain.
Research on neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to rewire itself, shows how repeated thoughts and behaviors can build new pathways in the brain and alleviate chronic pain.
“If the body is tense and in fight or flight, it doesn’t feel safe enough to let the mind relax and open and be receptive to change,” Minton said.
Minton believes the simple step of adding affirmations for 20 minutes a day has helped calm her nervous system, offering hope to millions that healing is possible with the power of the mind.

title: How to extinguish the 'firefighter' mindset
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Many years ago, trying to sleep under my desk at 4:15 a.m., I learned that the middle of the night is a clarifying (and inconvenient) time to restructure work habits. Sure, it was Wall Street; sleeping under one’s desk seemed inevitable. But as I snuggled under my blazer, I replayed the week.
The problem was clear: I was reactive, trapped in the undertow of other people’s decisions. I had to get proactive and stay that way.
In today’s environment, many are metaphorically cuddled up on the industrial carpet. When unpredictable events feel like the norm, it’s easy for us to become firefighters rather than proactive stewards of a mission or strategy.
As we cruise toward year-end reviews and 2027 goal setting, may I offer you the solution that usually keeps me from sleeping under my desk (even metaphorically)? Institute a quarterly check-in with yourself.
Set a recurring, quarterly 90-minute appointment right now. Automation makes it more likely to happen. Define the agenda and guard the time as you would a direct report’s review. Don’t reschedule. Link to a document that will serve as your agenda and take notes there each quarter. If you already review quarterly reports or have another quarterly process, that’s great. Piggyback on that with some qualitative data.
What’s energizing vs. draining
You don’t need many questions to figure out where you can tweak your work style and improve your days. For most people, I find these three questions bring up clear focus areas for the coming quarter:
- What aspects of your work felt energizing — and what felt draining?
- Was your attention spent where it matters most, or was your attention hijacked to reactively solve problems?
- What proactive improvement would have the biggest impact in the next quarter?
Functionally, this is a mini-audit of your energy, attention and focus. You’re probably thinking that answering those three questions took less than 90 minutes. Exactly! Now you have time intentionally set aside to plan the quarter, prioritizing that single impactful change.
If shifting your energy is your top priority, plan to use the energizing work as the engine of your day and try to offload whatever drains you. For many, “draining work” is also work they’re not great at.
True leadership is playing to your strengths … and weaknesses. Brainstorm ways to get the draining work off your plate. If you can’t delegate or outsource it, try concentrating it into “bummer chunks” in your schedule and giving yourself a little treat when it’s done.
Common issues
Planning to protect your attention can be trickier, but here are some common patterns:
Fire drills. Frequent “fire drills” indicate that your processes need restructuring to ensure earlier intervention or evaluation.
Other people’s messes. Routinely cleaning up other people’s messes is resolved by creating a shared understanding of roles and responsibilities, ensuring that decisions, actions and accountability sit with the right people.
Moving targets. Wasting time and attention on “moving target” work because you didn’t get the right information upfront can be reduced by using written, shared intake templates for frequent project types and by defining hand-off processes.
Watch for ‘energy vampires’
If the thing that’s sapping your attention doesn’t fit neatly into one of these categories, this review is the perfect time to try to identify a unique energy vampire. In any case, mapping out systems, processes and information flow is almost always time well spent.
If you don’t have a clear winner for which action would give the biggest bang for the buck, make your best guess. Write down the whole list of ideas, but commit to solving just one. You can always revisit the list to keep going if your quarter allows.
Now go forth and execute the plan. When the next quarterly check-in pops up, revisit your notes from the previous quarter. Did it go as you hoped? Is there work left to do? And were you solving structural problems rather than metaphorically sleeping under your desk?
Aim for progress, not perfection. Good luck!

title: Poll: U.S. Senate, Maine governor races tight
text:
MAINE (WABI) - We are exactly one week away from the midterm election.
According to the Marist Poll published Tuesday, October 27, the race for the Maine U.S. Senate seat is close.
Democratic challenger Troy Jackson has a 2-point lead over incumbent Senator Susan Collins, 49% to 47%.
The poll factors in Mainers who are likely to vote in the election. The margin of error for likely voters is 6.6 points.
Among registered voters, Jackson has a 9-point lead. The margin of error for registered voters is 4.1 points.
In the race for Maine governor, Republican Bobby Charles and Democrat Hannah Pingree are tied at 44%, according to the poll. Independent Rick Bennett received 6% of votes. The remaining 6% of voters are undecided.
The poll surveyed 1,449 Mainers.
