title: Trump promised to revive American manufacturing, but is it working? What the data shows
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump promised to revive American manufacturing, but is it working? What the data says ahead of midterms
President Donald Trump has announced some new factory investments ahead of midterm elections, but our Get the Facts Data Team found that manufacturing jobs have fallen slightly nationwide since the beginning of his second term.
Trump promised to revive American manufacturing, but is it working? What the data says ahead of midterms
President Donald Trump has announced some new factory investments ahead of midterm elections, but our Get the Facts Data Team found that manufacturing jobs have fallen slightly nationwide since the beginning of his second term.
President Donald Trump has pointed to new investments as evidence that his policies are reviving American manufacturing in the lead-up to midterm elections, but our analysis found that employment in the sector has remained relatively steady since the start of his second term.
Experts say it'll take several years to fully evaluate how Trump's tariffs and tax reforms will influence job numbers nationwide.
Voters had mixed views about his approach in the battleground state of Michigan, the heart of America's automobile industry.
Tariffs squeeze businesses
Detroit Axle ships thousands of packages carrying automotive parts directly to consumers each day.
Mike Musheinesh, the chief executive of Detroit Axle, said the company used to remanufacture all of its parts in Michigan, where the family business started in 1990 with just a handful of employees.
As the business expanded, it started importing most of its products from other countries. That supply chain has left the company with a steep tariff bill under the second Trump administration.
Musheinesh said that he used to pay the federal government $2,500 in tariffs for a container of brake rotors that are made in China. Now, he's paying $52,000.
Musheinesh said rapidly evolving import taxes have forced him to raise prices on his customers.
"We thought that, hey, the only way to survive is to be able to increase prices. If you don't increase prices, you're going to be selling for a loss," Musheinesh said.
Musheinesh said his ultimate goal is to produce more products in the United States, even if it costs him more, but there are barriers. He said a lack of workforce training and government assistance, in addition to tariff uncertainty, have caused him to hold off on expanding his U.S. footprint.
"If the government is taking all of your revenue for tariffs, you really have nothing left to invest," Musheinesh said.
"The government seems like all they do is support these big, multibillion-dollar enterprises when they're talking about manufacturing," he added. "Nobody has encouraged and nurtured the small father and son, like it's always been, to grow their manufacturing and to help make this country a little more prosperous."
Supply chain shakeup
Dr. Hung-Chung Su, an operations management professor at the University of Michigan-Dearborn, said major manufacturers are also assessing the impact of tariff costs on their bottom line.
Parts often cross Michigan’s border with Canada several times during the assembly process, and those deeply connected supply chains are being tested during the ongoing trade war with America’s northern neighbor, according to Dr. Su.
"They will revisit their existing supply chain structures and try to make changes. We don't know what kind of changes they are going to make," Su said.
Trump argues that his tariffs are already pressuring companies to bring manufacturing jobs back to the United States. A tax reform law passed by the Republican-led Congress last year seeks to further that goal by offering new incentives to build in America.
The law, often referred to as the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," is paying off, according to a study from the National Association of Manufacturers that credits the legislation with supporting six million jobs.
Asked about the impact of the law, Su said, "It is easier for companies to make investments in Michigan, in which some of the companies actually did, if you look at Ford and GM."
During a campaign rally on Saturday, Trump also announced that Audi plans to establish its first U.S. production site in Georgia, which is expected to create approximately 4,500 jobs.
Despite these wins, Su stressed that it will take several years to fully determine how Trump’s policies will influence employment numbers nationwide, especially as automation continues to transform the industry.
What the data shows
An analysis from our Get the Facts Data Team found that manufacturing employment has held relatively steady under Trump’s second administration.
The manufacturing sector had roughly 12.67 million employees when Trump started his current term. That number had fallen slightly to 12.65 million, a 0.15% decrease, as of September 2026, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Manufacturing employment remains far lower than the total at the turn of the century. The sector has lost approximately five million employees since 2000, with significant losses reported during the 2008 financial crisis. Job growth began to stabilize in the late 2010s and continued until the COVID-19 pandemic.
Employment in motor vehicle and parts manufacturing followed a similar trend. The sector has lost 17,000 employees since Trump returned to office and nearly 300,000 employees since the George W. Bush administration.
Construction spending – the amount spent on building factories, buildings, or other structures for the industry – has also fallen since Trump returned to office, according to data from the U.S. Census Bureau. In August 2026, manufacturing construction spending was $170.7 billion, 21% less than what was spent one year prior after adjusting for inflation.
In contrast, construction spending rose under former President Joe Biden, reaching $250.4 billion by the end of his term after adjusting for inflation.
The findings seem to contradict Trump’s recent statements. While campaigning in Detroit over the summer, he declared that there are "more plants being built than at any time in the history of our country."
A work in progress
Brian Pannebecker, a retired autoworker in Michigan who founded the group Autoworkers for Trump, said it’s too soon for the president to declare victory. He said it took decades for plants to close and that won’t change overnight.
"Yes, it is too soon for him to brag about it, and he has a bad habit of doing this, exaggerating and embellishing his accomplishments," Pannebecker said. "I think he envisions, five or ten years down the road, us returning to a manufacturing powerhouse."
It’s a worthy cause, according to Pannebecker, even if it causes some short-term pain for consumers dealing with higher prices.
"We have to have jobs. It doesn't matter if costs are up for the product. If you don't have a job, you can't buy it anyhow,” Pannebecker said.

title: High schools Tuesday: Thornton boys soccer survives a test
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Precieux Mbolela scored off a corner kick by Matthias Sunderland with 32:40 left in the second half, lifting top-seeded Thornton Academy to a 1-0 win over ninth-seeded Marshwood in a Class A South boys soccer quarterfinal Tuesday in Saco.
Thornton (12-1-2), the No. 3 team in the Varsity Maine Top 10, advances to face the winner of a game Wednesday between No. 5 Deering and No. 4 South Portland.
Lucas Stolf made five saves for Thornton, while Jack Eardley of Marshwood (7-6-3) had 12 saves.
PINE TREE ACADEMY 5, RANGELEY 0: Fitzroy Hakizimana had two goals and assist, Lucky Kabeya and Camden Brace each added a goal and an assist, and the top-seeded Breakers (13-0) handled the eighth-seeded Lakers (3-8-1) in an eight-person South quarterfinal in Freeport.
Santiago Lopez also scored and Rhett Tyson had an assist.
LEWISTON 3, BANGOR 1: Abdirauf Hersi scored in each half and the top-ranked Blue Devils (14-1) fought off a challenge from the eighth-seeded Rams (4-9-2) in a Class A North quarterfinal in Lewiston.
The Blue Devils led 2-0 at halftime after goals from Hersi and Nathan Dimandja. Bangor cut into the deficit early in the second half, but Hersi got his second goal with about five minutes remaining.
Lewiston, the No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine Top 10, next faces the winner of a Wednesday quarterfinal between Hampden Academy and Camden Hills.
GIRLS SOCCER
FREEPORT 1, LINCOLN ACADEMY 0: Keeley Furtney’s direct kick from 40 yards bounced into the goal, and the fourth-seeded Falcons (11-4) shut out the fifth-seeded Eagles (9-5-1) in a Class B South quarterfinal in Freeport.
Freeport advances to face to winner of a game on Wednesday between No. 1 Cape Elizabeth and No. 8 Morse.
GREELY 6, POLAND 2: Victoria Zandan scored twice in the first half, sparking the sixth-seeded Rangers (8-5-2) to a win over the third-seeded Knights (11-2-2) in a Class B South quarterfinal in Poland.
Greely benefited from an own goal about five minutes into the game when a corner kick deflected into the net off a Poland defender. Zandan made it 2-0 less than two minutes later, then extended the lead to 3-0 before Poland got on the board when Phoebe Paradis scored late in the first half.
Hannah Hussey, Lydia Berthiaume and Tess Waterhouse added second-half goals for Greely. Poland’s Gabby Lenahan scored midway through the second half.
HALL-DALE 3, NORTH YARMOUTH ACADEMY 2: The third-seeded Bulldogs (11-2-2) rallied from a two-goal deficit in the second half to beat the sixth-seeded Panthers (10-5) in a Class C South quarterfinal in Farmingdale.
Clare Sturtevant had two goals and an assist for Hall-Dale, which next faces second-seeded Maranacook. Sophia Murch was the other goal scorer.
Delphine Daniels scored twice for NYA.
MARANACOOK 2, WAYNFLETE 0: Caroline Harper scored two goals for the second-seeded Black Bears (14-1) in a Class C South quarterfinal against the seventh-seeded Flyers (5-9-1) in Readfield.
Evelyn Stevenson had an assist. Stella Stewart earned the shutout in net.
WINDHAM 2, WESTBROOK 1: Emily Wardwell, Grayson Cornish and Lexi Woodcock scored in the penalty kick shootout, and the Eagles (11-3-1) beat the Blue Blazes (8-7-1) in a Class A South quarterfinal in Windham.
Windham Libby Hartwell made a save in the shootout and finished with eight saves for the second-seeded Eagles, who will face No. 3 Kennebunk in the semifinals.
Wardwell scored early in the second half to give the Eagles a 1-0 lead. Ava Bolden got the tying goal.
Greta Krantz stopped 19 shots for the Blue Blazes.
FIELD HOCKEY
CHEVERUS 6, NOBLE 0: Mary McCartney scored four times and the top-ranked Stags (15-0) rolled to a Class A South quarterfinal win over the Knights (9-7) in Portland.
Cheverus, the three-time defending Class A champion, advance to face No. 4 Sanford/Kennebunk in the semifinals.
Sydney Brunelle and Avery Tinker each added a goal and an assist. Jaylee Radford had an assist.
Lauren Merchant stopped 19 shots for Noble.
SANFORD/KENNEBUNK 4, FALMOUTH 2: Reese Beaudoin had two goals and two assists, Paige Sevigny and Ella Tederous also scored, and the fourth-seeded Spartans (10-5) defeated the fifth-seeded Navigators (9-6) in a Class A South quarterfinal in Sanford.

Dempsey also founded the annual Dempsey Challenge in Lewiston, a walk, run, and cycling fundraiser that has raised more than $20 million for the center since its inception.

title: Did you know there are live stingrays in Tampa Bay's stadium?
text:
Did you know there are live stingrays in the outfield of Tropicana Field?
While the Brewers and Rays meet for Game 3 of the World Series, fans at the ballpark can find another attraction in the outfield: a tank filled with stingrays.
Stingrays have been at Tropicana Field for years, and Stephanie Sutton of Hearst sisters station WISN got up close and personal with them before the game.
The stingrays swim around during games, though fans may also see them resting on the bottom, said Christy Barrett, a curator at the Florida Aquarium.
Many longtime visitors stop by to see the animals and have favorite stingrays, Barrett said. While they don't have official names, some fans have their own names for them.
"But I think a lot of people are surprised to see it here," Barrett said.
Home run balls have landed in the tank in the past, Barrett said. A net now protects it, and a ball had bounced off the net shortly before the interview.

title: Scarborough girls soccer pulls away to take down Thornton Academy
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SCARBOROUGH — The shot off Maya Casey’s foot didn’t seem to have much of a chance to find the net.
But it did. And there was no stopping the Scarborough girls soccer team from there.
Casey’s goal in the 24th minute put the Red Storm ahead to stay, and No. 1 Scarborough got goals from five players en route to a 5-1 victory over No. 9 Thornton Academy in a Class A South quarterfinal Tuesday evening.
“It was really, really amazing, especially after last year. We started off our playoffs with a really close game against Marshwood,” said Casey, a sophomore. “To come out early felt amazing. … I feel really awesome. I’m so happy for the team.”
Scarborough (14-0-1) has reached the last four Class A state finals, but coach Craig Roberts knew that with a bevy of freshmen and sophomores playing key roles, playoff poise was hardly a given.
“We have a lot of girls that don’t have playoff experience, don’t have varsity experience,” he said. “I thought we had a really even temperament. Even after they scored, we didn’t panic, we didn’t get frustrated.”
KEY MOMENT
• Scarborough went ahead 5:27 into the game when freshman Wren Bodah knocked in Josie Duncan’s corner kick, but the Golden Trojans (7-7-2) pulled even just 2:17 later. Julia Collins took the ball down the left and got the ball past keeper Vera DiSotto, and Duncan accidentally directed it into the net while trying to clear it.
• Exactly 16 minutes later, the Red Storm struck again. Casey, sidelined most of the year because of a hip flexor strain, shook a defender and tried a shot from a tight angle near the left corner. The ball got through the defense and hit twine just inside the left post with 16:16 to go in the half.
“I was really surprised,” she said. “I was looking near post, but I wasn’t expecting it to go in. I really just wanted to take a leap of faith and put it out there. … I just wanted to be risky this time.”
• From there, the Red Storm rolled. Scarborough finished with a 20-4 advantage in shots and added goals from Hayley Meehan with 10:37 left in the first half, from Scarlett Floyd with 37:51 left in the game, and from Maggie Booth with 7:34 to play.
“This team definitely has faith in everyone,” Booth said. “Everyone steps up. We don’t just rely on one girl.”
UNSUNG HERO
• Thornton Academy, already without center back Jacey Springer because of illness and center midfielder Charlotte Beane because of an injury suffered in the second minute, lost keeper Adeline Polletta when she was hurt while diving after Casey’s goal.
Enter senior Madison Tripp, who made 11 saves and helped keep the Trojans in it.
“Maddie came in, she’s a senior, she stepped up,” Thornton coach Ellie Agreste said. “She was a field player last year. … She got a friend to train her after practice throughout the season. She was ready for this moment.”
STAT LEADERS
• Scarborough: Wren Bodah (goal), Maya Casey (goal), Hayley Meehan (goal), Scarlett Floyd (goal), Maggie Booth (goal), Josie Duncan (two assists), Jill Morris (assist), Vera DiSotto (three saves)
• Thornton: Madison Tripp (11 saves), Adeline Polletta (four saves)

How a disability payment error nearly cost this father his home
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
STONE MOUNTAIN, Ga. (InvestigateTV) — Henry Adams almost lost his house after a disability payment error caused a mortgage trial payment to bounce, kicking him out of a loan program that he entered while trying to take care of his wife through her cancer battle.
Adams held up a photo of his wife, Ellen Adams, and their daughter, Caitlin, on the back deck of their family home.
“This is us in the house when we first got here. Caitlin was so little,” he said. “She’s 21 now.”
The Adams lived in the home for almost two decades, during years in which the couple served as pastors in Atlanta. Their homeless outreach ministry was even featured in a local media outlet.
Adams said he survived cancer years earlier but was left with a disability. “I went through chemo and they was able to kill it but it left me with a disability,” he said, describing swelling in his leg.
He receives disability income from his previous employer, AT&T, and later found at-home work in cybersecurity, but Ellen Adams’ condition worsened after a years-long battle with breast cancer.
“I needed to watch her,” Adams said, describing frequent medical appointments and treatment.
As health costs mounted, Adams said finances tightened. “Things were getting really tough.”
Falling behind on mortgage payments, Henry Adams enrolled in an FHA loan modification program through U.S. Bank. The program paused the mortgage for several months, then required three consecutive on-time trial payments to qualify for final approval of the loan modification.
Hours after Adams admitted his wife to the ICU for what would be the final time on April 1, he received a call from the bank.
The scheduled disability direct deposit did not arrive, the mortgage payment bounced, and he was immediately removed from the loan program trial.
“If you miss that trial payment, there is no do-over,” Adams said. “There is no grace.”
AT&T’s disability provider later acknowledged what it described as a “systemic issue” that delayed payments by two days. Recipients were notified in a letter dated April 8.
“They had a glitch in their system,” Adams said. “They didn’t alert the thousands of people that they were servicing, so none of us knew that our direct deposits would not be in the bank by the last day of the month.”
Adams said the bank told him he owed nearly $10,000 in back payments and faced immediate foreclosure. “I never thought I’d be facing foreclosure in the house we celebrated in,” he said. “We had our baby here. We grew her up here.”
When asked who should be held accountable, Adams said, “I hate to blame the long-term disability department... but now we could possibly be homeless.”
Hours before Atlanta News First Investigates met with Henry Adams, Ellen Adams died at the hospital.
In a recording from one of Ellen Adams’ sermons before she became ill, she preached: “Jesus got it... He said, ‘I got something for you, I’m not gonna leave you like this, I’m not gonna leave you in sorrow.’”
They were words that would ring true for her husband years later.
We contacted AT&T, U.S. Bank and the federal loan provider to inquire about the payment delay and whether an exception was possible.
Within days, U.S. Bank worked out a policy exemption with the FHA program allowing Adams to restart the trial period in July.
“When [the bank] called me, I could not stop crying on the phone,” Adams said. “God rescued us and he used you all to rescue us, to help us, to support us.
“You came and sat down, and you listened, when a lot of other people wouldn’t listen,” Adams, who is now focusing on raising money for his wife’s funeral in early June, said.
Tips to avoid issues from payment delays:
- Try to pay loan payments early when possible
- Check your bank accounts often to verify deposits arrived
- Ask your lender about hardship exceptions if payment issues occur
“The client’s mortgage is an FHA loan, and we are required to follow their servicing guidelines which include a number of automatic actions if the requirements are not met,” a US Bank spokesperson said. “That said, we value our longstanding relationship with Mr. Adams and acknowledge the unfortunate circumstances involved, and we have worked directly with the FHA on a policy exception and will be in a position to offer reinstatement to the trial plan.”
“This unfortunate incident stemmed from a system error at our third-party benefits provider and affected a small number of people who receive long-term disability payments from us,” said an AT&T spokesperson. “We have apologized to Mr. Adams for the disruption this caused and are working closely with our vendor to help ensure this does not happen again.”
We reached out to AT&T’s third-party benefits provider for comment and did not receive a response.

title: Missing woman reportedly found alive in Mexico, but her family has doubts
text:
PHOENIX (KPHO/Gray News) — Mexican authorities said a missing Arizona woman was believed to have been found in Tijuana, but family members say they have doubts.
Shayna Feinman, 35, was reported missing in March 2024.
A Tijuana security force said Feinman was found on Oct. 23 after reports of a woman matching her description in an Encino neighborhood.
The security force said the woman was confirmed to be Feinman, but Yavapai County Sheriff’s Office officials initially said they couldn’t independently confirm her identity because of “insufficient evidence.”
Feinman’s sister Kara added that she did not recognize the person in Mexico and didn’t have hard evidence that the person was indeed her sister.
Kara said this wasn’t the first time Feinman was reported to have been spotted.
Feinman’s sister called these types of reports with little evidence from law enforcement agencies disheartening to the family.
Tijuana officials said they took the woman in question to a safe location to await contact with the Feinman family and U.S. authorities.
Details were not immediately shared about how Feinman may have ended up in Mexico.
Yavapai County Sheriff’s deputies said Feinman vanished without a trace on March 9, 2024, while walking to a friend’s house.
Two men were arrested in connection with her disappearance in 2024. Loved ones said they have been holding onto hope of her return.
The Yavapai County Sheriff’s Office updated its investigation, stating that the woman in Tijuana was indeed believed to not be the missing woman.

title: EPA response to 2023 Ohio train derailment will be investigated by agency watchdog
text:
The Environmental Protection Agency’s response to the disastrous 2023 East Palestine train derailment will be investigated after local residents of the small town on the Ohio-Pennsylvania border and Vice President JD Vance pressed for the review.
The Inspector General of the EPA announced the investigation Tuesday to assess the agency’s response to the worst rail disaster in more than a decade and the subsequent health and environmental concerns that have developed despite the EPA’s assurances to the public that no toxic levels of chemicals lingered in the community weeks and months later.
An assortment of chemicals spilled and caught fire after the failed bearing sent the Norfolk Southern train careening off the tracks late one Friday night in February 2023. Residents evacuated as officials decided three days later to blow open five rail cars and burn the vinyl chloride inside.
The National Transportation Safety Board determined the “vent and burn” move that generated a massive black plume of smoke and sent chemicals drifting across several states was unnecessary. But at the time, the officials in charge of the emergency response worried the tank cars might explode and do even more harm.
Jami Wallace and other East Palestine residents have been pushing for this investigation — much like they pressed the EPA initially to test for whether cancer-causing dioxins were released in their hometown — so she said “I’m going to cry” when she heard the news. Since the derailment, Wallace has kept track of more than 80 people who live in the area and have developed cancer, although it’s difficult to prove that every illness is directly linked to the derailment.
“It’s like we’ve had to push them along the way for every single thing they did, and then they didn’t even do it right,” said Wallace, who promised never to give up the fight. “We’re not going to stop when you poison our kids.”
The recent political request from Vance and the head of the EPA helped get the investigation started. But multiple complaints from residents and whistleblowers have also been made in the years since the derailment.
The Inspector General’s office said this investigation will determine whether the EPA fulfilled its responsibilities and whether the EPA had “sufficient data to support the agency’s public communications” assuring residents they were safe to return home and live in the small town. Testing experts questioned whether the test data EPA shared with the public obscured the risks and whether the agency could determine just how dangerous it is to be exposed to this cocktail of chemicals. Health standards are generally based only on exposure to a single chemical.
Wallace said she’s not sure how much good might come out of this investigation, but it will continue to put a bit of light on the lingering concerns around East Palestine.
“If nothing else, at least we’re getting attention again,” Wallace said. “And people know that we’re here and that we are not OK.”
Norfolk Southern agreed to a $600 million class action settlement with residents, but that money has been largely tied up in the courts and questions about the initial settlement administrator mishandling the funds. A group of residents has also sued because they argue the class action attorneys misled them and pressured them into signing the deal.
A separate federal settlement that includes a $15 million fine for the railroad and $55 million to pay for decades of medical exams and groundwater testing has been under review for more than two years without a judge approving it.
Norfolk Southern is seeking to merge with Union Pacific and create the nation’s first transcontinental railroad. But that $85 billion deal still faces an extensive review by the Surface Transportation Board.

title: South Portland personal care agency accused of defrauding MaineCare
text:
South Portland personal care agency accused of defrauding MaineCare in long-running scheme
6 people have been arrested in connection with the case, U.S. Attorney's Office says
South Portland personal care agency accused of defrauding MaineCare in long-running scheme
6 people have been arrested in connection with the case, U.S. Attorney's Office says
A South Portland personal care agency and six people have been indicted for healthcare fraud conspiracy after the company was accused of defrauding MaineCare, the state's Medicaid program, out of hundreds of thousands of dollars for services that were never provided, according to federal prosecutors.
The U.S. Attorney's Office said Noora Abd, the owner and operator of Community Home Health Care, LLC, and five of the company's employees were arrested Tuesday morning as a result of an indictment that was handed down by a federal grand jury on Thursday, Oct. 22.
Abd, 37, and Faysal Kalayaf Manahe, 51, were charged with healthcare fraud conspiracy and obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation.
Mohammed Alkhalaf, 41, was charged with healthcare fraud conspiracy and making false statements.
Adel Al Rashid, 47, Sura Almohammed, 47, and Ether Alyaseen, 46, were all charged with healthcare fraud conspiracy.
The indictment states that Community Home Health Care, through Abd, billed MaineCare for personal care services and was paid. But according to the indictment, the defendants submitted false electronic visit verifications claiming to have performed personal care services for clients when, in fact, the services had not been performed.
Federal prosecutors said the indictment goes on to state that since 2020, Community Home Health Care and Abd submitted numerous claims totaling more than $600,000 to MaineCare for personal care services purportedly provided to a single client.
"Healthcare fraud, in all its forms, costs all of us, and today's arrests should make it clear that if — as alleged in the indictment returned last week — you steal from our healthcare system for your own financial gain, you too will be shut down and brought to justice," said Andrew Benson, U.S. attorney for the District of Maine. "Protecting the integrity of all our federally funded healthcare programs for those who need them is truly paramount."
Benson spoke about the indictment in a news conference held on Tuesday. He was joined by members of the FBI's Boston Division, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, Homeland Security Investigations New England and IRS Criminal Investigation. You can watch that news conference in the YouTube video embedded below.
Benson said the investigation remains ongoing, and that the Maine Attorney General's Office and the state's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit provided support to federal agencies during the investigation.
If the defendants are convicted of healthcare fraud conspiracy, they face up to 10 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000 or twice the total loss due to fraudulent claims, and up to three years of supervised release. The charges of obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation and making false statements each carry a maximum of five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release.
What we know about Community Home Health Care
On Aug. 5, the Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) announced that it had suspended payments to five MaineCare providers due to credible fraud allegations. Maine's Total Coverage chief investigative reporter Norah Hogan found that Community Home Health Care, LLC in South Portland was one of the five providers that had their MaineCare payments suspended by the state.
Hogan spoke with an employee at Community Home Health Care in August. The employee spoke with her off camera while he was cutting final checks. He said the company had laid off 125 home health aides and told 165 patients to find services elsewhere, because the business could not operate without MaineCare reimbursements. The employee referred all other questions to the company's lawyer, who did not respond to a request for comment at the time.
In addition, Hogan found that Community Home Health Care received a notice of violation from DHHS in December 2025. According to that notice, DHHS reviewed records from Oct. 1, 2016, through March 31, 2019, and found more than $49,250 in MaineCare overpayments to Community Home Health Care. A DHHS spokesperson said that Community had repaid that debt.
Trump administration's allegations of fraud in Maine
On Jan. 23, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced that an audit revealed Maine made at least $45.6 million in improper fee-for-service Medicaid payments for rehabilitative and community support (RCS) services provided to children diagnosed with autism.
Two weeks later, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said in a social media post that Maine needed to "clean up its act" when it came to Medicaid fraud. CMS also sent a letter to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, in which it asked Gov. Janet Mills to explain how MaineCare — the state's Medicaid program — prevents fraud, identifies when fraud happens, bans providers from billing the system and recovers misspent funds. Mills responded to that letter by saying Maine was facing "a political attack" from President Donald Trump.
During his State of the Union address on Feb. 24, Trump accused Maine of fraud and announced a "war on fraud" that would be led by Vance. In a statement responding to Trump's claim, a spokesperson for Mills said Maine would "not be intimidated by the president's threats" and said addressing fraud allegations should be a joint effort between the state and federal government.
On March 6, Mills announced that her administration had responded to the CMS request for information about MaineCare and said the state was conducting oversight to ensure MaineCare providers are held to high standards, adding that the state has robust enforcement mechanisms to identify fraud.
Vice President JD Vance visited Maine on May 14 and said the state may be the third- or fourth-worst state when it comes to fraud.
"Outside of Minnesota and California, which are probably No. 1 and No. 2, if they're the gold medalist and silver medalist — I heard somebody shout out New York — maybe New York is the bronze medalist, but let me be honest, maybe Maine is the bronze medalist," Vance said. "What you have in Maine is a festering problem where people have been taken advantage of and they've been stolen from, and your government hasn't done anything about it."
On Aug. 3, Oz was in Maine to further look into alleged fraud in the state. The following day at a news conference in Philadelphia, Oz said that billing by the top 10 providers in Maine has dramatically increased over the last six years. He said the catalyst for the fraud issue was the COVID-19 pandemic. In a statement responding to Oz's claims, the Maine Department of Health and Human Services said that it has been actively working with CMS in response to the Office of the Inspector General report that was released in January.

title: Savannah Chrisley is expecting her first child with mystery fiancé Jason
text:
(Gray News) - Savannah Chrisley is expecting her first child with her fiancé, Jason.
“I’ve prayed for this life. I’ve cried for this life. And there were moments I truly wondered if this life would ever be mine,” she said in an Instagram post.
Chrisley, 29, shared the news on her podcast, Unlocked with Savannah Chrisley, and on Instagram.
“The past few years have taken me through fires I never imagined I’d have to walk through. Seasons of heartbreak, loss, and moments when I didn’t know if I would ever make it to the other side. I wondered if I would ever find my forever… if I would ever feel safe enough to truly breathe again. And then God sent me J. Right in the middle of the heartbreak. Before all the pieces were put back together. And somehow, he began healing parts of me he never broke," Chrisley wrote on Instagram.
Chrisley shared a video of herself holding ultrasound photos and kissing Jason with her hand on her pregnancy bump.
“For the first time in a long time, I feel safe. I feel fulfilled. I can finally exhale. I found my forever in you. And just when I thought my heart couldn’t hold any more love, God gave us our sweetest blessing yet… we’re having a BABY!" she continued in the Instagram caption.
In her podcast episode sharing the news, Chrisley said that she and Jason have been together since last July and first connected “in the world of politics.” She said Jason proposed to her in December in the Cayman Islands.
“The ring is insane and it’s everything I ever wanted,” she said.
Chrisley also said that their age gap is “huge.”
“I would rather 20 phenomenal years with someone than 50 meh years with someone,” she said.
Chrisley said that when she first saw Jason, she was still working to get her parents, Todd and Julie Chrisley, released from prison.
Julie and Todd Chrisley served more than two years in prison for financial crimes before receiving a full presidential pardon from President Donald Trump in May 2025.

title: As hunting season ramps up in Maine, the state's Hunters for the Hungry program is ready
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As hunting season ramps up in Maine, the state's Hunters for the Hungry program is ready
Hunting season is underway in Maine with expanded archery season for deer. Maine Resident Only Day for the deer hunt is on Oct. 31, and firearms season starts on Nov. 2.
Moose season wraps up this week in Maine with the antlerless-only hunt.
With hunters in the woods and a growing need for help putting food on the table for families across Maine, the state is reminding hunters of the Hunters for the Hungry program.
The program, run through the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF), the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, state biologists, Maine State Troopers, and hunters, supplies wild game meat, which is lean and high in protein, to food pantries, soup kitchens, and homeless shelters around Maine.
Hunters for the Hungry was founded in 1996 and accepts donations of bear, deer, and moose meat. Last year, hunters donated about 10,000 pounds of meat, surpassing the 9,600 pounds donated the year before.
Video in the media player above is from reporting on the program in 2025.
"This program allows hunters to give back in a meaningful way, turning their harvest into life-saving meals for neighbors in need," said Gus Nelson, Director of The Emergency Food Assistance Program (TEFAP) in Maine.
Hunters can donate their game to a participating processor and the meat processing costs will be paid for by DACF. Hunters can also donate a few pounds and keep the rest.
Interested hunters must contact approved meat processors and make sure the processor has the capacity to accept the donation. There are 32 approved processors for the 2026 hunting season, covering 12 of Maine's 16 counties. That is up from the 26 approved processors last year.
Meat processors that are interested in participating should call 207-287-3491 or email H4H@maine.gov.
Donated game must be legally harvested, tagged, and field dressed.
Meat must be properly cared for – follow food safety guidelines, keep it cold, and transport it to an approved processor in a timely manner.
The program is unable to accept donations from animals harvested in the "Do Not Eat" advisory area.
In July of this year, a report found that more than 200,000 Mainers struggled to access enough food in 2024, showing food insecurity is increasing across the state.
Data from Feeding America’s annual "Map the Meal Gap" report estimated that 14.5% of Maine residents experienced food insecurity in 2024, which is up from 13.8% the year before.
The report estimated more than 203,000 people, including nearly 50,600 children and more than 31,000 adults age 60 and older, did not have consistent access to enough nutritious food.
The study also found that Maine continues to have the highest child food insecurity rate in New England.

title: Jay-Z will headline the Super Bowl halftime show at SoFi Stadium in Southern California
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself.
The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he had one request when the league first reached an agreement with Roc Nation: that Jay-Z take the stage himself “whenever the moment felt right to him.”
“From ‘Reasonable Doubt’ to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey,” Jay-Z said in a statement. “Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world’s biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true.”
After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his celebration of the 30th anniversary of “Reasonable Doubt,” the mogul’s 1996 debut album. The concerts included three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium and sold-out performances in London and Paris ahead of a stop at SoFi Stadium over the weekend.
Jay-Z’s Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league’s entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told Goodell, “If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now.”
Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.
Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog also includes the albums “The Blueprint” and “The Black Album,” and hit songs such as “Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem),” “99 Problems” and “Empire State of Mind,” his collaboration with Alicia Keys.
Last year, “Reasonable Doubt” was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
His recent concerts brought out a rotating cast of guests. At SoFi Stadium, his daughter Blue Ivy played piano on “The Story of O.J.” and “Dead Presidents,” while Scarface, John Legend and DJ Khaled joined him on opening night. Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too $hort appeared during Saturday’s finale.
Earlier in the run, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and Nas were among the guests at Yankee Stadium.
Jay-Z has built a career as an executive and entrepreneur. The Brooklyn rapper co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.
Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021. He is also a four-time Emmy winner.
Roc Nation will executive produce the halftime show, with Hamish Hamilton directing.
The halftime show has collected Emmys in recent years. Bad Bunny’s performance in February won a record seven, including best variety special (live), while Kendrick Lamar’s show last year won for music direction.

title: Letter to the Editor: Thirty Years of Intrigue, and Betrayal
Maine secretary of state visits Maranacook High School on mock election day
text:
READFIELD, Maine (WABI) - Students at Maranacook High School met with Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows on Tuesday, which was mock election day across the state.
“Mock Election Day is civics in action. This is a great opportunity for students to practice voting before they turn 18,” Bellows said.
Mock ballots cast statewide
A total of 115 schools across Maine cast mock ballots Tuesday for governor, the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate.
Bellows met with students to answer questions about polling places, election monitoring and bipartisan dialogue.
Student and principal perspectives
For one sophomore, seeing the ballot table in the hallway was a push to learn more.
“I want to know about what’s going on in the world and not just base it off what my dad says, or what my parents are saying, or what teachers are saying,” said Rorie Sage, a sophomore.
Principal Michele LaForge said participation has increased over her five years at the school. The attitude is shifting and remaining civil across four towns with different views.
“I get fewer people telling me that their vote doesn’t matter,” LaForge said.
Mock ballots and voting habits
Bellows cited research that practicing voting early builds lifelong voters. She hopes the mock ballots build that habit.
“It’s important to have a voice in today’s society,” said Serenity Longfellow, a sophomore.

title: Alex Pretti’s parents say federal government is shielding agents involved in his killing
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — The parents of intensive care nurse Alex Pretti said Tuesday the federal government is shielding the immigration enforcement officers involved in their son’s killing, and no one from the government has reached out with any substantive information for nine months.
Michael and Susan Pretti called for the Department of Justice to hold accountable those who shot their 37-year-old son during President Donald Trump’s ramp-up in deportations targeting Minnesota. Federal prosecutors disclosed in recent court filings they had stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the January killings of Pretti and Renee Good by federal officers.
“The federal government went on TV and lied about Alex,” said Susan Pretti, his mother. “They tried to slander his memory to cover up their crime. Not only was it wrong, but it was shameful.”
Within moments of his Jan. 24 death, Trump administration officials sought to portray Pretti, a U.S. citizen and nurse at a veterans hospital, as an armed disruptor intent on doing harm to federal agents when he brought his own gun to a Minneapolis street where officers clashed with protesters. Kristi Noem, the then-Homeland Security secretary, painted the Veterans Administration hospital nurse as a domestic terrorist who violently resisted federal agents. Court records show he had no criminal record.
Video shot by bystanders that day showed Pretti only had a mobile phone in his hand. No footage has since emerged showing him brandishing a weapon or attacking federal agents in the moments before he was killed.
The Prettis spoke Tuesday at a news conference organized by an attorney representing the family, calling their treatment by the Trump administration “cruelty.” They said they decided to speak out after being “stonewalled” by U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and the top federal prosecutor in Minnesota, U.S. Attorney Dan Rosen.
“At every turn, they have ignored us, misled us, and shielded Alex’s killers,” said Michael Pretti, his father. “We are a family who love this country. We trust in the institutions of this country. We believe in the rule of law – and that people should be held accountable through that law.”
After months of reaching out to Rosen’s office, the federal prosecutor agreed to meet with them in July. But the family and their attorney, Steve Schleicher, said that meeting raised more questions than answers, with Rosen refusing to provide even basic information about the status of the federal investigation into Pretti’s death.
A spokesman for Rosen’s office had no comment when reached by The Associated Press on Tuesday. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Pretti family’s remarks.
Minnesota officials sued the Trump administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings of Pretti and Good. The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don’t have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don’t trust the federal government to investigate itself.
The state is still seeking the cellphones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews.
Pretti’s parents recounted how they first learned of his death when they were called by a reporter for The Associated Press.
“We learned about his death from the media as we saw him being shot repeatedly in the back after helping a woman from his community, a fellow Minnesotan, who had been shoved to the ground viciously,” Michael Pretti said. “No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex. No one from the federal government has called us since.”
He said the videos of his son’s killing haunt his family every day.
“I think it haunts many Americans to see a U.S. citizen who was peaceful and in his community shot multiple times on the back, in the back, while on the ground,” the father said, calling his family heartbroken.
“We wish we didn’t have to be here,” he said. “We wish Alex was alive. We wish we were simply in Minneapolis to visit with Alex. For him and me to chat about cars, hiking, biking, or anything that came to our mind. This administration has taken that away from us forever.”

title: UMaine goaltending duo pulls off rare feat with back-to-back shutouts
text:
The University of Maine men’s hockey team accomplished a rare feat in Friday and Saturday night’s 3-0 victories over Colgate at the Alfond Arena.
For just the third time in the program’s 50-year history, the Black Bears swept a team with back-to-back shutouts involving two different goalies.
The Swedish tandem of Petter Wickstrom Stumer and Albin Boija did the honors, with Wickstrom Stumer making 24 saves Friday night and Boija stopping 17 shots Saturday.
Wickstrom Stumer, a Canisius University transfer, is from Stockholm, while Boija is from Sundsvall, which is 225 miles from Sweden’s capital.
The last time it happened was in November 2002, when Jimmy Howard made 17 saves in a 5-0 victory over Mercyhurst and Frank Doyle followed that with a 25-save, 7-0 triumph the next night.
Prior to that, Blair Marsh registered 15 saves in a 5-0 win over Boston College on Feb. 18, 1995, and Blair Allison rejected 22 shots the next night in a 4-0 victory.
Technically, two UMaine goalies combined for back-to-back shutouts over Merrimack on Nov. 1-2, 2024, although Boija earned both victories and played all but seven minutes.
Boija made 15 stops in the 5-0 win in the opener and made 15 more the next night before Patriks Berzins came on in a mop-up role with seven minutes remaining and finished with four saves in the 6-0 triumph.
The fact Colgate is now 0-6 and has scored only five goals shouldn’t overshadow the performances turned in by Wickstrom Stumer and Boija, especially in the first periods. Colgate was the better team in the first period both nights and should have taken leads into the intermission.
Wickstrom Stumer’s 12 saves in Friday’s first period featured a pair of important multiple-save sequences during goalmouth scrambles.
Boija had 10 stops in the first period Saturday when the Black Bears were outshot 10-5.
It was the perfect scenario for UMaine head coach Ben Barr, who wants his two goalies pushing each other and competing for the starting job.
Boija was a second team All-American two years ago but dropped off significantly last year to the point where he actually lost his job at the end of the year to freshman Mathis Rousseau.
He knows he has to get back to that standard of two years ago, and the team needs him to do so because UMaine is going to be in a lot of close, low-scoring games.
However, the 6-foot-6 Wickstrom Stumer showed that he is capable of performing at a high level, and if he can continue to do so, that will give Barr and assistant/goalie coach Alfie Michaud the nice luxury of having two potential elite-level goalkeepers they can rely on.
The team’s sluggish starts are a concern, but the way the Black Bears played in the last two periods, especially Saturday night, was encouraging. UMaine outshot Colgate 27-7 over the final 40 minutes and held Colgate to one shot on goal in the middle period.
The Black Bears’ speed, tenacity and aggression took over the game.
This is the deepest of Barr’s six teams at UMaine, and he has pointed out that it is his most mobile defense corps. Goal scoring is the big question mark, but the early signs are positive with 10 players registering at least three points, including eight with four and five with at least five. Fifteen have dented the scoresheet with at least a goal or an assist.
And the defense corps has been getting involved in the offense which will help significantly.
Last year’s defense corps produced 19 goals in 35 games and the current blue-liners have already scored five times in six games led by sophomore Loic Usereau’s three goals and Bemidji State transfer Isa Parekh’s two. Parekh also has three assists and sophomore Lukas Peterson has five assists, which is second on the team to senior center Max Scott’s six.
Up front, UMass Lowell transfer Lee Parks has a five-game goal-scoring streak, and his five goals tie him for fifth in the country among players at the 56 schools who have already played a game this season. The six Ivy League schools have yet to play a regular season contest.
He is tied for seventh in goals per game (.83). The junior right wing’s two game-winning goals tie him for first.
Parks, who also has an assist, is on a line with longtime friend Will Gerrior, who has set him up on three of his goals with nice cross-ice passes. Left wing Gerrior has four assists, and the center of that line, senior alternate captain Max Scott, has a team-high six assists. Scott’s 1.2 assists per game is tied for ninth in the nation.
Barr also has a well-seasoned line involving players who have combined to play 306 college games between them.
That line features graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler (1 goal, 3 assists), senior center and alternate captain Sully Scholle (1 goal, 3 assists) and senior right wing Charlie Russell, who will look to find the scoresheet for the first time this weekend when UMaine visits Boston University at 7 p.m. Friday and 6 p.m. Saturday for its first two Hockey East games.
Senior left wing and Robert Morris transfer Tanner Klimpke is tied for second in the country with three power play goals, and he also has three assists. He was on a line with Arizona State transfer Sam Alfano (2 goals, 1 assist), who was the right wing. Falmouth’s Brock James centered that line Friday, and vastly improved Jaden Lipinski centered them Saturday, which gave UMaine a line with a pair of 6-foot-4, 210-pounders in Lipinski and Alfano and a 6-2, 182-pound Klimpke.
Barr is comfortable playing any of his 16 forwards and nine defensemen on a given night.
UMaine, ranked 19th in the weekly national USCHO poll, will get severely tested by a highly skilled BU team ranked 14th in one poll and tied for 13th in the other and that has 18 NHL draft picks, including 11 who were selected in the top two rounds.

title: DiMillo’s co-owner to receive lifetime achievement award
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Steve DiMillo, co-owner of DiMillo’s on the Water in Portland, has been named this year’s Lifetime Achievement Award winner by HospitalityMaine.
The trade group, which represents the state’s lodging, restaurant and hospitality industry, recently announced the award. DiMillo and others will be honored at HospitalityMaine’s annual awards dinner on Nov. 16.
The DiMillo family opened DiMillo’s on the Water, a floating restaurant and Portland landmark, in 1982. The family’s restaurant roots in Portland stretch back to 1954, when Tony DiMillo opened Anthony’s on Fore Street.
“Steve is a kind and generous man and tireless supporter of Portland’s restaurant and hospitality community and businesses throughout Maine,” said Becky Jacobson, retired executive director of HospitalityMaine.
The group has also named Paige Gould, co-owner of Portland’s Central Provisions and Tipo, as well as Finestkind in Saco, as Restaurateur of the Year. Chef Jose Ochoa of Natalie’s at Camden Harbour Inn won the Chef of the Year award.
The awards ceremony is part of the annual HospitalityMaine Summit, slated for Nov. 16-17 at the Portland Sheraton at Sable Oaks. Tickets for the awards reception and dinner are $110; register for the event online at HospitalityMaine.com.

title: Bangor credit union branch breaks ground at State Street and Broadway
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The County Federal Credit Union (CFCU) broke ground Tuesday morning on a new branch in Bangor.
The branch is planned for the corner of State Street and Broadway. Bangor officials and others were at the site to see plans and congratulate CFCU Tuesday.
The new location is a move from the credit union’s previous Bangor location on Main Street, which it leased. It will be CFCU’s ninth branch.
CFCU President Ryan Ellsworth said expanding operations south is the natural progression after the credit union merged with Penobscot Federal Credit Union in 2021.
“Aroostook County has not shown significant growth over the years, population has been decreasing slowly for a number of years, and if you project that out, we’re afraid that our membership’s going to be much smaller, 10, 20 years from now,” Ellsworth explained. “And we want more members to have access to our great team and our great services.”
Ellsworth adds that CFCU is always looking for ways to expand, and the new Bangor branch will not be “the last next step.”
Construction is expected to be finished sometime in the summer. Doors will most likely open in July.

title: Serial killer Ted Bundy linked to another 1970s homicide
text:
PARK CITY, Utah (AP) — DNA connects serial killer Ted Bundy to the death of another Utah teenager, authorities announced Tuesday, exactly 52 years after her body was discovered in the woods by a hunter.
Bundy has been dead since 1989, but the tally of his confirmed victims continues to grow due to advances in DNA testing. He killed at least 30 women and girls in multiple states in the 1970s, and many more escaped or survived with injuries.
Investigators are satisfied that Bundy was responsible for killing 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith in 1974, a death that had long been listed as a cold case, Summit County Attorney Margaret Olson said at a news conference.
They were able to close the case by making crucial connections with DNA found on Smith and Laura Aime, another Bundy victim whose case was resolved last April in Utah County. Bundy’s DNA was on file in Florida, where he was convicted and ultimately executed.
Besides that evidence, Smith’s death showed hallmarks of Bundy’s “pattern, motive, means and opportunity,” Olson said.
Decades-old evidence was key to the case
Utah’s state crime lab got new technology in 2023 that extracts DNA from samples even if they are small, degraded from age or contain DNA from multiple people.
“This case demonstrates the importance of preserving evidence,” said Salt Lake County Sheriff Rosie Rivera, whose department has also investigated homicides linked to Bundy.
“We have to solve these cases to the best of our ability,” she said, explaining the importance of tapping science, even so many years later. “Nobody is just going to walk away and just blame everything on Ted Bundy, even though many cases have been that way. Here in the state of Utah, we take it very seriously.”
Smith’s relatives were contacted about the findings but declined to attend the news conference and declined to speak to reporters, the Summit County Sheriff’s Office said. Her parents are deceased.
Smith’s father was police chief in Midvale, south of Salt Lake City. She was at a pizza parlor and a restaurant before she disappeared on Oct. 18, 1974, The Salt Lake Tribune reported at the time. Nine days later, her body was found in Summit County.
“With every case closure, may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out,” Utah County Sgt. Mike Reynolds said.
Bundy investigations are not finished
Bundy was executed by electric chair in Florida in 1989 after being convicted of three murders, including the killing of two women at the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University.
He gave a series of confessions in his final days, including to some crimes that were previously unknown to police. Not all of those cases have been confirmed.
Besides Florida and Utah, authorities said Bundy had victims in Colorado, Idaho and Washington state. They said they’re especially working to solve the 1974 death of 16-year-old Nancy Wilcox of Utah.
Solving the Smith homicide “does not close the book on Ted Bundy,” said Det. Ben Pender of the Salt Lake County Sheriff’s Office, which has the Wilcox investigation. “Information kind of leads to Ted Bundy but again we’re not for certain on Nancy Wilcox. We’re going to continue to work that case.”

title: A mystery fire truck has been driving through a small southern Maine town
text:
A fire truck unknown to any local departments has been spotted on roads near Lake Arrowhead with its lights and sirens activated, the Limerick Fire Department reported on social media.
“Please know this vehicle is not associated in any way with the Limerick Fire Department or any surrounding town,” the department said, adding that the truck is believed to be privately owned.
“No emergency response was occurring at the time this vehicle went through the area,” the department said.
Owning a fire truck privately in Maine is not illegal, but operating lights and sirens is limited to vehicles working in certain official capacities.

title: Maine's "Mr. Halloween" has 14,000 candy bars to give away this year
text:
Maine's "Mr. Halloween" has 14,000 candy bars to give away this year
Halloween is on Saturday, and kids in costumes will be going door to door looking for candy.
One of the most popular destinations each year is at Peter Geiger's business at 70 Mt. Hope Avenue in Lewiston. He has been giving away thousands of candy bars each year for more than 30 years.
Geiger was the editor of the Farmers' Almanac before selling the publication earlier this year to Farmers’ Almanac LLC, a New York–based company.
Geiger will release the secret password for his trick-or-treat special on Friday, Oct. 30, even though the trick-or-treating itself is on Saturday.
On Monday, he gave Maine's Total Coverage a sneak peek of what will be happening.
Thanks to a donation from Reny's, he told us that he will have more than 14,000 king-sized candy bars to give away this year to kids of any age.
"This has become such an event in Lewiston and Auburn and I want to make it as much fun as I could possibly do," Geiger said. "I think what really drives me on this is the fact that it's families. They're having fun, they're laughing, they're dressed up in all kinds of costumes.
The event is a little different each year.
Last year, Geiger had 10,000 candy bars, allowing each person with the secret password to take three. He also had a witch's cauldron filled with 8,500 mini-bars that visitors were able to grab by the handful. And visitors number 1,000, 2,000 and 3,000 last year each got a five-pound chocolate bar.
There were also dozens of inflatable and mechanical creatures and a DJ. In 2026, Geiger says he will have even more inflatables and characters, as well as a bubble machine.
In 2024, Geiger handed out 8,260 king-sized candy bars.

title: Grand jury refuses to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, AP sources say
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department on Tuesday failed to secure a grand jury indictment against a former White House staffer who provided dramatic but disputed testimony against President Donald Trump before a House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection, according to two people familiar with the matter.
A grand jury in Washington rejected prosecutors’ request to return an indictment against Cassidy Hutchinson, said the people, who spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the case. It’s the latest setback in the Justice Department’s efforts to persuade grand jurors in the nation’s capital to bring politically sensitive cases.
Details of prosecutors’ allegations against Hutchinson were not immediately clear, but Republican lawmakers had accused her of lying under oath in her explosive testimony in 2022 about Trump’s behavior on Jan. 6, when a mob of his supporters stormed the Capitol to halt the congressional certification of his election loss to Democrat Joe Biden.
The effort to indict Hutchinson was hardly isolated. It is part of a surge in politically sensitive actions by the Justice Department in the run-up to next week’s midterm elections targeting perceived adversaries of the president, including a new attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey and a search by federal agents of the home of outspoken Trump critic and Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.
It’s highly unusual for grand juries to decline to return indictments, but the Justice Department under Trump has been rebuked by citizens in the nation’s capital in a number of high-profile cases. A grand jury in Washington earlier this year declined to indict Democratic lawmakers in connection with a video they recorded urging U.S. service members to follow established military protocols and reject orders they believe to be unlawful.
An attorney for Hutchinson didn’t immediately return a phone message seeking comment Tuesday.
Hutchinson said Trump was angry and defiant on Jan. 6
Hutchinson’s testimony, at a surprise hearing announced just 24 hours earlier, was seen at the time as particularly powerful given her proximity to power as special assistant to Mark Meadows, Trump’s chief of staff.
Hutchinson described an angry, defiant president who was trying to let armed protesters avoid security screenings at a rally that morning to protest his 2020 election defeat and who later grabbed at the steering wheel of the presidential SUV when the Secret Service refused to let him go to the Capitol. And when the events at the Capitol spiraled toward violence, with the crowd chanting “Hang Mike Pence,” she testified that Trump declined to intervene.
Trump at the time denied much of what Hutchinson said on his social media platform, Truth Social. He called her a “total phony” and “bad news.”
Hutchinson’s description of the altercation inside the presidential SUV was regarded as particularly explosive, even as she acknowledged during her testimony that she was relaying what she had heard from a White House security official and did not have firsthand knowledge of the episode because she was not there.
Her account was quickly disputed.
In March 2024, House Republicans released a previously undisclosed transcript of the Select Committee’s interview with a Secret Service officer who drove the presidential SUV. That transcript of the presidential limo driver contradicted some of Hutchinson’s testimony but corroborated other aspects of her account, including Trump’s attempt to join the mob scene at the Capitol.
The driver said he did not see the altercation that Hutchinson described.
But the driver said Trump “never grabbed the steering wheel.”
“I didn’t see him, you know, lunge to try to get into the front seat at all,” the driver said.
Hutchinson has alleged that members of Trump’s inner circle dangled job opportunities and financial assistance while she was cooperating with the committee. She also testified that her own lawyer — a former ethics counsel in the Trump White House — told her “the less you remember, the better.”
“It feels ridiculous, because in my heart I knew where my loyalties lied, and my loyalties lied with the truth,” she told the committee. “And I never wanted to diverge from that.”
The U.S. House of Representatives impeached Trump in 2021 on allegations that he incited the mob that attacked the Capitol, but he was later acquitted by the Senate. The Justice Department under Biden charged Trump with felony offenses, accusing him of illegally working to overturn his 2020 election loss in the run-up to the Capitol attack, but then-special counsel Jack Smith abandoned the case after Trump’s 2024 presidential victory. Longstanding Justice Department policy says sitting presidents cannot face criminal prosecution.
Hutchinson, a native of Pennington, New Jersey, previously worked in the White House Office of Legislative Affairs and interned for Republicans, including Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection at https://apnews.com/hub/capitol-siege.

title: We compared AI travel videos with real listings; here’s what we found
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (InvestigateTV) — A scroll through social media can make a mountain cabin, beachfront rental or luxury resort look like an easy escape. But some AI-generated travel videos may not accurately show the property a viewer would book or the price a viewer would pay.
We reviewed TikTok posts promoting real hotels, resorts and vacation rentals. The posts included TikTok labels stating they were generated with artificial intelligence and that the creator earns commission. Several directed viewers to major booking services, including Expedia and Booking.com.
In multiple examples, the apparently AI-generated video did not appear to match the property’s official listing or other photos.
In others, the price promoted in the video was not a deal we could locate when we checked the listing.
Using AI to create travel posts is not inherently illegal. The concern is whether commercial posts create a misleading impression about a real property, price, amenity, review or travel experience.
What we found
Altered exterior and living room
One TikTok video promoted a real rental home in the Blue Ridge Mountains. But a comparison with the property’s listing showed apparent differences in the home’s exterior and the layout and furnishings of the living room.
The linked property was real. The video, however, appeared to present an altered version of it.
The same post promoted a price of $93 per person per night. The video did not identify travel dates, occupancy, taxes, fees or other terms for that price.
When InvestigateTV/Atlanta News First checked the listing, the rate displayed was about $865 per night.
The video did not state travel dates or terms for that price, and we didn’t find the advertised deal on the booking link or the property’s official booking sites.
A doorway changes — and so does the neighboring home
Another AI-generated video promoted a beachfront rental in Panama City Beach.
In the video, the kitchen appeared to connect directly to a bedroom.
The actual property listing showed that opening leads outside. A side-by-side comparison also showed differences in the neighboring house.
Different properties in one video
A separate video presented features as part of the Gaylord National Resort at National Harbor, outside Washington, D.C.
But we found the video appeared to combine features from more than one Gaylord resort.
Among them: an outdoor lazy river that is not located at Gaylord National.
Other advertised deals
We also reviewed posts promoting specials such as three nights for about $359 at Pine Mountain Callaway Resort And Gardens in Georgia.
We could not find that offer through the listed booking link or the property’s official website when we checked October 2026.
Who earns when viewers book?
The posts we reviewed included TikTok’s “Creator earns commission” label. That label indicates the creator may receive a commission when a qualifying purchase is made through a link, but it does not by itself verify every claim in a video about a property, price or availability.
TikTok told us it requires AI generated content labels on realistic scenes or people, adding that misleading AI content would prohibit the account from making a commission. The misleading content would need to be caught in the platforms own general moderation or by a user reporting it.
Expedia said the accounts we shared with them “don’t appear to be connected to Expedia’s affiliate program and the discounts featured in the videos are not an Expedia affiliate offering.”
Booking.com did not respond by our deadline.
What to check before booking
Atlanta-based travel agent Nicholas Santine of TravelMation said travelers should not rely on a social media video alone when deciding where to book.
“Google the location. Google the hotel... See reviews. Look at review photos. Look at other people’s experience. Go beyond what the influencers and what the algorithm wants you to see,” Santine advised.
He added that booking through direct links on an app may not be the safest route.
“Go to the exact website,” he said. “Don’t trust the link. Don’t trust everything you see. You know, if it’s too good to be true, it probably is.”
Santine said a real-life travel agent is the safest best to avoid losing money or showing up to a place that isn’t as advertised.
Most travel agents will be licensed, and they are primarily free to use. The agent receives commission from the resorts and amenities.
Before booking a trip promoted on social media:
- Search for the property independently 
  - Do not rely only on the link in the post
- Compare the video with the official listing
  - Check the hotel’s website or the rental listing on sites such as Airbnb or Vrbo
- Compare like with like 
  - Use the same travel dates, number of guests, taxes and fees before deciding whether a price matches
- Look beyond the creator’s video 
  - Review several recent traveler photos and reviews
  - Be cautious if comments look generic, repetitive, limited or disabled
- Check the disclosures 
  - Look for AI, advertising, affiliate and sponsorship labels
- Protect your payment 
  - Avoid sending deposits through direct messages, wire transfers, crypto, gift cards or unfamiliar payment apps
  - A credit card may provide options to dispute some charges
- Save your evidence 
  - Keep screenshots of the post, booking page, terms and receipts if something goes wrong
What the law says
There is no single U.S. law requiring every AI-generated travel post to carry a label. But existing consumer-protection and advertising law can apply when commercial content makes a materially misleading claim.
The Federal Trade Commission said its truth-in-advertising standards apply to endorsements on social media. A paid endorsement or other relationship that could affect how viewers judge a recommendation may need to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously.
Federal rules also address certain fake consumer reviews, testimonials and fake indicators of social-media influence, such as bots or accounts that do not reflect real people’s activities or experiences.
In Georgia, the Fair Business Practices Act declares unfair or deceptive practices in consumer transactions unlawful. The law includes conduct that causes confusion about the source, sponsorship, affiliation or geographic origin of goods or services.
The bottom line: an AI label does not itself prove a post is deceptive or necessarily resolve whether it is.
The key question is whether the content leads consumers to believe that a property, price, deal, review or personal endorsement is real or verified when it is not.
Encountered a potentially misleading travel post?
TikTok advises users who see a post containing AI-generated content that goes against its guidelines, including AI impersonation, to report it:
From the TikTok app
- Go to the post and tap the Share button or press and hold the post, then tap Report
- Tap Misinformation, then tap Deepfakes, synthetic media, and manipulated media
- Tap Submit
From a web browser
- Go to the post and hover over the More options button at the top, then click Report
- Click Misinformation, then click Deepfakes, synthetic media, and manipulated media
- Click Submit
