title: Music icon Donnie Iris dies at 83
text:
Donnie Iris, rock icon and music legend, dies at 83
Donnie Iris, a rock legend, died Monday at the age of 83, according to friend and concert promoter Rich Engler.
Video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
The Ellwood City, Pennsylvania, native first came to fame with his band The Jaggerz, best known for their hit "The Rapper." He then went on to have a successful solo career with his band The Cruisers, making hits such as "Ah! Leah!" and "Love is Like a Rock."
Earlier this month, Iris announced his retirement from future performances after experiencing health issues.
He gave his final performance at the grand opening of Citizens Live at The Wylie in Pittsburgh's historic Hill District neighborhood.
In a statement announcing his retirement, he said, "Music has given me far more than I could ever put into words. From the earliest days to every chapter of my life, your support has been a constant source of joy and inspiration. Thank you for your loyalty, your energy, and your love through all the years. It has been my great honor to make music for you."
A cause of death has not been released. In 2023, Iris began receiving treatment for bladder cancer.
Those who worked with him and called him a friend say the man on stage was the same as the man off stage.
"He was a wonderful man and a wonderful representative of Pittsburgh music. So he's done us all proud," musician Shari Richards said.
Rich Engler, a longtime concert promoter who began working with Iris in 1966, praised his vocal abilities and passion.
"The volume he and the high notes that he could hit, and everything with such passion like 'Ah! Leah!' And all the high notes. I can't even possibly do it. And he knocked audiences out, even down to the last," Engler said.
Engler, who produced numerous shows with Iris over the years, shared a memorable moment from their time working together.
"I probably produced at least 20 or 30 shows with them over the years, and probably one of the most famous. I pulled out a poster of Donnie Iris and the Cruisers and special guest Bon Jovi. I mean, wow," Engler said.
Friends say Iris embodied his music and left a lasting impression on those who knew him.
"We're going to miss him personally, forever. But his songs will live on forever," Engler said.
Even those who grew up listening to Iris' hits were shocked and saddened to hear of his passing. They've been playing his biggest hits to honor him.
"It's a weird feeling. I mean, local legend, you know, Donnie Iris, I'm just going to be listening to "Ah! Leah!" the entire way home as a tribute," said Michael Caponi.

title: Why can’t we hunt mourning doves in Maine?
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
I have never hunted mourning doves, or any kind of dove for that matter, but I would like to. Every winter, several doves sun themselves atop the woodpile under our south-facing front porch. When I go down to replenish the living room wood supply, they blast off like a rocket.
I’ve often wondered if my wingshooting abilities are still good enough to match their speed. I would like to find out, but I can’t because Maine is one of just nine states that ban dove hunting or do not list doves as a legal migratory game bird. Of the six New England states, Rhode Island is the only one with a dove hunting season in its 2026-27 Hunting and Trapping Regulation Guide.
A friend of mine in Texas, however, hunts doves. While hunting grouse with him in Piscataquis County a few weeks ago, he told me dove hunting is highly anticipated each year in his home state. It’s a really big thing, and doves are the most popular game bird in Texas.
He didn’t know how many doves are hunted annually but guessed the number was in the tens of thousands, given the split season and generous bag and possession limits.
Being the curious type, I researched the numbers a few days after his departure from the Portland airport. According to the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, some 300,000 to 350,000 resident and nonresident hunters pursue doves in Texas each year.
The department doesn’t publish the number of mourning doves killed each fall, but Texas has the largest dove population in the country and leads the nation in dove hunting. The state accounts for more than 30% of the national total, according to the report. You do the math. The numbers run into the millions.
On our way home from the grouse trip, my Texas friend was surprised when I mentioned that we don’t hunt doves in Maine. He wondered why, and I thought it was a good question.
Mourning doves are migratory birds protected under the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act. Although the law protects them nationally, the federal framework allows states to establish hunting seasons and set bag and possession limits.
Forty-one states have dove hunting seasons, but Maine is not one of them.
In its official migratory game bird regulations, the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife lists three bird families: Anatidae, which includes ducks and geese; Rallidae, which includes rails and gallinules; and Scolopacidae, which includes woodcock and snipe.
Mourning doves belong to a different family, Columbidae, which is not included in the list of huntable migratory birds. Because Maine has not established an authorized hunting season for them, mourning doves cannot legally be hunted or possessed as game.
That explains the legal reason we can’t hunt mourning doves here. But why hasn’t Maine established a season when federal guidelines allow it?
While researching this column, I couldn’t find official figures or estimates of Maine’s mourning dove population, or determine whether recent studies or surveys had been conducted. I found only indications that doves have been here for a while and that their numbers and range may be increasing. Whether that’s true, I have no idea.
I can’t recall seeing a dove as a kid, but I see them now.
Perhaps dove numbers are not large enough to support a hunting season, and the MDIFW is right on the money not to include the family Columbidae on its list of huntable migratory birds.
But I think there are other factors at play that help answer the question: Will we ever hunt doves in Maine?
My thinking is that Mainers generally consider mourning doves gentle songbirds, and hunting them is not high on anyone’s priority list. Like Sunday hunting, bear baiting and some other topics, dove hunting would no doubt prove controversial and spark a firestorm of protests from anti-hunting groups and birdwatchers.
Who needs the hoopla, especially when Maine hunters can pursue grouse, woodcock and a long list of other migratory game birds?
So the answer is no. I don’t believe we’ll ever hunt mourning doves here in Maine, or at least not anytime soon.
But that’s OK. I’ve long been a grouse-loving fan, and still am. I can always shoot down to Rhode Island or take my friend up on his open invitation to give it a try in Texas.
It’s a long way to go, but I would really like to find out if my wingshooting is still up to the challenge.

title: UMaine faculty, students hold emergency town hall over planned staff cuts
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Orono, Maine (WABI) -University of Maine faculty and students gathered Monday night for an emergency town hall in response to expected cuts to staff positions at the university.
Unions, students and legislators spoke out against the staff layoffs. Speakers said every professor, counselor and advisor makes a difference in the lives of students, and that removing them would have a negative impact on the school.
The town hall comes after UMaine President Joan Ferrini-Mundy recently outlined mounting financial pressures in a letter to the university community.
She pointed to shifting federal funding, deferred building maintenance and inflation as major driving factors.
Ferrini-Mundy said the university has exhausted short-term fixes and its core reserves have dwindled, leaving leadership facing difficult decisions, including potential staff and faculty layoffs.
Not everyone is on board with the proposed cuts.
“We want there to be a parallel review with administration costs versus cutting the lowest paid employees, faculty and staff. We need to make sure that any cuts that are made aren’t impacting students. My hope is to really increase state appropriations and really elect the right legislators who are pro-public education,” said Sara Abronze, President of Universities of Maine Professional Staff Association.
“It’s these kind of faculty staff that actually are the kind of people I interface with as a student who have made it possible for me to be a student. And I think they shouldn’t be the ones on the chopping block,” said Maeve Durkee, a University of Maine senior.
A draft budget with the administration’s priorities will be submitted in January.
Decisions on program cuts and staffing will be finalized by June 30.

title: FBI raids mansion as part of an investigation into former Rep. Eric Swalwell
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal law enforcement agents searched a Beverly Hills home early Tuesday as part of an investigation into Eric Swalwell, who resigned from Congress amid a wave of sexual misconduct allegations, two people familiar with the investigation told The Associated Press.
Agents searched the home of wealthy developer and Swalwell donor Stephen Cloobeck, where the ex-Congressman spent time before resigning from office in April, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation.
Swalwell, D-Calif., has denied criminal wrongdoing.
Messages seeking comment were left for Swalwell’s lawyer and for a lawyer who represented Cloobeck in another matter.
Cloobeck, who founded the Diamond Resorts International timeshare company and ran last year for California governor, contributed more than $23,000 to Swalwell’s congressional campaigns since 2017, federal campaign finance records show.
He told the New York Post in April that he cut ties with Swalwell as accusations against him mounted.
“I am no longer associated with a man that takes advantage of women,” Cloobeck told the newspaper. “I support women’s rights.”
In May, Cloobeck was charged with witness intimidation in an unrelated case. He has pleaded not guilty. In August, the online prediction market platform Kalshi temporarily banned him after it said he bought $10,000 worth of contracts on his short-lived gubernatorial candidacy.
Tuesday’s search is the latest escalation in the federal investigation of Swalwell — one of several probes begun after a woman came forward with allegations that he sexually assaulted her twice, including when she worked for him.
The San Francisco Chronicle, followed by CNN, first reported the allegations. CNN also reported that three other women alleged various kinds of sexual misconduct by Swalwell, including sending them unsolicited explicit messages or nude photos.
Around the same time, another woman came forward with allegations that Swalwell raped her at a Southern California hotel in 2018. She said she had one glass of wine and believes that Swalwell drugged her. She said she planned to make a report to law enforcement.
Asked about the search at Cloobeck’s address, FBI spokesperson Lourdes Arocho said: “Early this morning the FBI conducted an operation in the Los Angeles region related to an ongoing criminal investigation. We have no further comment.”
In August, federal agents seized electronic devices from Swalwell at the San Francisco airport and searched his Washington home.
Swalwell, an Iowa native, was elected in 2012 and represented a House district east of San Francisco. He launched a presidential run in April 2019 but ended it a few months later after failing to catch on with voters.
The seven-term lawmaker had been seen as one of the leading candidates in California’s gubernatorial race before dropping out after the allegations surfaced.
The office of Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg has said it is also investigating Swalwell after a former staffer told CNN and the Chronicle that Swalwell raped her at a hotel while he was in New York City for a charity gala in 2024.
In a statement, Bragg’s office encouraged “survivors and anyone with knowledge of these allegations to contact our Special Victims Division.”
Los Angeles prosecutors were also said to be weighing charges.
Swalwell was one of Republican President Donald Trump’s top Democratic antagonists in Congress. He was a prominent member of the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees during Trump’s first term and served as one of several Democratic prosecutors for Trump’s second impeachment after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.
Swalwell was removed from the Intelligence Committee by then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., in 2023 based on Swalwell’s contact with a suspected Chinese spy, Christine Fang.
Fang was reported to have come into contact with Swalwell’s campaign as he was first running for Congress in 2012 and to have participated in fundraising for his 2014 campaign.
Federal investigators alerted Swalwell to their concerns and briefed Congress about Fang in 2015, at which point Swalwell says he cut off contact with her. He was not accused of wrongdoing and a House Ethics Committee investigation that was opened in 2021 closed two years later without any action.

title: Special needs teacher accused of pouring hot sauce on student’s tongue as a punishment
text:
HOUSTON COUNTY, Ala. (WTVY/Gray News) - An Alabama special needs teacher is facing child abuse charges after deputies say she poured hot sauce on a student’s tongue.
Heather Varner Hunter, a 46-year-old special needs teacher at Cottonwood Elementary School, allegedly used hot sauce to punish a student for sticking out their tongue in September. A Houston County Sheriff’s Office investigation followed.
Jail records show Hunter was arrested Monday afternoon. She is no longer employed by the Houston County School System, according to Superintendent Brandy White.
White said the school system cooperated fully with authorities, and all information has been turned over to the Alabama Department of Human Resources.
Hunter was named Teacher of the Month in March, according to 95.5 WTVY-FM. She said she had taught at Cottonwood for eight years and spent 18 years as an educator.
Hunter was released after posting a $2,500 bond.

title: Physical therapist takes simple approach to end her chronic pain
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Research from the National Library of Medicine shows more than 30% of the world’s population suffers from chronic pain.
That’s 2.4 billion people who might feel hope after hearing Allyn Minton’s story.
The Nashville-based licensed physical therapist has been pain-free for a full year, thanks to a breakthrough she says has changed her mind.
Minton opened Swell Studio after turning to the low-impact exercise in her 20s.
She had injured her back while transferring a patient. She learned to manage her pain with daily, core-strengthening exercise and physical therapy. That is, until debilitating pain returned every year, on a certain day.
“Over the years, as I would get stressed through times in my life, my dad getting cancer and passing away, my back would start to just go out on me,” Minton said. “I went to the doctor, and he said, ‘Allyn, you were here last year to the day.’”
The debilitating pattern repeated itself, until one year ago.
Mind-body connection
“As I started calming the nervous system and looking at those thoughts, slowly with the repetition of affirmations — it’s that repetition that’s key — my thoughts started to change. And my back pain disappeared,” Minton said.
A 2022 review of multiple studies in the Harvard Gazette explains how adding psychological therapies with physical ones, including reframing negative thoughts, can change how the body feels pain.
Research on neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to rewire itself, shows how repeated thoughts and behaviors can build new pathways in the brain and alleviate chronic pain.
“If the body is tense and in fight or flight, it doesn’t feel safe enough to let the mind relax and open and be receptive to change,” Minton said.
Minton believes the simple step of adding affirmations for 20 minutes a day has helped calm her nervous system, offering hope to millions that healing is possible with the power of the mind.

title: Rainbarrow Art Studio marks 20 years in the county
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LITTLETON, Maine (WAGM) - Local artist Frank Sullivan has spent 20 years painting and drawing at Rainbarrow Studio, a dream that began with a plan written down on paper to move his family to Maine and create art.
For 20 years, Sullivan has been coming into his studio, picking up a brush and creating work he says he cannot always predict.
“I always challenge myself in the way that I work. I never know what a painting or a drawing is going to look like when I begin it,” Sullivan said.
Sullivan said that uncertainty is part of what keeps him creating, tracing back to why he came to Maine in the first place.
“It feels like quite an accomplishment and it seemed to come up very quickly, but when I came up here to Maine, I just had a dream and not much else of turning this old building into an art studio and becoming an artist and I didn’t really know what was going to happen,” Sullivan said.
Turning a shell of a building into a studio
The building that became Rainbarrow Studio needed work, and Sullivan spent months transforming it into a gallery and art studio.
“It was really just a shell of a building with exposed rafters, no electricity. There was an overhead door in the front. The windows in the back didn’t open. So, and I’m not really a carpenter or an architect, but I kind of mapped out a design,” Sullivan said.
By September 2006, the studio was ready. Sullivan opened it to the public, began teaching classes, and made art inspired by the county.
“I’m just really grateful that I’ve been able to remain here doing this and thrive and the community has been so welcoming and supportive,” Sullivan said.
Twenty years later, the studio is still a place where Sullivan makes art.

title: Terwilliger Family Light Show brings Halloween magic — and holiday tradition — to Hancock County
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) - Halloween lights, music and community spirit are shining bright in Ellsworth.
The Terwilliger Family Light Show runs Friday through Sunday, drawing crowds for a free, music-synced show like no other.
From 48 channels to 38,000
Bob Terwilliger says it started in his childhood with old-fashioned string lights — and blown fuses.
“This starts back in my childhood believe it or not. I used to go crazy with regular old fashioned lights when I was a kid.”
In November 2020, the family decided to try a full show with just 48 light channels. Now, they run 38,000 channels — taking a full week to set up.
“In 2020, we decided to kick it up a notch because we figured everybody needed a little something to look forward to.”
A community tradition
Every year, letters pour in about the show — a reminder of why they keep it free.
“We get letters every year from children, from parents. Some of them tug at your heart strings pretty hard, not going to lie.”
“After seven years, we’re seeing people say things like you know this is our tradition... this is on our list of places that we have to stop at every year, so it’s nice to see that this is becoming a part of other peoples traditions.”
“I’ve had a very good life, I feel like we’re very blessed and this is definitely worth it... sharing something bright for the community.”
How to watch + give back
- When: Friday through Sunday through Oct. 31
- Cost: Free
- Listen: Tune to 96.9 FM
- Pick a song: Enable location services on the family’s website and add to the queue
- Give back: Donation boxes benefit the SPCA of Hancock County and The Grand Theatre. The family also promotes STEM through xLights.org.
What’s next
The Halloween show ends Oct. 31, then the Christmas show kicks off on Black Friday.
For details, follow the link to their Facebook page or website.
If you go — please be mindful of neighbors and drive down the road to turn around.

title: 6 citizens sue Trump, saying media ban deprives them of news as audience stakeholders
text:
6 citizens sue Trump, saying media ban deprives them of news as audience stakeholders
In the increasingly bitter legal standoff between President Donald Trump and media outlets whose reporting he dislikes, a new and crucial third party has emerged: citizens who watch and read the news and need it to do their jobs.
A lawsuit filed Monday on behalf of six such citizens — essentially representing the wider public audience — argues that it’s not only the rights of news organizations that are violated when Trump bans them from White House premises. Even more fundamentally, the lawsuit argues, such bans violate the public’s right to independent reporting about its president and government.
“The ultimate injury here … is to the democratic public,” says the suit, filed in federal district court in New York against Trump and three key aides, including the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles.
“The First Amendment protects the public’s right to know what its government is doing,” said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute, which filed the lawsuit on behalf of the plaintiffs, along with the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School.
Related video: Betsy Klein: CNN denied access to White House
“The White House cannot decide what information Americans receive by punishing critical reporting,” Fallow said in a statement. “When the White House expels reporters because of their coverage and threatens others with expulsion, it isn’t just the press that suffers — the public loses access to independent reporting and gets something closer to government propaganda.”
The Trump administration, asked for comment on the lawsuit, responded in a statement that it attributed to an unidentified White House official: “No person may demand access to the Oval Office.” It said media that peddle “misinformation and defamation are completely capable of reporting their manufactured stories from directly outside.”
The plaintiffs all rely on White House news for their work
The six plaintiffs are all people who say they rely on independent and diverse White House reporting for their teaching, journalism or advocacy. They include a noted human rights advocate, a political journalist, a Yale history professor, a high school civics teacher, a legal journalist, and a student journalist at the University of Pennsylvania.
The complaint filed Monday recounts how various news organizations that have been targeted by Trump are already battling the administration in the courts. These cases include the current lawsuit by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, whose journalists were banished from the White House in September.
A federal judge recently extended an order preventing the White House from enforcing the ban while the case makes its way through the legal system. Still affected, though, is CNN’s pool coverage of Trump. The White House has been denying the network its usual slots in the video pool covering the president’s activities and travel, and CNN has threatened further action.
Also continuing is the legal case involving The Associated Press, whose reporters were barred last year from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events in retaliation for the outlet’s decision not to follow Trump’s lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, to the Gulf of America.
The New York Times is also involved in litigation, over a Pentagon policy requiring escorts for journalists on its grounds. And ABC is fighting back against the Trump administration in a dispute over renewal of its broadcast licenses.
This lawsuit seeks more wide-ranging relief
The new lawsuit filed Monday, though, is different from previous legal action against the president — first, in that the plaintiffs are ordinary citizens, shifting the focus from news gatherers to news consumers, and thus implying a much larger pool of stakeholders.
The lawsuit reframes the current debate over White House access in at least one key way. The public right to receive information is part of established law, said Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight Institute. However, nobody has yet asserted this right in relation to the White House press corps and the issues currently at stake.
“We wanted to put the injury to the public at the center of the conversation,” Jaffer said.
“It’s one thing for CNN to say, ‘We are here because the public needs us,’” he said. “It’s another for a member of the public to say that interference with the White House press corps undermines our right to information about the government.”
In addition, the litigation seeks more wide-ranging relief.
The suit, which names Trump as a defendant along with Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran, calls not merely for reinstatement of access that has already been impacted, but for a broad injunction that would protect from retaliation every news outlet that covers the White House —- now, and in the future.
“Defendants’ policy of restricting the access of disfavored news organizations deprives the public of the reporting of those organizations,” the complaint says. It also “inevitably deprives them of the independent reporting of other news organizations as well, since every journalist who reports from the White House must now account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked.”
“Plaintiffs ... seek a declaration that the policy is unconstitutional because it imposes restrictions on a limited public forum that are viewpoint-based and unreasonable,” the complaint adds. “They also seek an injunction barring defendants from enforcing the policy.”
Plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a high school teacher and a student journalist
Plaintiff Ethan Young, a student at the University of Pennsylvania and editor-in-chief of The Daily Pennsylvanian, said in an interview that White House reporting has become increasingly important at his college newspaper during Trump’s second term.
“Over the last two years we’ve seen college campuses be a key avenue where President Trump’s policies have really affected people across the country, and Penn’s campus is no stranger to that,” he said.
“So I use White House reporting almost daily to look at what’s happening in both national higher education trends, but also just general federal policy changes, to see what might impact Penn,” Young said. “You never know what policy could have an impact on the Penn student body.”
Especially important to Young and his colleagues at the paper is a diversity of news outlets to choose from.
“We are not in the room. We are not in Washington,” Young said. “The benefit of having access to a variety of publications ... means I am constantly seeing different questions being asked of White House officials.”
And more often than not, he said, that means he’ll get the answer to a question he has, too.
The other plaintiffs are:
— Kenneth Roth, former longtime executive director of Human Rights Watch and a lecturer at Yale’s law school and school of global affairs.

title: A one-city ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine brokered by First Lady Melania Trump is in effect
text:
MYKOLAIV, Ukraine (AP) — A localized ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia took effect early Tuesday ahead of a humanitarian mission led by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, as missile attacks resumed in Kyiv.
Meanwhile, Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister spoke on the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, officials said, in their first-known direct contact since shortly after Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
After the conversation with Putin, the two Nordic leaders had a telephone conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, according to Zelenskyy’s office.
Russia and Ukraine began observing a localized ceasefire in a devastated southern Ukrainian city Tuesday, before a planned humanitarian mission brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, but Moscow kept up its deadly missile attacks on other cities in the meantime.
The local pause in fighting started at 3 a.m. to allow an aid mission into the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky later this week. The situation in Oleshky is desperate, with food and medical supplies running perilously low for the up to 2,000 people still there, as drones and land mines restrict movement.
Deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine, as Moscow’s full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark in February, has undermined previous attempts at limited ceasefires, which quickly unraveled or never took hold.
The humanitarian truce was a high-stakes operation for both Moscow and Kyiv, with both sides keen to win U.S. President Donald Trump’s favor.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators as well as the militaries of the two countries confirmed in separate statements that the Oleshky ceasefire had begun.
Nordic leaders speak by phone to Putin and Zelenskyy, officials say
The call, confirmed by the offices of Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, followed an Oct. 20 meeting in Oslo between the two Nordic leaders, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff.
The call was held in consultation with Ukraine, according to the official statements by the two Nordic countries. Stubb and Støre initiated the call to discuss the war and upcoming trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States that are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in November.
The two European leaders spoke on behalf of their own countries and not the whole of Europe, the statements said.
“The discussion was frank and substantive,” Stubb said. “We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions.”
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs,” Støre said. “The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation.”
Melania Trump and Pope Leo worked for a truce in Oleshky
According to her office, Melania Trump led talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine after meeting with U.N. officials who briefed the American first lady on the situation in Oleshky.
Up to 2,000 people are stranded in the city, unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the U.N. The partly occupied Kherson region of Ukraine where Oleshky is located is notorious for the dangers of Russian drone attacks on soldiers and civilians.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that “so far there have been no reports of violations.”
Pope Leo XIV spoke earlier this month with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging them to allow humanitarian aid into Oleshky and the safe evacuation of civilians, the Vatican said.
Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened.
The Kremlin said at the time that Putin voiced support for the Vatican’s plea, and an agreement was reached to coordinate efforts in this regard.
Moscow and Kyiv have blamed each other for the humanitarian crisis.
Russia, as the occupying power, must under international law ensure that civilians under its occupation live safely. Ukraine has repeatedly tried to negotiate a humanitarian corridor for evacuations and aid delivery with Moscow.
The aid mission is planned ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered talks between delegations from Russia and Ukraine expected next month that will seek to lay the groundwork for detailed peace negotiations later.
Lull in Oleshky uneasy, a Ukrainian official tells The AP
The local ceasefire is due to last through Saturday, or longer if needed. Its geographical scope was unclear, though it was centered on Oleshky and other nearby parts of the Kherson region.
Oleshky is about 550 kilometers (340 miles) southeast of Kyiv, where the Dnipro River separates Russian and Ukrainian forces. Oleshky sits across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, the region’s administrative capital. Russian forces seized Kherson in the early stages of the 2022 full-scale invasion, but retreated across the river several months later.
The Ukrainian-held side of the Kherson region was quiet Tuesday. Only Russian reconnaissance drones were in the sky, local authorities said, though they cautioned it was too early to draw any conclusions and that they didn’t trust Russia.
“It’s too early to say. Let’s wait and see, because you can’t trust the enemy, especially the Russians,” Yaroslav Shanko, head of the Kherson city administration, told The Associated Press.
“There have been previously announced ceasefires more than once, and they had no effect on Kherson … and, let’s say, a lull like this is sometimes even frightening.”
Shanko acknowledged the situation was unusual. He typically travels with a portable drone detector that constantly picks up drones overhead, but it had gone silent. He said he still kept glancing at it, but it showed nothing.
The quiet stands in contrast to daily life in the city, where people are wounded or killed nearly every day, he said.
City services plan to use the pause to carry out utility work that is usually too dangerous because of constant drone activity.
Russian missiles kill at least 3 civilians in Ukraine, officials say
Minutes after 3 a.m., multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded in multiple parts of the country.
Late Monday, the capital also came under attack, when Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 10 injured, city officials said. In Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.
“It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post shortly afterward.
___
Susie Blann and Derek Gatopoulos contributed to this report from Kyiv.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: A dinosaur fossil that looks like a mini T. rex just sold to a mystery buyer for a giant $47 million
text:
A dinosaur fossil that looks like a mini T. rex just sold for a giant $47 million
A dinosaur that looks like a miniature T. rex is now one of the world's most expensive fossils.
The rare skeleton of a Nanotyrannus — recently confirmed to be a distant cousin of Tyrannosaurus rex, not just a young specimen — sold for $47.3 million to a mystery buyer at auction in New York City on Tuesday, according to Sotheby’s. The auction house had expected it to fetch anywhere from $6 to $9 million.
The blockbuster price tag for “Jodi,” as the skeleton is nicknamed, makes it the second-priciest set of dinosaur bones ever sold. This summer, a T. rex fossil known as “Gus” sold for a record $50.1 million at Sotheby's.
The new owner of “Jodi” has, for now, chosen to remain anonymous after outbidding five other prospective buyers online and by phone during the roughly 12-minute live auction, Sotheby’s said.
A Nanotyrannus was about half the length of an adult T. rex, and the two creatures coexisted during the Cretaceous period some 67 million years ago. Nanotyrannus had relatively longer forelimbs and larger hand claws, as well as more slender, blade-like teeth than its famous cousin.
“Jodi” is one of only three such skeletons known to exist. Standing 6.5 feet tall and stretching nearly 20 feet, it has been on display at the auction house’s upper Manhattan headquarters since earlier this month, and is considered almost 70% complete.
The dinosaur is named after Jodi Pierson, the Montana rancher who discovered it on her land in 2019.
Sotheby’s, in a statement, thanked the team of professional fossil hunters whose efforts to discover and excavate the specimen were the focus of the Discovery Channel documentary series “Dino Hunters” in 2020.
“Their commitment to understanding and preserving this remarkable specimen has helped bring us to this moment, a testament to the fact that we can all make major contributions to science,” said Cassandra Hatton, Sotheby’s head of science and natural history.
However, some scientists have opposed such private sales, saying “Jodi” and other significant fossils should be displayed in museums or other institutions so they can be studied by researchers and viewed by the public.
Scientists for decades weren't even sure whether Nanotyrannus represented a distinct type of dinosaur or merely a juvenile T. rex. But research published last year concluded that it was in fact a distinct genus of dinosaur.

title: Israel’s polls close as Netanyahu seeks another term in office. Here’s what exit polls are showing
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli voters delivered a rebuke Tuesday to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with exit polls indicating voters gave his opponents a solid majority in the next parliament. Whether those disparate parties can form a government is uncertain and will likely take weeks of haggling.
The easiest path would involve Netanyahu’s main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, partnering with Arab-led parties, but that could prove politically difficult and potentially alienate other opposition factions.
Exit polls released early Wednesday by major Israeli TV stations suggested that Netanyahu’s bloc and Eisenkot’s each won about 51 seats, and Arab parties won about 18. That would set the stage for weeks of political jockeying before a prime minister is declared — or another round of elections is called.
Eisenkot said the exit polls show a “lack of confidence” in Netanyahu and he vowed to form a new government. Arab voters celebrated the exit polls while supporters of far-right parties aligned with Netanyahu expressed disappointment.
Netanyahu had yet to make a public statement early Wednesday, hours after the exit polls were released.
Like all surveys, exit polls are subject to potential error. Preliminary results are expected in the coming hours. Final results are expected in the coming days and may vary from the exit polls.
An inconclusive result would leave Israel in political limbo after the country’s first national election since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
The race was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s nearly unbroken 17-year rule, which had left Israelis bitterly divided on a host of issues even before the deadliest attack in the country’s history. The resulting wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, along with settler violence in the occupied West Bank, have stoked worldwide outrage, straining ties with Israel’s closest allies and fueling a rise in antisemitism.
Among Israelis, the election was broadly viewed as a struggle over the character of the state, pitting Netanyahu and his ultranationalist and religious allies against those seeking to preserve its liberal and secular foundations. The opposition may soon have to grapple with the social divisions — between right and left, and between Jews and Arabs — that have widened during Netanyahu’s long and polarizing rule.
The process of coalition building will begin
Voter turnout was the highest since 1999, with more than 77% of eligible voters casting ballots, according to the Central Elections Committee. Over 7 million people were eligible to vote, and tens of thousands reportedly arrived from overseas.
Israel’s president will be tasked with asking the party leader with the best prospect of forming a government, usually one with the most seats, to cobble together a coalition. If Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud emerges as the largest party, he could claim that right.
Meanwhile, there will be heavy pressure on Eisenkot to reach a deal with the Arab parties, while Netanyahu and his allies are likely to cast any such alliance as illegitimate and even treasonous.
Netanyahu had warned earlier that Arab parties could make or break the election, saying they were receiving “truly massive support” and heading to the polls in “unprecedented numbers.”
If no one can cobble together a majority coalition, new elections could be held early next year. Israel held five elections between April 2019 and November 2022 because of a similar stalemate.
No single party has ever won an outright majority in the country’s 120-seat parliament, forcing political leaders to forge coalitions. Minority governments are also possible, but they must rely on support or cooperation from parties outside the government to pass legislation.
Netanyahu’s current coalition peaked at 68 members before it began to disintegrate over the past year.
Eisenkot says exit polls point to ‘lack of confidence’ in Netanyahu
As the exit polls were broadcast, supporters at Eisenkot’s party headquarters jumped for joy, chanting his name.
In a speech early Wednesday that focused on national unity, he pledged to form a government and promised “a new era — an era of hope” for Israelis.
“Today, Israel went out to a referendum over the leadership that will lead Israel in the coming years,” Eisenkot said to cheers from supporters. “The people decided in favor of change.”
Eisenkot warned Netanyahu not to “dare use Israel’s security for your political needs” while he is a caretaker prime minister, an apparent reference to reports that the Israeli leader considered an attack against Iran in the sensitive days leading up the election.
At Netanyahu’s party headquarters, filled mainly with media, the few supporters present chanted Netanyahu’s name, draping themselves in flags with his face on them and kissing posters.
Netanyahu’s supporters see him as a steady hand and a consummate statesman who has led Israel through a war of redemption after the country’s darkest hour. They think he is protecting Israel’s security and Jewish identity in the face of international pressure and liberal elites at home.
His detractors see him as a polarizing leader who, beset by an ongoing corruption trial, dragged out the war in Gaza and its hostage crisis for political reasons. They say he is undermining Israel’s independent judiciary and weakening its democratic underpinnings. And they accuse him of abetting the system that has allowed ultra-Orthodox religious Jews to avoid military conscription.
“The present government is driving the country into the ground,” voter Angela Bengur said in Jerusalem.
Eisenkot is viewed by supporters as a capable leader with sterling security credentials who, along with his likely governing partners, could act as a bulwark against creeping illiberalism. As someone personally touched by the conflict — his son and two nephews were killed in Gaza — his backers believe that he feels deeply the pain that still courses through Israel.
Parties that likely would support Eisenkot have vowed to improve Israel’s international standing and work to conscript ultra-Orthodox men while bolstering the independence of the judiciary.
The elections are about “who serves and who evades service — who takes an active part in building this country and who doesn’t,” said voter Nisso Shitrit in Tel Aviv’s Jaffa neighborhood.
Oct. 7 and its aftermath were a major focus of the election
The election is Israel’s first national vote since the Oct. 7 attack that sparked the war in Gaza and related conflicts. In Tel Aviv, families of some killed on Oct. 7 or former hostages held a moment of silence during the vote.
“Remember all those whose voices are no more,” said Yona Adam, whose daughter Mapal Adam was killed.
Israel has found itself increasingly isolated over its conduct in Gaza and the West Bank. Public support among Americans has plummeted, and partners in Europe and elsewhere have slapped sanctions on Israel. Netanyahu faces an international arrest warrant over alleged crimes against humanity in Gaza, allegations he denies.
Also hanging over the election were lingering tensions with Iran. Netanyahu ramped up threats ahead of the vote, warning Tehran it would face “a devastating blow” if it attacked Israel.
___
Associated Press writers across Israel contributed to this report.

title: Aging Untold: Hospice doesn’t have to happen at home
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore compassionate hospice care options beyond the home, focusing on comfort, dignity and family support.
Plus, we share practical advice for older adults stepping up to raise school-aged kids and navigating today’s modern classrooms.
Then, a breast cancer survivor opens up about the emotional toll of chemotherapy-induced hair loss and how she reclaimed her identity and strength.
Hospice care is about comfort, dignity and quality of life.
It isn’t tied to one setting, the Aging Untold experts said. Hospice care can happen in a hospital, in independent living, assisted living, or in a private home.
“For me, it’s whatever brings comfort to the family,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said. “At this point, we’ve got to make sure that the person’s comfortable, that they’re being provided the care and the dignity they deserve.”
Some older adults are raising school-age kids again at a time when school looks nothing like what they remember.
But school itself has changed for everyone, not just older caregivers.
“You may be the oldest member in the PTA, but you’re not probably the most confused,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
The Aging Untold experts say to remember that you have been through this before and find resources that are available to you, including librarians, teachers, tutors, school counselors and parent liaisons.
Hair has always been Lisa Steinhauser’s craft, artistry and expression.
When she started treatment after a diagnosis of triple-negative breast cancer, her hair began to fall out, and that was difficult.
Steinhauser decided to shave off the remaining hair, and her grandchildren did it for her.
Steinhauser said she is now clear of the disease, and she wants people to know there is hope.
The Exoneree Band is using the power of music to heal, to tell their stories and to build a brotherhood unlike any other.
The members were convicted of crimes they did not commit and collectively lost decades of their lives before DNA evidence cleared their names. While they are grateful for their freedom, the scars of their time in prison run deep.
The band members live in different parts of the country and come together to create a sound that is both a celebration of their freedom and a testament to their resilience.
Their setlist is a mix of cover songs, often with a twist to reflect their unique journey, and deeply personal original music.

title: Alex Pretti’s parents say federal government is shielding agents involved in his killing
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — The parents of intensive care nurse Alex Pretti said Tuesday the federal government is shielding the immigration enforcement officers involved in their son’s killing, and no one from the government has reached out with any substantive information for nine months.
Michael and Susan Pretti called for the Department of Justice to hold accountable those who shot their 37-year-old son during President Donald Trump’s ramp-up in deportations targeting Minnesota. Federal prosecutors disclosed in recent court filings they had stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the January killings of Pretti and Renee Good by federal officers.
“The federal government went on TV and lied about Alex,” said Susan Pretti, his mother. “They tried to slander his memory to cover up their crime. Not only was it wrong, but it was shameful.”
Within moments of his Jan. 24 death, Trump administration officials sought to portray Pretti, a U.S. citizen and nurse at a veterans hospital, as an armed disruptor intent on doing harm to federal agents when he brought his own gun to a Minneapolis street where officers clashed with protesters. Kristi Noem, the then-Homeland Security secretary, painted the Veterans Administration hospital nurse as a domestic terrorist who violently resisted federal agents. Court records show he had no criminal record.
Video shot by bystanders that day showed Pretti only had a mobile phone in his hand. No footage has since emerged showing him brandishing a weapon or attacking federal agents in the moments before he was killed.
The Prettis spoke Tuesday at a news conference organized by an attorney representing the family, calling their treatment by the Trump administration “cruelty.” They said they decided to speak out after being “stonewalled” by U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and the top federal prosecutor in Minnesota, U.S. Attorney Dan Rosen.
“At every turn, they have ignored us, misled us, and shielded Alex’s killers,” said Michael Pretti, his father. “We are a family who love this country. We trust in the institutions of this country. We believe in the rule of law – and that people should be held accountable through that law.”
After months of reaching out to Rosen’s office, the federal prosecutor agreed to meet with them in July. But the family and their attorney, Steve Schleicher, said that meeting raised more questions than answers, with Rosen refusing to provide even basic information about the status of the federal investigation into Pretti’s death.
A spokesman for Rosen’s office had no comment when reached by The Associated Press on Tuesday. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Pretti family’s remarks.
Minnesota officials sued the Trump administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings of Pretti and Good. The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don’t have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don’t trust the federal government to investigate itself.
The state is still seeking the cellphones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews.
Pretti’s parents recounted how they first learned of his death when they were called by a reporter for The Associated Press.
“We learned about his death from the media as we saw him being shot repeatedly in the back after helping a woman from his community, a fellow Minnesotan, who had been shoved to the ground viciously,” Michael Pretti said. “No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex. No one from the federal government has called us since.”
He said the videos of his son’s killing haunt his family every day.
“I think it haunts many Americans to see a U.S. citizen who was peaceful and in his community shot multiple times on the back, in the back, while on the ground,” the father said, calling his family heartbroken.
“We wish we didn’t have to be here,” he said. “We wish Alex was alive. We wish we were simply in Minneapolis to visit with Alex. For him and me to chat about cars, hiking, biking, or anything that came to our mind. This administration has taken that away from us forever.”

title: UMaine faculty, students hold emergency town hall over planned staff cuts
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Orono, Maine (WABI) -University of Maine faculty and students gathered Monday night for an emergency town hall in response to expected cuts to staff positions at the university.
Unions, students and legislators spoke out against the staff layoffs. Speakers said every professor, counselor and advisor makes a difference in the lives of students, and that removing them would have a negative impact on the school.
The town hall comes after UMaine President Joan Ferrini-Mundy recently outlined mounting financial pressures in a letter to the university community.
She pointed to shifting federal funding, deferred building maintenance and inflation as major driving factors.
Ferrini-Mundy said the university has exhausted short-term fixes and its core reserves have dwindled, leaving leadership facing difficult decisions, including potential staff and faculty layoffs.
Not everyone is on board with the proposed cuts.
“We want there to be a parallel review with administration costs versus cutting the lowest paid employees, faculty and staff. We need to make sure that any cuts that are made aren’t impacting students. My hope is to really increase state appropriations and really elect the right legislators who are pro-public education,” said Sara Abronze, President of Universities of Maine Professional Staff Association.
“It’s these kind of faculty staff that actually are the kind of people I interface with as a student who have made it possible for me to be a student. And I think they shouldn’t be the ones on the chopping block,” said Maeve Durkee, a University of Maine senior.
A draft budget with the administration’s priorities will be submitted in January.
Decisions on program cuts and staffing will be finalized by June 30.

title: Kitten rescued from transfer station dumpster in Somerset County
text:
BINGHAM, Maine (WABI) - This past weekend, a roughly three month old kitten was found in a tied plastic bag at a transfer station in Concord Township, just outside Bingham in Somerset County.
The kitten is alive and being cared for, thanks to the vigilance of an employee.
“I kept hearing a kitten meowing, and then I kept looking, and I see a bag moving,” said Peter Abraham, the transfer station manager for the town of Bingham. “So, I went back to the garage, and I got my pick pole, and I pulled the bag apart, and the kitten was in the bag.”
That was when he called Tina Tibbetts, Bingham’s new animal control officer.
“It upset me a lot. It upset a lot of people in Bingham, knowing that someone couldn’t just bring him to the Humane Society. You don’t have to throw an animal into the dump,” said Tibbetts.
Tibbetts and other town officials say this incident shows the crucial need for animal welfare resources in Maine.
A candlemaker by trade, Tibbetts has no history of working with animals, but she stepped up when she saw a need in her rural community.
“I saw the sign. I love animals, and I knew Bingham needed an animal control officer. Nobody wanted the job,” said Tibbetts.
The kitten, now named “Dumpster,” is one of more than 70 animals Tibbetts has helped relocate in just two weeks of working for the town as ACO out of her own home. She’s hoping to raise money for a small, heated animal shelter in Bingham, as well as an animal food pantry.
Donation boxes are being left at local businesses. Anyone from outside the area looking to donate can call Tibbetts at 995-1196 or message Tina Marie Tibbetts on Facebook.
As for Dumpster, Tibbetts says he may have found a forever home with her and her family, and seems to be in good shape—except for some fleas.
If you have any information regarding how the kitten ended up in the transfer station dumpster, you’re asked to contact the Somerset County Sheriff’s Office.
The Town of Bingham also urges anyone who finds themselves unable or unwilling to care for an animal there to call their local animal shelter, ACO, town office, or even your local dispatch center’s non-emergency line.

title: Rep. Pingree talks federal support, sustainability with Maine fiber farmers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON, Maine (WABI) — Maine Congresswoman Chellie Pingree met with farmers in Knox County to address the growing hurdles facing local fiber producers and discuss the future of the state’s textile industry.
During a visit to Meadowcroft Farm, owner Nanne Kennedy highlighted how a lack of infrastructure and cuts to federal grant programs complicate the post-production process.
“Trying to turn your commodity into a saleable product — we don’t have a lot of infrastructure manufacturing options, certainly not locally,” Kennedy said. “Everything I do is within a five-hour radius. That’s really important to me.”
Kennedy pointed out the economic and energy disparities between natural fibers and fossil-fuel-based synthetics, noting how local natural fiber growers lack comparable support.
“[It is] much cheaper to take something soft and fluffy to make something soft and fluffy, but we don’t have the support to do that,” said Kennedy.
Following a tour of Meadowcroft Farm, a roundtable took place with area farmers to discuss additions to a draft of the Farm to Fabric Act.
The proposed legislation aims to expand federal agriculture funding, including both food and fiber production. The roundtable follows Pingree’s introduction of the Textile Waste Reduction Act last month.
“This administration has cut back on a lot of the programs that are important to farmers, so it’s good to see where those cuts are hurting farmers,” Pingree said.
Roundtable discussions centered on high entry costs for new producers, utilization of waste wool, and the broader environmental toll of synthetic textiles.
“70% of our clothing is made from fossil fuels, polyesters, and synthetics,” Pingree said. “Not only does it add a lot of questions for what people are wearing, but it ends up in our waste stream. There’s a lot of fast fashion now, and clothing is thrown away very quickly.”
Pingree emphasized that boosting domestic fiber processing creates both economic opportunities for growers and sustainable alternatives for consumers.
“We want to support more clothing that is sustainable, lasts longer, but also gives more opportunities to our American farmers — whether it’s cotton, linen, flax, or wool,” Pingree said. “And wool is a product that we make a lot of in Maine, so we want to support that.”

title: What Maine’s latest loon count revealed
text:
Maine Audubon estimates that 2,770 adult loons and 276 chicks were on lakes in southern Maine this summer, down from the previous two years.
The estimates are based on the organization’s 43rd annual Loon Count, held July 18. A record 1,861 volunteers surveyed 438 lakes statewide.
Maine Audubon has used the annual count to track loon populations south of the 45th parallel since 1983. That region has enough lakes surveyed to produce a reliable population estimate, but there is not enough data from northern Maine to estimate the population statewide.
The lower numbers this year may reflect conditions that made loons harder to spot, including fog, wind and smoke from Canadian wildfires. Some loons also had not hatched their eggs by the time of the count, according to Maine Audubon.
The organization said the lower estimates are not necessarily cause for concern. Loon pairs do not raise chicks every year, and some successfully fledge young only every other year or every few years.
Long-term studies such as the annual count focus on population trends over time rather than individual yearly estimates. The population does not need to grow every year to remain healthy and stable, according to Maine Audubon.
“The next few years will allow us to truly understand what trends we’re seeing in the adult and chick populations,” said Mady Eori, the organization’s community science manager.
Eori said long-term monitoring is important for identifying potential threats to Maine’s loon population.
In northern Maine, volunteers counted 515 adult loons and 40 chicks on 125 lakes. A separate group surveying remote lakes over a weeklong period counted 53 adults and three chicks.
People interested in participating in next year’s count in northern Maine can contact conserve@maineaudubon.org. More information about the annual count is available at maineaudubon.org/loons.

title: Elect Republicans to turn Maine around
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Dick Bradstreet of Vassalboro is a state senator.
An old adage says that elections have consequences. It’s true and we can see that big time here in Maine.
For nearly a decade, Democrats have had complete control in Augusta, and what do they have to show for it? You’ve heard it all: Much higher electricity costs, big increases in property and other taxes, failing schools, a huge budget shortfall and the list goes on and on. These issues are Maine problems and I believe they’re caused by the passage of bad policies. So why do we keep electing people who make the bad policies?
Many Democrats are blaming everything on Donald Trump, and of course all Republicans. It’s a good campaign strategy because it takes our eyes off their failures and forces us to see Republicans as the real villains. But the issues that are specific to Maine were here before Trump took office and will remain long after his tenure is done unless we do something about it on election day. I think they’re hoping we all have short memories.
Has anyone asked Hannah Pingree where the hundreds of millions of dollars in new programs she is proposing so that she and her legislative allies can get elected will come from? It seems to me that all of them are becoming more and more extreme, even to the point where they have rejected the most progressive governor we have ever had in favor of catering to the radical wing of their party. Sadly, it seems the old reasonable Democrats who would work to find consensus on important issues have been tossed aside. It’s not the party it used to be.
Normally, more government spending can be partially covered by economic growth. Did you know that the state’s own forecasting commission has predicted zero job growth over the next five years? Can you wonder why?
Our remote location here in the northeast and our cold climate already put many Maine businesses at an economic disadvantage, so you’d rationally think that the Legislature would do whatever it could to help our businesses be successful. Not in Maine, from what I see. We Republicans have sat in countless committee meetings and long legislative sessions in strong opposition to the passage of destructive legislation, but the unified Democrats tend to get their way. You would hope that enough of them would see the need to join in opposition to bad policy, but the reality I see in Augusta is that they are hard pressed by the powers that be to fall in line with the party dictates. It’s sad, but that’s the way I think it is.
The proof of bad policies, created and passed by those who make bad policies, is in the conditions mentioned above that our state is suffering from right now. Why would any right-minded person vote for legislators who repeatedly support legislation that hurts our state? It makes no sense.
I believe the majority party in Augusta is very partisan. Compare this to Sen. Susan Collins, who has repeatedly been accused of being a President Donald Trump sycophant yet was ranked the most bipartisan member of the Senate in 2023. I thought that’s what we wanted — people who can work across the aisle compared to the totally partisan candidate who is running against her.
Both parties in these elections are focused on “winning.” I think it’s high time for Mainers to finally win. The only way I see to accomplish this is to vote out the people who have created the mess we’re in and instead choose candidates who will fix it.
If we want to turn Maine around, we’ll need sensible, rational people in our Legislature and an experienced, focused and able chief executive as our next governor. I think that person is Bobby Charles. Together, they can bring common sense and accountability back to Maine. Our best chance to do that is for all open-minded people to cast votes for Republicans so that we can finally set Maine back on the right track.

title: Does Biddeford prohibit camping in city parks?
text:
Yes.
Biddeford’s parks ordinance prohibits overnight camping, including tents and other temporary shelters. Erecting any tent or shelter requires a recreation director’s permit. City parks generally close at dusk, and unauthorized structures may be removed.
The ban predates the city’s recent efforts to address homelessness. In 2024, officials adopted a plan prohibiting camping on all city-owned land, ordered encampments closed and arranged overnight accommodations at the nonprofit Seeds of Hope.
Encampments remain an issue. At an Oct. 6 City Council meeting, General Assistance Administrator Jacob Hammer said code enforcement had responded to encampments over 50 times since July 1, issuing trespass warnings and directing people to move. Public Works had conducted 10 cleanups costing more than $5,000.
Hammer proposed a pilot program pairing code enforcement with a housing navigator to address encampments and connect people with housing. The proposal was referred for further review.

title: Bowdoinham officials want to make contentious first 4-way stop permanent
text:
The light at the intersection of Main Street and River Road in Bowdoinham has been blinking red in all directions since July 28. The Select Board voted unanimously on Oct. 13 to ask the Maine Department of Transportation make the town’s test run of its first four-way stop permanent.
The Maine Department of Transportation has the final say, and is reviewing survey data to decide whether to make the change official.
The new traffic feature, including the light and stop signs, have sparked debate among locals at Select Board meetings and in Facebook groups.
The intersection was flagged for improvement after the town used a grant to assess Bowdoinham’s walkability. The Masonic Lodge, a large building at the intersection, obstructs the view around the corner when coming up Main Street from the waterfront. Drivers need to inch into the intersection before they can tell if it is safe to turn or not, said Town Manager Nicole Briand. The town also explored making lower Main Street a one-way road, but encountered significant opposition from the boating community according to Yvette Meunier, director of planning and development.
In 2025, Bowdoinham trialed a temporary crosswalk at the same intersection. At the same meeting, the Select Board voted to accept a grant to build a permanent crosswalk. The town hopes to design it this winter and do the construction this spring, said Briand.
The town conducted a survey during the trial period for the four-way stop, and the results were mixed. Fifty-five percent of respondents said that the stop did not make the intersection safer, 36% said it did, and 8% were unsure.
Walkers and bikers tended to like the stops, according to the survey. People driving trailers had the least positive responses. Drivers had different opinions based on which direction they came through the stop.
“I think one of the arguments against the four-way stop is that folks don’t think it’s necessary because there hasn’t been many accidents at that end,” said Briand.
Comments from the survey and Facebook mentioned there has been confusion about how the four-way stop works. At the meeting, Select Board Chair Joanne Joy suggested that the town newsletter include four-way stop instructions, “just to remind folks who haven’t really had to look at it since they were getting their license in the first place.”
Briand said she thinks the contentiousness of the issue really comes down to uneasiness around change.
“It’s a change that a lot of folks don’t think is necessary. Change can be difficult, especially if you don’t agree with it,” she said.

title: How to use AI to budget for the holidays without overspending
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Holiday expenses often extend well beyond gifts and food, and those additional costs can add up quickly.
Cherry Dale, vice president of financial education at Virginia Credit Union, said the first step to managing holiday spending is a simple list — before ever opening an AI tool like ChatGPT or Claude.
Dale recommends listing everything planned for November and December spending, including travel, decorations, gifts and hosting costs. She said AI can help organize a budget, but personal information such as a name or banking details should never be entered.
Dale said general, non-identifying details can still produce a useful, personalized budget.
“You can put generic things like, ‘Hey, I’m hosting eight people for Thanksgiving, and I have six adults, two children. I would like to create a traditional Thanksgiving meal. Can you map out a budget for me with all of this information?’” Dale said. “And it will spit out approximate cost per person.”
Dale said AI tools can suggest a menu and grocery list, or help identify gift ideas that fit a specific budget.
“Use AI — put in, like, ‘I would like a gift for a child that’s interested in piano or theater, or maybe it’s sports. What is something under $10 that would be simple for me to create or to give?’” Dale said. “And it can give you some very specific suggestions to stay within the budget.”
For those looking to save further, Dale recommends thinking beyond store-bought gifts. She said a gift of time or a shared experience can carry more meaning than a purchased item.

title: VIDEO: Great white shark lunges at woman reaching to touch it
text:
VIDEO: Great white shark lunges at woman reaching to touch it
A close encounter with a great white shark off Tybee Island, Georgia, took a startling turn when a woman reached out to touch the animal — and the shark suddenly swung its head and lunged toward her.
Video of the encounter was shared on Facebook by Jimmy Lee Armel of the Knot Lucky White Shark Tagging Program.
"One second, Jen, one of our veterans, is laying her hand on a wild white shark like it's the family dog, and the next second that shark whips around and lunges toward her," Armel wrote. "Everybody on the boat felt that one in their chest."
Armel said Jen was never in immediate danger because the crew had control of the situation and the shark did not get close enough to harm her. Still, he said its reaction offered a clear reminder that great white sharks are powerful wild animals that must be treated with respect.
Tagging sharks for science
The Knot Lucky program catches, tags, and releases great white sharks to help researchers study their movements and behavior.
Each tagged shark is also given the name of a fallen service member, combining the program’s scientific work with its mission of honoring those who died in service.
This shark was not tagged, however. Armel said the crew never had a safe opportunity and would not force the process.
"The shark's safety and the crew’s safety come first, every single time," he wrote.
The crew released the shark, allowing it to swim away without a tag.

title: Walden Renewables to hold another community session Oct 29th
Risks spelled out for Anthropic investors include possible harms from runaway AI
text:
(AP) - Any time a company looks to start selling shares on Wall Street, it’s required to disclose potential risks for investors. In the case of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic, that has included the possibility that its products could threaten nothing less than humanity itself.
The risks laid out by the San Francisco company in its filing Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission included discussion of bad actors potentially using AI models to build deadly weapons or the technology itself going rogue with untold consequences.
Of the 335 pages outlining Anthropic’s finances, executive compensation, dividend policy and the like, 93 pages are devoted to “risk factors” — the things that could hurt potential shareholders’ investments. Rival SpaceX’s listed risk factors, in comparison, took up 38 out of more than 250 pages.
In selling itself to investors, Anthropic presents its own initial public offering as a step toward mitigating the risks it believes AI poses.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” write the company’s founders in a letter to prospective shareholders in the IPO filing. “Anthropic is a deeply values-driven organization, founded in large part to help the world realize AI’s benefits and avoid its dangers.”
Still, the risks are many. They range from the mundane — the possibility it won’t be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — to involvement in cyberattacks and the spread of dangerous misinformation.
Here is a look at some of the risks Anthropic details:
The technology’s rapid development
Anthropic said it’s possible its models could develop so quickly the company won’t be able to implement adequate safety measures, “which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in September that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet. The warning — and now Anthropic’s move to sell shares — comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also act on their own to carry out other, more harmful tasks.
As AI systems “become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the SEC filing said, there’s a risk that such systems could “take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.”
“Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier AI could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business,” Anthropic said.
Now that the AI models are themselves contributing to Anthropic’s own research and development, it’s possible that AI could progress “beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models,” according to the filing. This, the document said, could adversely affect Anthropic’s business.
Malicious actors could cause mayhem with the technology
The filing discussed concerns that advanced AI systems, if not developed and operated with enough safeguards and oversight, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.”
The company said it would be harmed if use by bad actors causes damage, “or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse.”
Anthropic sketched out the prospect of bad actors using AI models to build chemical weapons or authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens. In September, the company disclosed that it had blocked efforts to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapon development.
The company could run up against limits on processing power
Compute — the computing power or resources needed to build, test and improve AI models — is expensive and in high demand. Anthropic notes that if it’s unable to secure adequate compute, or if “we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers.”
Anthropic mentioned community opposition to data centers as a risk to its business. Data center development “has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources,” the filing said, adding that if regulators impose new requirements or charges as a result, its ability to do business could suffer.
In addition, the company relies on a small number of customers, including SpaceX and Microsoft, and distribution channels for a large portion of its revenue. This means that even if just one of its big customers decides to scale back — or drop the company altogether — Anthropic said it could see its prospects and finances suffer.
Mitigating the risks
In some ways, AI’s enormous risk, combined with its enormous potential, is Anthropic’s main selling point. The company has tried to position itself as a responsible AI company, and courts business customers by emphasizing safety-mindedness.
“We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology,” the filing said.
Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Research, said IPO deals have to display “very clearly” what risks people face when they invest their money in a newly public stock.
“That’s one of the things that’s great about our capital markets here domestically is the level of transparency that you must commit to, to be a publicly traded corporation on a U.S. exchange requires you to outline those risks in a very clear way, so that people understand if they want to participate by offering their hard-earned money and help finance this type of a deal,” he said.
___
AP Business Writer Bernard Condon and AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed to this story.
