title: Judge extends court-ordered block on Trump's renovation plans for public golf course in Washington
text:
Judge extends court-ordered block on Trump’s renovation plans for public golf course in Washington
A federal judge agreed Monday to extend an order blocking the Trump administration's renovation plans for a century-old public golf course in the nation's capital.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a preliminary injunction that temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the East Potomac Golf Course. The administration must give 10 days' notice in writing before making any "irreparable modification" to any "forms or features" to the course while the lawsuit is active.
"The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees.' The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law," Reyes wrote.
Reyes expressed astonishment that the government has asked her to "not to believe the sitting President" and disregard Trump's statements about his plans for the golf course renovations.
"This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more," Reyes wrote. "It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."
On Oct. 18, Trump announced plans on social media to close the golf course for 15 months, starting Nov. 15, and redevelop the 106-year-old park and course despite a court challenge by the D.C. Preservation League and two golfers. A day later, Trump posted that the work would start immediately.
Reyes, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Joe Biden, previously ordered the administration to suspend work on the project until at least Oct. 26.
The plaintiffs challenging the project claim the work is inflicting irreversible damage. At a hearing, the judge excoriated the government after workers cut down at least 400 trees over a holiday weekend with little notice to the plaintiffs.
The course renovation project is part of the Republican president's aggressive campaign to leave his personal imprint on Washington's historic landscape, including his plans to construct a huge ballroom at the White House, to build a massive arch and to add his own name to the Kennedy Center.
Reyes rejected the administration's request for her to recuse herself from the case. The government questioned her impartiality and accused her of engaging in "egregious" behavior from the bench during an emergency hearing in the case.
In Monday's ruling Reyes stressed that she had hoped the parties could have resolved their dispute without judicial intervention. She noted that she had denied plaintiffs' previous requests.
"The Court would much prefer not to have to resolve Lorax v. Once‑ler redux. Indeed, for months, the Court declined to intervene," she wrote.
But she said the government forced her hand by bulldozing hundreds of trees without any notice, doing "what it assured all it would not do."
Democracy Forward President & CEO Skye Perryman, whose organization is co-counsel representing the plaintiffs, DC Preservation League and two golfers, called the ruling "a big win that will rightly protect East Potomac Park from further irreparable harm." She added, in an email, that the move will stop activities "while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court."
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: The Latest: Trump goes to Texas as his Iran war damages GOP hopes for Congress
text:
President Donald Trump takes his midterm campaign blitz to Texas, where Senate candidate Ken Paxton is locked in a tight race against Democrat James Talarico. And Secretary of State Marco Rubio will join Trump to show off a newly arrived oil tanker filled with Venezuelan crude to be processed in Texas refineries, according to a congressional aide and two U.S. officials.
Meanwhile, the Iran war, which Trump often describes as a “little detour,” has emerged as an unforced liability for a president who promised to keep the U.S. out of foreign wars. Republican strategists privately acknowledge it’s severely damaging party efforts to retain control of Congress as gasoline price hikes drive up costs across the economy and new hostilities emerge.
And two former FBI officials charged with lying to Congress about investigations involving Hunter Biden have a preliminary hearing Tuesday. Lawyers for Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides call the charges baseless and politically motivated, the latest in a series of splashy investigative actions by the Justice Department as Americans go to vote.
Here’s the Latest:
Republicans try to shake voter frustration over the Iran war
GOP strategists privately acknowledge that the Iran war is severely damaging their push to retain control of Congress for the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
They point to voters like Noor Dubow, who says he’s regularly voted for Republicans who align with his economic views, even though he’s never been a fan of Donald Trump or the president’s dehumanizing rhetoric toward immigrants. Not this year — Dubow says his early midterm election ballot tipped more toward Democrats because of his frustration over Trump’s war with Iran.
“Where are the Republicans in Congress?” asked Dubow, 44, a dispatcher at a trucking logistics firm in Columbus, Ohio, where he has a bird’s eye view of the surging fuel prices disrupting the economy. “Why aren’t the Republicans holding Trump accountable?”
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker steps up spending in Mississippi, Kansas and South Carolina
The billionaire Democrat, who is on the cusp of reelection and considering a 2028 presidential bid, is directing some last-minute campaign spending on Senate Democratic nominees in traditionally Republican states.
Pritzker’s Ready for the Fight PAC is making a $1 million ad buy for Scott Colom against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi and spending $500,000 for Adam Hamilton against GOP incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas.
Shared first with The Associated Press, the plan also includes money for voter turnout in Mississippi and South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews wants to unseat Sen. Darline Graham. All three would be upsets as Democrats seek to flip the Senate.
First lady MK Pritzker meanwhile said she donated $500,000 to Democrat Amy Acton’s Senate campaign in Ohio because of her opponent’s controversial ad featuring her estranged mother.
Political ad spending in the midterm elections has set a new record
With spending on campaign ads now reaching $11.21 billion, the 2025-2026 midterms have become the most expensive ever, according to AdImpact, which tracks media spending.
A week out from Election Day, total spending and reservations has topped the $11.20 billion spent in 2023-2024 period, which included the presidential contest.
The latest figure has not been adjusted for inflation.
Trump vows to appeal temporary hold on renovation of Washington golf course
The president says he’ll appeal a federal judge’s order putting a temporary hold on his plans to renovate a Washington golf course.
“The Development of this World Championship Public Facility must begin, immediately, if it is to be completed in a timely and seasonal manner,” he posted on social media.
Trump said the East Potomac Golf Course could hold major events once renovated and would remain public with reduced rates for residents of the nation’s capital.
Judge Ana Reyes’ preliminary injunction temporarily bars the removal or damage of any more trees on the course, ordering the administration to give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any of the course’s “forms or features.”
“The Court earlier stated, ‘I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees.’ The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law,” Reyes wrote.

title: Deaths of Mount Desert woman, 2 grandchildren ruled accidental drownings
text:
ROQUE BLUFFS, Maine (WABI) - The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner has ruled the deaths of a Mount Desert woman and her two young grandchildren found in Roque Bluffs last month accidental drownings, according to an update from Maine State Police.
Sharon Bukulmez, 61, of Mount Desert, along with 5-year-old Kinsley Grubb and 3-year-old Sawyer Grubb, both of Bar Harbor, were found dead Sept. 20 inside Bukulmez’s vehicle in Pond Cove near the boat ramp at the end of Schoppee Point Road.
Search launched after trio failed to arrive in Machias
According to investigators, Bukulmez and the two children were last seen leaving a family function in Jonesboro around 8:30 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 19. The trio was headed to Machias but never arrived.
After family members raised concerns, law enforcement launched a search. The Bar Harbor Police Department obtained Bukulmez’s cellphone location data, which traced her phone to the water in Roque Bluffs.
State troopers, along with the Maine State Police Dive Team and Maine Marine Patrol, responded and located the submerged vehicle in Pond Cove around 7 a.m. Sunday, Sept. 20. First responders recovered the vehicle and the bodies of Bukulmez and the two children from the water. The Washington County Sheriff’s Office and the U.S. Coast Guard also assisted at the scene.
State police said the circumstances surrounding how the vehicle entered the water remain under investigation.

title: Scarborough boys soccer edges Biddeford in A South prelim
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SCARBOROUGH — The game was chippy, tight and intense, just the way the Scarborough boys soccer team anticipated it would be.
“We all knew it was going to be a rivalry going in. It was going to be heated,” senior midfielder Connor Casey said. “We definitely didn’t overlook them going over here.”
Evan Sharifipour headed in Papa Osei’s cross for the only goal of the game, and second-seeded Scarborough slipped past No. 10 Biddeford, 1-0, in a Class A South quarterfinal Tuesday night.
The Tigers had already proved their ability to stay with the defending state champions in a 1-0 loss 11 days earlier, and the rematch also had a dearth of goals and scoring chances. In their place were physical defense and some verbal jousting.
Once again, it added up to a Scarborough victory.
“Scarborough High School playoff nights, that’s what we live for,” Osei said. “It’s just fighting hard for every ball. When we make mistakes, having the next guy ready to cover you. It’s that team mentality.”
JUMPING AHEAD
• Scarborough (11-2-2) scored the only goal it needed with a highlight-reel hookup in the 16th minute. Osei brought the ball down the right sideline and boomed a long cross into the box in front of the net.
The senior wasn’t looking for a target.
“I see we’ve got a clump of people back post,” he said. “I know if we drop it in there, eventually it’s going to fall to somebody. Just get it in that spot.”
Osei’s ball found one. Sharifipour ran up and got his head square on the cross, putting the ball in the net with 24:09 to go in the half.
“It was beautiful,” Sharifipour said. “It came over the keeper, I sprinted from the top of the 18 to the box, and I just tapped it in. … If I missed, it would have been terrible.”
CHIPPY AND CHIRPY
• The goal came only 1 minute and 15 seconds after emotions between the rivals briefly bubbled over. Nsimba Ilunga outran the Biddeford defense to win a loose ball for a breakaway, but in the process he collided with Tigers keeper Tyler Pelletier, who was racing up to make a play on the ball.
After the collision, players gathered and traded pushes and shoves before the group was broken up and play resumed. Just over a minute later, Osei connected with Sharifipour.
“These two teams are so competitive, we know there are going to be some chippy moments,” Osei said. “That was big for us to get motivated and then use that to score.”
• The two teams kept up the intensity, tackling aggressively and taking opportunities to try to unnerve the other.
Casey, the dynamic Scarborough midfielder, was hounded by Biddeford defenders whenever he took the ball on the attack.
“I’ve got to really praise our mental toughness. They were talking the whole night,” he said. “We didn’t let it faze us. We’re just really happy to get the result.”
PLAYING TOUGH
Biddeford coach Paul Illiano credited his team for taking the perennial power to the limit again. The Tigers (7-7-2) outshot the Red Storm, 7-6.
“It was tough. We knew it was going to be tough. I liked the way we finished the game, just couldn’t find a goal,” he said. “(It was) pack mentality on defense, just one guy to the ball at a time, and the rest of the guys in a position to support. … We were pretty good at that tonight, just couldn’t get it done on the other end.”
UNSUNG HERO
Though he wasn’t involved in the only goal, junior Joseph Walker was a difference-maker for the Scarborough attack. He was strong on the ball and skilled at bringing it up through the midfield, but he also got back on defense and was an effective 1-on-1 matchup.
GAINING MOMENTUM
In the preseason, Scarborough coach Mark Diaz said his team had holes to fill, but the talent to fill them. Sure enough, the Red Storm have won seven straight games and have gone unbeaten in their last 11 after a 1-2-1 start.
“We’re just playing more like a team now,” he said. “We’re close to where everyone’s on the same page. When you get that, you’ve got a shot. And we’re close.”
STAT LEADERS
• Scarborough: Evan Sharifipour (goal), Papa Osei (assist), Joshua Serafin (seven saves)
• Biddeford: Tyler Pelletier (five saves)

title: Savannah Chrisley is expecting her first child with mystery fiancé Jason
text:
(Gray News) - Savannah Chrisley is expecting her first child with her fiancé, Jason.
“I’ve prayed for this life. I’ve cried for this life. And there were moments I truly wondered if this life would ever be mine,” she said in an Instagram post.
Chrisley, 29, shared the news on her podcast, Unlocked with Savannah Chrisley, and on Instagram.
“The past few years have taken me through fires I never imagined I’d have to walk through. Seasons of heartbreak, loss, and moments when I didn’t know if I would ever make it to the other side. I wondered if I would ever find my forever… if I would ever feel safe enough to truly breathe again. And then God sent me J. Right in the middle of the heartbreak. Before all the pieces were put back together. And somehow, he began healing parts of me he never broke," Chrisley wrote on Instagram.
Chrisley shared a video of herself holding ultrasound photos and kissing Jason with her hand on her pregnancy bump.
“For the first time in a long time, I feel safe. I feel fulfilled. I can finally exhale. I found my forever in you. And just when I thought my heart couldn’t hold any more love, God gave us our sweetest blessing yet… we’re having a BABY!" she continued in the Instagram caption.
In her podcast episode sharing the news, Chrisley said that she and Jason have been together since last July and first connected “in the world of politics.” She said Jason proposed to her in December in the Cayman Islands.
“The ring is insane and it’s everything I ever wanted,” she said.
Chrisley also said that their age gap is “huge.”
“I would rather 20 phenomenal years with someone than 50 meh years with someone,” she said.
Chrisley said that when she first saw Jason, she was still working to get her parents, Todd and Julie Chrisley, released from prison.
Julie and Todd Chrisley served more than two years in prison for financial crimes before receiving a full presidential pardon from President Donald Trump in May 2025.

title: Women who accused Alexander brothers of rape to speak at their sentencing
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Three brothers who exploited their wealth, proximity to celebrities and access to luxury real estate to help them drug and rape dozens of women are likely to face lengthy prison terms Tuesday when they are sentenced for sex trafficking.
Nearly a dozen victimized women are expected to make statements at the New York sentencing of twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, and Tal Alexander, 40, who were convicted in March.
Prosecutors have asked U.S. District Judge Valerie E. Caproni to give them life prison sentences. The brothers’ lawyers have asked for the minimum: 15 years.
Oren and Tal Alexander were once nicknamed real estate’s “A Team” for their ultra high-end sales and celebrity clientele. After smashing sales records at industry powerhouse Douglas Elliman, the brothers started their own firm. Alon Alexander ran their family’s private security company.
The brothers projected an exclusive lifestyle of yachts, private jets and waterfront mansions in Miami, but prosecutors said they began sexually assaulting women as early as 2001 or 2002, when they were in high school, and over time developed a pattern of drugging and raping women who they enticed to join them on luxury getaways.
At least 70 women were raped or sexually assaulted by the men, prosecutors said in a court filing that called the brothers “serial rapists.”
Defense lawyers said the brothers apologize to the women they insulted or offended for conduct they admit was “insensitive toward the feelings of certain women at certain times.” They also maintained their innocence.
The trio were arrested in 2024 and have been held without bail ever since.
The judge, Caproni, has said she believes the brothers should not be incarcerated at the same prison because they were a bad influence on one another. The brothers’ lawyers plan to argue that they belong together, even behind bars.

title: Manhunt underway for convicted murderer who escaped from prison, officials say
text:
LAKE COUNTY, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) – A convicted murderer is on the run after escaping from a prison in Tennessee.
Officers at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Lake County discovered inmate Jacob Morley was missing late Sunday night.
Surveillance footage shows Morley breached a perimeter fence and left the facility in his prison uniform.
Authorities released video of him allegedly stealing a white 2008 Ford F-350 during his escape around 1 a.m. Monday.
The truck has a Tennessee license plate 138BBQV and is marked with Lindamood Planting Company on the side.
Morley is serving a life sentence for first-degree murder in the 2022 killing of Cody Birchfield in Carter County, officials said. He was also convicted of abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary.
Morley was found guilty on Feb. 3 and sentenced to life with chance of parole.
According to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, Morley has now been added to the Tennessee Most Wanted List and should be considered dangerous.
A reward of up to $2,500 is offered for information leading to his arrest. Anyone who sees him or has information is asked to call 911 or 1-800-TBI-FIND immediately.
Morley is the second inmate to escape Tennessee Department of Corrections custody in less than a week.

title: A New ‘Simpsons’ Episode Mocks Disney World’s Biggest Flop
text:
A New ‘Simpsons’ Episode Will Mock Disney World’s Biggest Flop
The November 8 episode of The Simpsons — the 815th in the history of the extremely long-running animated sitcom — is called “The Kosmic Kruiser.” The photos from the show, the description of the show, and the inclusion of a very notable guest star make it clear: The Simpsons is taking aim at one of the most notorious flops in the history of Walt Disney World.
(Disney, as you are no doubt aware, is currently the corporate owner of The Simpsons.)
Fox’s official description for the episode:
At Krustyland amusement park, Bart and Lisa break into an abandoned ride ... I'm sorry; did I say ‘abandoned’?
All signs point to a Simpsons parody of the Star Wars: Galactic Starcruiser, the already-defunct Star Wars hotel that opened in 2022 as a unique immersive experience for hardcore fans. Instead of a typical Disney hotel, the Starcruise was designed to mimic a lavish cruise — only instead of traveling on the high seas, your “ship” took you across the “galaxy” to “Baatu” (aka Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge theme park in Disney’s Hollywood Studios theme park).
Each visit to the Starcruiser was highly themed, with busy itineraries for each guest blending immersive experiences, character interactions, lightsaber training, and live performances. It was billed as the ultimate Star Wars experience ... but it was also one of the most expensive Star Wars experiences, and Disney ultimately shuttered the experiment after less than two years in operation.
Which should make for excellent fodder for a Simpsons episode!
READ MORE: A Controversial Simpsons Character Finally Returned to the Show After a Years-Long Absence
One of the most notable critics of the Galactic Starcruiser was Jenny Nicholson, whose fascinating four-hour video about her unsatisfying experience at the hotel has more than 17 million views on YouTube. And Nicholson herself will reportedly provide a voice for “The Kosmic Kruiser,” bringing the whole story full circle.
The Simpsons is no stranger to mocking Disney and its theme parks. The fourth episode of the show’s brilliant sixth season was called “Itchy & Scratchy Land,” and followed the Simpsons as they tried to survive a trip to a theme park inspired by Bart and Lisa’s favorite cartoon (and also by jokes that the writers wanted to make about Walt Disney World). The episode later helped to inspire The Simpsons ride at various theme parks — although, ironically, those rides are Universal parks, not a Disney ones. (Disney did not yet own The Simpsons when those rides were built.)
Of course, this episode was released many years before Disney acquired 20th Century Fox, and with it The Simpsons. Do we think they will pull their punches this time?

title: 'I asked to tighten this': 911 call reveals moment after video board fell onto Florida student
text:
'I asked to tighten this': 911 call reveals moment after video board fell onto Florida student
Family members are continuing to search for answers after a 5-year-old boy was killed by 120-pound video board that fell on him at a Florida elementary school. Weeks later, newly released 911 recordings revealed believed issues with the board prior to the incident.
Hearst sister station WESH said a distressed caller told emergency dispatchers that she asked someone to “tighten this the other day” moments after the board fell onto Bellamy Dawkins-Morris at Riviera Elementary School.
“I have a student who (unintelligible) a Promethean board off of the door, off the wall, and landed on him,” the caller said.
About a minute later, she said, “He’s not responsive.”
The caller then said, “And I asked (unintelligible) to tighten this the other day.”
Following his death, the district issued a statement, saying it would inspect all video boards districtwide.
“The district has completed its inspection of more than 3,000 boards and found no pattern of improper installations," the district said in the statement. "We are currently awaiting the final inspection report.”
“It is abundantly clear that there were failures associated with this particular equipment that caused the tragic and unfortunate death of Bellamy,” attorney Maegan Bridwell said.
Bridwell said the firm visited Riviera Elementary on Friday.
“We’re still in the endeavor to find out why this happened and how it happened, and we’re prepared to pursue litigation against those entities responsible, especially in light of the information that we’ve received as of the past couple of weeks since this has happened,” she said.
Palm Bay police said the investigation remains active.
The district has not said whether there were issues with the board that fell on Oct. 7, 2026.

title: It's true: There is a fungus among us
text:
Autumn is a time when we think of the natural world winding down in preparation for winter. While there is some truth to that, an entire kingdom (Fungi) is emerging all around us. Yes, there is a fungus among us. And above us. And below us. Fungus is, quite literally, everywhere.
Sometimes, fungi gets a bad rap. For some people, the word conjures images of out-of-control biological experiments in the refrigerator. For others, fungus is a dreaded ailment. While there is truth to these connotations, fungi are an integral part of the natural world.
Ever-present, fungi grow in vast networks on, and inside, organic matter where moisture, warmth, and nutrients are available. The mycorrhizae (which translates to “fungus-root”) are mutually beneficial associations between soil fungi and the roots of most vascular plants. Autumn’s cool temperatures and frequent rainfall create ideal conditions for the normally-underground fungal networks to sprout surface-fruiting bodies. And with our wetter and cooler-than-usual summer, there seems to be more mushrooms than ever this year.
Fungi facilitate decomposition, breaking down dead wood, leaves, and animal debris, cycling carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorous back into the soils, thereby making them available for plants. Through their mycorrhizal networks, they supply plants with water and minerals. Their vast, underground networks capture and store massive amounts of carbon, with the side benefit of being one piece in the puzzle of climate regulation. Some fungi even break down environmental contaminants such as heavy metals, hydrocarbons (the basis of petrochemicals) and some types of plastics.
The fungi propagate primarily through spore dispersal (spores are the fungal equivalent of plant seeds, though far simpler). The vast majority of spores are released into the air, where billions can be found at any given time. This can happen naturally or through disturbance: think of those puffballs we all liked to pop when we were kids and cloud of powder they released. Those were spores. Fungal spores can even be found in fog and clouds.
Fungi occur in water both fresh and marine, too. Microscopic and filamentous fungi live in streams, ponds, and lakes where they break down dead leaves and wood. This, in turn, feeds aquatic insects and small animals.
There are thousands of species of marine fungi, found in from coastal estuaries to deep-ocean sediments. For those who like to geek out on nature, there is a Marine Fungi database (marinefungi.org).
Fungi come in a diverse array of forms, shapes, and sizes, ranging from microscopic to the Humongous Fungus in Oregon. This latter is a mostly underground network consisting of thread-like mycelium. Above ground, small Honey Mushroom clusters pop up. The Humongous Fungus covers 3.5 square miles, weighs up to an estimated 35,000 tons, and is more than 2,000 years old (some estimates put it at over 8,000 years).
Although taxonomists have formally described nearly 150,000 species of fungi in the world, estimates suggest there could be as many as 5 million. In Maine, the number of macrofungi (fungi visible to the naked eye) is estimated at more than 2,000 (with thousands more microscopic species).
College of the Atlantic and Acadia National Park maintain the Acadia Herbarium which contains more than 15,000 botanical specimens, including 691 species of nonlichenized fungi (remember, lichen are a symbiotic relationship between fungus, algae and yeasts). To learn more about this incredible resource, browse coa.edu/about/herbarium.
Perhaps the most commonly observed species of fungi on Mount Desert Island are the shelf funguses, also known as bracket funguses (botanists call them polypores). These woody, leathery, shelf-shaped fruiting bodies, or “conks,” jut from the side of trees and dead wood like fairy shelves. Shelf fungi can be found year-round. To the untrained eye, they all look alike; however, with some sleuthing, you should be able to identify the commoner species (iNaturalist and Seek apps are helpful).
Red-belted Polypore is recognizable for its fan shape and distinctive reddish-orange band near the margin (biologist-speak for edge). They grow up to nearly a foot wide and 4 inches deep.
The diverse coloration of Turkey Tail is reminiscent of its namesake. Similar only in having a fowl-based name, is Chicken of the Woods, which grows in clumps of yellowish shelves.
Foot-wide Artist’s Conks are the shelf fungus of choice for, well, artists. The upper side is a hard, woody texture; the underside is soft. It seems every summer camp in Maine has a mantle strewn with stylized conks. Take a pointed stick to draw in the soft parts. Over time, it hardens with drawn areas developing a rich brown, which contrasts with the white surrounds.
When we think of mushrooms, the “capped” forms are what come to mind. Common capped mushrooms include Brick Cap, Brittlegills, False Chanterelle, Butterball, and Deceivers.
This time of year, I have been seeing mushrooms everywhere. Many species have colorful names. My favorite is Robust Clitocybe.
These large, funnel-shaped mushrooms frequently grow in “fairy rings.” The underground mycelial network of the fungus starts from a single point, then spreads outward radially in search of nutrients. The physical manifestation we see above ground, sprout at the edge of the network, results in circles, or fairy rings. Many fungal species do this.
Some people like to forage for mushrooms, especially morels. Take great care in foraging as many mushroom species are poisonous; you want to be absolutely certain of your harvest. Many mushrooms have specific cooking instructions to render them safe. I knew a botanist who failed to properly prepare their mushroom meal and ended up needing a kidney transplant.
Enjoy this blast of life springing up across our coastal Maine landscape as we head into the next season. A final cautionary note to those interested in the edible landscape: please do not gather mushrooms in Acadia National Park where it is prohibited.
To learn more about mushrooms, I have long considered David Arora’s “Mushrooms Demystified” an invaluable resource. It is thick and heavy and worth its weight in, well, mushrooms.

title: UMaine United holds emergency town hall to discuss potential faculty and staff cuts
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Monday, Oct. 26, UMaine United, a group of University of Maine unions and organizations, hosted an emergency town hall meeting in the Donald P. Corbett Business Atrium to protest proposed staff and faculty cuts. The event featured eight speakers and two emcees as well as a mixer after speeches concluded. The hosts also encouraged attendees to sign a petition demanding that administrators pause any planned layoffs.
The town hall came after UMaine administrators announced a projected $19 million budget deficit that may result in staff and faculty layoffs. On Oct. 21, administrators released a letter detailing their plans for resolving the deficit, including reducing the unaccounted-for $9 million gap to $3 million. However, these plans still rely on staff retrenchments, albeit the elimination of vacant positions.
Speakers at the town hall included graduate and undergraduate students, legislators, professors and union representatives.
Democratic state Rep. Amy Roeder, who represents House District 23 and is an adjunct theater professor at UMaine, raised the question of the budget deficit’s impact on students.
“I have a question about these proposed cuts. What exactly are students supposed to get less of? Less feedback on their work, less help finding the courses they need to graduate, longer waits for counseling, fewer people answering their financial aid questions?” said Roeder. “You cannot reduce the people available to students and promise students a credible education.”
Democratic state Sen. Mike Tipping, who represents Senate District 8 and is up for reelection in November, stated that students and community members have power as a significant source of university funding.
“You pay a majority of the costs, you should have a majority of the say,” said Tipping.
He added that the state has been “systematically underfunding” public education for decades, and advised the community not to “take these cuts lying down.”
Lisa Neuman, the president of Orono’s chapter of the Associated Faculties of the Universities of Maine (AFUM), highlighted the importance of retaining faculty, especially following the 17% loss in 2022.
“We cannot cut our faculty by 10%,” said Neuman. She also asserted that there was not enough available data to support administrators’ decision to initiate layoffs.
Brian McGill, president of the UMaine Faculty Senate, pointed out that there had been a distinct lack of shared governance in the way university administration had been handling the budget deficit.
“How’d we get here, where are we going, what are the consequences of these cuts and what’s the impact gonna be?” asked McGill. “We’re taxpayers and this is a public institution and every single taxpayer has the right to know this information.”
Sara Abronze, the statewide president of the UMaine Professional Staff Association (UMPSA), demanded a full review of administrative costs and called for increased transparency.
“This issue should have been discussed with our labor unions first,” said Abronze. “We are being starved of the resources required to fulfill our mission [as an R1 university].”
She added that since every dollar spent on the university generates about $4 dollars in economic revenue, the university community “will not accept layoffs as a solution to state neglect.”
Jacquelyn Gill, a professor of paleoecology and plant ecology and one of the event’s emcees, offered her perspective as a faculty member.
“Our staff have been cut and cut and cut to the bone, and asked to do more things,” said Gill. She added, “I don’t know which of my colleagues are still going to be here next spring, next fall.”
Mo Drammeh, an undergraduate student, stressed the importance of faculty on the university’s credibility and what stance other students were likely to take.
“As it would turn out, students… side with their teachers,” said Drammeh.
The crowd began chanting “stop the cuts” of their own volition after the conclusion of Drammeh’s speech.
Andrii Obertas, a member of the UMaine Grad Workers Union (UMGWU), highlighted the importance of collaboration.
“An injury to one person is an injury to all,” said Obertas.
Aurora Green, president of UMGWU and the event’s second emcee, initiated “UMaine united” chants and emphasized the importance of fighting for the university.
Maeve Durkee, an undergraduate student, demanded that administrators look at administrative overhead and consider how these changes would affect students.
“I’m worried that the classes I’m gonna register for this week won’t actually be available next semester,” said Durkee.
She also mentioned the university’s contract with OpenAI, which was met with boos from the crowd.
“Administration has spent $1 million on an AI program that no one I know has actually used,” she said.
Event organizers plan to meet on the steps of Fogler Library at 9:30 a.m. on Oct. 29 to deliver their petition to the office of President Joan Ferrini-Mundy in Alumni Hall.

title: AT&T data breach settlement payments start soon. Here's what to know
text:
AT&T data breach settlement payments start soon. Consumers who filed could get up to $7,500
A federal court gave its final approval of the agreement terms this month.
AT&T data breach settlement payments start soon. Consumers who filed could get up to $7,500
A federal court gave its final approval of the agreement terms this month.
AT&T customers who filed claims for a settlement following two breaches in 2024 could soon start receiving payments – up to $7,500 for anyone eligible for the maximum amount for both breach events.
Related video above: Apple settlement offers some iPhone owners up to $95. Do you qualify?
Affected consumers had to file for the $177 million settlement by November of last year, according to CNBC.
The payout timeline has been revealed, as a federal court gave its final approval of the agreement terms early this month.
This story was originally published in MySA, a Hearst publication.
Here's what consumers need to know.
AT&T data breach settlement payout timeline
A memorandum opinion and order from the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, Dallas Division, requires that payments be distributed electronically or by paper check within 60 days of the "Effective Date."
Initially, "lawsuits were filed against AT&T in state and federal courts across the country," according to the filing website. "The lawsuits were consolidated" in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, Dallas Division.
When should we expect the AT&T settlement payout?
The settlement agreement defines the effective date as "10 days after the time for appeal of the Final Approval Order runs." This court granted final approval of the settlement on Friday, Oct. 2.
That means AT&T has 30 days to file an appeal under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(1)(A), making the deadline Monday, Nov. 2.
The agreement also states that "If an appeal is filed, then the Effective Date shall be 30 days after the last appellate court ruling affirming the Final Approval Order or 30 days after the entry of a dismissal of the appeal when there is no remaining right to appeal." This places the effective date around Thursday, Nov. 12, if no appeal or deadline-extending motion is filed. No official date has been announced; this is the best estimate.
Who qualified for AT&T settlement?
Two major data breaches occurred in 2024, according to court records. One happened in March and involved the leak of AT&T-specific fields contained in a data set released on the dark web. The other occurred in July. During the second instance, "certain limited data had been illegally downloaded from an AT&T workspace on a third-party cloud platform hosted by Snowflake, Inc.," according to the settlement website. AT&T said on its website that the data appeared to be from 2019 or earlier.
Despite some exceptions, anyone involved in the leaks, which included Social Security numbers, phone numbers, addresses and more for some 7.6 million active customers and 65.4 million former customers, is considered a member of the AT&T 1 Settlement Class or the AT&T 2 Settlement Class.
Eligible members would have received emails from the domain "attsettlement@e.emailksa.com." Anyone unsure whether they qualified can call 833-890-4930 for information.
Why is there a class action lawsuit against AT&T?
Several plaintiffs joined a consolidated class action against AT&T after it announced the pair of data breaches, with allegations including that savings had been "fraudulently drained from their accounts," that they noticed "unauthorized loans taken out in their name," and that "credit ratings dropped precipitously due to fraudulent activity on their accounts," among other claims.
In December 2024, representatives from a class action suit filed in Montana and another in Texas agreed to early-stage mediation, agreeing to a $149 million payout for the March data breach and a $28 million settlement for the July incident.
How much is the AT&T settlement payout per person?
An AT&T 1 Settlement Class Member can receive up to $5,000 if they can show proof that the losses were "fairly" traceable to the March data incident and submit a claim form by the deadline listed on the settlement website.
An AT&T 2 Settlement Class Member can receive up to $2,500 if they can show proof that the losses were "fairly traceable" to the July incident and submit a claim form by the deadline listed on the settlement website.
The deadline to file a claim for either class eligibility has passed.

title: Training helped this longtime shelter dog find an Aroostook County home
text:
After living in an Aroostook County shelter for more than a year, 5-year-old shepherd mix Mosey earned himself a permanent place on the sofa next to his new human mom when training taught him good dog manners.
In August, The Houlton Humane Society partnered with Purpose Pups, a Newburgh-based dog training business, to help the shelter’s dogs learn basic obedience, socialization and integration skills to give them a fighting chance at staying in their adoptive homes.
“Dogs know nothing unless we show it to them,” said Tyler Jones, Purpose Pups’ owner, who has now trained more than 6,000 dogs.
Like most Maine shelters operating at or near capacity, the Houlton shelter has experienced a surge in the number of surrendered dogs who wait a long time for adoption or are returned after a few days. Experts point to the economy and a lack of affordable housing as part of the problem.
“These dogs are sitting here way too long and we need to be trained to help them get the best second chance at life,” said CJ Virgie, Houlton Humane Society director. “We’re their last stop and we need to give them the best tools that we possibly can.”
That’s why Virgie, who has worked with Jones over the years, decided to start weekly training sessions at the shelter. Jones first taught the shelter staff, then the dogs, and the staff and dogs together before passing on the lessons to new owners.
When dogs come into the shelter, they should be evaluated for character traits and then enter six weeks of obedience training. When they’re ready to be adopted, there’s a transition session with the owner, Jones said.
“All the things the dogs learned in those six weeks are now translated to the owner. They know it’s up to them to continue it, and [it] sets both the handler and the dog up for success,” he said.
Mosey, the pup who had been at the shelter the longest, started in the initial training sessions with shelter staff and easily learned all his commands such as “sit,” “wait,” “heel” and “leave it.”
A lot of times people’s hearts are in the right place with wanting to adopt, but they don’t succeed because they don’t realize when you adopt a shelter dog there’s a lot of baggage that comes with it, Jones said.
“It doesn’t mean that shelter dogs are bad, it means they need more attention, more compassion, more empathy to be successful,” he said. “I find a lot of owners don’t get dogs based on their lifestyle. They say, ’He is so cute.’ OK, great, but what breed is that, and what do we need to do to give that dog enrichment to be successful?”
Houlton resident Eileen Voisine suddenly lost her dog in August.
“He started having seizures and he died in less than 24 hours,” she said. “He was my companion and we had been through so much together. It was very lonely. “
But when she saw Mosey at the shelter, she was smitten, although his shelter bio said it was unknown if he was good with children or cats. Voisine has both, including six great-grandchildren 6 and under, she said.
Still, she wanted to give it a try, so she started fostering Mosey to learn more about him.
“Right away he made himself at home,” she said. “And he’s been wonderful, but Tyler had already started working with him.”
Nonetheless, she didn’t dare walk him outside because he was pulling her while leashed. With her health issues — hip replacements, serious back surgery and a terrible accident that affected her legs — she could not afford an outdoor tumble, she said.
Jones worked with Mosey on such things as impulse control, heeling properly, “stay” and “come” commands and basic handling techniques to make the dog more adoptable.
“I think we definitely did that with Eileen and Mosey and I was happy to be a part of that story,” Jones said.
Voisine trained her other Houlton rescues, but this was her first experience with a professional trainer, she said. The experience helped her decide to adopt Mosey.
“He’s a very loving dog, a very sweet dog, and I feel sad he was [at the shelter] for so long. He’s a good companion and he follows me everywhere,” she said. “As soon as I got him he decided he liked the love seat, and I sit on half of it and he sits on the other side.”
Jones has been teaching Voisine how to continue training Mosey through weekly public sessions, which has become part of their daily routine. Now, they go for daily outdoor walks.
“It’s a cool story,” Jones said. “I listened to what Eileen said and that she wanted to be able to walk him outside. I really targeted his heeling and his ability to do that. I think it’s awesome because it shows that when you put in the time to establish a great foundation and put in the love, consistency, it works.”
For more information, contact the Houlton Humane Society, 207-532-2862.

title: Nancy Joan (Myers) Stevens
text:
Nancy Joan (Myers) Stevens, 91, of Gardiner, died peacefully Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026 at Dionne Commons in Brunswick.
Born in Altoona, Pa. on Jan. 12, 1935, she was the last child of John and Lydia (Wilson) Myers. She met and married Prince Stevens, who was in the Air Force and moved to many locations during that time, retiring to their home in Gardiner. Nancy devoted her entire life to her family, her grandchildren, and beyond. Her kindness was felt by everyone she met, and she will truly be missed.
Nancy was predeceased by her parents; husband, Prince Stevens; brothers and sisters; and grandsons, Cameron Stevens and Jason Spaulding.
Nancy is survived by children, Vyrl Romanella, Eric (Diane) Stevens, Beth (Tim) Goodwin, Alec (Terry) Stevens, and John (Mondy) Stevens; and grandchildren, Tricia Bowman, Ethan Stevens, Ivan Stevens, Crystal Sweeney, Blake Goodwin, Ford Stevens, Karita Parlett, Nicole Gruszewski, Lydia Arcidy, Jared Stevens, Laura Mistarz, Benjamin Goodwin, and Austin Dow. There are also 21 great-grandchildren and one great-great-grandchild.
A memorial service will be held at 1 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026 at the Gardiner First Baptist Church, at 47 Church St. in Gardiner. A committal service will take place at the Maine Veterans Cemetery, at 163 Mt. Vernon Road in Augusta on Monday, Nov. 9 at 10 a.m.
Arrangements and guidance are in the care of Staples Funeral Home and Cremation Care in Gardiner.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared with the family on the obituary page of the Staples Funeral Home website at staplesfuneralhome.com.

title: Lewiston caseworker sues Maine DHHS alleging retaliation for concerns he raised
text:
LEWISTON — An Office of Children and Family Services employee filed a civil lawsuit Thursday under the Maine Whistleblower’s Protection Act and the Human Rights Act in Androscoggin County Superior Court against the Maine Department of Health and Human Services.
The suit — filed by Auburn resident Sergey Miller, a child protective caseworker in the Lewiston office since 2024 — alleges officials have retaliated against him for raising concerns in January 2026 about child safety and the handling of findings that allege abuse.
Miller said his issue with DHHS officials began in mid-January 2026 when he refused an overnight assignment he reported as unsafe. Some two weeks later, on Jan. 26, he alleges an assistant program manager directed him to change an unrelated finding on child abuse, an action he considered unethical due to the nature of the recorded findings.
Miller said in an email that the record of child abuse included video of how children were being treated, and “everyone below the administrators that worked the case” agreed on it.
“I was told to change it,” Miller said. “I said ‘no,’ in writing … (and) the next day I received my first discipline. The finding was changed anyway, in the record, by an administrator who had interviewed no one. No reason was recorded. No one who had worked the case was asked a question.”
Miller’s written warning included his use of foul language with superiors and refusal of the overnight assignment, according to the lawsuit.
Despite issues up to that point, the lawsuit says Miller received a performance evaluation Jan. 30 rating him as meeting or exceeding expectations in every category but one and recommending him for a raise.
According to the lawsuit, in mid-February Miller reported further concerns about a supervisor’s child safety decisions and met with supervisors about the issue. He also issued written reports from April to May about two child protective cases and how findings were handled. Miller said after a transfer request was denied in May due to discipline, he notified supervisors he would be asking the Child Welfare Ombudsman to review another child welfare case.
About a week-and-a-half later, he received a written reprimand over correspondence with administrators and a separate job-performance warning. Miller filed a union grievance contesting discipline and his transfer denial.
“I asked to transfer out from under that supervisor,” Miller said. “In April I was told two supervisors had openings and nothing barred the move. In May, the program administrator denied it, ‘consistent with practice,’ because I had active discipline. That practice is not written anywhere.”
On June 6, Miller told his managers that he filed a complaint with the Maine Human Rights Commission, according to the lawsuit. In a meeting on June 8, DHHS officials discussed investigating Miller after learning of his ombudsman report and the next day placed Miller on paid administrative leave taking away his access to their systems and reassigning his cases, according to the lawsuit.
Miller also filed a federal civil rights lawsuit in July against five DHHS officials for First Amendment violations and against the department itself under the Maine Whistleblowers’ Protection Act. The federal counts, Miller said, say the department retaliated against him for refusing to alter a child protective finding and for reporting a case to the Child Welfare Ombudsman.
The state moved to dismiss the case in September, but the matter is still pending. Miller said he opted to drop the count against the department under the Maine Whistleblowers’ Protection Act in order to bring the most recent case in Superior Court.
In the civil lawsuit, Miller asks for a transfer out of the “supervisory chain of people who did this” so he can go back to work, have discipline removed from his record, damages and a written declaration that the rule denying his transfer does not exist.
“One side is accountable for breathing the wrong way — the other side is accountable for nothing,” Miller said. “The people who did this have never had to say, in writing, what I did or what rule I broke. I would like them to have to. I want to work there.”
The Department of Health and Human Services said Monday that it cannot answer questions pertaining to pending litigation.

title: Zookeeper dies after leopard attacked her in the animal’s enclosure
text:
AMSTERDAM (AP) — A longtime zookeeper at a safari park in the Netherlands died Tuesday from injuries she suffered when she was attacked by a leopard in its enclosure over the weekend.
The Beekse Bergen Safari Park said in a statement that the woman, whose name has been withheld in accordance with Dutch privacy law, had passed away after she suffered serious wounds to her head and neck on Saturday while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards. “Her passing deeply affects us all, and we sympathize intensely with her family, friends, and loved ones,” the zoo in the southern town of Hilvarenbeek said in a statement, which was made together with her family. The woman began working at the zoo when she was 17 and spent nearly all of her 40-year career there.
An investigation is underway to determine why the woman was in the enclosure with the leopards. Zoo staff are typically not permitted to be in the same space as predatory animals.
According to the zoo, the woman was able to alert colleagues via a walkie-talkie that she had been hurt. An ambulance and a trauma helicopter were dispatched to the park at around 11 a.m. local time on Saturday.
The woman underwent emergency surgery, but her condition worsened Sunday evening and the zoo said they did not expect her to survive. The safari park said an area in the park will be set up where condolences can be left.

title: 6 arrested in alleged MaineCare fraud scheme
text:
Six people have been arrested in an alleged MaineCare fraud scheme.
Noora Abd, 37; Faysal Kalayaf Manahe, 51; Adel Al Rashid, 47; Sura Almohammed, 47; Ether Alyaseen, 46; and Mohammed Alkhalah, 41, have been charged with healthcare fraud conspiracy, while Abd and Manahe also have been charged with obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation and Alkhalaf also was charged with making a false statement, according to the U.S. attorney’s office.
The arrests were announced during a Tuesday morning press conference.
The six allegedly participated in a scheme to defraud MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, through Community Health Care LLC, a South Portland-based personal care agency owned and operated by Abd.
They allegedly submitted false documentation to MaineCare for services provided to Community Health Care’s clients but were never actually provided, according to the U.S. attorney’s office.
Numerous claims submitted for a single client totaled $600,000.
“Health care fraud – in all its forms – costs all of us, and today’s arrests should make it clear that if, as alleged in the indictment returned last week, you steal from our health care system for your own financial gain, you too, will be shut down and brought to justice,” U.S. Attorney Andrew B. Benson said in a statement.
Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey said that it can take years to build cases like this, requiring “sustained diligence” from investigators at the state and federal level.
“I hope today’s announcement serves as an important reminder that federal and state officials are working continuously to protect public dollars for the intended beneficiaries,” Frey said in a statement.
For months, the Trump administration has targeted Maine over failure to prevent MaineCare fraud. That was the subject of Vice President JD Vance’s May visit to Bangor International Airport.
This year the state has yanked MaineCare licenses from some providers and sanctioned others over fraud allegations. Gateway Community Services has figured centrally in the debates over the state of MaineCare. It has been the subject of fraud allegations, and late last year the Maine Department of Health and Human Services halted payments to it.
If convicted of healthcare fraud conspiracy, the defendants face up to 10 years in prison, a fine of $250,000 or twice the total loss due to fraudulent claims, and up to three years of supervised release. If convicted of obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation, the defendants face up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release. If convicted of making false statements, the defendant faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release.

title: Who’s a Good Boy? Maine’s Most Popular Dog Breed Revealed
text:
Who’s a Good Boy? Maine’s Most Popular Dog Breed Revealed
Dogs. Man’s best friend. Our four-legged companions. The lovable, tail-wagging bundles of joy that somehow manage to make life infinitely better just by being around. A gift from the gods that we truly don't deserve.
If you're a dog lover, you know exactly what I'm talking about. Their loyalty is unmatched, their affection is endless, and their ability to brighten even the worst day is downright remarkable. Whether they're protecting the family, playing fetch, or simply curling up next to you on the couch, dogs have a special way of making everything better. Dogs are about as close to perfection as it gets.
How Can Dogs Positively Affect Your Health?
They can even help improve your health. According to the American Kennel Club, dogs can lower stress, improve heart health, promote a more active lifestyle, reduce loneliness, and even lessen the threat of allergies.
As you can probably tell, I’ve been a dog owner my entire life, and for me, it’s rescue dogs all the way! But that doesn’t mean I don’t have a soft spot for every breed out there.
With that in mind, I thought it would be fun to do a little research to figure out the most popular dog breed in Maine. Thankfully, the fine folks over at House Sitter have already done the heavy lifting. The site analyzed every house-sitting request it has received to determine the most popular breed in each state.
What is the Most Popular Dog Breed in Maine?
As for Maine, according to House Sitter, a true classic came in at number one: the venerable golden retriever.
The golden retriever is the ultimate family dog. Goldens are easy to train, gentle with children, good with other pets, and always up for a walk. Sure, keeping them clean can be a chore, but they more than make up for it with their affectionate nature and goofball charm. They also make amazing service and working dogs. Quite frankly, they are pretty damn perfect.
Seriously, who doesn't love a goldie? Every single one I have ever met has been mild-mannered, sweet, and just about perfect. While I have never owned one, I would certainly rescue one if I ever had the chance. Honestly, I'd love to see it try to corral our cats. That would be quite enjoyable to watch.
Maine was not alone in its love of goldies. Seven other states had the popular dog listed at number one, including one other New England state, Vermont. I always liked those Green Mountain folks.
READ MORE: Maine’s Acadia National Park Earns National Praise as a Top Fall Destination
While eight states is a solid number for the goldie, it pales in comparison to the most popular dog breed overall, the Labrador retriever, which led the way in a whopping 28 states. Very impressive indeed.

title: Thousands of Mainers are scrambling to find new Medicare coverage amid plan terminations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Thousands of Mainers are scrambling to find new Medicare coverage amid plan terminations
As of September, more than 13,111 people were enrolled in nine Medicare Advantage plans that won’t be offered in 2027
Thousands of Mainers are scrambling to find new Medicare coverage amid plan terminations
As of September, more than 13,111 people were enrolled in nine Medicare Advantage plans that won’t be offered in 2027
Many Maine seniors are scrambling to choose their Medicare coverage after Martin’s Point terminated several Medicare Advantage plans.
An 8 Investigates analysis of Medicare enrollment data found that five other carriers are also cutting plans, affecting thousands of Mainers. As of September, more than 13,111 people were enrolled in nine Medicare Advantage plans that won’t be offered in 2027. Roughly 31,788 people were enrolled in 11 plans that will no longer offer coverage in their county.
"Particularly when your plan is being discontinued, it’s really important that you choose a new plan for next year so that you don’t have any gaps in coverage come January," said Chloe Gray, volunteer program manager at Age Maine.
Gray oversees Age Maine’s Medicare counseling program. This year, all of the agency’s one-on-one appointments are booked, and requests for help have nearly doubled. Last October, the agency received roughly 850 calls. As of Monday, it has already received more than 1,500 calls this month.
"We did see a lot of premiums increase for next year, and some of the extra benefits on plans were reduced," Gray said. "That’s pretty much across the board that we saw that happening to plans on Medicare Advantage plans and costs going up on prescription drug plans as well for original Medicare."
Seniors whose plans aren’t being terminated are also feeling the impact of significant changes, including higher premiums, reduced vision, dental and prescription coverage, and changes to provider networks.
"It seems like almost every year I have to swap plans because the coverages change or the physicians, the primary cares, they come and go," said John St. Hilaire, who attended a Medicare enrollment counseling session with his wife, Laurie.
The St. Hilaire sign up for a counseling session every year and usually book their appointment months in advance. John doesn't think they should have to jump through hoops to ensure good coverage, but they're happy for the assistance.
"We’re just lucky that people like this, at Age Maine, are there for the people," Laurie said.
Medicare open enrollment ends Dec. 7, but people enrolled in plans that were terminated will have until the end of the year to choose a new plan. People enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans can also switch plans between January and March, if needed.
Although counseling sessions are booked, other resources are available, including a comparison tool on the Medicare website, informational videos and a hotline.

- Call 1-800-MEDICARE at 1-800-633-4227 with general Medicare questions and for help enrolling in plans
While personal Medicare counseling sessions are booked at aging agencies across the state, many offices offer walk-in-clinics where you can receive assistance in person.

title: Ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump starts in southern Ukraine
text:
Local ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump starts in southern Ukraine as Russia attacks other areas
A localized ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia took effect early Tuesday ahead of a humanitarian mission brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, as missile attacks resumed in Kyiv.
The local pause in fighting started at 3 a.m. to allow an aid mission into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine later this week.
Video above: Melania Trump on new women's health NIH division
According to her office, Melania Trump led talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine after meeting with U.N. officials who briefed her on the situation in the town.
The aid mission is planned ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine expected next month aimed at ending the war after more than 4½ years of fighting.
Up to 2,000 people are stranded in Oleshky with dwindling food and medicine. They are unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the U.N.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators, as well as the militaries of the two countries, confirmed in separate statements that the ceasefire had begun.
The local ceasefire is due to last through Saturday, or longer, though deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine has thwarted previous attempts at ceasefires.
Video below: First lady slams Jimmy Kimmel for ‘hateful and violent rhetoric’
Minutes after 3 a.m., multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded in multiple parts of the country.
Late Monday, the capital also came under attack, when Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 10 injured, city officials said. In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.
“It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote in an online post shortly afterward.
Oleshky is in the partially occupied Kherson region, about 550 kilometers (340 miles) southeast of Kyiv, where the Dnipro River separates Russian and Ukrainian forces.
It was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Further calamity struck in June 2023 when floodwaters inundated the town due to a dam collapse.
Oleshky sits across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, the region’s administrative capital.
Russian forces seized Kherson in the early stages of the 2022 invasion but retreated across the river several months later.
Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened.

title: Venison From Maine Woods Feeds Families Through Hunters For The Hungry
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Hunters Are Helping Feed Families in Need
If you love to hunt but don't need/want the meat for yourself, the Hunters for the Hungry program can help you donate it to Maine's food-insecure.
Maine Wild Game Hunters Can Donate Their Harvest to Feed the Needy
My husband enjoys hunting, and he typically gets one or two deer each year. But it's just the two of us, so we end up with venison in our freezer when the next season rolls around.
READ MORE: Still No Proof of Bigfoot in Maine
Bow hunters have been in the woods for weeks, and firearms season starts this weekend, so venison will soon fill freezers all over the state.
And some hunters will have venison they don't want or need.
Maine Hunters for the Hungry Program Provides Game Meat to the Food Insecure
The Maine Hunters for the Hungry program provides places to donate the meat to people in need.
Hunters for the Hungry is a collaboration between the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, state biologists, Maine State Troopers, and hunters.
It supplies lean, high-protein game meat to food pantries, soup kitchens, and homeless shelters, providing thousands of nutritious meals for Maine's most vulnerable populations.
How to Donate Game Meat to Maine's Hunters for the Hungry Program
And the process is pretty easy.
If you have bear, deer, or moose meat to donate, contact an approved meat processor.
The Department of Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry will cover processing costs.
Game must be legally harvested, tagged, and field-dressed, and kept cold, before arriving at the processing facility.
You don't have to donate the entire animal, either. If you want to donate a few pounds of meat, the program will happily accept it.
One warning: Hunters for the Hungry cannot accept donations from animals harvested in the 'Do Not Eat' advisory area.
It will make the hunt even sweeter knowing your donation will give food-insecure families a delicious Maine meal.

title: Mother who traveled to Las Vegas on a work trip arrested after unsupervised child was injured and hospitalized, deputies say
text:
KISSIMMEE, Fla. (Gray News) - A mother who traveled to Las Vegas on a work trip was arrested after one of her children was injured and hospitalized, according to deputies.
According to the Osceola County Sheriff’s Office, a child called 911 after a dumbbell fell on her 9-year-old brother’s head on Oct. 21.
When deputies responded to the home, they found that four children, ages 14, 12, 11 and 9, were home unsupervised.
Fire rescue took the 9-year-old child to the hospital.
The responding deputy called the children’s mother, Irene Miller, 50. She told the deputy that she has been working in Las Vegas since Oct. 18, and would return on Oct. 23.
Miller said she had a babysitter coming from Tampa every morning to get the children ready for school and to check on them after school, but she did not require her to stay at night.
The 9-year-old returned home after being treated and discharged from the hospital.
Authorities contacted the children’s father and agreed to take them to his home.
Detectives met Miller when she got off her flight from Las Vegas on Oct. 23.
Miller is charged with four counts of child neglect without great bodily harm. She was booked into the Orange County jail.

title: Man arrested after series of late-night burglaries targeting women home alone, sheriff says
text:
GREENVILLE COUNTY, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - South Carolina authorities are asking for additional victims to come forward after a series of late-night burglaries targeting women home alone.
Greenville County Sheriff Hobart Lewis said investigators were made aware on Oct. 16 of multiple burglaries that shared “some very concerning similarities.”
In each burglary, a suspect entered or attempted to enter homes occupied by women who were alone at the time, Lewis said.
Investigators identified the suspect as 25-year-old Terron Lamon Banks.
Through their investigation, detectives said they linked Banks to four burglaries in September, including one where he entered an apartment through an unlocked window while a woman was sleeping.
Banks’ charges include four counts of first-degree burglary, one count of grand larceny and one count of voyeurism.
According to the sheriff’s office, Banks was able to be taken into custody at a bus station in Spartanburg County as he was trying to board a bus to Atlanta.
“We have a great relationship [with] adjoining counties,” Lewis said. “Certainly relieved to have him in custody before he got out of the county and possibly harmed somebody else.”
Deputies said they are also actively investigating five other incidents in the area that had similar circumstances that could be connected to Banks.
DNA evidence has been collected and submitted to the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division for processing.
The sheriff said Banks is not originally from Greenville and has a criminal history.
“Obviously, this guy probably did not just start doing this in Greenville County,” Lewis said. “Hopefully we can bring some justice maybe to some of those victims in another part of the country.”
Anyone who believes they were a victim of Banks or has further information has been asked to call the Greenville County Sheriff’s Office at 864-467-5300.
“Be vigilant. Watch your surroundings, keep your doors locked, keep your windows locked,” Lewis said. “Don’t be afraid to arm yourself. If you’re comfortable doing that, be aware of where that firearm is and don’t be afraid to use it.”

title: Bangor Symphony and guest cellist bring Hemingway’s work in beautiful sonic portrait
text:
I have not been a fan of Ernest Hemingway’s writing — too many short sentences and too much toxic masculinity. I’m having to rethink that assessment after hearing cellist Zuill Bailey’s dynamic performance of Michael Daugherty’s “Tales of Hemingway for Cello and Orchestra” Sunday, Oct. 18.
Bailey perfectly performed the piece with the Bangor Symphony Orchestra at the Collins Center for the Arts in Orono. It was the centerpiece of the symphony’s concert titled “Force of Nature” that opened its 131st season.
Daugherty composed what has been called “a sonic portrait” of the author’s best known works for Bailey in 2015. Since then, the cellist has performed it more than 60 times. In four movements, it vividly brings to life Hemingway’s novels, “For Whom the Bell Tolls,” “The Old Man and the Sea,” “The Sun Also Rises” and the short story “Big Two-Hearted River.”
This piece requires the cellist to pluck and strum strings and tap the body of Bailey’s instrument, a rare Matteo Gofriller cello built in 1693. At times Sunday, Bailey appeared to be wrestling rather than dancing with the music. He is a charismatic performer who channels the notes with his entire body and appears to conquer rather than conjure them, something Daugherty requires of a soloist. Playing “Tales of Hemingway” for a celllist is akin to athletes running the Appalachian Trail, or so it seemed Sunday.
Conductor and Music Director Lucas Richman and the orchestra embraced this unorthodox concerto with gusto and precision. It was an incredibly memorable performance.
Also on the program were Peggy Stuart Coolidge’s “New England Autumn,” which musically reflected the vibrant colors of the leaves outside and a country fair. The concert concluded with a lovely interpretation of Robert Schumann’s Symphony No. 2 in C major.
This season, the orchestra is partnering with the Gracie Theatre at Husson University to offer a chamber music series featuring guest artists and BSO musicians. The Gracie, which seats 490 compared with the Collins Center’s 1,435, is an intimate space that allowed the audience to get up close and personal with the players on Oct. 19.
Concertmaster Mitchell Newman (violin), Simon Bilyk (violin), Laura Gallucci (viola) and Noreen Silver (cello) joined Bailey on stage for Franz Schubert’s String Quintet in C major, a rare chamber music piece featuring two cellos. Bailey opened the concert with Johann Sebastian Bach’s Solo Sonata and a piece by Pablo Casals, considered to be one of the greatest cellists of all time.
This series, which will feature guest violinist Julian Rhee at 6:30 p.m. Feb. 1 and soprano Natalia Santaliz and mezzo-soprano Erin Wagner at 6:30 p.m. April 22, is a welcome addition to the symphony’s offerings. It’s an opportunity to hear some beautiful music and see how musicians bring it to life.
Sunday’s concert, “Force of Nature,” may be streamed through Nov. 6 at watch.bangorsymphony.org.

title: 📚 BIG NEWS, BANGOR! Local School Teacher Publishes First Children’s Book! ✏️

Bangor, Maine, Teacher Publishes First Children’s Book
From the classroom to the bookshelf!
Rachel Ortiz, is a teacher at John Bapst Memorial High School, who has just had her first kids book published, "The Adventures of Pip Quilliam: A Prickly Kind Of Brave"
Five years of writing in notebooks, jotting down ideas, rewriting & tweaking little details have all led to this moment, that all started 6 years ago, with a simple walk through the woods with her son, when they stumbled upon a baby porcupine.
As the mother of a son with profound autism, Rachel has spent years seeing the world through a slightly different lens. Raising her son has taught her so much about acceptance, individuality, and the importance of recognizing that everyone has a place in this world

What's the book about?
Pip Quilliam, is a young porcupine with a big smile and a kind heart. There’s just one problem: His quills make the other animals in the Maine woods a little nervous!
No matter how friendly Pip tries to be, the fawns, raccoons, and other creatures keep their distance. Just when he starts to think he’ll always be alone, he meets Tommy Tortuga, a cheerful wood turtle who isn't afraid to be his friend.
As the two explore the woods together, the other animals begin to see Pip differently. And when danger strikes, Pip’s quills and courage might just save the day!
The Adventures of Pip Quilliam: A Prickly Kind Of Brave: is a charming Maine woodland adventure about friendship, kindness, and embracing what makes us all different. It’s an important reminder that everyone deserves a chance to belong.

title: 1 in 1800 Senior Spotlight: Scarlett Downes On Arts at Bates
text:
Scarlett Downes ’28 can be found across the art scene at Bates, whether in WRBC, Snaggletooth Literary Arts Magazine, the Bates Dance Department, or “Bates Plays”. In continuation of the Bates Student series 1 in 1800, we feature Downes, a junior double-majoring in Dance and Rhetoric, Film, and Screen Studies.
What made you choose Bates?
At first, I was really interested in Colby, after hearing about it from my camp counselor when I was a counselor-in-training. I soon realized though that I did not love the preppy vibes that Colby was giving but did want to be in Maine, so I revisited Bates! I was really drawn in by how established the arts seemed here. I didn’t even know how good the dance program was, but [I] appreciated that there was one.
What are you involved in on campus?
I am a DJ for WRBC, our campus radio station, and co-host a show Friday’s 11:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. called The Cursed Sisters. I also work at the Digital Media Studios where I rent out equipment to fellow students. I wanted to work there because I am a Rhetoric, Film, and Screen Studies major and I am super interested in film and video production. It’s a great way to get to know the equipment and it’s fun to use.
I am also very involved in the Bates Dance Department. This semester I am involved in a thesis work as a dancer and choreographic collaborator which will be performed in the Fall Dance Concert this November! I am also involved with Snaggletooth, our campus literary magazine, and this semester conducted a Mosh interview for the upcoming issue with my friend who is a drummer.
What have been a few of your favorite memories at Bates?
There are so many, but honestly, what’s coming to mind right now is the “Bates Plays” nights. This year was Wilco and the last two years was Big Thief. Lots of friends, music, vibes, and dancing.
I would also say working with guest artist/choreographer Jenna Riegal last spring semester. She set a new dance work for six dancers, including myself. It was such a joy to work with her and probably one of my favorite dance pieces I’ve been in at Bates. All those rehearsals were so fun and got me through those cold winter days.
If there is one thing Bates could do differently, what would it be?
Bates pours a lot of money into sports and athletics, and as someone involved in the arts here, I do think they could put a lot more energy, time, and money into the arts departments and facilities. The arts are so important, and after being drawn to Bates because of its emphasis in the arts, I would really like to see a larger commitment to them from the institution.
What are you most looking forward to for the rest of the semester/year?
I am really looking forward to the Fall Dance Concert as well as continuing to dream up my own thesis in dance I will create next year. I want to combine video production with dancing and hopefully perform in the Immersive Media Studio.
In terms of the rest of the school year, I am really looking forward to studying abroad in Prague, if my visa gets approved, which I did make a mistake on. I am going to take some film classes at FAMU (Film and TV School of the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague) which will be super cool. I am also very excited to travel around Europe while I am abroad. I am taking German this semester, so I am hoping I will be able to go to Germany in the spring and say “Guten Morgen” to people.
Editor’s Note: Downes’ answers have been edited for length and clarity. This story was edited on Oct. 27 to correctly identify Downes’ class year.

title: Sen. Angus King endorses Matt Dunlap in Maine CD2 race
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A major endorsement in the race for Maine’s Second Congressional District came in Tuesday morning.
“I think Matt will make a great member of Congress, and I look forward to working with him,“ said Independent Senator Angus King, who is officially endorsing Democrat Matt Dunlap.
Dunlap will square off against former Governor Paul LePage at the polls on November 3rd.
King says Dunlap made a strong impression on him when they worked together in the State House when King was governor and Dunlap was a lawmaker.
“When you serve as governor, you get to know a lot of legislators, but one I particularly remember is Matt Dunlap because he was tough and smart and a strong advocate for his district,” King said in a video message. “He also has been a great advocate for the sportsmen and women of Maine. In fact, he has a hunting license. He can represent the whole second district in Congress, and that’s what we need.”
“When Senator King was Governor, we worked closely on major issues for Maine sportsmen. I’m honored to have his support and endorsement, and look forward to the chance to work with him to lower prices if elected,” Dunlap said. “Mainers are frustrated by high prices on home heating oil, groceries, hockey sticks, and pretty much everything else under the sun. We’ve got to end the war that’s keeping gas prices high and end the tariff taxes that are keeping grocery prices high.”
King has also endorsed Hannah Pingree for governor.
LePage senior campaign adviser Brent Littlefield commented on the endorsement, saying: “The last time Angus King endorsed in a race Governor LePage was in he endorsed Eliot Cutler. Matt Dunlap is now in the same company as Eliot Cutler.”
