title: Someone’s been driving a fire truck around Limerick for months. It’s not the fire department.
text:
Someone has been driving a fire truck around Limerick with lights flashing and sirens blaring for months, but they’re not associated with the local fire department or any other agency.
A Maine State Police spokesperson says the incident has been addressed with the vehicle’s owner.
The Limerick Fire-Rescue Department notified the public of recent reports of a fire truck driving in the area of Lake Arrowhead in a social media post on Sunday.
“Please know this vehicle is not associated in any way with the Limerick Fire Department or any surrounding town. This vehicle is believed to be personally owned,” the department said in its post, which included a short video clip of the truck.
The department encouraged members of the public to share information about, and video of, such incidents with Maine State Police.
Shannon Moss, spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety, said in an email Tuesday evening that the owner of the vehicle has been identified and “the issue has been resolved.”
Moss said in a follow-up email Wednesday morning that the vehicle’s owner has not been charged with a crime but was reminded of laws regarding use of sirens and emergency lights. She added that it wasn’t clear whether the owner was the one driving.
The vehicles permitted by state law to utilize emergency lights include fire department vehicles, which are defined as vehicles “owned by, registered to and maintained by a governmental agency or political subdivision that is equipped and used primarily for response to a fire or emergency situation.”
Moss said only one such incident, on Sunday evening, was reported to state police. But Fire Chief Jared Welsh said in an email Tuesday that there have been multiple reports of such instances over the course of a few months.
Welsh said members of the public reported hearing sirens and seeing the truck but detected no signs of an emergency in the area.
While he believed it was only a few times per month, Welsh said comments on the department’s Facebook post indicate it’s likely been occurring “much more often, possibly multiple times a week.”
Moss said there have been no reported incidents since Sunday.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 28 to add additional information from the Department of Public Safety.

title: We compared AI travel videos with real listings; here’s what we found
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (InvestigateTV) — A scroll through social media can make a mountain cabin, beachfront rental or luxury resort look like an easy escape. But some AI-generated travel videos may not accurately show the property a viewer would book or the price a viewer would pay.
We reviewed TikTok posts promoting real hotels, resorts and vacation rentals. The posts included TikTok labels stating they were generated with artificial intelligence and that the creator earns commission. Several directed viewers to major booking services, including Expedia and Booking.com.
In multiple examples, the apparently AI-generated video did not appear to match the property’s official listing or other photos.
In others, the price promoted in the video was not a deal we could locate when we checked the listing.
Using AI to create travel posts is not inherently illegal. The concern is whether commercial posts create a misleading impression about a real property, price, amenity, review or travel experience.
What we found
Altered exterior and living room
One TikTok video promoted a real rental home in the Blue Ridge Mountains. But a comparison with the property’s listing showed apparent differences in the home’s exterior and the layout and furnishings of the living room.
The linked property was real. The video, however, appeared to present an altered version of it.
The same post promoted a price of $93 per person per night. The video did not identify travel dates, occupancy, taxes, fees or other terms for that price.
When InvestigateTV/Atlanta News First checked the listing, the rate displayed was about $865 per night.
The video did not state travel dates or terms for that price, and we didn’t find the advertised deal on the booking link or the property’s official booking sites.
A doorway changes — and so does the neighboring home
Another AI-generated video promoted a beachfront rental in Panama City Beach.
In the video, the kitchen appeared to connect directly to a bedroom.
The actual property listing showed that opening leads outside. A side-by-side comparison also showed differences in the neighboring house.
Different properties in one video
A separate video presented features as part of the Gaylord National Resort at National Harbor, outside Washington, D.C.
But we found the video appeared to combine features from more than one Gaylord resort.
Among them: an outdoor lazy river that is not located at Gaylord National.
Other advertised deals
We also reviewed posts promoting specials such as three nights for about $359 at Pine Mountain Callaway Resort And Gardens in Georgia.
We could not find that offer through the listed booking link or the property’s official website when we checked October 2026.
Who earns when viewers book?
The posts we reviewed included TikTok’s “Creator earns commission” label. That label indicates the creator may receive a commission when a qualifying purchase is made through a link, but it does not by itself verify every claim in a video about a property, price or availability.
TikTok told us it requires AI generated content labels on realistic scenes or people, adding that misleading AI content would prohibit the account from making a commission. The misleading content would need to be caught in the platforms own general moderation or by a user reporting it.
Expedia said the accounts we shared with them “don’t appear to be connected to Expedia’s affiliate program and the discounts featured in the videos are not an Expedia affiliate offering.”
Booking.com did not respond by our deadline.
What to check before booking
Atlanta-based travel agent Nicholas Santine of TravelMation said travelers should not rely on a social media video alone when deciding where to book.
“Google the location. Google the hotel... See reviews. Look at review photos. Look at other people’s experience. Go beyond what the influencers and what the algorithm wants you to see,” Santine advised.
He added that booking through direct links on an app may not be the safest route.
“Go to the exact website,” he said. “Don’t trust the link. Don’t trust everything you see. You know, if it’s too good to be true, it probably is.”
Santine said a real-life travel agent is the safest best to avoid losing money or showing up to a place that isn’t as advertised.
Most travel agents will be licensed, and they are primarily free to use. The agent receives commission from the resorts and amenities.
Before booking a trip promoted on social media:
- Search for the property independently 
  - Do not rely only on the link in the post
- Compare the video with the official listing
  - Check the hotel’s website or the rental listing on sites such as Airbnb or Vrbo
- Compare like with like 
  - Use the same travel dates, number of guests, taxes and fees before deciding whether a price matches
- Look beyond the creator’s video 
  - Review several recent traveler photos and reviews
  - Be cautious if comments look generic, repetitive, limited or disabled
- Check the disclosures 
  - Look for AI, advertising, affiliate and sponsorship labels
- Protect your payment 
  - Avoid sending deposits through direct messages, wire transfers, crypto, gift cards or unfamiliar payment apps
  - A credit card may provide options to dispute some charges
- Save your evidence 
  - Keep screenshots of the post, booking page, terms and receipts if something goes wrong
What the law says
There is no single U.S. law requiring every AI-generated travel post to carry a label. But existing consumer-protection and advertising law can apply when commercial content makes a materially misleading claim.
The Federal Trade Commission said its truth-in-advertising standards apply to endorsements on social media. A paid endorsement or other relationship that could affect how viewers judge a recommendation may need to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously.
Federal rules also address certain fake consumer reviews, testimonials and fake indicators of social-media influence, such as bots or accounts that do not reflect real people’s activities or experiences.
In Georgia, the Fair Business Practices Act declares unfair or deceptive practices in consumer transactions unlawful. The law includes conduct that causes confusion about the source, sponsorship, affiliation or geographic origin of goods or services.
The bottom line: an AI label does not itself prove a post is deceptive or necessarily resolve whether it is.
The key question is whether the content leads consumers to believe that a property, price, deal, review or personal endorsement is real or verified when it is not.
Encountered a potentially misleading travel post?
TikTok advises users who see a post containing AI-generated content that goes against its guidelines, including AI impersonation, to report it:
From the TikTok app
- Go to the post and tap the Share button or press and hold the post, then tap Report
- Tap Misinformation, then tap Deepfakes, synthetic media, and manipulated media
- Tap Submit
From a web browser
- Go to the post and hover over the More options button at the top, then click Report
- Click Misinformation, then click Deepfakes, synthetic media, and manipulated media
- Click Submit

title: Can ‘You Can See Everything’ Be Nominated For Best Picture?
text:
Can ‘You Can See Everything’ Get Nominated For Best Picture?
The higher its box office total, the more rapturous its reviews, the more people will start to wonder: Does You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes have a shot at a nomination for Best Picture at next year’s Academy Awards? And beyond that: Can it get nominated in the first place? After all, no prior documentary in the 90+-year history of the Academy has ever received a Best Picture nom. That would suggest that the odds are not in Fielder and Oppeheim’s favor.
They may not be, but it’s not technically impossible even if it has never happened (yet). A documentary can be nominated for Best Picture, provided it meets the same eligibility requirements as any other feature film that wants to win the biggest Oscar.
READ MORE: The Worst Movies Where Actors Played Multiple Roles
According to the Academy’s eligibility rules, any film that wants to be considered for Best Picture must be meet three distinct requirements.
Rule 1
A week of being “publicly exhibited for paid admission” in one of six different U.S. markets: Los Angeles, New York, the San Francisco Bay Area, Chicago, Dallas-Fort Worth, and Atlanta. That run must last “at least seven consecutive days” with screenings “at least three times daily” with “at least one screening beginning between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m. daily.” The film must also “be advertised during its qualifying theatrical release in a manner normal and customary to theatrical feature distribution practices.”
Rule 2
After that initial run the film must play “in nine additional markets, separate and in addition to the market being utilized for the film’s General Entry qualifying run, resulting in a total of at least ten markets” among the top 50 markets in the country. This is known as a “Best Picture Expanded Theatrical Run,” and it must occur within 45 days of the film’s qualifying run.
Rule 3
The third: “The motion picture must meet the requirements of two out of the four Representation and Inclusion Standards.”
Long story short: Yes, You Can See Everything can receive a Best Picture nomination, in addition to a nomination for Best Documentary.
But will it?
Again, it’s never happened before. And there are reasons to think it’s a long shot. The Director’s Guild of America recently ruled that You Can See Everything cannot compete for its top award, outstanding directorial achievement in theatrical feature film. That’s because that group’s rules explicitly state that “re-releases, animated films and documentaries are not eligible” for that category at the DGA awards. You Can See Everything can compete for outstanding directorial achievement of a documentary film at the DGA Awards — but it’s that “theatrical feature film” award that’s often considered a key forerunner to the Academy Awards. And You Can See Everything definitely won’t win that one.
Of course, there are a lot of preliminary awards before the Oscars, many of them voted on by critics groups, many of whom have been overwhelmingly ecstatic in their praise of the film. If the movie wins a few of the key critics’ awards — and You Can see Everything keeps performing well in theaters — that could be enough momentum to help it break new ground at the Academy Awards.

title: Here’s how to keep your pet safe during Halloween
text:
(CNN) - Halloween brings hazards for pets, according to the American Veterinary Medical Association, which says emergency animal clinics see a spike in cases during October.
Dr. Jen Quammen, president of the American Veterinary Medical Association, said the biggest hazard may not be candy.
“I think sometimes the biggest Halloween hazard isn’t exactly the candy; it might be the front door. The doors opening over and over. There are strangers in costumes,” Quammen said.
Keep pets secure
Quammen said pet owners should make sure pets are microchipped and have ID tags and collars in case they slip out an open door. She said owners should also consider this before taking pets trick-or-treating.
“I would always encourage folks to know their pet,” Quammen said. “I think I would just consider that the pet gets a vote in this conversation.”
Candy dangers
Unattended candy can be dangerous for pets. Chocolate is not the only concern. Treats made with a sugar-free sweetener called xylitol can also be harmful.
Quammen said pet owners should contact their veterinarian or poison control if pets get into either type of candy.
“And the other thing about candy is our pets don’t really usually unwrap it. They also eat the wrappers, and those can be an issue as well if they get swallowed,” Quammen said.
Costume tips
Best Friends Animal Society recommends the following when dressing up pets:
- Keep costumes comfortable
- Don’t put pets in anything that restricts movement
- Make sure pets can see clearly
- Remove any small parts that can be chewed off and swallowed
- If pets show signs of distress, opt for a festive bandana instead
Quammen said preparation is the top tip for a safe Halloween: “A little bit of preparation can really keep Halloween super fun and keep your pet out of the ER.”

title: ‘Dune’ Prepares For an Epic Finale With Final Part Three Trailer
text:
‘Dune’ Prepares For an Epic Finale With Final ‘Part Three’ Trailer
In just a few short years, Dune has gone from unfilmable to one of the biggest franchises in Hollywood. title: Maine secretary of state visits Maranacook High School on mock election day
text:
READFIELD, Maine (WABI) - Students at Maranacook High School met with Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows on Tuesday, which was mock election day across the state.
“Mock Election Day is civics in action. This is a great opportunity for students to practice voting before they turn 18,” Bellows said.
Mock ballots cast statewide
A total of 115 schools across Maine cast mock ballots Tuesday for governor, the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate.
Bellows met with students to answer questions about polling places, election monitoring and bipartisan dialogue.
Student and principal perspectives
For one sophomore, seeing the ballot table in the hallway was a push to learn more.
“I want to know about what’s going on in the world and not just base it off what my dad says, or what my parents are saying, or what teachers are saying,” said Rorie Sage, a sophomore.
Principal Michele LaForge said participation has increased over her five years at the school. The attitude is shifting and remaining civil across four towns with different views.
“I get fewer people telling me that their vote doesn’t matter,” LaForge said.
Mock ballots and voting habits
Bellows cited research that practicing voting early builds lifelong voters. She hopes the mock ballots build that habit.
“It’s important to have a voice in today’s society,” said Serenity Longfellow, a sophomore.

title: American Legion national commander visits the county to learn the challenges that local veterans face
text:
STOCKHOLM, Maine (WAGM) - American Legion National Commander Jay Bowen spent most of this week in Aroostook County learning about the challenges veterans face.
Visits to county American Legion posts
Bowen visited multiple American Legions in the county. At the Stockholm American Legion, where News Source 8 met up with Bowen, the room was filled with veterans from Caribou, Van Buren and Madawaska.
Bowen said one concern keeps coming up.
“A lot of times they have to travel great distances just to get VA medical care,” Bowen said. “And a lot of times they have to go through things like community care or VA telehealth, which is okay, but it doesn’t really replace the care that they get when they go to a VA facility.”
VA operates in 10 locations across the state of Maine.
Community care and telehealth
Community care allows veterans to receive care outside the VA, while telehealth provides care remotely. Bowen said those options can be helpful, but they don’t always provide the same veteran-specific experience.
“Their primary care provider may see one veteran out of 25,” Bowen said. “So they don’t really have the understanding or the background to be able to help that veteran as well as they could through the VA system.”
Testimony before Congress
Bowen said the conversations he is having with veterans in Maine could help him speak to lawmakers about those challenges. He is scheduled to testify before Congress in February.
“So in February, when I get the opportunity to testify before Congress and talk about veterans issues and challenges, I can speak a little bit more intelligently about some of those things,” Bowen said.
Lloyd Woods, Maine’s representative on the American Legion’s National Executive Committee, said hearing those concerns is part of the organization’s larger mission to support veterans.
“The commander said it really, really well to be part of the solution. Like he said, if you’re not part of the solution, then you’re part of the problem,” Woods said. “So it’s a very good thing for us to be part of the solution to assist any veteran that we can in any way that they need, either medically or physically or financially. However we can do it, we do it.”
Next stop on nationwide tour
Bowen’s visit to Aroostook County is one stop on a nationwide tour. His last day in the county was Wednesday, October 27th. He will continue the tour in St. Louis.

title: Man arrested after series of late-night burglaries targeting women home alone, sheriff says
text:
GREENVILLE COUNTY, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - South Carolina authorities are asking for additional victims to come forward after a series of late-night burglaries targeting women home alone.
Greenville County Sheriff Hobart Lewis said investigators were made aware on Oct. 16 of multiple burglaries that shared “some very concerning similarities.”
In each burglary, a suspect entered or attempted to enter homes occupied by women who were alone at the time, Lewis said.
Investigators identified the suspect as 25-year-old Terron Lamon Banks.
Through their investigation, detectives said they linked Banks to four burglaries in September, including one where he entered an apartment through an unlocked window while a woman was sleeping.
Banks’ charges include four counts of first-degree burglary, one count of grand larceny and one count of voyeurism.
According to the sheriff’s office, Banks was able to be taken into custody at a bus station in Spartanburg County as he was trying to board a bus to Atlanta.
“We have a great relationship [with] adjoining counties,” Lewis said. “Certainly relieved to have him in custody before he got out of the county and possibly harmed somebody else.”
Deputies said they are also actively investigating five other incidents in the area that had similar circumstances that could be connected to Banks.
DNA evidence has been collected and submitted to the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division for processing.
The sheriff said Banks is not originally from Greenville and has a criminal history.
“Obviously, this guy probably did not just start doing this in Greenville County,” Lewis said. “Hopefully we can bring some justice maybe to some of those victims in another part of the country.”
Anyone who believes they were a victim of Banks or has further information has been asked to call the Greenville County Sheriff’s Office at 864-467-5300.
“Be vigilant. Watch your surroundings, keep your doors locked, keep your windows locked,” Lewis said. “Don’t be afraid to arm yourself. If you’re comfortable doing that, be aware of where that firearm is and don’t be afraid to use it.”

title: Patricia Ann Ropp | Obituaries
text:
Patricia Ann Ropp began her journey to the next great adventure with her usual grace and determination, at home with her three loving children by her side, on Oct. 19, 2026.
Trish was born on March 27, 1947, in Truro, County Cornwall, England, to Capt. Henry Thomas and Mary Patricia Mill. At age 8, the family emigrated to Melbourne, Australia. A fourth-generation descendant of famed royal family portrait artist Polly Pearce, Trish attended the National Gallery of Victoria Art School. At 21, Trish emigrated to the States, landing in Terre Haute, Ind., where she met her beloved husband of 32 years, David Edwin Ropp. One of their first dates was to attend her brother’s wedding in Belize; however, Mother Nature had other plans and canceled their flights south. Already at the airport, Dave asked Trish where she wanted to go instead, and she replied she had always wanted to visit Bar Harbor; off they went, not knowing they would fall in love with Maine and each other on the way.

title: Bangor Councilors vote to end Zoom public comment
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Zoom public comment for Bangor City Council meetings is officially a thing of the past.
Councilors voted 6 to 2 Monday night to stop offering Zoom participation.
Councilor Susan Faloon who introduced the order said since Zoom participation resumed in January after a brief pause, there has only been one instance where a resident meaningfully participated in comment and was not disruptive. She added the city is not legally obligated to allow virtual comments.
Those who opposed the order said if councilors are permitted to join via Zoom, residents should be permitted the same accommodation.
Faloon added that anyone who cannot attend due to medical reason should contact the city and ask for an accommodation.
You can still comment in person in council chambers and submit a written comment ahead of time.
Councilors Joe Leonard and Wayne Mallar voted against the order. Councilor Daniel Carson was not in attendance.

title: York’s unofficial Lorax speaks for a beloved tree
text:
YORK — For six days, James Kences hadn’t eaten anything. Just sixteen half glasses of fruit juice, nine cups of tea.
“The sort of constant discomfort of not having eaten really keeps me on edge in terms of just the anger that I need to have,” Kences, York’s town historian, said of his hunger strike Thursday morning.
Behind him, a tall honey locust loomed over a clipboard waiting for signatures that could save it from being cut down next week. He paced, hungry, with his hands clasped behind his back and his hair tucked into a tan hat. “Vocal local,” it read.
Bewildered drivers passed the intersection at York Street and Long Sands Road, staring at the man dressed in an ochre orange pullover with a screen-printed portrait of the tree. The Lorax of York.
On Nov. 3, the decades-old tree in the center of town is due to be felled as part of the York Village revitalization plan. Officials have described it as a visual hazard, causing further confusion at an already perplexing intersection. The most efficient and affordable option to make the intersection safer, is to take down the tree, which is not native to Maine. Kences thinks there are better solutions, like carefully excavating its roots to relocate it.
The longtime York resident initially began gathering support to save the tree in a Facebook group. Comments asked him how they could help. He told them he’d be standing in front of the tree every morning and waiting at the library in an effort to collect 100 signatures before the Select Board meeting on Monday.
His first day on the ground, Kences gathered just over a dozen supporters. The next day, a few dozen more, and by a Thursday afternoon deadline, he’d garnered 124. Per town ordinance, the Select Board is required to hold a public hearing and create a ballot question for any petition that meets the 100-signature requirement.
“If I didn’t do it, who would?” Kences said.
‘I DIDN’T KNOW ABOUT IT’
Voters approved the revitalization plan a decade ago after officials tabled a handful of efforts to revamp the area dating to the ’60s, Town Engineer Dean Lessard said on Oct. 8.
By the time Kences began petitioning, the intersection was already a construction zone. The grass had already been ripped up. A dozen large concrete pipes lay in the dirt beside the tree and the wires used to light the honey locust every year had been clipped.
Members of the Select Board say residents have known of the tree’s fate — and the relocation of a soldier’s monument that sits in the same intersection — since 2016. Some residents say that’s not true, and have joined Kences in his quest to save the tree.
“A lot of people are like, ‘Well, we had 10 years to do this,’” resident Lana Dufour-Kosacz said after scrawling her name on the petition Thursday morning. “I didn’t know about this.”
Kences said the town wasn’t transparent enough about the consequences of the project, and that 10 years is plenty of time for people to change their minds. By Monday’s meeting, 227 people agreed. Several residents said at the meeting that they didn’t recall the vote, and that there should be a new one. Others, including two arborists, said chopping down a perfectly healthy tree angered them.
Resident Mike Lee told the board he believed the scope of the revitalization project had changed since he and his neighbors voted in 2016.
Officials discovered a $100,000 shortfall in funding based on 10 years of inflation when it came time to set the plan into action, Lessard, the engineer, said on Oct. 8. Officials filled the gap by using money meant for the second phase of the project. Lee and resident Susan Gillis said the funding breakdown changed what voters thought they approved years ago.
Kences also thinks that killing the honey locust will pave the way for developers to build structures that would destroy the old-town charm of York Village.
“I want this tree not only to be recognized as a tree,” Kences said. “I want it to become symbolic of the town’s population, pushing back against unscrupulous developers who cynically and manipulatively go over town government again and again and again to get their way.”
A tenth of a mile down the road — the distance Kences had ridden his bike countless times to be with the tree — his home faces an uncertain fate. He lives on the upper floor of a bagel shop, which is slated to either be demolished or moved to make room for an apartment building.
As he prepared to speak to the Select Board on Monday, Kences pulled a copy of “The Lorax” by Dr. Seuss out of a reusable shopping bag that also held a tall drinking glass — the one he’d been filling with juice during his hunger strike. As he took the stand, he handed the glass to a perplexed board member without explanation and it was passed down the line to the other members.
“The honey locust is a personal friend of mine,” Kences said, recalling several past protests against a handful of town issues. “I felt strong because of the strength it offered.”
OFFICIALS UNDER STATE, FEDERAL PRESSURE
At Monday’s meeting, Select Board members reminded residents that the town is at the mercy of long-standing plans already approved by state and federal entities. Just 10% of the funding will come from local contributions, while another 10% will come from the state and 80% from the federal government.
The town also has a contract with a construction company, which it must pay upon the project’s estimated completion in November 2027.
“Any change to that contract, is not just the town’s choice to make,” said Peter Joseph, the town manager. “There’s pretty significant consequences if we stand in the way of moving forward something that’s 90% funded by entities other than the town.”
Joseph said breaking agreements with other people’s money could open the town up to the possibility of litigation. And changing the project could take officials back to the design phase, delaying it another 18 to 24 months.
In recent weeks, residents on Facebook pleaded for alternatives to removing the tree. Kences’ idea to excavate its roots and relocate it could cost the town $50,000.
“The problem with that is not necessarily the dollars, although that’s a pretty significant amount of money for the town, it’s also the timing, and that takes a pretty significant amount of time,” Joseph said.
The Select Board is due to continue the discussion at its next meeting on Nov. 9, and could set a date for a public hearing about the tree, pending an evaluation from the town’s attorney about the legality of the petition. Board members noted that the attorney’s opinion could be moot because the tree is slated to come down before the next meeting.
“We care,” board member Mary-Anne Szeniawski told voters on Monday. “Sometimes we’re in a position where, what some people might want, we can’t provide.”

title: New polls show Maine Senate race neck and neck, governor campaign heating up
text:
New polling released Tuesday says Democrat Troy Jackson holds a slim lead in Maine’s U.S. Senate race, while Republican Bobby Charles has made gains in the state’s gubernatorial campaign.
One survey of more than 1,400 voters, published by the Marist Poll just a week before the midterms, showed Jackson with a two-point lead over Republican Sen. Susan Collins among likely voters, 49% to 47%. The result is within the poll’s margin of error of +/- 6.6 percentage points.
Another poll by Echelon Insights and NetChoice, also released Tuesday, sampled 413 Maine residents and found more encouraging results for the Democrat: Jackson holds a seven-point lead among voters who have already cast their ballots, 51% to Collins’ 44%. That poll’s margin of error was +/- 6.3%. However, Republicans have tended to vote later than Democrats in recent elections.
Both Senate polls are in line with previous surveys, which have shown a tight race for months.
Perhaps more surprising is the Marist poll’s findings in the state’s gubernatorial race, which veered from Echelon’s findings and previous polling results.
Charles and Democrat Hannah Pingree both polled at 44% among likely voters, Marist found. Six percent of respondents said they’re backing independent Rick Bennett, and another 6% were undecided.
The split is wider between registered voters, of whom 51% supported Pingree and 40% backed Charles. Bennett received support from 7%.
Still, Marist’s poll is the first to show such a tight race for governor. Charles has trailed by double digits in most previous surveys and has been at a significant fundraising disadvantage compared to Pingree.
Echelon’s poll aligned more closely with trends established in previous surveys. Of Maine voters who have already cast their ballots, 51% told Echelon they voted for Pingree. Just 38% said they backed Charles, and 7% supported Bennett.
Independent voters, a crucial demographic in both races, are breaking toward Democrats, Marist’s poll found. Half of the survey’s unaffiliated respondents said they’re backing Jackson in the race for Senate, compared to 41% who back Collins. Some 43% said they plan to cast their vote for Pingree, while 35% said they were backing Charles.
Echelon’s poll did not differentiate its results by respondents’ political affiliation.
President Donald Trump remains widely unpopular in Maine, both surveys found. Some 57% of respondents to Marist’s poll (Including 70% of independents) are unhappy with Trump’s second term so far, along with 62% of those surveyed by Echelon.
Just under half of those polled by Marist, 41%, said they’re casting their vote “against the president” in this year’s midterms. That aligns with nationwide trends, which show discontentment with the White House is fueling Democrats’ hopes — and Republicans’ fears — of significant Democratic gains in Congress this November.

title: 7-year-old shoots first buck. It was bigger than most shot in Maine.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Waylon Bourgoin is only 7 years old, but he already has a 225-pound deer to his name.
The young hunter shot his first buck Saturday evening during Maine’s youth hunting days while hunting with his father, Tyler Bourgoin.
Waylon shot a doe last year, but this season he had a bigger goal in mind. He wanted to shoot a buck — and a big one at that.
On Friday, the pair passed on several young bucks while holding out for one of the larger deer they had captured on trail cameras. One of the bucks they hoped to harvest showed up Friday afternoon at another hunting spot, prompting them to move stands for Saturday.
“Lo and behold one of the bigger ones we’ve been watching stepped out and he made it count,” Tyler said.
Waylon shot the buck with a 6.5 Creedmoor from an elevated hunting tower on their family farm in Corinth, which was farmed by Waylon’s great-grandparents many years ago.
Tyler said he and his son had spent plenty of time practicing shooting together.
“Right after I said he went down, he started crying saying he just shot a huge buck.”
The family is submitting Waylon’s deer for his first “patch buck” recognition through The Maine Sportsman.

title: Cornell student suspended after 2023 alleged assault was then placed in co-ed dorm, professor says
text:
Cornell student suspended after 2023 alleged assault was then placed in co-ed dorm, professor says
One of the seven Cornell University students disciplined in connection with an alleged 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house returned to campus this fall after a three-semester suspension and was placed in a co-ed dorm with a roommate who had no idea about his past, according to a professor familiar with the housing arrangement.
Video above — 'You deserve to be safe': Bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
University housing officials then left the accused student in that shared room for two weeks after the woman who made the allegation filed a lawsuit in September publicly accusing him of rape, psychology professor Corinna Loeckenhoff said at a Faculty Senate meeting. Meanwhile, Cornell students shared the accused student’s name and dorm location on social media.
“This was a clear security risk,” Loeckenhoff told Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff at the Oct. 14 meeting, according to a recording obtained by The Associated Press.
“Cornell’s own records show that, at the very least, he admitted to taking drugs and having sex with an intoxicated person,” Loeckenhoff said. “Why was Housing Services not aware of this? They had no clue until the shocked roommate contacted them and asked them for a room change,” she said.
Kotlikoff faces a possible no-confidence vote from faculty this week. Debate on the issue resumes Wednesday. In response to questions from the AP, Cornell said it would examine how the dorm room situation was handled.
“The university will review whether concerns were raised with housing or other offices and, if so, whether appropriate accommodations were provided,” the university said.
Cornell explains decision to allow student's return
The woman, identified in court papers by the pseudonym Jane Doe, sued Cornell and seven men last month, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in 2024.
All those men have denied her allegations, saying either the sex was consensual or they weren't involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter, and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York's attorney general.
Cornell disciplined several members of the Chi Phi fraternity following a monthslong Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write “reflection” papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times.
One of the expelled students later enrolled at Nova Southeastern University in Florida. The university said it was unaware of the allegations when it admitted him and acted immediately after learning of them. It declined to say what action it took or whether he remains enrolled, citing federal student privacy laws.
The student who returned to Cornell this fall had been suspended for three semesters.
Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney representing the student, said his client maintains the encounter was consensual. He cautioned against treating all seven accused students as equally responsible.
“These are seven different people, with different circumstances, and each deserves to be judged on the evidence concerning him,” Miltenberg said.
In her lawsuit, Jane Doe accused the student of having sex with her without her consent alongside another fraternity member and later joining other men in snorting ketamine from her body.
Details of the allegations remained largely out of public view until Jane Doe filed her lawsuit, rattling students and faculty.
Cornell anthropology professor Noah Tamarkin said students in one of his classes didn't think accused students should be back on campus.
“The other students in the class are uncomfortable with it,” Tamarkin told the AP.
Cornell’s media relations office said in a statement that students who complete a suspension and fulfill other sanctions “regain the same rights and responsibilities as their classmates, including eligibility for housing.”
Cornell president says disciplinary committee decided punishment
Loeckenhoff raised her concerns during a Faculty Senate meeting at which professors were debating whether to pass a resolution expressing no confidence in Kotlikoff’s leadership.
She declined to elaborate on her remarks, citing student privacy concerns. The roommate declined an interview request made through an intermediary.
Kotlikoff replied at the meeting that the decision to allow the student to return to campus was made by the university’s disciplinary panel, not him.
“It’s something you might disagree with — I may disagree — but we didn’t hear the evidence,” Kotlikoff said.
However, Kotlikoff acknowledged the university’s duty to respond to concerns about the student’s presence on campus.
“If we didn’t do that, I pledge to look into what happened there,” he said.
Kotlikoff was serving as interim president when the woman reported the assault in 2024. He suspended the fraternity, publicly condemned the behavior of the men involved and convened a task force on sexual assault. But he's faced criticism for not following up with the woman or doing more to push for a criminal investigation or harsher discipline.
Privacy rules limit sharing info on discipline
Federal privacy law does not categorically prohibit universities from sharing a student’s disciplinary history with housing officials.
The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act allows universities to share student records with school officials who need the information to carry out their responsibilities, according to U.S. Department of Education guidance.
The law allows colleges to disclose some information when a student has been found responsible for violating school rules involving violence, including forcible sexual assault, or a nonforcible sex offense.
Kristi Patrickus, an attorney and board member of the Association for Student Conduct Administration, said universities have leeway to restrict campus housing access for students returning from suspension, even if they are allowed to resume classes. But federal privacy protections generally prevent universities from warning roommates about another student’s disciplinary history.
“There are not really any exceptions that allow us to tell a roommate, like, ‘Hey, this person is returning from suspension. Be careful,’” Patrickus said.
David Karp, director of the Center for Restorative Justice at the University of San Diego, has studied how colleges handle students returning from suspensions for sexual misconduct. He said universities often focus on disciplinary sanctions without adequately addressing the needs of those involved or the broader campus community.
“I don’t think it meets people’s needs very well, even if it meets university compliance needs,” Karp said.
Associated Press writer Michael Biesecker in Pittsburgh contributed.

Patrick Dempsey was named People magazine’s Sexiest Man Alive for 2023 at age 57.

Dempsey also founded the annual Dempsey Challenge in Lewiston, a walk, run, and cycling fundraiser that has raised more than $20 million for the center since its inception.

title: What should you do with art supplies that have toxins?
text:
Reports of undisclosed chemicals in hundreds of art products and toys have left Maine parents and educators questioning whether it is safe to keep using the markers, clay and fingerpaints in their homes and classrooms.
Public health advocates say there are no easy answers.
“That’s a tricky question,” said Emily Carey Perez de Alejo, director of Defend Our Health, the Portland-based public health organization that recently audited hazardous chemical filings in several states. “The most likely appropriate response is to discard them in the regular trash when you are finished using the product.”
While using up the supplies, parents and teachers should increase room ventilation, stop children from drawing on their bodies and enforce hand-washing immediately after craft time, said Perez de Alejo.
Defend Our Health found that some companies, including Crayola, reported hazardous chemicals such as formaldehyde in its products in other states but not in Maine.
The group is calling on Crayola to remove the carcinogen from its products and give Maine buyers full refunds or nontoxic replacements. Perez de Alejo said safe disposal of spent products should fall on product manufacturers, not the consumers.
Crayola said its products are safe to use and that the formaldehyde found in them is the result of contamination, which does not need to be reported in Maine and was mischaracterized in disclosures to other states.
Companies that make children’s goods with high-risk chemicals should set up stewardship programs like those that exist for batteries and lightbulbs, Perez de Alejo said. This would allow buyers to return used markers to retail stores for safe collection.
Without a take-back program, the tossed supplies face a grim environmental trajectory in Maine.
Municipal hazardous waste facilities generally reject such household items, like Teflon-coated cookware that contains forever chemicals, Perez de Alejo said. Consumers have no choice but to throw such items into ordinary household trash.
That trash ultimately ends up buried in landfills like the state-owned Juniper Ridge Landfill near Old Town. Over time, chemical preservatives in buried plastic goods turn into landfill runoff, or effluent, which must then be treated or discharged into local watersheds, she said.
Gail Carlson, a Colby College environmental studies professor who studies the impact of toxic chemicals in local environments, says “there is little we can do” with toxic household goods that are not eligible for hazardous waste pickup or a manufacturer take-back program.
That is why states like Maine adopt laws mandating extended stewardship programs, she said.
“We are left with unfortunate waste disposal options,” Carlson said. “I might suggest capping the markers, sealing the finger paint and clay and storing them in a plastic sealed box. Label the box ‘contains formaldehyde.’ And check with local hazardous waste officials.”
Maine wouldn’t have to do this if it just banned formaldehyde in children’s products, she noted.
Carlson warned against incinerating the spent art supplies. Under high heat, formaldehyde will volatilize and escape into the air. Carlson said there is no safe level of exposure.
Doctors say chemicals pose a higher risk to children because their bodies are still growing. For example, the American Academy of Pediatrics says prolonged exposure to formaldehyde can trigger severe allergies and is tied to increase cancer risks.
Crayola maintains that its products are safe and earned nontoxic seals from the Art and Creative Materials Institute, which means toxicologists have evaluated Crayola formulas for acute and chronic hazards. But those evaluations are proprietary and not shared with the public.
“Crayola does not intentionally add formaldehyde to any of its products,” said the company’s corporate communications manager Karen Kelly. “Contaminant-level formaldehyde, however, is reflected by virtue of two preservatives.”
The reason for the contradictory reporting is based on how the states worded their product laws.
Washington and Oregon continue to list formaldehyde as a Crayola additive. In those states, laws focus on a chemical’s functional intent. Crayola adds a preservative to a marker, it degrades into measurable formaldehyde in the marker, so it is deemed a hazard.
Maine’s Kids Safe Product Act requires a company to disclose if it adds one of nine high-hazard chemicals to a product intended for use by children under 12, including formaldehyde. Under the law, the product containing a properly documented high priority chemical can still be sold.
Crayola argues it does not have to disclose the formaldehyde found in its art products to Maine because it adds an ingredient that creates it, not the regulated chemical itself. Under Maine law, that would make the formaldehyde a contaminant, not an additive.
Kelley said the company submitted corrections to Washington and Oregon requesting that the chemical be reclassified as a contaminant instead of an additive in its filings there, too. 
To successfully claim the contaminant exemption in Maine, however, the company must have internal testing proving the formaldehyde byproduct falls below 100 parts per million. That’s equal to about a drop of ink in a standard two-liter soda bottle.
Perez de Alejo argues Crayola is putting children at risk by flouting the intent of Maine’s law. “I’m not sure consumers can trust Crayola to be honest about what’s in their product,” Perez de Alejo said. “Without public disclosure and real state oversight, parents are left guessing.”
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection is working on a way to share chemical disclosure reports with the public, said Deputy Commissioner David Madore. The agency contacted Crayola after learning it had filed formaldehyde disclosures in other states.
Crayola has since submitted a certificate of compliance attesting that its products are free of intentionally added formaldehyde, Madore said. The DEP has asked Crayola to provide proof that it is trying to minimize the presence of formaldehyde in the manufacturing process.
The state did not ask for Crayola’s internal testing to confirm the amount of formaldehyde in its products fell below 100 parts per million concentration levels. Kelly is reviewing the Portland Press Herald’s request for those records.

title: An intergenerational duo teams up to make greeting cards
text:
LANSING, Mich. (InvestigateTV) - Riley Haughey sits at her kitchen table with a tackle box of tools, drawing her newest critter with markers.
“I just really like the close up of looking at how markers go onto the paper. It kind of is like magic for me,” Riley said.
“This is like top notch printing I feel like,” Riley said.
The printer is 85-year-old Tony Klain.
Klain has no grandchildren of his own. He became a friend of the Haughey family six years ago when they were backyard neighbors.
“He’s so kind,” said Whitney Haughey, Riley’s mother.
When the family was looking for a cost-effective way to get Riley’s Critters on greeting cards to help pay for Riley’s dance classes, Klain stepped up.
“He was like, I can do it,” Whitney said.
At his home office, Klain uploads Riley’s animal art and cleans up imperfections.
“We’ll call it Cherry the squirrel,” Klain said while working on one card.
He preserves Riley’s signature mark, a paw print in the shape of a heart, and her brush strokes.
“I don’t like to change what she’s done,” Klain said.
The work is familiar to Klain. His wife Phoebe did similar artwork.
“My wife did the same thing and so that’s kind of cool,” Klain said.
The artistic connection to Klain’s wife has helped mend his broken heart.
“Actually, when my wife died, she left a whole bunch of journals, and she did a lot of really neat drawings and stuff,” Klain said.
Klain perfected his Photoshop talent by turning his wife’s art into a collection of calendars. He pulled drawings from her journals and scanned them to match each month.
Now the 85-year-old is matching wits with an 11-year-old in a friendship built on art.
Riley gives a nod of approval when she sees the finished product.
“It looks good,” Riley said.
“Makes my day every time I do it,” Klain said.

title: 'I'm with the right guy': Man spends months panning for gold to craft engagement ring
text:
'I'm with the right guy': Man spends months panning for gold to craft engagement ring
When it comes to marriage proposals, some people really go for the gold. And one Colorado man took that idea quite literally.
He spent months working on a surprise for his longtime girlfriend — and the results were one-of-a-kind.
Jack Vulcani, who spent months panning for gold to create an engagement ring, loves the hunt for gold along Clear Creek in Colordao.
The process takes time, and the payoff isn't always obvious.
"The smallest gold you've ever seen, but it's right there," Vulcani said.
Each fleck connects him with nature.
"That's really also kind of what got me to love it so much," he said.
All that time along the river gave Jack plenty of time to think about how to pop the question to his longtime girlfriend, Joanne.
"I just sat down, thought about it really long and hard, and eventually a thought just kind of popped in my head: What if I were to make the ring myself? And I just thought, you know, perfect."
Jack started collecting, one tiny piece at a time.
"I was like, 'This is going to take forever,' and for some reason that got me going, you know?" Vulcani said.
He was right — it took months. But eventually, he had enough gold to make his idea a reality.
So he took his little vial out of the mountains and into a jewelry shop, where he met Zak Allen.
"It was definitely memorable," Allen said."I initially kind of got excited, just because it's like, 'Well, that's a new thing.'"
"They asked a few times, they're like, 'It's seriously just from up in the mountains?' I was like, 'Yeah, it's all up from the mountains.' They were really blown away. It was a great reaction," Vulcani said.
Vulcani's gold wasn't like anything Allen had worked with before.
"I've never worked with such pure gold before. It was like, in theory, yes, I could do it. Have I done it? No, but I'm willing to try," Allen said.
Allen melted down the gold and found a way to cast it.
"To spray everything off and see the first time, it went great, was absolutely amazing and really exciting."
Vulcani had the ring. Now he needed the perfect way to share it.
So he took Joanne on a hike and pulled out his phone.
"I'm just watching this video of him gold-panning, and I'm like, 'This is cute, but I don't know why we're doing this right now,'" Joanne recalled. "And then halfway through the video I realized, 'Oh, this is the process of you making the ring,' and I just started crying. I blacked out a little bit, but it was a really special moment."
Jack Vulcani knows his proposal set the bar pretty high.
"I just wanted to make her day, not crush anybody else's dreams," he said.
The best relationships take time and work. And just like their ring, this one seems built to last.
"It just really reinforces that I'm with the right guy," Joanne Vulcani said.
"No matter how far we are separated apart, even when we're at work, I still look down and know that what's on her finger is still is tying us together every time I get to see it," Jack Vulcani said.
There was still enough gold left over for Jack to have a wedding band made for himself as well.
In the end, Joanne said yes — and the couple recently tied the knot.

title: Breast cancer survivor faced hair loss during chemotherapy and reclaimed her identity
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (Aging Untold) — Hair loss is often the most common and visually striking side effect of chemotherapy, especially for women.
Lisa Steinhauser, a breast cancer survivor, said she lost her hair and part of her identity during chemotherapy. Now she inspires patients to find strength during their own battle.
Hair as part of her identity
“So when I knew I was going to lose my hair, that was pretty hard because I had a lot of it,” she said.
Hair has always been Steinhauser’s craft, artistry and expression.
Diagnosis and treatment
In December 2021, Steinhauser went in for a routine mammogram, and she said doctors found a spot they were concerned about.
“I really was not expecting it to be anything at all, but it was,” she said.
She was diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive, invasive type of breast cancer. Treatment is intense.
“It was not fun,” Steinhauser said. “I went every three weeks.”
Shaving her head
Steinhauser’s hair began to fall out during treatment.
“Being in the shower and washing my hair and having those handfuls come out,” she said.
Steinhauser decided to shave off the remaining hair.
“I decided that that was not going to define me,” she said.
Her grandchildren shaved her hair off for her.
“I am going to still be that fun, spunky person that I’ve always been,” she said. “I just rocked the bald.”
Message to others
Steinhauser said she is now clear of the disease, “NED — no evidence of disease.”
She said she wants people to know there is hope.
“No matter what’s happening, you don’t know. There is going to be hope and just keep fighting,” she said.
Dr. Rhea Rogers shares her story
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said she identifies with Steinhauser. The same thing happened to her during cancer treatment. When Rogers’ hair was falling out, she shaved her head.
“I identify with her. You know, just depends on how people view their identity. And, you know, some people are just tied to their hair and all that, but really it’s your heart,” Rogers said.
Rogers shared a similar message of hope that Steinhauser did.
“Just don’t give up,” she said.

title: Woman arrested after 4-year-old found dead in Atlanta townhome
text:
WASHINGTON, Ga. (WRDW/Gray News) - A woman was arrested Tuesday morning after a 4-year-old boy was found dead more than an hour away in an Atlanta townhome, authorities said.
Wilkes County Sheriff Darrell Powers said Jasmaine Smoak was arrested and booked into the Wilkes County Detention Center.
According to WRDW’s sister station, Atlanta News First, Atlanta police responded to a gated community in the 3500 block of Cardinal Drive SW on Monday night for a welfare check.
Officers forced their way into the home “based on information received during the welfare check,” Atlanta police said.
Once inside, officers found the child dead. Emergency personnel attempted lifesaving measures but were unsuccessful, police said.
Powers said deputies worked closely with Atlanta homicide detectives to locate Smoak using license plate reader technology.
Smoak is charged with second-degree cruelty to children and concealing the death of another.
Atlanta police said Smoak is a friend of the child’s mother.
The circumstances surrounding the boy’s death remain unclear.

title: Alex Pretti's parents say federal government is shielding agents involved in his killing
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — The parents of intensive care nurse Alex Pretti said Tuesday the federal government is shielding the immigration enforcement officers involved in their son’s killing, and no one from the government has reached out with any substantive information for nine months.
Michael and Susan Pretti called for the Department of Justice to hold accountable those who shot their 37-year-old son during President Donald Trump’s ramp up in deportations targeting Minnesota. Federal prosecutors disclosed in recent court filings they had stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the January killings of Pretti and Renee Good by federal officers.
“The federal government went on TV and lied about Alex,” said Susan Pretti, his mother. “They tried to slander his memory to cover up their crime. Not only was it wrong, it was shameful.”
Within moments of his Jan. 24 death, Trump administration officials sought to portray Pretti, a U.S. citizen and nurse at a veterans hospital, as an armed disruptor intent on doing harm to federal agents when he brought his own gun to a Minneapolis street where officers clashed with protesters. Kristi Noem, the then-Homeland Security secretary, painted the Veterans Administration hospital nurse as a domestic terrorist who violently resisted federal agents. Court records show he had no criminal record.
Video shot by bystanders that day showed Pretti only had a mobile phone in his hand. No footage has since emerged showing him brandishing a weapon or attacking federal agents in the moments before he was killed.
The Prettis spoke Tuesday at a news conference organized by an attorney representing the family, calling their treatment by the Trump administration “cruelty.” They said they decided to speak out after being “stonewalled” by U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and the top federal prosecutor in Minnesota, U.S. Attorney Dan Rosen.
“At every turn, they have ignored us, misled us, and shielded Alex’s killers,” said Michael Pretti, his father. “We are a family who love this country. We trust in the institutions of this country. We believe in the rule of law – and that people should be held accountable through that law.”
After months of reaching out to Rosen’s office, the federal prosecutor agreed to meet with them in July. But the family and their attorney, Steve Schleicher, said that meeting raised more questions than answers, with Rosen refusing to provide even basic information about the status of the federal investigation into Pretti’s death.
A spokesman for Rosen’s office had no comment when reached by The Associated Press on Tuesday. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Pretti family’s remarks.
Minnesota officials sued the Trump administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings of Pretti and Good. The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don’t have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don’t trust the federal government to investigate itself.
The state is still seeking the cellphones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews.
Pretti’s parents recounted how they first learned of his death when they were called by a reporter for The Associated Press.
“We learned about his death from the media as we saw him being shot repeatedly in the back after helping a woman from his community, a fellow Minnesotan, who had been shoved to the ground viciously,” Michael Pretti said. “No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex. No one from the federal government has called us since.”
He said the videos of his son’s killing haunt his family every day.
“I think it haunts many Americans to see a U.S. citizen who was peaceful and in his community shot multiple times on the back, in the back, while on the ground,” the father said, calling his family heartbroken.
“We wish we didn’t have to be here,” he said. “We wish Alex was alive. We wish we were simply in Minneapolis to visit with Alex. For he and I to chat about cars, hiking, biking or anything that came to our mind. This administration has taken that away from us forever.”
__
Biesecker reported from Pittsburgh.

title: Noah Wyle named People Magazine's sexiest man alive

Actor Noah Wyle was named People Magazine's Sexiest Man Alive on Tuesday.

title: Maine must seek state solutions to homelessness
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rep. Grayson Lookner, D-Portland, represents House District 113 in the Maine Legislature.
There was a sharp rise in panhandling in Maine in the years following the financial crisis of 2008. Back then, it wasn’t controversial to chalk it up to the hard times we all were having.
There was broad recognition that for all of the conditions that may lead to an individual becoming homeless, the trend was primarily due to economic and financial conditions largely beyond those individuals’ control.
That’s changed, especially in cities that have traditionally been generous in their approach to helping people experiencing homelessness, like Portland. One need only to open a local Reddit thread or scan a newspaper’s opinion section to hear the latest upsetting episodes of people feeling unsafe around those who are struggling with extreme unmet needs in public.
People are demanding solutions, as they should.
When things become as heated as they are in an election year, it can be hard to look at the bigger picture, but we need to.
As with many of the problems we currently have, the roots of today’s homelessness crisis can be traced to the Reagan era. Back then, “deinstitutionalization” was having a moment, and it was a good and necessary idea. Many voters alive today (myself included) are not old enough to remember the horror stories of the thousands of people with mental illness being put into faceless institutions for years on end to languish in neglect and sometimes to face unspeakable abuse.
The idea behind deinstitutionalization was that we would close the big asylum-style hospitals and replace them with robust community-based supports for housing, employment and ongoing treatment — methods that were more effective at restoring people to social functioning and more humane. The problem was that we fulfilled the first half of that equation without fully committing to the second, and the community-based supports we have today are wholly inadequate for the scale of our crisis.
That — coupled with the ongoing divestment from public housing since that time — has helped to create the situation today where we have crises that exacerbate and magnify each other.
That is not to say that solutions don’t exist. At the beginning of the pandemic, the federal government instituted a national Emergency Rental Assistance (ERA) program to keep people housed when they couldn’t work. Much of this funding was spent on housing people who were experiencing homelessness in hotels. The program lasted for several years, and worked brilliantly for its intended purpose.
During that time, many advocates in Maine understood that although there was a light and the end of the tunnel concerning the pandemic, in regards to homelessness that light was an oncoming train. They foresaw that when ERA expired, there were going to be huge homeless encampments if no alternatives were put in place, and planned accordingly.
I introduced a bill to establish an ERA program for Maine in 2021 that would have extended the federal program. That bill was seen as too radical at the time, but the Legislature finally did establish a small eviction prevention program. Not insignificant, but also not nearly enough to address the scale of the problem.
Between the Department of Corrections and counties’ budgets for jails, we are spending nearly $400 million a year on jails and prisons in Maine. The county jails describe themselves as the de facto homelessness and mental health providers in our state.
We could drastically reduce the roughly 2,000 Mainers we incarcerate annually at a cost of roughly $100,000 per individual if we only had alternative systems. Nobody was complaining about visible homelessness and needle waste between 2020 and 2022 not because it didn’t exist, but because it didn’t exist in public due to the ERA program.
There are many solutions that we could pursue as well that would be equally effective if we could muster funding on par with spending on jails and prisons. Since the federal government has abandoned its role to create effective national solutions to homelessness, like ERA and public housing, the state has to create alternative systems.
An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. Otherwise, our cities will be left holding the bag, and our institutions will swell with people who might have been helped in our communities.

title: Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges
text:
Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges
President Donald Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi, as he continued a closing midterm rally blitz that has highlighted Republicans' challenges ahead of an election that could drastically shift power in Washington and statehouses across the country.
"I'm here because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance," Trump told the crowd, his voice audibly hoarse, as he worked to boost Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who is facing a surprisingly stiff challenge from Democrat Scott Colom.
Colom was spotted at the rally site, too, creating the rare spectacle of Trump's staunchest supporters interacting directly with a figure the president would soon go on to denigrate as a "Marxist radical" and "fake" and "shameless phony who pretends to be a moderate" from the stage.
Mississippi, among the nation's most reliably Republican states, is not where the GOP envisioned needing a late-October stop from the president. But Colom is one of many Democratic underdogs who have managed to expand the House and Senate battleground maps because of widespread voter discontent over inflation, the Iran war and other aspects of Trump's second presidency.
He said he had planned to go to the rally site to listen to what was on Trump supporters' minds.
"They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said ahead of the president's arrival.
Trump's event kicks off a week of aggressive campaigning that will include more stops in states he won comfortably in 2024, including Texas, South Carolina and Iowa. Trump also plans to hold a rally Saturday in Salina, Kansas, officials announced late Monday, marking his second visit to the state in less than two weeks.
Democrats, including progressives, are expanding their efforts
Top Democratic candidates and their surrogates were also greeting voters — more than 30 million of whom have already cast ballots, according to data collected by The Associated Press from election administrators across the country — as they try to end Republicans' threadbare majority in the House, take over a Senate majority that was once thought secure for Republicans and end the GOP's national advantage in state capitals.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats' 2024 presidential candidate, campaigned in Wisconsin with Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who faces Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Trump ally, for governor. Crowley would be the state's first Black governor if elected to lead the battleground state.
"This is a tight race because the stakes are so high," Harris said at the event billed as a "Women for Crowley" rally.
Meanwhile, in Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced himself from an ad created by a political action committee called Rebellion PAC that blames high grocery prices on U.S. support for Israel.
"This ad is not affiliated in any way with the Abdul for Senate campaign," a spokesperson for El-Sayed, Roxie Richner, said in a statement about the spot, which features a couple discussing U.S. support for Israel as they shop for groceries.
"Apparently it's costing us a lot of money to drop bombs on Gaza," the woman says.
The ad had been condemned by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic primary.
The way to win Michigan "is not by blaming the high costs of our goods on the only Jewish homeland in the world," Stevens wrote on X.
El-Sayed, who would be the country's first Muslim senator, has denounced antisemitism while fiercely criticizing Israel for its military operations in Gaza — a position that has been a frequent point of attack for both Republicans and supporters of Israel in his party.
Vance campaigning in other Republican states
Vice President JD Vance returned to Kansas to stump for Sen. Roger Marshall, who finds himself in a tight contest with Democratic nominee and pastor Adam Hamilton. Hundreds of people were gathered inside the warehouse of a steel-fabricating company in north Topeka in a state where Democrats haven't won a Senate race since 1932.
Marshall, who has raised far less money than Hamilton, told the crowd that Trump is on the ballot, even if his name doesn't appear, because of how Democrats will thwart his agenda if they win control of Congress.
"Democrats are coming out like it's a presidential year," he said, calling on the GOP to match Democrats' energy.
Jace Sullivan, a 50-year-old electrician from Topeka who describes himself as "85% Republican," said Trump supporters need to "circle the wagons" and get out to vote.
Wearing a red "JD Vance for President 2028" shirt, he said he thinks Trump is rightly working to keep Iran from getting nuclear weapons.
"Gas prices are high and it does suck, but it's a means to an end," Sullivan said.
Trump, at the Mississippi rally, said he had, in fact, expected gas prices to rise even higher than they had.
"It worked out fine and it'll be over soon," he said of the war with Iran.
Earlier, Vance was in Belgrade, Montana, to campaign with Republican Aaron Flint, who is facing Democrat Sam Forstag in the race for the state's 1st Congressional District, and Republican Senate candidate Kurt Alme.
Despite the visits to ruby red states, Sen. Tim Scott, who serves as chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told The Associated Press Monday that GOP candidates are "closing very strongly" in races across the country, including South Carolina, which Trump is set to visit for the second time in as many weeks to stump for GOP Sen. Darline Graham.
"One of the reasons why we will be in the majority is because he has invested the time and the energy on the campaign trail," Scott said on the sidelines of U.S. Rep. Russell Fry's 3rd Annual Freedom Fry event.
Trump to rally in another reliably Republican state
But it's Trump's visit to Mississippi that perhaps brings the midterm landscape into the sharpest relief with just a week of campaigning left.
To be sure, Hyde-Smith, who is vying for her second full term, remains the favorite in a state Trump won three times by an average of nearly 20 percentage points.
But Colom, a local prosecutor who would make history as Mississippi's first Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction, is looking to parlay inflation, Trump's lagging popularity and Hyde-Smith's mistakes into an upset.
Senate Democrats' super PAC has been a late entry in the contest, with a $1.2 million investment. Mississippians have not chosen a new Democratic senator since 1947, and Democrats last won a Senate race there when that senator, the onetime segregationist John Stennis, won his last reelection in 1982.
In New York, meanwhile, one of the party's most vulnerable House members pulled from Trump's campaign playbook. Rep. Mike Lawler, who is in a tight race with Democrat Cait Conley in New York City's northern suburbs, manned a McDonald's drive-thru — mimicking something Trump did two years ago, even as Lawler has tried to emphasize his independence from the president.
___
Barrow reported from Atlanta and Colvin from New York. Associated Press reporters John Hanna in Topeka, Kansas; Meg Kinnard in Columbia, South Carolina; Laura Turbay in St. Paul, Minnesota; Jonathan J. Cooper in Phoenix; Seung Min Kim in Belgrade, Montana, and Anthony Izaguirre in New York contributed.

title: Bangor credit union branch breaks ground at State Street and Broadway
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The County Federal Credit Union (CFCU) broke ground Tuesday morning on a new branch in Bangor.
The branch is planned for the corner of State Street and Broadway. Bangor officials and others were at the site to see plans and congratulate CFCU Tuesday.
The new location is a move from the credit union’s previous Bangor location on Main Street, which it leased. It will be CFCU’s ninth branch.
CFCU President Ryan Ellsworth said expanding operations south is the natural progression after the credit union merged with Penobscot Federal Credit Union in 2021.
“Aroostook County has not shown significant growth over the years, population has been decreasing slowly for a number of years, and if you project that out, we’re afraid that our membership’s going to be much smaller, 10, 20 years from now,” Ellsworth explained. “And we want more members to have access to our great team and our great services.”
Ellsworth adds that CFCU is always looking for ways to expand, and the new Bangor branch will not be “the last next step.”
Construction is expected to be finished sometime in the summer. Doors will most likely open in July.

title: Frenchman Bay Conservancy’s Pumpkin Hike returns to Ellsworth Riverwalk for Halloween celebration
text:
ELLSWORTH — Frenchman Bay Conservancy, in partnership with the Ellsworth Public Library and Heart of Ellsworth, invites the community to celebrate the 8th annual Pumpkin Hike along the Ellsworth Riverwalk Trail from 5 to 7 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 28.
This free, family-friendly event will transform the Riverwalk into a glowing display of jack-o’-lanterns carved by community members. Visitors of all ages are invited to enjoy an evening walk along the illuminated trail, celebrate the Halloween season, and vote for their favorite pumpkin creations. Costumes and festive attire are encouraged.
The pumpkins will remain on display through Sunday, Nov. 1, giving residents and visitors additional opportunities to experience the trail throughout Halloween weekend.
Visitors will have the opportunity to vote for their favorite pumpkins, with winners announced during the first week of November and prizes generously donated by local Ellsworth businesses.
The Pumpkin Hike is free and open to the public, with no registration required to attend. Visitors should park at the Ellsworth City Hall parking lot and walk to the trail. Accessible parking will be available at the Ellsworth Public Library.
For more information about the Pumpkin Hike and pumpkin carving opportunities, visit https://frenchmanbay.org/event/pumpkin-hike-grand-opening-lighting-2/.

title: Champion the Cure Challenge sets $1 million goal in 2027
text:
BREWER — A cancer diagnosis may feel overwhelming, but having a sense of hope can go a long way for patients and families who are facing this complicated disease. Each year, thousands of people come together at Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center’s Champion the Cure Challenge to celebrate and encourage members of the cancer community.
The 2026 Challenge raised more than $850,000, brightening the path for cancer survivors, family, friends and caregivers. Funds raised expand resources and research for patients with cancer, advancing technology and equipment, targeted treatments, as well as nurse navigation.
More than 29,000 community members have helped raise $9.5 million since 2010, and there’s more work to be done.
“To support our patients, families, and staff, we’ve set our largest annual goal to date,” Ava Collins, MHA, FACHE, Northern Light Health chief executive, Central Region – Bangor, said. “In 2027, we plan to raise $1 million at Champion the Cure Challenge, and we’ll need more commitment and momentum than ever to meet that target.”
It’s never too early to start planning to make a difference for loved ones with cancer. Save the dates for these upcoming events:
- Walk, Run, Cycle on Saturday, Aug. 21, 2027
- Motorcycle Ride and Car Show on Sunday, Aug. 22, 2027
“When our generous community members give back at the Challenge, we strengthen vital resources for our patients who deserve world class care close to home,” Collins said.
Learn more about Champion the Cure Challenge and start building a team today at CTCChallenge.org.
