title: 3 Alexander brothers each get 30 years in prison for sex trafficking after women talk of being raped
text:
3 Alexander brothers each get 30 years in prison for sex trafficking after women talk of being raped
Three brothers convicted of exploiting their wealth and access to luxury real estate to drug and rape dozens of women were sentenced Tuesday to 30 years in prison.
U.S. District Judge Valerie E. Caproni announced the punishment for Tal, Oren and Alon Alexander — known collectively as the Alexander Brothers — after 11 accusers spoke in court. Some of the women choked up as they described how the assaults stole their innocence and left them haunted by nightmares and fearing men.
“It took one night, only a few hours, one invitation to completely wreck the girl I once was,” one woman, using a pseudonym to protect her identity, said as she stood at a lectern just feet from the brothers in a Manhattan courtroom.
Twins Oren and Alon, 39, and Tal Alexander, 40, were convicted in March of sex trafficking.
The brothers speak for themselves
None of the brothers testified during the trial, but each spoke Tuesday before they were sentenced.
Oren Alexander addressed the packed courtroom first, saying, “I am not here to discount what they have said,” referring to the women.
He said he and his brothers came of age at the height of hookup culture and, looking back and now as a father, he regrets many of the things he said about women at that time. However, he insisted that they never broke the law.
“My brothers and I have never drugged or raped anyone. We never trafficked anyone for sex and we never conspired to hurt anyone,” he said.
Tal Alexander also denied that he drugged or raped anyone. He asked the judge to be assign him to same prison as his brothers; saying their parents, both 70 years old, hope to visit them every weekend, which might be difficult if they’re at different lockups.
Alon Alexander said he, too, has evolved from his regrettable past, noting that not a single woman has accused him of wrongdoing in the eight years he’s been committed to his wife: “Over time, that became my life: work, home, children, parents, community.”
Victims describe a lasting dread
The accusers who spoke in court — and another whose statement was read by a prosecutor — were among at least 70 women who prosecutors say were assaulted by one or more of the brothers over the last two decades in posh locales including the Hamptons on Long Island and in Aspen, Colorado.
Lindsey Acree, an artist and gallery owner, testified that she was raped by Tal Alexander and another man at a Hamptons home in 2011 after taking a drink that she said left her feeling paralyzed. Scrapping her prepared remarks, she told Caproni that a life sentence wouldn’t begin to do justice for the women whose lives were irreparably harmed.
“This has wasted my damn time. It’s wasted your time. It’s wasted everyone in this room’s time,” Acree told the judge. Turning to the brothers, she said: “For why? For you. Because you did some really messed up stuff.”
“The biggest thing is why? Why did you do this?” Acree asked. “I don’t understand the cruelty. I don’t understand the hatred towards women.”
Another woman who testified that Tal Alexander raped her in August 2014 said she carried “a quiet funeral in me for the person I might have become had this not happened to me.”
“Every second that Tal raped me in that shower felt like an eternity of terror,” said the woman, who used a pseudonym.
Another woman speaking about her rape in the Hamptons, said: “What looked like a beautiful place became for me a mansion of horror, a mansion of dark secrets.”
Prosecutors had sought life prison sentences while the brothers’ lawyers had requested the 15-year mandatory minimum.
Stars of the New York real estate scene
Oren and Tal Alexander were once nicknamed real estate’s “A Team” for their ultra-high-end sales and celebrity clientele. After smashing sales records at industry powerhouse Douglas Elliman, the brothers started their own firm. Alon Alexander ran their family’s private security company.
The brothers projected an exclusive lifestyle of yachts, private jets and waterfront mansions in Miami, but prosecutors said they began sexually assaulting women as early as 2001 or 2002, when they were in high school, and over time developed a pattern of drugging and raping women whom they enticed to join them on luxury getaways.
In remarks before the sentence was announced, Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth Espinosa told the judge that the brothers’ “callousness, carelessness, cruelty” in repeatedly drugging and raping women over many years warranted a life prison term, especially since all their victims would be serving life sentences of pain.
“Women overcame all the forces telling them this was their fault, they should stay quiet, that no one would believe them,” the prosecutor said. “Despite that pain, so many came forward, and 11 women testified at trial.”
Alon Alexander’s lawyer, Howard Srebnick, called a life sentence a “death in prison sentence.”
In court papers, defense lawyers said the brothers apologize to the women they insulted or offended for conduct they admit was “insensitive toward the feelings of certain women at certain times.” They also maintained their innocence.
The trio were arrested in 2024 and have been held without bail ever since.
The judge, Caproni, has said she believes the brothers should not be incarcerated at the same prison because they were a bad influence on one another. The brothers’ lawyers plan to argue that they belong together, even behind bars.

title: Woman dies after being hit by car in McDonald’s parking lot
text:
WHITE OAK, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A woman died after being hit by a vehicle in the parking lot of a fast-food restaurant, authorities said.
White Oak police responded to the fatal crash around 4:35 p.m. Oct. 21 in the McDonald’s parking lot in the 600 block of East U.S. Highway 80.
During the investigation, officers determined a woman walked out of the building, crouched in the driveway and began looking in her purse when a vehicle drove around the building and hit her, authorities said.
Officers determined the woman was not visible to the driver due to rounding a blind corner and the woman being so low to the ground, according to a release.
Paramedics took the woman to a hospital, where she later died, according to the release.
Police determined the crash was an accident, and no criminal charges will be filed, according to the release.
“Any incident involving the loss of life is a tragedy,” a department spokesperson wrote. “Our thoughts are with the family of the victim.”

title: 18-year-old charged in hate-motivated attack after luring victim through dating app, police say
text:
ELLISVILLE, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - An 18-year-old in Missouri was charged in a hate-motivated attack after allegedly luring a victim through a dating app, according to authorities.
Around 2:20 a.m. Oct. 21, the victim went to Bluebird Park to meet a man named Adam, whom he had been talking to on a dating site.
When the victim met the man he thought was Adam, the suspect, identified as Abdulwareth A. Alahmad, told him, “I actually hate gay people,” and four men who were hiding in nearby bushes approached him.
The group then punched the victim in the head and torso. When he fell to the ground, the group continued punching and kicking him.
According to charging documents, during the attack, the group used slurs and told the victim they wanted his belongings. The victim dropped his iPhone 16 during the attack and was able to get in his car while the taunts continued. The phone was later found smashed at the park.
The victim drove to the Ellisville Police Department.
The attack was captured on surveillance video. Detectives said Flock cameras captured Alahmad leaving the park.
The victim identified Alahmad in a photo lineup.
Alahmad is charged with first-degree assault and property damage motivated by discrimination.

title: Maine woman and grandchildren drowned after driving off boat ramp, medical examiner rules
text:
A 61-year-old woman and her two grandchildren drowned after their car went off a boat ramp into Pond Cove in Roque Bluffs last month, according to the official cause of death released by the state medical examiner on Tuesday.
Their manner of death has been ruled accidental.
Sharon Bukulmez, of Mount Desert, and her two grandchildren, 5-year-old Kinsley Grubb and 3-year-old Sawyer Grubb, both of Bar Harbor, were heading home to Machias on Sept. 19 after the wedding of her son and the children’s parents in Jonesboro but did not arrive as expected.
They were found dead the next day in a submerged vehicle beyond the boat ramp on Schoppee Point Road, where the roadway leads directly into the water with no barrier.
It was not the first fatality at that boat ramp. In 2013, two women, one of whom was five months pregnant, drowned after their minivan went into the water on a foggy, rainy July evening.
After the most recent tragedy, Roque Bluffs officials claimed they had been trying for years to revamp the boat ramp area in a way that would have forced traffic into a sharp right turn. But they said the plan was delayed by the state.
A metal gate has since been installed at the end of the road, Fox 22 Bangor reported.
Maine State Police said on Tuesday that they are continuing to investigate the circumstances around the incident.

title: Stillwater River Trail Of Lights Returns To Orono. Free Holiday Tradition Draws Thousands To The Area
text:
Folks In Orono Are Gearing Up For Their 7th Season Of Lights And Whimsy As They Set Up The Stillwater River Trail Of Lights
While it may still be a few months away, folks in Orono are prepping for this year's holiday season early...
...Because it takes a lot of time and effort to put something this dazzling together!
If you haven't yet made the trek out 92 Bennoch Road, off of Brownie's Park (or Brownie's Beach as the locals call it) along the Stillwater River to check out the Stillwater River Trail of Lights, you should add it to your Christmas bucket-list for this year.
Read More: Halloween Events In Orono Bring Trick-or-treating And Adult Fun
What started as a fun little light display 7 years ago has turned into a must-see holiday tradition for many, with picture-worthy pop ups along the way.
According to one of the event organizers, Anthony Francis, while they may not know the exact total number of who makes it through the path each year, it's well into the thousands.
"It is difficult to estimate attendance because the Trail is free and does not require tickets, but we received roughly 200,000 requests for directions last season. It has become a tradition for many families, with multiple generations returning year after year. We have celebrated engagements, weddings, and countless family milestones along the Trail. The event also brings meaningful activity to Orono and its local businesses during the holiday season."
As is the case in many situations, something this fabulous doesn't just come together overnight. It takes many hands many months to make this magic happen.
"We are incredibly grateful for the support of our sponsors, including presenting sponsor University Credit Union, Harvest Moon for Santa’s List, Harvey RV & Marine for the main photo area, the Town of Orono and Sunbelt Rentals for lift support, Sargent’s Construction, and Northeast Paving."
"Several sponsors have also provided volunteers who have worked alongside our small core group. The exact number of people involved changes throughout the setup as different businesses and volunteers join us."
Set up for this year's display started at the beginning of September.
"The trail is growing, the lights are going up, and Christmas will be here before we know it!"
With help from a team of community members, volunteers and local businesses, this year's display is slowly starting to take shape.
"We are happy to share that all of the overhead lighting is complete, including new sweeping teal sections and red-and-green zigzag lights. We are now working on the trees, displays, photo areas, and pathway markers."
"Section five is officially in the air! A big shout-out to Andrew and Ryan from A.M. Smart construction LLC for braving the rain and spending the past two days hanging lights with me. We added a canopy of red-and-green zigzag lights over the trail. We may be working backward through the sections, but the Stillwater River Trail of Lights is moving forward and reaching new heights!"
"The Trail is located largely on private property and is generously shared with the public. We ask visitors to stay on the marked trail, respect all signs and barriers, keep pets leashed, and clean up after them. Visitors should also dress for winter conditions and be prepared for snow, ice, mud, and uneven ground."
Organizers say they should be up and running and ready for visitors for the first weekend in December.
"The Stillwater River Trail of Lights will open as planned on Friday, December 4, 2026. The lights will be on nightly from 4 to 9 p.m., weather permitting."
And they say they've got something really fun in the works for one special night this season.
"December 18 will be an especially exciting night. The Town of Orono is planning to coordinate fireworks with the lights, and the trolley will also return."
There is a small parking lot area at the beginning of the trail that can fill up quickly. It's recommended that you pay attention to the traffic signs and watch out for pedestrians walking to and from the area when you do make it into the lot. And at times, it can get a little slick, so appropriate footwear is important.

title: Dollar General sued for allegedly charging customers at register more than advertised
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) - The Federal Trade Commission has sued the bargain chain Dollar General for what it characterized as “long-running deceptive pricing practices” by charging customers more once they reach the register than the prices that are displayed on shelves and in advertisements.
Twenty states joined in the complaint, filed by the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee. It said that Dollar General failed to correct the issue despite what it said was “extensive corporate knowledge of the problem.”
“Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” wrote Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection.
Dollar General, based in Goodlettsville, Tennessee, just outside of Nashville, did not immediately return a request for comment from The Associated Press.
The states joining the FTC lawsuit include: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin, according to the FTC.
Americans have become frustrated with higher prices, and also what they perceive to be new methods used by restaurant chains and major retailers in setting prices including the use of artificial intelligence tools.

title: Toyota issues recall for more than 220,000 vehicles: See model affected
text:
Toyota issues recall for more than 220,000 vehicles: See model affected
Toyota has issued a recall after it said that some vehicles with second-row back seats may fail to remain secure in the event of a crash.
Related video above: How to stay ahead of recalls
According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the company said 228,367 vehicles are being recalled over the potential issue.
The company said on Oct. 20 that "certain 2022-2026 Sienna Hybrid 7-passenger vehicles" are affected.
According to the safety report issued, some seat backs that are not secured in a locked position may fail to properly restrain occupants, increasing the risk of injury during a crash.
NHTSA said Toyota dealers will update the supplemental restraint system electronic control unit software. For vehicles equipped with the "Mobility as a Service" package, dealers will also replace the two second-row seat backs.
The company said owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out Dec. 7, and customers can contact Toyota's customer service number at 1-800-331-4331 to see if their vehicle is affected.

title: Trump plans to loosen restrictions on methane emissions from oil drilling
text:
BILLINGS, Mont. (AP) — President Donald Trump is expected to announce plans Tuesday to loosen a Biden-era rule that aimed to reduce planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.
Trump was to deliver the announcement as he campaigned in Texas, according to an administration official speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record ahead of the official announcement.
The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices amid the U.S. war in Iran. Methane is responsible for about a third of planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions, scientists estimate.
Cuts in methane emissions have emerged in recent years as a global priority to slow the rate of climate change. Oil and gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane, which is the main component in natural gas and far more potent to the atmosphere than carbon dioxide in the short term.
The invisible gas leaks from equipment and is sometimes released into the atmosphere by oil drillers or burned off as a waste byproduct during crude production.
Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin previewed the changes last month, saying they would eliminate the agency’s “Super Emitter Program” that requires companies to investigate and repair major methane releases from oil and natural gas facilities. The agency would also set less restrictive standards for small oil and gas wells.
The loosening of the emissions rule comes as Trump and Republicans in Congress have been methodically dismantling climate policies enacted under former President Joe Biden. That’s included the revocation of a scientific finding that was central to U.S. action on greenhouse gas emissions, lower fuel economy standards for vehicles and a move to repeal emission restrictions for coal and natural gas power plants.
Environmental groups criticized the latest rollback.
“It will impose a heavier pollution burden on our front-line communities and make our energy sector less efficient,” said Max Lopez, an Environmental Law & Policy Center attorney.
Zeldin has said the methane rule would have cost $18 billion and was holding back the U.S. energy industry.
“The Trump EPA is committed to fixing this so the U.S. can reach its full energy potential,” he said last month.
The Biden methane rule was announced by officials including former Vice President Kamala Harris during a 2023 U.N. climate conference in the United Arab Emirates. Federal officials under Biden said it would prevent an estimated 58 million tons (52.6 million metric tonnes) of methane emissions by 2038.
While previous EPA regulations focused only on new oil and gas wells in the U.S., the Biden rule regulated existing wells. Operators also would have needed to plug leaking methane from smaller wells that produce just 6% of the nation’s oil and gas while accounting for up to half of all methane emissions from oil and gas fields.
The final rule was published in 2024 but never went into effect. The EPA last year imposed an 18-month delay to give companies time to meet new inspection requirements and other provisions.
The rule was crafted to be coordinated with a methane fee, approved in the 2022 climate law. The fee program would have levied a “waste emissions charge” of as much as $1,500 per metric ton of methane on energy producers that exceed a certain level of methane emissions.
The fee marked the first time the U.S. government directly imposed a fee, or tax, on greenhouse gas emissions. Congress repealed it weeks after Trump took office.
___
Gruver reported from Fort Collins, Colorado.

title: Maine’s loon population declines but loon counters up
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Maine’s loon population has gone down but there was a record amount of volunteer loon counters this year.
According to the Maine Audubon, there are an estimated 2,700 adults and 276 chicks in Southern Maine.
The numbers for the Northern portion of the state were not given by officials due to limited data being collected.
However, of the 125 lakes in Northern Maine that were counted, the Maine Audubon says there were 515 adults and 40 chicks.
Across the entire state, nearly 1,900 volunteers took part.
This was the 43rd year of the annual loon count.
Volunteers can learn more by visiting the Maine Audubon’s website.

title: Where to find Halloween events on Mount Desert Island
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND — A chill in the air, the swirling of fallen leaves in the wind and the rising of a bright full moon can mean only one thing: Halloween is fast approaching. The holiday falls on a Saturday this year, so ghouls and goblins can take part in festivities all weekend long.
Ledgelawn Avenue trick or treating
Trick-or-treating will take place on Ledgelawn Avenue again this year. The road will be closed from 3:30-8:30 p.m. on Halloween. The Bar Harbor Mount Desert Police Department will set up a mobile command post and encourage trick-or-treaters to stop by and say hello.
Book trick or treat
Southwest Harbor Public Library will host their book trick-or-treat event Friday, Oct. 30, 1-5 p.m. The event is for babies, kids and teens to show off their costumes and pick out a free book to bring home. If you can’t make it on Friday, the library will continue the event on Saturday from 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Registration is not required for the event, and more information can be found on the Southwest Harbor Public Library’s website.
Aid Society of Otter Creek
Drop by Otter Creek Hall to enter a pumpkin into the Aid Society of Otter Creek’s pumpkin carving contest before 6 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 29. Voting will take place Friday night through Saturday night. Then find out if your pumpkin is a winner on Saturday at their costume social from dusk until 8 p.m. Winners will be announced at 6 p.m. For information, visit aidsocietyofottercreek.org/events.
MDI YMCA
Trunk or treat returns to the MDI YMCA Oct. 30, 4:30-6 p.m., in the YMCA parking lot. To volunteer your trunk or learn more, call (207) 288-3511.
Birch Bay Retirement
Village
Another safe option for collecting treats is Birch Bay Retirement Village’s annual Trail of Treats event Oct. 30, 4:30-6 p.m. For more information, contact Susanne Hopkins: susanne.hopkins@birchbayvillage.us or 288-8014 x 5211.
Camp Beech Cliff
The annual Trail of Treats event is returning to Camp Beech Cliff for its seventh year on Saturday, Oct. 31, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Local organizations and nonprofits will have stations set up along the trick-or-treat route. Registration is required at campbeechcliff.org/halloween-happening or (207) 244-0365.
Paradis Ace Hardware
All day Oct. 30 and 31, during store hours, Paradis Ace Hardware in Bar Harbor will host a trick-or-treat event. Donut holes, hot cider, hot cocoa and coffee will be available as well as candy treats for the kids.
Trenton Elementary School
Looking for a way to get some of the sugar-induced energy out? Trenton Elementary School is hosting a costume fun run for kiddos aged 5 and up Oct. 31. Race one is 0.4 miles and for children ages 5-11 and race two is 1.1 miles for kids 12 and up. The event starts at 9 a.m. at Trenton Elementary School, with a $5 entry fee benefiting the school’s athletic program. Costumes are encouraged and prizes will be awarded to the top runners in each race.
Connors Emerson
Elementary School
To keep the festivities going all weekend, Evergreen Yurts will host a pumpkin walk fundraiser Sunday, Nov. 1, 4:30-7:30 p.m., to raise money for Connors Emerson Elementary School and PTSA. Visitors can enjoy a walk on the yurt loop road that will be illuminated with carved pumpkins. Contact kate@evergreenyurts.com for more information.
“Rocky Horror Picture Show”
For the slightly older crowd, College of the Atlantic will host Downeast Shadowcast Ensemble for their performance of “Rocky Horror Picture Show” at the Gates Auditorium. Adults 18 and over can come do the time warp Oct. 30 at 9 p.m. and Oct. 31 at 6:30 and 9 p.m. Admission is free, and goodie bags are available for purchase. Costumes are encouraged. title: Letter: Matt Dunlap is true outdoor sportsman

title: Jay-Z will headline the Super Bowl halftime show at SoFi Stadium in Southern California
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself.
The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he had one request when the league first reached an agreement with Roc Nation: that Jay-Z take the stage himself “whenever the moment felt right to him.”
“From ‘Reasonable Doubt’ to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey,” Jay-Z said in a statement. “Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world’s biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true.”
After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his celebration of the 30th anniversary of “Reasonable Doubt,” the mogul’s 1996 debut album. The concerts included three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium and sold-out performances in London and Paris ahead of a stop at SoFi Stadium over the weekend.
Jay-Z’s Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league’s entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told Goodell, “If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now.”
Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.
Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog also includes the albums “The Blueprint” and “The Black Album,” and hit songs such as “Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem),” “99 Problems” and “Empire State of Mind,” his collaboration with Alicia Keys.
Last year, “Reasonable Doubt” was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
His recent concerts brought out a rotating cast of guests. At SoFi Stadium, his daughter Blue Ivy played piano on “The Story of O.J.” and “Dead Presidents,” while Scarface, John Legend and DJ Khaled joined him on opening night. Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too $hort appeared during Saturday’s finale.
Earlier in the run, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and Nas were among the guests at Yankee Stadium.
Jay-Z has built a career as an executive and entrepreneur. The Brooklyn rapper co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.
Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021. He is also a four-time Emmy winner.
Roc Nation will executive produce the halftime show, with Hamish Hamilton directing.
The halftime show has collected Emmys in recent years. Bad Bunny’s performance in February won a record seven, including best variety special (live), while Kendrick Lamar’s show last year won for music direction.

title: Raising school-aged grandkids: how to handle homework and school in a digital age
text:
(Aging Untold) — For some older adults, this chapter of life was supposed to mean retirement. Instead, they are raising school-age kids again, navigating online portals, teacher apps and school meetings that look nothing like the school they remember.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing how older caregivers can manage the digital side of modern schooling — and why their experience still matters.
“You’re not probably the most confused”
When the day-to-day of supporting a child’s education starts to feel overwhelming, older adults should know they are not alone.
“I think it might be important to know that you may be the oldest member in the PTA, but you’re not probably the most confused,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said. “There are many younger parents that are still trying to learn to navigate the online portals and the tablets that their kids have, not having textbooks.”
Cradduck pointed out that school itself has changed for everyone, not just older caregivers.
“School isn’t what it once was, and math doesn’t math anymore. There’s this new math thing,” Cradduck said. “There’s a lot of things that have changed. But for our older community that are managing and helping school-age children, there’s a lot of help for you.”
Cradduck said the most important step is figuring out what resources are available. (See below for resources.)
“I think that’s the most important thing to find out is what resources are available to you, and how can you tap into it and make sure that you find a tutor that can help with some of the things you’re not maybe the best at,” Cradduck said.
Leaning on what’s worked before
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said older adults should remember that they have been through this before.
“It might look different, but the younger parents — they haven’t helped kids go all the way through school,” Ambrose said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke encouraged older caregivers to draw on past experience and to ask for help.
“Think of all the difficult things you’ve been through, and look at what did you do then that made that successful,” O’Rourke said. “So one of them is asking for help. I love the library — the librarians will help with the Wi-Fi and the app and give you other resources.”
O’Rourke also pointed to school staff as a resource.
“If you go into the school counselors, the guidance counselors, the parent liaison people, just stop and then know your weak spot,” O’Rourke said.
Board-certified physician Dr. Rhea Rogers recommended that older adults also talk to the teachers so they understand the situation.
Consistency matters more than perfection
She noted the added weight older caregivers carry when they take on this role.
“Because as an older adult who thought they were going to retire, you’re doing two jobs,” Rogers said. “You’re still trying to navigate your own health, your own decisions and things that pertain to you. Then you’ve got to also look at this other person.”
Rogers said children don’t need a perfect caregiver — they need steadiness.
“Really, for a child, they just need consistency. You don’t have to be a perfect caregiver. They just need to know that they matter,” Rogers said.
Reframing the role as mentorship
Cradduck said older caregivers often have more time and presence to offer than younger, working parents.
“If you’re at that retirement age and you’ve retired, most of the moms and dads are both working, and you do have that better quality time to be able to sew into the children,” Cradduck said. “Mentorship is what we’re to do when we age.”
O’Rourke added that older caregivers don’t need new credentials to contribute.
“What do you need to learn? You’ve already learned. You’ve already gotten educated. So use that — use what you have,” O’Rourke said. “Think about the other parents being exposed to you, like your generation, and what you can give just by being there.”
Ambrose agreed that the impact goes beyond the day-to-day logistics.
“Just that love, consistency, willingness — and these kids will remember that. That’s quite a legacy,” she said. “Grandparents have a big impact on kids anyway.”
Ambrose closed with a reframe for caregivers who feel stretched thin.
“It might sometimes seem like an interruption, but it could be disguised as your greatest legacy,” Ambrose said.
Resources
- Librarians
- Teachers
- Tutors
- School counselors
- Parent liaisons
Key takeaways
- You’re not alone in feeling lost. Many younger parents are also struggling to navigate school portals, apps and tablets — it’s not just an older-generation problem.
- Find out what resources exist first. Libraries, tutors, school counselors and parent liaisons can help fill in the gaps older caregivers may feel around technology or coursework.
- Draw on what already worked. Past experience solving hard problems — including asking for help — is a skill older caregivers already have.
- Reframe the role as mentorship. Older caregivers often have more unhurried time than dual-working parents, and that presence is valuable on its own.
- This can be a legacy, not just a burden. What feels like an interruption to retirement may be remembered by kids as a defining relationship.

title: This Maine transplant answers all your Acadia-related questions
text:
A Maine transplant is helping fill an online void for Acadia National Park, which, run by the federal government, has never had an extensive digital footprint.
That’s become even more apparent with the recent funding cuts and staff layoffs under the Trump administration, perhaps most explicitly with the springtime decision to eliminate the park’s spokesperson.
But in today’s modern age, when many visitors and locals rely on social media and websites for national park information, Acadia’s online void leaves a gap in advice. Although the park has its own website, it sometimes lacks up to date information. Instead, people lean on park rangers for advice. Yet with funding cuts and trouble filling open positions, having fewer park staff has resulted in less in-person guidance.
Amid the park’s shrinking online and in-person presence, an army of social media users have appeared to offer advice and lessons on all things Acadia. Amy Faber, a New Jersey-born blogger who moved her family to Ellsworth four years ago explicitly for her love of the national park, is among them, and arguably their most enthusiastic voice.
Faber, who had vacationed in Acadia since 2008 before she made the move, consistently answers park-related questions on various Acadia Facebook pages — often sending long, comprehensive messages on the best ways to enjoy the park despite the large crowds.
“People always ask questions, and I was one of those people at some point that didn’t know the trails or didn’t know what I was getting into,” Faber said. “I don’t mind helping people figure out alternative things to see besides Beehive, Sand Beach and Jordan Pond. Sometimes I’ve been in the park on July 4th and had a summit to myself [but] then driven through the Ocean Drive and [it’s] totally chaotic. I’ve been on the Triad and haven’t seen anybody.”
Faber estimated she’s hiked roughly 90% of Acadia’s trails.
In a recent Facebook post inquiring about a short to medium-length hike for a pregnant woman, roughly 25 people responded with suggestions. Faber was one of those commenters, as she often is.
She recommended Hunters Beach, but advised the hikers to be mindful of fallen leaves that can hide roots and rocks this time of year. She also linked to her blog, Faber Adventures, where the mother of 13-year-old twins chronicles her weekly visits to the national park.
Faber’s suggestions are intended for visitors and locals alike. She urges out-of-towners to embrace the crowded spots, and not to be discouraged by bad weather, when fewer tourists are likely to be hiking even though rain and fog brings about a mystical, fairy tale-like aura.
She also encourages visitors to invest in their own map — not the one distributed for free by park officials, which tends to highlight main roads and popular attractions. Instead, Faber recommends the one produced by Map Adventures, which outlines the entirety of Mount Desert Island’s interconnected roads, trails, carriage roads and parking lots.
Faber, whose plans of moving to Maine were expedited after the sudden death of her sister in New Jersey, often advises visitors to check a summit’s weather forecast in addition to Bar Harbor’s, noting that mountain temperatures can drop substantially with windchill.
Faber’s suggestions always account for variables, including the inquirer’s age and fitness level.
In a late September social media post asking about recommended paths up Cadillac for a family with two large-breed dogs, Faber replied with a detailed summary of how her own hound mix fares on the various summit trails. After explaining the conditions of the north and south ridge trails, she settled on recommending the south ridge, qualifying that the day’s weather should also be considered.
For locals, Faber’s advice is simple: take advantage of the park.
“I would just say appreciate what an incredible place Acadia is and the fact that you get to live so close by. Even if you don’t visit in the summer because it’s too crowded, visit in the spring and late fall,” Faber said. “Embrace the trails that people don’t visit. For the carriage roads, go early. Be off of them by 10 a.m.”
Faber — who recently completed the MDI Marathon, her fourth 26-mile, long-distance race, after training throughout the summer on the park’s sprawling system of gravel roads — suggests early morning trips to the carriage roads as rental bicycles typically begin pouring into the park by late morning.
Sergeant Mountain, Acadia’s second highest peak, is among Faber’s favorite hikes in the park, as is Cadillac Mountain, though specifically during the winter months when the road leading up the summit is closed, she said.
“Acadia is a healing place for me. [It’s] where I go to find balance,” Faber said. “I don’t need to go to church, I just need to go there. I feel it so much in my soul, so I don’t mind helping people because it’s given me so much.”

title: 18-year-old charged in hate-motivated attack after luring victim through dating app, police say
text:
ELLISVILLE, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - An 18-year-old in Missouri was charged in a hate-motivated attack after allegedly luring a victim through a dating app, according to authorities.
Around 2:20 a.m. Oct. 21, the victim went to Bluebird Park to meet a man named Adam, whom he had been talking to on a dating site.
When the victim met the man he thought was Adam, the suspect, identified as Abdulwareth A. Alahmad, told him, “I actually hate gay people,” and four men who were hiding in nearby bushes approached him.
The group then punched the victim in the head and torso. When he fell to the ground, the group continued punching and kicking him.
According to charging documents, during the attack, the group used slurs and told the victim they wanted his belongings. The victim dropped his iPhone 16 during the attack and was able to get in his car while the taunts continued. The phone was later found smashed at the park.
The victim drove to the Ellisville Police Department.
The attack was captured on surveillance video. Detectives said Flock cameras captured Alahmad leaving the park.
The victim identified Alahmad in a photo lineup.
Alahmad is charged with first-degree assault and property damage motivated by discrimination.

title: Dunlap delivers closing congressional message ahead of Election Day
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, was in Bangor on Tuesday to deliver his closing message ahead of Election Day next week.
Dunlap, the current state auditor, was joined by several supporters. Maine AFL-CIO president Cynthia Phinney spoke about Dunlap’s union support. Erin Oberson, a registered nurse and co-president of the Maine State Nurses Union, spoke about the importance of implementing Medicare for All. Sportsmen Ed Pineau and Jeff McCabe spoke about Dunlap’s history with hunting and land protection.
Dunlap’s primary opponent, Jordan Wood, and former 2nd District U.S. Rep. Michael Michaud also supported him Tuesday. Both spoke about their lifelong ties to Maine, along with Dunlap’s. They said Dunlap would be available all year to constituents, referencing an admission by Dunlap’s Republican opponent, former Gov. Paul LePage, about spending winters in Florida.
Voting is already underway, and polls close Nov. 3.
Dunlap said he wanted to share one message before then.
“So here’s my promise. If you send me to Congress, I’ll never forget where I came from and I will never forget who sent me,” Dunlap said. “I’ll be your neighbor first and your congressman second. And I’ll come home every chance I get because home is where the work is.”
In a statement, King described Dunlap as “tough and smart and a strong advocate for his district.”

title: Report calls Select Board member’s husband ‘key aggressor’ in western Maine brawl
text:
A Brownfield Select Board member and her husband helped initiate a fight that turned physical at a board meeting in August, an investigator found.
Select Board member Tracie Peek-Antolin violated town policies when she instigated an altercation with Anna Maxwell, the town’s recreation director, according to the report conducted by a labor lawyer with the firm Bernstein Shur.
The 12-page report details how a “long-standing schism” between supporters of Maxwell and those of her fired predecessor exploded. The report states that Peek-Antolin is friends with the dismissed recreation director.
It marked the first official account of the fight, which drew a police investigation and capped months of division in the town of 1,600 on the New Hampshire border. The brawl also put the focus on a board member who was not a target of a recall push that voters rejected by large margins in September.
The report, written by employment lawyer Matthew Tarasevich, called Peek-Antolin’s husband, the similarly named Tracy Antolin, a “key aggressor.” He allegedly pushed and punched Maxwell while Peek-Antolin herself “stood to the side and did not intervene.”
Neither Antolin nor Peek-Antolin could be reached for comment. Select Board Chair Ricky Emery did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.
The parking-lot brawl was caught on video from an adjacent playground, which officials were informally inspecting. The footage shows Antolin in a physical altercation while two Select Board members try to break up the fight. Police were called to the scene, which remained tense. Antolin and Peek-Antolin left before any law enforcement arrived, the report said.
Tarasevich found some of Peek-Antolin’s comments to Maxwell, many of which are redacted from the version of the report released by town officials, constituted harassment under town policy. The lawyer also noted that policy forbids officials from engaging in conduct that reflects “unfavorably” on the town.
Peek-Antolin violated this “for obvious reasons,” he concluded, saying her conduct “was completely unacceptable as an elected official.”
Much of the context for the fight was redacted from the version of the report that was released to the public. But the broader feud over the position of recreation director has divided the town before. It contributed to the attempt to recall the other two Select Board members, Emery and Selectman Brian Fortier, which failed last month.
The report stated that “possible criminal conduct” occurred during the fight, but it made no findings regarding alleged criminality.
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: Environmental officials recommend new air monitoring near South Portland oil tanks
text:
Environmental officials recommend new air monitoring near South Portland oil tanks
Maine environmental officials want more air monitors near South Portland oil tanks after a state study found elevated benzene levels; leaders are set to discuss next steps at a city council workshop Tuesday night.
Environmental officials recommend new air monitoring near South Portland oil tanks
Maine environmental officials want more air monitors near South Portland oil tanks after a state study found elevated benzene levels; leaders are set to discuss next steps at a city council workshop Tuesday night.
Officials with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection are recommending that the South Portland City Council support a year-long study of benzene levels between petroleum terminal fences and nearby homes, after a state study found long-term levels of benzene at two sites were higher than the state's safety guideline.
According to the report, the elevated long-term benzene levels are due to fumes from petroleum tank terminals.
One of the terminals at 102 Mechanic St., which is operated by Citgo, had long-term benzene levels from November 2019 to November 2025 that were double Maine's acceptable risk level.
The city of South Portland partnered with the Maine DEP and the Maine CDC on the study. Officials from both agencies are set set to discuss its findings with city leaders Tuesday evening at a workshop at South Portland High School.
Officials also plan to discuss next steps in light of the data, which, after six years of monitoring, found that the air at the South Portland Terminal had the highest long-term average of benzene concentrations, with some locations there averaging as much as 4.5 times Maine's Ambient Air Guideline.
The study found that the CITGO terminal also had elevated long-term benzene concentrations along its fenceline.
In the study the Maine DEP cautioned that the fenceline results "should not be interpreted as demonstrating that nearby residents are exposed to the same concentrations."
At the same time, the study noted that its findings reinforce the need for more data to answer the primary unanswered question: how quickly do benzene levels decrease as air moves beyond the tank farms and into residential neighborhoods?
The Maine DEP says that an additional year-long "fenceline step-out VOC study" is needed to answer that question.
Environmental officials are now recommending that city leaders support installing to 12 new monitors at different distances between 300-900 feet from the South Portland Terminal and 16 monitors near the CITGO terminal.
Officials say this separate study would "fill an important gap" and better determine whether and to what degree benzene concentrations extend into nearby neighborhoods.
Long-term exposure to benzene has been linked to dizziness, headaches, blood disorders and cancer.

title: How to use AI to budget for the holidays without overspending
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Holiday expenses often extend well beyond gifts and food, and those additional costs can add up quickly.
Cherry Dale, vice president of financial education at Virginia Credit Union, said the first step to managing holiday spending is a simple list — before ever opening an AI tool like ChatGPT or Claude.
Dale recommends listing everything planned for November and December spending, including travel, decorations, gifts and hosting costs. She said AI can help organize a budget, but personal information such as a name or banking details should never be entered.
Dale said general, non-identifying details can still produce a useful, personalized budget.
“You can put generic things like, ‘Hey, I’m hosting eight people for Thanksgiving, and I have six adults, two children. I would like to create a traditional Thanksgiving meal. Can you map out a budget for me with all of this information?’” Dale said. “And it will spit out approximate cost per person.”
Dale said AI tools can suggest a menu and grocery list, or help identify gift ideas that fit a specific budget.
“Use AI — put in, like, ‘I would like a gift for a child that’s interested in piano or theater, or maybe it’s sports. What is something under $10 that would be simple for me to create or to give?’” Dale said. “And it can give you some very specific suggestions to stay within the budget.”
For those looking to save further, Dale recommends thinking beyond store-bought gifts. She said a gift of time or a shared experience can carry more meaning than a purchased item.

title: Susan Collins fought for Social Security for some, but inaction on insolvency may mean lower benefits for all
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
David Dancause is a retiree who is active in the Maine outdoor community serving on the Maine Outdoor Adventure Club board of directors.
A recent letter to the editor in the Bangor Daily News from a Susan Collins supporter praised the senator for her leadership and pointed to the Social Security Fairness Act as proof, which got me thinking. If Collins considers bringing Social Security benefits to more people a legacy achievement, then I want to set the record straight: The big generational problem I believe Collins has largely ignored is Social Security solvency.
If Collins saw fairness as a concern, why has she not taken the lead on the far larger problem: Social Security solvency? Trustees project the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will exhaust its reserves in 2032, leaving ongoing revenue sufficient for only about 78% of scheduled benefits. For Maine, the implications are enormous. At 78 cents on the dollar, the shortfall approaches $2 billion a year less for Maine OASI beneficiaries. That 78 cents on the dollar translates to a $478 cut from the $2,000 average Maine monthly check!
Congress and Collins should have prevented this looming crisis decades ago. They still can, but they no longer have painless choices, which now include raising revenue, further increasing the retirement age, trim benefits or COLAs, or combining them.
Social Security solvency has been an issue throughout Collins’ 30 years in the Senate. In 2011, she called for reform “to ensure long-term solvency” and warned that “the longer we wait to act, the more difficult the task.” She ended with this ominous line: “The moment of truth is here.”
In 2011, Collins warned that delay would make the task harder. She was right. The question is why she didn’t follow with action.
This year, when AARP asked how she would strengthen Social Security, Collins called for a bipartisan commission. Sounds to me like more lip service. After decades of warnings and commissions, where was Collins’ fight on solvency? Collins’ warnings throughout these decades, without action, look less like rolling up her sleeves to fix it and more like a way to avoid owning it.
The Social Security Fairness Act expanded benefits for public employees and spouses. Give Collins credit. But adding $196 billion in costs while the trust fund may run dry deserves another word: reckless. The Tax Policy Center argued that its cost comes at the worst possible time for the program’s solvency.
Maine’s former senator Margaret Chase Smith once held the record for consecutive votes. No one remembers her for that! People remember her for recognizing a moment that demanded political courage and acting despite the risk. Her “Declaration of Conscience” became her legacy.
Just this July, Maine’s other senator, Angus King, joined a bipartisan group of Republican and Democratic senators trying to force action on Social Security solvency (the PROMISE Act). Collins, a senator from the nation’s oldest state, did not. I think Collins should sign on and show us a plan that does more than study the problem.
Will 10,000 consecutive votes really be the best measure of Collins’ 30 years or more, as she has been touting? She knew Social Security’s financing problem was coming and warned about delay, but took no meaningful action. And here is the irony: if Collins wins another six-year term — likely her last — her final Senate year would be 2032, just as the Trust Fund could run dry.
But imagine we could roll back the clock a decade or more and give Collins one chance to confront a generational problem while there was still plenty of time to make the solution less painful. Would anyone care about 10,000 votes? Or would we ask Collins to work really hard to fix Social Security solvency, and make that vote one that truly truly counts?

title: ‘McMillan & Wife’ actress Susan Saint James dies at 80
text:
(Gray News) - Emmy-winning actress Susan Saint James has died. She was 80 years old.
Saint James, who starred in “McMillan & Wife,” “Kate & Allie” and “The Name Game,” died Monday after being diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, according to People.
Her family said she was “generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up,” in a statement to People.
Saint James “never met a stranger” and “taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people,” her family said.
“Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story,” her family said.
After retiring from Hollywood in 1989, she made appearances on “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” and “Suits.”
She was married to longtime NBC executive Dick Ebersol for 45 years. In 2004, their 14-year-old son, Teddy, died in a plane crash in Colorado.
Saint James received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2008.

title: U.S. Senate debates left Maine wanting
text:
Cynthia Cushing, LMSW, of Readfield is currently pursuing a Ph.D. from the University of Maine, focusing on gerontology, social work and technology. In January 2026, she founded the Maine Coalition for Social Connection.
On Oct. 15 in Bangor, Maine voters got 15 seconds that explain where our politics has gone. A young man stood up in the middle of the final Senate debate to shout about data centers, and before security even reached him, the debate had stopped being about anything he — or any of us — actually came to hear.
The young man was Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old Bowdoin student. He said he was terrified — that AI data centers are destroying our climate and poisoning our water — and he asked Sen. Susan Collins a question a lot of Mainers have asked in one form or another: “Thirty years, for what?” As he was being led out, Sen. Collins remarked, “So this is obviously one of Troy’s supporters.” Troy Jackson answered, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
That was it. That was the moment. In the week since, Mainers have been treated to wall-to-wall coverage of those 15 seconds — who was rude, who regrets what, whose temperament is fit for the Senate. Jackson went on national television to say he does not regret his words. The Collins campaign called his reaction “very telling.” Almost none of the coverage has been about what either candidate plans to do for the people of Maine. The exchange was replayed for a week because it was good television, not because it told voters anything.
Here is the part that should trouble us most. The remark that started it all — the suggestion that the protester was Jackson’s supporter, planted or otherwise — was not true. Elgie has said that there was “zero coordination” with the Jackson campaign and that he does not know Troy Jackson at all. He acted on his own, as a volunteer with a climate group. An unverified claim was broadcast across the state, and turned out to be false. Unsurprisingly, the truth reached only a fraction of the audience that saw the original video.
I am not writing to defend either candidate’s behavior in that moment. A United States senator should not state a guess as a fact. A man who wants to be a senator should not tell anyone to shut up. I am writing because of what the moment crowded out.
That debate — the last one before we vote — included real exchanges about healthcare, about the people who may run our federal agencies, about the cost of energy. The protester himself was raising a question that matters here: what large data centers would mean for our electric bills and our water. None of that is what Maine has spent a week talking about. We spent it on 15 seconds of accusation and insult.
Somewhere along the way, we have accepted a different idea of what a debate is. A debate is supposed to be a job interview. Two people are asking us for one of the most powerful jobs in the country, and the interview questions are simple ones: What will you do about the cost of healthcare? What will you do about heating our homes and keeping the lights affordable? How will you represent people who did not vote for you? When a debate becomes a contest of who can land the sharpest accusation, we the employers walk out of the interview knowing less than when we sat down.
There is a small detail from that night that I keep coming back to.
Jackson has shaken Collins’ hand after every one of their debates, including this one. Two people who disagree about nearly everything still manage that much. It suggests the problem is not that our candidates are incapable of basic decency. The problem is what the format — and the coverage, and honestly, our own appetite for the clip — rewards.
By now, both campaigns have spent millions telling us what is wrong with the other candidate. I would like to hear something else. I would like each of them to spend their remaining time answering the only question that matters: what will you do for us?
Maine deserves that debate. We haven’t had it yet.

title: New York woman is convicted of Islamic State training after becoming a teen bride to a fighter
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A New York woman whose father took her to Syria as a teenager and arranged her marriage to an Islamic State fighter was convicted Tuesday of receiving weapons training from the militant group.
Prosecutors said Halima Salman, a U.S. citizen, pledged loyalty to the extremist group and willingly participated in its activities. Jurors were shown a video of her holding an assault rifle, a photo of her with the group’s flag, and loving text messages she sent her husband.
“The evidence shows that the defendant received military training from a violent, brutal, terrorist organization — an organization that is responsible for attacks across the world,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda Shami told the jury in a closing argument.
The defense sought to portray Salman, now 27, as a teenager who was unwittingly trapped in Syria’s civil war, first by her father and later by an extremist husband whose orders she had to follow.
“You try to leave, it is death,” Salman testified. She said she refused to be “married off” at age 18 and repeatedly tried to get a divorce.
Salman burst into tears on hearing the verdict, as did one of her relatives in the front row. After the judge left the courtroom to speak to jurors before setting a date for sentencing, one of Salman’s relatives reached across the railing between the audience and the courtroom well to comfort her. The jury had begun deliberating Thursday.
Despite its defeat in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria two years later, the Islamic State group still has sleeper cells that carry out deadly attacks in both countries, where they once declared a caliphate.
Born in Brooklyn, Salman was 17 when her father took the family on what she thought was a trip to visit relatives in Turkey in 2017. Instead, the van crossed into Syria, where masked gunmen surrounded them. Salman said she was frightened and confused, and had no idea where her father was taking them.
“I do blame my father for a lot of things that happened,” she testified.
She said she spent three months in housing run by the Islamic State group before reuniting with her family. They moved twice because their homes were hit by airstrikes.
On the first day of her marriage, Salman recalled, her husband told her: “Get up, stupid wife, it’s time for you to be a wife.”
She spent much of the marriage doing domestic labor for her husband and mother-in-law. Her father died after being injured in an airstrike in 2018.
Prosecutors insisted Salman was dishonest and had more agency in Syria than she claimed. They got her to concede during cross-examination that she once sent a religious song about Osama bin Laden to her husband. Prosecutors also disputed Salman’s account of a poor marriage, citing two loving text messages she sent to her husband.
Salman’s husband took a video of her holding an assault rifle, which prosecutors said she had been trained to use. When she testified, Salman said she was only complying with her husband’s request to carry the rifle.
She recalled her last year of marriage was particularly harrowing, with constant bombings leaving them sometimes living in the streets, where she recalled seeing “dead bodies everywhere.”
The couple eventually fled with other refugees in a truck, where she told her husband they were going to separate, and Salman testified that she never saw him again.
She was detained in Baghouz, Syria, in 2019 by forces opposed to the Islamic State group. She was arrested by U.S. authorities when she returned to New York in 2024.

Senior US official says Flavio Bolsonaro and family will be granted U.S. visas after election loss
text:
Senior US official says Flavio Bolsonaro and family will be granted U.S. visas after election loss
A senior State Department official says Brazilian opposition candidate Flavio Bolsonaro and his family will be granted U.S. visas after his weekend loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in a hotly contested race that bucked a trend of conservative electoral results in Latin America.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to visa privacy laws, said “the State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsanaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States.”
Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has left Brazil for the United States following a stunning loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s election, according to multiple media reports.
A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday; his campaign manager Rogério Marinho also refused to comment.
Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.
Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil’s election was “rigged.”
Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied.
Bolsonaro was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss. Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After that defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.
The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud.
Bolsonaro raises questions about election he lost
Bolsonaro initially asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that prompted authorities to extend voting by two hours.
On Monday, he urged the electoral court to investigate alleged election fraud and nullify Lula's and Vice President Geraldo Alckmin's candidacies, which the electoral court has never done before.
“I never thought about leaving the country,” Bolsonaro said in a video published on his social media channels. "I will hand over my passports and I will defend myself from this aberration. It is a clear attempt to intimidate me. But I will not be silenced."
To overturn the result, Bolsonaro would have to present evidence of fraud affecting Lula's 4.4 million-vote margin and convince the eight-member electoral court before the results are certified on Dec. 18.
Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.
Bolsonaro said in a video posted Monday on his social media channels that he had no plans to leave Brazil and instead was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court.
Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil's Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. In one, he's accused of using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In the other, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker.
He has denied any wrongdoing in both cases, and has claimed Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who is heading one of the investigations, is a Lula ally. Prosecutors suspect the funds from the banker were used to pay his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro’s, expenses and to promote Flávio Bolsonaro’s political agenda with the Trump administration, documents show.
Mauricio Marcon, a lawmaker of Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party, also questioned de Moraes’ objectivity on Tuesday. “Seven minutes after the election, Alexandre de Moraes ordered his passports to be seized,” Marcon said. Bolsonaro "will represent us in a free country. He will continue to be our leader."
Brazilians had earlier taken to social media to ask where Bolsonaro was. Reporters gathered outside his home in the capital, Brasilia, but he did not appear.
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Security of Argentina denied reports the Brazilian senator had entered the country. Brazilian media outlets reported that many Bolsonaro allies had been unable to reach him.
Paulo Figueiredo, a close ally of Bolsonaro's who lives in the United States, was asked about the senator's whereabouts and did not answer directly.
“At this moment — following months of intense work that were unfairly thwarted — I have no desire to speak with the press. I kindly ask that you do not persist. Should I have a statement to make on any matter, I will reach out,” Figueiredo said.

title: Mother who traveled to Las Vegas on a work trip arrested after unsupervised child was injured and hospitalized, deputies say
text:
KISSIMMEE, Fla. (Gray News) - A mother who traveled to Las Vegas on a work trip was arrested after one of her children was injured and hospitalized, according to deputies.
According to the Osceola County Sheriff’s Office, a child called 911 after a dumbbell fell on her 9-year-old brother’s head on Oct. 21.
When deputies responded to the home, they found that four children, ages 14, 12, 11 and 9, were home unsupervised.
Fire rescue took the 9-year-old child to the hospital.
The responding deputy called the children’s mother, Irene Miller, 50. She told the deputy that she has been working in Las Vegas since Oct. 18, and would return on Oct. 23.
Miller said she had a babysitter coming from Tampa every morning to get the children ready for school and to check on them after school, but she did not require her to stay at night.
The 9-year-old returned home after being treated and discharged from the hospital.
Authorities contacted the children’s father and agreed to take them to his home.
Detectives met Miller when she got off her flight from Las Vegas on Oct. 23.
Miller is charged with four counts of child neglect without great bodily harm. She was booked into the Orange County jail.

title: Trump administration asks Washington to set aside ballots from 400 voters it says may be noncitizens
text:
Trump administration asks Washington to set aside ballots from 400 voters it says may be noncitizens
The Trump administration on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it alleges registered to vote without U.S. citizenship, less than two weeks after making a similar demand in California.
The announcement is the latest sign of the administration's attempts to sow doubts about the election or its outcome in states with races that will help determine control of the U.S. Senate and House.
In a letter to Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, the Justice Department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by the more than 400 people in prior elections. It asked the state to set aside any ballots they might cast in next month's midterm until state officials can confirm they are legally eligible to vote. The state has more than 5 million registered voters, and the state issues mail ballots to all of them.
One listed voter last cast a ballot in 1994
At a news conference, Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney in Seattle, said he believed the 405 voters identified so far represented "the tip of the iceberg."
"Because of limitations the state has placed on our investigation, we've only been able to uncover a fraction of the total number," he said.
Hobbs said he was reviewing the DOJ's request. His office noted that the data shared by the department included the last time each of the 405 people voted. One was in 1994.
"The timing of this request — one week before the General Election — is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results," Hobbs said.
Much of the list was built based on "recent contacts" with suspected noncitizens, Floyd said, because federal officers are now routinely checking to see if the people they interact with are registered to vote.
Lack of state cooperation a problem, DOJ says
Without access to those state records, proving someone illegally voted will be difficult, Floyd said. The Justice Department has demanded information including addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers.
The effort is the latest by the administration to identify noncitizen voters, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine public confidence in elections.
Meanwhile, Washington officials have noted that changes in U.S. Postal Service operations have disenfranchised thousands of legitimate voters.
Voting is underway
The Washington request marks the third time this month that the Justice Department has brought a direct state challenge as voting is underway. All three states — Washington, California and Alaska — have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in the nation's Capitol.
The race for Washington's 3rd Congressional District is one of the most competitive in the country in this year's midterm elections. Democrats are counting on Rep. Maria Gluesenkamp Perez winning reelection as crucial to their strategy of retaking the majority in the U.S. House. She has won twice in a district that also has supported Trump each time he's been on the ballot.
The Justice Department sued in California as part of a similar attempt to require the state to set aside mail ballots from up to 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. Another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent doesn't win.
In California, a panel of federal appellate judges heard rare Sunday arguments and questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand. On Monday, they declined to rule on the expedited timeline the DOJ requested and sent it back to a lower court.
The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections.
Prior allegations have been overstated
Los Angeles County Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration's list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, people with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States.
The Justice Department told Washington it anticipates sending the state an additional list of people it suspects are not citizens prior to Election Day. It also noted that some of the people it suspects registered without citizenship may have since become naturalized.
Investigations into prior allegations of noncitizen voters have revealed far fewer instances than the Trump administration has claimed. In Nevada, Trump's administration alleged there were 1,500 potential noncitizen voters on the rolls but subsequent investigation found zero.
In Maricopa County, which includes Phoenix, the county recorder, who is a Trump supporter, announced that there were 207 possible noncitizens on the county's rolls. The Republican County Attorney determined there were actually eight. ___ Boone reported from Boise, Idaho.

title: A Batesies Ballot Guide to 2026 Midterms
text:
The Nov. 3 midterm election is expected to draw millions of young voters. A report by Tufts University’s Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) estimates that 49 million young people ages 18-29 are eligible to vote in this year’s midterm elections.
Below is a voting guide to the key national, state and local races for Bates students voting in Maine. When possible, candidates’ positions are expressed in their own words, as reported by news outlets or published on their campaign website.
Additional resources, including walking groups and shuttle rides courtesy of the Harward Center for Community Partnerships, are listed below. For additional information, please reach out to Associate Director of Democratic Engagement and Student Activism, Jenna Dela Cruz Vendil.
U.S. Senate
Incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins will compete with former Maine State Senate President Troy Jackson for one of Maine’s U.S. Senate seats.
In a voter guide published by the League of Women Voters of Maine (LWVM), Collins touted her long record of service and work on the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee.
Collins said, “I am focused on bipartisan solutions to issues … like lowering the cost of health care and prescription drugs, strengthening Maine’s workforce, expanding housing options, making childcare more affordable, and funding lifesaving research into diseases like Alzheimer’s.”
Collins’ official campaign website lists similar accomplishments, including lowering costs for healthcare and medications related to Alzheimer’s disease and diabetes.
Troy Jackson, former Maine State Senate President, took the Democratic candidacy after Graham Platner withdrew from the race in early July.
Jackson’s campaign has consistently emphasized his blue-collar roots and status as a fifth-generation logger.
Jackson’s official campaign website stresses his humble upbringing as “a poor kid in a town of poor kids” and lists among his top priorities passing Medicare for all, lowering the cost of prescription drugs, dismantling and abolishing ICE, passing a federal right to abortion and ensuring comprehensive civil rights legislation.
Maine Governor
The Maine gubernatorial election pits three candidates against each other as they vie to replace term-limited Janet Mills: Republican Maine State Sen. Rick Bennett (running as an Independent), Republican lawyer Bobby Charles and former Democratic Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree.
Bennett, who currently serves in the Maine State Senate as a Republican until 2025, has emphasized an independent platform during this race. He touts an environmental, non-partisan approach to government, saying in an interview with NBC’s News Center Maine, “I would not want to serve as Governor with a party label after my name.”
Charles, a lawyer who previously served as Assistant Secretary of State for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs from 2003 to 2005, emphasizes curbing crime, cutting taxes and ending “ideological agendas” in schools, according to his official campaign website.
Pingree, the second woman to serve as Maine’s Speaker of the House from 2008 to 2010, takes affordability as one of the most pressing issues on voters’ minds. Her official campaign website outlines plans to curb childcare and gas costs and renew her emphasis on climate work.
U.S. House of Representatives (CD-2)
Bates is located in Congressional District 2 (CD-2), which elects a representative to the U.S. House of Representatives. This election cycle, Maine’s auditor Matthew Dunlap (running as a Democrat) and former Republican Maine governor Paul LePage will vie for the spot.
Dunlap, who has served as Maine state auditor since 2021, cites affordability as the focus of his campaign on his official campaign website.
Paul LePage, who served as Maine governor from 2011-2019, is centered on lowering costs, securing the border and promoting Social Security and Medicare, according to his official campaign website.
Lewiston Mayor
The ballot will offer voters a choice among mayoral candidates Carl Sheline (incumbent), Brian Beaulieu, Ricky LaChapelle, Jay Rodrigue and Charles Soule. A recent Sun Journal article covered each candidate’s goals for the office of mayor.
Ballot Questions
Lewiston voters will also decide five ballot questions:
- Question 1: Amendments to Syringe Service Program Ordinance
- Question 2: City Charter Commission
- Question 3: City Charter amendment regarding filling a vacancy on the City Council
- Question 4: City Charter amendment regarding vacancies on the City Council
- Question 5: City Charter amendment regarding City Council action on school budget
A sample ballot with elaborated explanations of each question is available on the City of Lewiston’s website.
Resources and Where to Vote on Nov. 3
Bates students registered to vote with their campus address should go to the Lewiston Armory on 65 Central Ave., unless living in 96 Campus Ave. or John Bertram Hall, in which case their polling location will be Montello Elementary School. Every hour, on the hour, a Harward Center shuttle will be waiting to transport students to the Montello poll location.
Additionally, the Harward Center will host walking groups departing every 15 minutes for the Lewiston Armory. These groups will meet at the Bates Votes table in front of Commons. Check out the Harward Center’s website on 2026 elections for more details.
Voters interested in information about minor-party candidates in the Senate, Governor and House races should see the Secretary of State’s list on upcoming elections.
