title: Study looks at changes to Mt. Katahdin’s tree line
text:
BAXTER STATE PARK, Maine (WABI) - According to a new study, the landscape atop Maine’s highest peak is changing through a process known as alpine greening.
“This study uses satellite imagery from the past 40-plus years to look at long-term changes in kind of the environment of the alpine zone on the summit of mountains across New England and eastern Canada, above tree line, where the climate is too harsh for trees to grow,” said Jonathan Chipman, the researcher at Dartmouth College who commissioned the study.
“What we found is that over the past four decades, there’s been a gradual greening process above tree line on these mountains,” said Chipman, notably, “Mount Katahdin, other mountains in Maine, in New Hampshire, and in eastern Quebec.”
“In some cases, trees are starting to spread up into areas that were formerly above tree line. Climate warming is contributing to this.”
Chipman went on to say that alpine zones, meaning zones above the tree line where larger vegetation cannot grow, are likely to keep shrinking.
“What we will probably see is the alpine zones, especially the smaller ones, disappearing on these mountains,” and “many of the smaller alpine summits will basically be turning over into forest,” said Chipman.
Nava Tabak, Natural Resource Director at Baxter State Park, said long-term data is key.
“It’s very hard to detect these changes year to year. And that’s why these studies like the ones that you’re asking about are so important because they allow us to look over longer periods of time to see that, to actually be able to detect those changes,” said Tabak.
Tabak also said alpine sedge communities appear to be bearing the brunt of these long term changes.
“Rare plants are, by their definition, somewhat more sensitive to these changes in population, sensitive to becoming extinct,” said Tabak.
Operating as a public trust, Baxter State Park takes a hands-off wilderness approach, focusing on managing people, not plants, to let systems adapt naturally.
On stewardship, Tabak stressed staying on the trails.
“One of the most impactful thing, things people can do when they come to visit an alpine area is to stay on the marked trails.”

title: Maine Averaged 21 Deer Crashes Per Day in 2025
text:
Most drivers in Maine will tell you that there is enough to worry about when behind the wheel without adding wildlife into the mix.
From excessive speeders to distracted drivers and beyond, keeping an eye out for a moose or a deer often times seems like an afterthought.
But according to driving data released by AAA for 2025, thinking about collisions with deer specifically shouldn't be an afterthought at all because it's happened about once-per-hour every single day last year.
There Were 7,672 Deer involved Vehicle Crashes in Maine For 2025
Over the last several years, there have been more than 32,000 vehicle accidents in Maine that have involved deer. In 2025 alone, there were 7,672 deer crashes averaging out to more than 21 per day.
Maine ranks number 9 in the nation in odds of having a deer-related vehicle crash and those odds are set to increase over the next few months.
That's because deer mating season has arrived in Maine and during the peak of rutting season in November, deer crashes around the state typically spike. Roughly 20% of the deer crashes in 2025 took place in November.
The Cost From Deer-Related Crashes in Maine Can Be Expensive
While frightening, deer crashes in Maine rarely prove to be fatal for drivers. What they can be is incredibly expensive.
Depending on the severity of the impact, repair costs on vehicles average anywhere from $3,000 to $6,000 per accident.
Injuries and damage costs rise when drivers attempt to swerve and avoid a deer, often causing motorists to hit guardrails, trees or other vehicles.
Deer activity during mating season is most prominent in the early morning hours and around the evening commute.

title: This fossil may look like a mini T. rex, but a Nanotyrannus just sold for a giant $47 million
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A dinosaur that looks like a miniature T. rex is now one of the world’s most expensive fossils.
The rare skeleton of a Nanotyrannus — recently confirmed to be a distant cousin of Tyrannosaurus rex, not just a young specimen — sold for $47.3 million to a mystery buyer at auction in New York City on Tuesday, according to Sotheby’s. The auction house had expected it to fetch anywhere from $6 to $9 million.
The blockbuster price tag for “Jodi,” as the skeleton is nicknamed, makes it the second-priciest set of dinosaur bones ever sold. This summer, a T. rex fossil known as “Gus” sold for a record $50.1 million at Sotheby’s.
The winning bidder for “Jodi” has, for now, chosen to remain anonymous after outbidding five other prospective buyers online and by phone during the roughly 12-minute live auction, Sotheby’s said.
A Nanotyrannus was about half the length of an adult T. rex, and the two creatures coexisted during the Cretaceous period some 67 million years ago. Nanotyrannus had longer forelimbs and larger hand claws, as well as more slender, blade-like teeth than its famous cousin.
“Jodi” is one of only three such skeletons known to exist. Standing 6.5 feet (2 meters) tall and stretching nearly 20 feet (6 meters), it has been on display at the auction house’s upper Manhattan headquarters since earlier this month, and is considered almost 70% complete.
The dinosaur is named after Jodi Pierson, the Montana rancher who discovered it on her land in 2019.
Sotheby’s, in a statement, thanked the team of professional fossil hunters whose efforts to discover and excavate the specimen were the focus of the Discovery Channel documentary series “Dino Hunters” in 2020.
“Their commitment to understanding and preserving this remarkable specimen has helped bring us to this moment, a testament to the fact that we can all make major contributions to science,” said Cassandra Hatton, Sotheby’s head of science and natural history.
However, some scientists have opposed such private sales, saying “Jodi” and other significant fossils should be displayed in museums or other institutions so they can be studied by researchers and viewed by the public.
Scientists for decades weren’t even sure whether Nanotyrannus represented a distinct type of dinosaur or merely a juvenile T. rex. But research published last year concluded that it was in fact a distinct genus of dinosaur.

title: Maine snubbed in US News & World Report’s ‘best places to retire’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Despite a reputation for attracting retirees, Maine didn’t get a single mention in U.S. News & World Report’s “250 Best Places to Retire in the U.S. in 2027” list.
It’s at least the second year in a row that Maine hasn’t made the list.
The recommendations were released Tuesday, and Texas and Florida cleaned up with 44 and 42 entries, respectively, followed by Michigan with 20, Indiana with 12, North Carolina and Georgia with nine apiece, and West Virginia with eight.
Numerous states appeared five times or more, but none of those were in the Northeast.
Just one New England municipality made the list, the Boston suburb of Newton, Massachusetts, which has held a spot since at least the 2025 list.
The list was created by applying demographic and geographic data to six categories that were weighted based on a public survey of 3,500 people, according to U.S. News & World Report.
Those categories, listed from most to least weighted, were: quality of life (including crime, weather temperateness, risks of extreme weather events, culture, air quality and walkability), value (cost), health care quality, retiree taxes, senior population/migration, and job market (based on Americans having “a variety of views on what it means to be retired”).

title: ‘You can’t go any higher’: American Airlines’ most senior flight attendant retires
text:

At 83, she is retiring at the top of American Airlines’ seniority list.
“It’s time. I’ve enjoyed every minute of it. I made No. 1 out of 30,000. You can’t go any higher, so I might as well hang it up,” Fair said in an interview with Forbes.
Her last trip was on an American Airlines flight from London to Charlotte, North Carolina, on Monday.
A crowd celebrated Fair when the plane landed at Charlotte Douglas International Airport.
Fair is a 2008 inductee of the North Carolina Transportation Hall of Fame and is also a member of the Tennessee Aviation Hall of Fame. Her career is also featured in an exhibit at the Sullenberger Aviation Museum.

title: Drought helps push Maine sewage pollution to record low in 2025
text:
Unusually low rainfall helped Maine set a record for the least amount of sewage pollution into waterways last year, according to a new state report.
Maine has been trying to eliminate combined sewer outfalls in dozens of towns and cities for decades. During heavy rains, these older systems carry combined stormwater and raw sewage into rivers and coastal waters.
Last year, about 153 million gallons of mixed water was discharged from combined sewer outfalls, half as much as the previous lowest record, according to the Maine Department of Environmental Protection.
There were 143 discharges in 2025, about a hundred fewer than the previous record in 2024.
The Department of Environmental Protection’s Mike Riley said that flash drought conditions last year helped avoid polluting discharges. But he said that the hundreds of millions of dollars invested in removing combined sewer outfalls also made an impact.
For example, the gallons discharged per inch of rainfall also hit a low record last year, Riley said.
“That last number takes into account dry vs. wet years,” Riley explained. “And that still being the lowest on record is a sign that investments that the communities are making on these [combined sewer outfall] abatement projects continue to pay off.”
Towns and cities spent $55.5 million on combined sewer outfall work last year, according to the Department of Environmental Protection. Riley said that over the years many of the simpler projects have been fixed and those remaining are more expensive and complicated works.

title: Letter: Mainers need Susan Collins now more than ever
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
You may not agree with every vote Sen. Susan Collins has ever taken, but I can tell you from my experience that she sees the needs of rural Maine and sends help.
When flood-level rain washed out our roads and breached Caratunk’s old bridges, our homes and travel means were at risk. These bridges were old and narrow bottlenecks that kept filling with gravel. I contacted every state agency I could to help us. The answer was always the same: The state was overwhelmed with bigger problems and had no money for a town our size. At one point, we were told Main Street might have to close.
Then help came from Collins in Washington. As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins secured $38.7 million to replace 11 aging, rural Maine bridges in poor condition, and Caratunk’s Main Street and Pleasant Pond bridges were included. That money came through a federal program she helped write specifically to fix old, rural bridges like ours. She saved our town from the next disaster before it happened. She saved our taxpayers from replacing expensive roads.
I believe Sen. Collins understands what small towns go through, and she has the seniority to deliver from D.C. With Augusta facing a $1.3 billion budget shortfall, rural towns can’t count on the state to step in. I believe Mainers need Susan Collins now more than ever before.
Elizabeth Caruso
Caratunk

title: Feds charge South Portland personal care agency with healthcare fraud
text:
The federal government has charged a South Portland personal care agency with healthcare fraud conspiracy, accusing it of obtaining Medicaid funds for services it never performed.
An indictment signed Oct. 22 was unsealed Tuesday morning, laying out the government’s allegations against Community Home Health Care LLC, its owner and five employees.
According to the document, investigators determined that the employees billed the state’s MaineCare program and received Medicaid funding for services that they knew they hadn’t provided. The allegations focus on personal care services that were reportedly provided to one unnamed client.
The owner and one employee have also been indicted on counts of “obstructing a health care crime investigation” for allegedly encouraging someone with knowledge of the situation not to speak with law enforcement after two related FBI raids in Augusta and Biddeford on June 23, according to the indictment.
Defense attorney Michael Conley said Tuesday that Community Home Health Care’s owner, Noora Abd, is presumed innocent.
“An indictment is an accusation. It is not a finding,” Conley said in an email. “The government writes it and presents it to a grand jury that meets in secret. No defense lawyer is in that room. No judge is in that room. Noora Abd was not in that room.”
An attorney for Faysal Kalayaf Manahe, who was also indicted on obstruction and healthcare fraud conspiracy counts, said his client is innocent and looks forward to trial.
“It seems to be a politically expedient prosecution,” attorney Thomas Marjerison said Tuesday.
Prosecutors said in the indictment that Maine had paid roughly $600,000 to Community Home Health Care since 2020 for a client to receive personal care support. The state later reversed $35,000 of that, according to the indictment.
“Healthcare fraud — in all its forms — costs all of us,” U.S. Attorney Andrew Benson said in a statement on Tuesday. Benson said if “you steal from our healthcare system for your own financial gain, you too, will be shut down and brought to justice. Protecting the integrity of all our federally funded healthcare programs for those who really need them is paramount.”
Prosecutors have not reported an actual loss, Conley wrote in a motion opposing the government’s request to hold Abd in jail pending trial. The indictment doesn’t detail which personal care services the government alleges were billed but not performed.
Prosecutors made similar requests to detain the other defendants, who, according to review of court records Wednesday morning, were ordered released on bail conditions. The defendants pleaded not guilty to their counts.
The Bangor Daily News reported that the hearings lasted roughly six hours, and that many people supporting the defendants were in attendance.
By 5 p.m. on Tuesday, a federal judge had ordered that several defendants be released on bail, including Abd, according to court records and attorneys.
Abd, 37, was arrested Tuesday at her home in Biddeford, according to her attorneys. She’s pregnant, and her three young children were immediately placed with her sister, they said. Abd’s attorneys said in a court filing that she has lived in Maine for more than 17 years without a criminal record, and that she’s known about the federal investigation since the FBI raids in June.
All of the defendants face up to 10 years in federal prison if convicted on the healthcare fraud conspiracy charge, according to court records. The obstruction counts carry another potential five years, and each count comes with a maximum of $250,000 in fines, or no more than twice the gross gain.
Jeffrey Grimming, the Homeland Security Investigations acting special agent in charge, said in a statement on Tuesday that the arrests “dismantled an elaborate alleged fraud ring dedicated to fleecing a system meant to help those in need.”
Abd’s employees have been accused of creating false entries in the state’s Electronic Visit Verification system, which the state uses to track Medicaid-eligible services as they’re performed, including the person who has performed the services and the date.
Mohammed Alkhalaf, an employee, has also been indicted on one count of delivering a false statement for denying the allegations during an FBI raid of a home in Augusta on June 23, according to the indictment. Property records show that Alkhalaf was one of the property owners.
Attorney Steve Smith, who was appointed to represent Alkhalaf, said on Tuesday that he had no comment at this time.
Investigators said in the indictment that they seized more than $116,000 in cash during an FBI search of the property in Biddeford, and more than $53,000 in cash from the search of Alkhalaf’s reported address.
Photographs of the search in Augusta captured by reporters show officials from the FBI and the Office of the Maine Attorney General. Both agencies declined at that time to comment on the nature of those searches.
Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey, whose healthcare fraud unit helped investigate, said in a statement on Tuesday that “federal and state officials are working continuously to protect public dollars.”
The Department of Justice said on Tuesday that the prosecution was part of a Homeland Security Task Force initiative established by President Donald Trump’s “Protecting the American People Against Invasion” executive order. The task force reportedly focuses on foreign gangs and transnational criminal organizations, according to the DOJ. Benson said Tuesday that all of the Community Home Health Care defendants are U.S. citizens, which is also reflected in court records.
Community Home Health Care is one of five reported agencies that the state had suspended Medicaid payments to, effective June 29, according to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. Another agency that had Medicaid payments suspended, Maine Connect Care, was included on a list of cases that the Office of the Maine Attorney General’s criminal division accidentally sent to members of the media earlier in October.
That document indicated that Maine prosecutors were waiting to hear back from the U.S. Attorney’s Office about whether federal criminal or civil charges would be pursued against the company, as well as another behavioral health provider that DHHS has taken action against, following allegations of Medicaid misuse.
Maine Connect Care did not respond to calls or emails last week.
Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, has criticized the state’s Medicaid program, saying in February that the state “needs to clean up its act.” In January, a federal audit reported that Maine made at least $45.6 million in improper Medicaid payments for autism support services in 2023. State officials pointed out at the time that the audit did not include findings or allegations of fraud.
In a news conference on Tuesday, Benson was asked whether to expect more Medicaid fraud indictments.
“I don’t want to comment on exactly what we anticipate, but I will say the investigation is ongoing,” Benson said.
Staff Writer Jake Freudberg contributed to this story.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 28 at 7a.m. to reflect that the defendants have been released.

Beloved high school football player hit, killed by allegedly drunken driver after game
text:
FEDERAL WAY, Wash. (KING) - Friends, family and teammates are mourning a 16-year-old Washington state student-athlete who was hit and killed by an allegedly drunken driver after a Friday night football game.
Deejay Tuiasosopo, 16, came from a family of standout athletes, including an all-star University of Washington quarterback – but his family says he was building his own legacy. The Federal Way High School junior played multiple sports, valued his education and cared about the people around him.
“He was always there for you. He always had a big smile on his face, no matter what was going on,” said Tuiasosopo’s friend, Stormie Corey. “He was lighting up every single room.”
After a Friday night football game, Tuiasosopo was standing on the sidewalk around 10:45 p.m. when two cars collided on Pacific Highway South in Federal Way. The crash sent one of the cars onto the sidewalk, hitting and killing the 16-year-old.
Police arrested the 29-year-old man driving the car that hit Tuiasosopo on suspicion of vehicular homicide. Investigators suspect he was driving under the influence.
“It didn’t feel real. It felt like I was stuck in a nightmare. Nothing can prepare you for that kind of moment,” Corey said. “He had so much life to live.”
Now, Tuiasosopo’s family, friends and teammates are left mourning his death, a loss that still doesn’t feel real.
“He wasn’t just a friend. He was a brother to me, and I just feel like all of us football players are going to remember this night,” said Chester Maletala, one of his football teammates. “We’re still going to have him spiritually in our hearts and in our head. We told ourselves already we’re going to make it to state for him.”
Tuiasosopo’s family said in a statement in part that “his energy, light and infectious presence reached far beyond what we, as his family, even realized.”
The suspect’s next court appearance is expected Wednesday. The investigation into the incident is ongoing.

title: Zookeeper dies after leopard attacked her in the animal’s enclosure
text:
AMSTERDAM (AP) — A longtime zookeeper at a safari park in the Netherlands died Tuesday from injuries she suffered when she was attacked by a leopard in its enclosure over the weekend.
The Beekse Bergen Safari Park said in a statement that the woman, whose name has been withheld in accordance with Dutch privacy law, had passed away after she suffered serious wounds to her head and neck on Saturday while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards. “Her passing deeply affects us all, and we sympathize intensely with her family, friends, and loved ones,” the zoo in the southern town of Hilvarenbeek said in a statement, which was made together with her family. The woman began working at the zoo when she was 17 and spent nearly all of her 40-year career there.
An investigation is underway to determine why the woman was in the enclosure with the leopards. Zoo staff are typically not permitted to be in the same space as predatory animals.
According to the zoo, the woman was able to alert colleagues via a walkie-talkie that she had been hurt. An ambulance and a trauma helicopter were dispatched to the park at around 11 a.m. local time on Saturday.
The woman underwent emergency surgery, but her condition worsened Sunday evening and the zoo said they did not expect her to survive. The safari park said an area in the park will be set up where condolences can be left.

title: Scarborough native Joe Cronin named Phillies assistant hitting coach
text:
PHILADELPHIA — The Philadelphia Phillies named Peter Fatse their hitting coach on Tuesday and hired Joe Cronin as assistant hitting coach. Edwar Gonzalez will remain on the Phillies’ staff as an assistant hitting coach.
Fatse and Cronin, a Scarborough native, were fired along with three other coaches and manager Alex Cora by the Boston Red Sox in April. Fatse was served as the Red Sox hitting coach for parts of five seasons from 2022-2026.
Cronin, who joined the Red Sox organization in 2021, was the team’s major league hitting strategy coach. He starred at Scarborough High and then Boston College before spending four seasons playing in the Minnesota Twins organization.
After being released by the Twins in 2020, Cronin joined the Red Sox as a player development intern in 2021. He became a development coach for the Greenville Drive (Boston’s Single-A minor league affiliate), then joined the major league team as a clubhouse analyst in 2023. Last season, he became Boston’s hitting strategy coach.
Fatse most recently worked as a hitting consultant for the Tampa Bay Rays, a role he began in June.
Fatse replaces Kevin Long, who was fired at the end of the season. The Phillies reached the playoffs for the fifth consecutive season but were eliminated by the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card Series.
“I am very excited to add Pete to our staff,” Phillies manager Don Mattingly said. “He has a track record of being a great communicator who prioritizes collaboration, and we truly feel that with his skillset and approach, he is a great fit for the organization.”

title: Who’s a Good Boy? Maine’s Most Popular Dog Breed Revealed
text:
Who’s a Good Boy? Maine’s Most Popular Dog Breed Revealed
Dogs. Man’s best friend. Our four-legged companions. The lovable, tail-wagging bundles of joy that somehow manage to make life infinitely better just by being around. A gift from the gods that we truly don't deserve.
If you're a dog lover, you know exactly what I'm talking about. Their loyalty is unmatched, their affection is endless, and their ability to brighten even the worst day is downright remarkable. Whether they're protecting the family, playing fetch, or simply curling up next to you on the couch, dogs have a special way of making everything better. Dogs are about as close to perfection as it gets.
How Can Dogs Positively Affect Your Health?
They can even help improve your health. According to the American Kennel Club, dogs can lower stress, improve heart health, promote a more active lifestyle, reduce loneliness, and even lessen the threat of allergies.
As you can probably tell, I’ve been a dog owner my entire life, and for me, it’s rescue dogs all the way! But that doesn’t mean I don’t have a soft spot for every breed out there.
With that in mind, I thought it would be fun to do a little research to figure out the most popular dog breed in Maine. Thankfully, the fine folks over at House Sitter have already done the heavy lifting. The site analyzed every house-sitting request it has received to determine the most popular breed in each state.
What is the Most Popular Dog Breed in Maine?
As for Maine, according to House Sitter, a true classic came in at number one: the venerable golden retriever.
The golden retriever is the ultimate family dog. Goldens are easy to train, gentle with children, good with other pets, and always up for a walk. Sure, keeping them clean can be a chore, but they more than make up for it with their affectionate nature and goofball charm. They also make amazing service and working dogs. Quite frankly, they are pretty damn perfect.
Seriously, who doesn't love a goldie? Every single one I have ever met has been mild-mannered, sweet, and just about perfect. While I have never owned one, I would certainly rescue one if I ever had the chance. Honestly, I'd love to see it try to corral our cats. That would be quite enjoyable to watch.
Maine was not alone in its love of goldies. Seven other states had the popular dog listed at number one, including one other New England state, Vermont. I always liked those Green Mountain folks.

While eight states is a solid number for the goldie, it pales in comparison to the most popular dog breed overall, the Labrador retriever, which led the way in a whopping 28 states. Very impressive indeed.

title: Terwilliger Family Light Show brings Halloween magic — and holiday tradition — to Hancock County
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) - Halloween lights, music and community spirit are shining bright in Ellsworth.
The Terwilliger Family Light Show runs Friday through Sunday, drawing crowds for a free, music-synced show like no other.
From 48 channels to 38,000
Bob Terwilliger says it started in his childhood with old-fashioned string lights — and blown fuses.
“This starts back in my childhood believe it or not. I used to go crazy with regular old fashioned lights when I was a kid.”
In November 2020, the family decided to try a full show with just 48 light channels. Now, they run 38,000 channels — taking a full week to set up.
“In 2020, we decided to kick it up a notch because we figured everybody needed a little something to look forward to.”
A community tradition
Every year, letters pour in about the show — a reminder of why they keep it free.
“We get letters every year from children, from parents. Some of them tug at your heart strings pretty hard, not going to lie.”
“After seven years, we’re seeing people say things like you know this is our tradition... this is on our list of places that we have to stop at every year, so it’s nice to see that this is becoming a part of other peoples traditions.”
“I’ve had a very good life, I feel like we’re very blessed and this is definitely worth it... sharing something bright for the community.”
How to watch + give back
- When: Friday through Sunday through Oct. 31

The Halloween show ends Oct. 31, then the Christmas show kicks off on Black Friday.

title: What are election monitors? Get the facts on the DOJ's record deployment
text:
What are election monitors? Get the facts on the DOJ's record deployment
Critics fear the program will be used to intimidate voters, which the Justice Department denies.
What are election monitors? Get the facts on the DOJ's record deployment
Critics fear the program will be used to intimidate voters, which the Justice Department denies.
The Justice Department is expected to launch its largest-ever election monitoring effort with a presence in all fifty states, but some advocates are concerned about how the decades-old program is evolving under the Trump administration.
Where will election monitors be deployed?
Kiersten Pels, a DOJ spokesperson, said there will be around 1,000 monitors deployed to counties across the country,  but a full list will not be shared until Election Day.
Election officials in some states, including North Carolina and New Mexico, hadn't recieved specifics from the DOJ as of Monday.
Officials in other states, including Arkansas, Georgia, Kansas, Maine, New Hampshire, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and South Carolina, have recieved notices about where monitors will be sent.
- Arkansas: Pulaski and Washington counties
- Georgia: Fulton, DeKalb, Gwinnett, Cobb, Chatham and Bibb counties
- Kansas: Johnson, Sedgwick, and Wyandotte counties
- Maine: Portland and Lewiston
- Massachusetts: Lowell and Boston
- New Hampshire: Manchester and Nashua
- Oklahoma: Oklahoma, Tulsa, and Muskogee counties
- Pennsylvania: Philadelphia, Allegheny, Luzerne and Lehigh
- South Carolina: Charleston County
Louisiana Deputy Secretary of State Trey Williams said they were informed "indirectly" about federal monitors but have not recieved official notification from the DOJ.
What's the purpose of the program?
Pels said monitors will "merely observe" and report any potential violations of federal law to the DOJ. She said those reports will be reviewed after Election Day. 
The program has been in place for decades to track compliance with civil rights laws, according to Nicole Hansen with the Campaign Legal Center.
"It's a program that has had a lot of success in uncovering instances of discrimination," Hansen said.
But critics fear the focus of the program is shifting under the Trump administration, which has repeatedly threatened to prosecute election officials who don't cooperate with election security efforts.
Some concerns were reported during primary elections. Wyoming's Republican Gov. Mark Gordon described the monitors’ behavior as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular." One county official said monitors asked to examine tabulators and inquired about the acquisition of new election equipment.
"It seems, this year, the Department of Justice election monitors are being used to hunt for fraud as opposed to protecting voters," said Carmen Daugherty, executive director of the Advancement Project.
Advancement Project and the NAACP filed a lawsuit earlier this month that aims to block the DOJ from deploying federal prosecutors and other federal law enforcement as part of the program.
"Our fear is that, if we see the deployment of prosecutors and federal law enforcement agents, that will have such a chilling effect, especially in Black and Brown communities, that folks will be afraid to come out and vote on Election Day," Daugherty said. "We have no issue with DOJ being neutral monitors."
The DOJ said the lawsuit is based on "unwarranted fear and baseless speculation" and rejected the notion that its election monitoring will intimidate voters.
"The NAACP’s self-serving fear-mongering is likely doing far more to deter lawful voting than our monitoring efforts," Pels said in a statement.
What can't election monitors do?
Hansen said that monitors are not supposed to question voters about their citizenship, interfere with election administration, or engage in political activity while they're on duty.
"So voters might have these very real fears, but they should also rest assured that there are critical federal laws to protect them from intimidation," Hansen said.
Amy Cohen with the National Association of State Election Directors said each state has different laws around who is permitted to be in a voting location and what they are authorized to do while they are in the voting location. She said voters who have concerns on Election Day should speak with a poll worker or reach out to their local election office.
Voters can also contact the nonpartisan Election Protection Hotline at 866-OUR-VOTE (866-867-8683).

title: Teenager charged in hit-and-run that killed 6-year-old getting off the bus
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A 17-year-old was charged in connection with a hit-and-run that killed a 6-year-old girl in Charlotte last week, according to authorities.
Charlotte police announced Monday that Lachevis Finnie, 17, was arrested in the hit-and-run death of 6-year-old Mariana Espinoza. He was charged with felony hit-and-run resulting in death.
Espinoza was hit by a car while crossing at the intersection last Friday in east Charlotte. Espinoza, a student at Devonshire Elementary School, had just gotten off the school bus.
Police said Espinoza was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries and died there the following day.
Doorbell camera footage obtained by WBTV on Monday shows the moments before Espinoza was hit.
Court documents filed Monday allege that Finnie was driving the Mercedes-Benz that hit and killed Espinoza.
Police had released a photo of the gray Mercedes-Benz, believed to be the car involved in the hit-and-run, Monday morning. By Monday evening, police said they identified Finnie as a suspect in the case after “conducting a traffic stop on the suspect vehicle.” The car had been seized as evidence.
An affidavit alleged Finnie did not stop after the collision and did not call 911. The document said he claimed he fled “due to being scared.” The affidavit also said Finnie “confessed to striking the child,” and has since been cooperative with the investigation.
Finnie appeared in Mecklenburg County court on Tuesday. During that appearance, he was appointed a public defender and had his bond set at $2.5 million. He was also ordered to complete a mental health evaluation.

title: Utah authorities connect serial killer Ted Bundy to another 1970s homicide
text:
Serial killer Ted Bundy is linked to another Utah teenager's 1974 killing through DNA testing
DNA connects serial killer Ted Bundy to the death of another Utah teenager, authorities announced Tuesday, exactly 52 years after her body was discovered in the woods by a hunter.
Bundy has been dead since 1989, but the tally of his confirmed victims continues to grow due to advances in DNA testing. He killed at least 30 women and girls in multiple states in the 1970s, and many more escaped or survived with injuries.
Investigators are satisfied that Bundy was responsible for killing 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith in 1974, a death that had long been listed as a cold case, Summit County Attorney Margaret Olson said at a news conference.
They were able to close the case by making crucial connections with DNA found on Smith and Laura Aime, another Bundy victim whose case was resolved last April in Utah County. Bundy's DNA was on file in Florida, where he was convicted and ultimately executed.
Besides that evidence, Smith’s death showed hallmarks of Bundy’s “pattern, motive, means and opportunity,” Olson said.
Decades-old evidence was key to the case
Utah's state crime lab got new technology in 2023 that extracts DNA from samples even if they are small, degraded from age or contain DNA from multiple people.
“This case demonstrates the importance of preserving evidence,” said Salt Lake County Sheriff Rosie Rivera, whose department has also investigated homicides linked to Bundy.
“We have to solve these cases to the best of our ability,” she said, explaining the importance of tapping science, even so many years later. "Nobody is just going to walk away and just blame everything on Ted Bundy, even though many cases have been that way. Here in the state of Utah, we take it very seriously.”
Smith's relatives were contacted about the findings but declined to attend the news conference and declined to speak to reporters, the Summit County Sheriff's Office said. Her parents are deceased.
Smith's father was police chief in Midvale, south of Salt Lake City. She was at a pizza parlor and a restaurant before she disappeared on Oct. 18, 1974, The Salt Lake Tribune reported at the time. Nine days later, her body was found in Summit County.
“With every case closure, may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out,” Utah County Sgt. Mike Reynolds said.
Bundy investigations are not finished
Bundy was executed by electric chair in Florida in 1989 after being convicted of three murders, including the killing of two women at the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University.
He gave a series of confessions in his final days, including to some crimes that were previously unknown to police. Not all of those cases have been confirmed.
Besides Florida and Utah, authorities said Bundy had victims in Colorado, Idaho and Washington state. They said they're especially working to solve the 1974 death of 16-year-old Nancy Wilcox of Utah.
Solving the Smith homicide “does not close the book on Ted Bundy,” said Det. Ben Pender of the Salt Lake County Sheriff's Office, which has the Wilcox investigation. “Information kind of leads to Ted Bundy but again we're not for certain on Nancy Wilcox. We're going to continue to work that case."

title: ‘You can’t go any higher’: American Airlines’ most senior flight attendant retires
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Gray News) - American Airlines’ most senior flight attendant is retiring after nearly 64 years with the company.
Carol Fair has worked as a flight attendant for 63 years.
At 83, she is retiring at the top of American Airlines’ seniority list.
“It’s time. I’ve enjoyed every minute of it. I made No. 1 out of 30,000. You can’t go any higher, so I might as well hang it up,” Fair said in an interview with Forbes.
Her last trip was on an American Airlines flight from London to Charlotte, North Carolina, on Monday.
A crowd celebrated Fair when the plane landed at Charlotte Douglas International Airport.
Fair is a 2008 inductee of the North Carolina Transportation Hall of Fame and is also a member of the Tennessee Aviation Hall of Fame. Her career is also featured in an exhibit at the Sullenberger Aviation Museum.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Jeffrey G. Sewall, 78, of Edgecomb and formerly of North Reading, Mass. and Sarasota, Fla., passed away on Oct. 22, 2026.
Jeff was born in Winchester, Mass. He proudly served in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam War. Following his military service, he lived in New Hampshire, where he served as a police officer with the Middleton Police Department. He later moved to Edgecomb – where he had spent many cherished childhood summers – and served for a decade as a deputy with the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office alongside his trusted K-9 partner, inspiring a lifelong love for German shepherds.
Jeff later relocated to Florida, where he ran a handyman business, driven by a lifelong desire to help others and work with his hands. Following his retirement, he returned permanently to his roots in Edgecomb. An avid outdoorsman, he loved hunting, fishing, and woodworking. He also played an active role in the congregation of the Edgecomb Community Church. Jeff took immense pride in being a veteran, a law enforcement officer, and a proud American.
Jeff was predeceased by his parents, Janet and Philip Sewall; his sister, Susan Merriam; the mother of his daughter, Joyce Sewall; and his late wife, Jeanne Wormelle. He is survived by his brother, Philip “Skip” Sewall Jr.; his daughter, Shandra Whitaker; his grandchildren, Hailey, Kayla, and Dylan; and his loving companion, Julie Tryder. He will be greatly missed by all who knew him.
A service honoring his life and military service will be Friday, Nov. 6, 2026 at 11 a.m. at the Edgecomb Community Church, at 15 Cross Point Road in Edgecomb.
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to German Shepherd Rescue of New England, gsrne.org, 978-443-2202, or P.O. Box 299, Wayland, MA 01778.
Arrangements are in the care of Hall’s of Boothbay. To leave online condolences for Jeff’s family, please visit hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: South Portland personal care agency accused of defrauding MaineCare in long-running scheme
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Maine announced Tuesday that an indictment has led to the arrests of six people in connection with an alleged long-running healthcare fraud scheme.
Federal prosecutors said a home healthcare agency in South Portland stands accused of defrauding MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, out of hundreds of thousands of dollars for services that were never provided.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office and federal law enforcement partners, including the FBI and the IRS, held a news conference Tuesday to discuss the indictment.
Trump administration’s allegations of fraud in Maine
On Jan. 23, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced that an audit revealed Maine made at least $45.6 million in improper fee-for-service Medicaid payments for rehabilitative and community support (RCS) services provided to children diagnosed with autism.
Two weeks later, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said in a social media post that Maine needed to “clean up its act” when it came to Medicaid fraud. CMS also sent a letter to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, in which it asked Gov. Janet Mills to explain how MaineCare — the state’s Medicaid program — prevents fraud, identifies when fraud happens, bans providers from billing the system and recovers misspent funds. Mills responded to that letter by saying Maine was facing “a political attack” from President Donald Trump.
During his State of the Union address on Feb. 24, Trump accused Maine of fraud and announced a “war on fraud” that would be led by Vance. In a statement responding to Trump’s claim, a spokesperson for Mills said Maine would “not be intimidated by the president’s threats” and said addressing fraud allegations should be a joint effort between the state and federal government.
On March 6, Mills announced that her administration had responded to the CMS request for information about MaineCare and said the state was conducting oversight to ensure MaineCare providers are held to high standards, adding that the state has robust enforcement mechanisms to identify fraud.
Vice President JD Vance visited Maine on May 14 and said the state may be the third- or fourth-worst state when it comes to fraud.
“Outside of Minnesota and California, which are probably No. 1 and No. 2, if they’re the gold medalist and silver medalist — I heard somebody shout out New York — maybe New York is the bronze medalist, but let me be honest, maybe Maine is the bronze medalist,” Vance said. “What you have in Maine is a festering problem where people have been taken advantage of and they’ve been stolen from, and your government hasn’t done anything about it.”
On Aug. 3, Oz was in Maine to further look into alleged fraud in the state. The following day at a news conference in Philadelphia, Oz said that billing by the top 10 providers in Maine has dramatically increased over the last six years. He said the catalyst for the fraud issue was the COVID-19 pandemic. In a statement responding to Oz’s claims, the Maine Department of Health and Human Services said that it has been actively working with CMS in response to the Office of the Inspector General report that was released in January.

title: P.I. Book Vending Machines Promote Good Attendance
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Elementary students in Presque Isle have a new way to dive into reading, thanks to new attendance-driven book vending machines. Pine Street and Skyway Elementary received donations toward the machines, which reward students for good attendance.
Elementary students in Presque Isle are earning their way to free books, thanks to the schools’ new book vending machines. Pine street Elementary held an assembly today to unveil their machine and explain to students how they can earn books.
Bill Guerrette, the Principal of Pine Street Elementary says: “We have an issue at Pine Street with truancy and truancy are kids who miss 10% of the school year and it could be for any reason. It could be a family vacation, could be sickness, could be whatever but it’s 10%. So, in 181 days it’s about 18 days of school and we were about at 33% of our kids were missing at least that much school. So, we were looking at a way that we could kind of promote attendance, promote literacy, and doing things as a family. And so, we thought the book vending machine would be a good way to do that.”
School officials reached out for donations toward the project. Presque Isle’s Kiwanis Club purchased the machines, and other businesses and organizations donated money and books to fill them. Students who attend school at least 90% of the time each month earn a token to spend on a book.
“I think it will make an impact. I think they’re excited about it and it will just be our job as adults to kind of sustain that excitement. Each month we are going to check with attendance records to see who’s been here at least 90% of the time and all of those kids will get a token for the month that they’ll get a chance to spend. So, we could be spending up to close to 200 tokens a month if attendance is really good. So, we’ve got to be prepared for that and have books ready to go,” continued Guerrette.
Several students at Pine Street Elementary picked out books from the machine during today’s unveiling. I asked some students how it felt getting the first books from the vending machine.
Walter Martinez Sanchez, a 1st Grader at Pine Street Elementary said: “Good!”
Mary Stevens, another 1st Grader added: “It was cool. It’s about a lot of books.”
With the new vending machines, the hope is that a free book will give students one more reason to come to school every day.

title: USPS recommends mailing ballots today in 34 states. Here's how to make sure yours counts
text:
USPS recommends mailing ballots today in 34 states. Here's how to make sure yours counts
The Postal Service advises voters in 34 states to mail their ballots by today to ensure they arrive by Election Day, while experts suggest exploring other return options if mailing is no longer viable.
USPS recommends mailing ballots today in 34 states. Here's how to make sure yours counts
The Postal Service advises voters in 34 states to mail their ballots by today to ensure they arrive by Election Day, while experts suggest exploring other return options if mailing is no longer viable.
With Election Day just a week away, Tuesday, Oct. 27, is an important date for millions of Americans planning to vote by mail.
The U.S. Postal Service recommends sending completed ballots at least seven days before they're required to arrive at election offices.
That makes today the recommended mailing date in 34 states where ballots must be received by Election Day, Nov. 3. Louisiana has an earlier deadline of Nov. 2.
Voters can still mail ballots afterward, but the Postal Service recommends allowing at least a week for delivery. And in some states, getting a ballot postmarked by Election Day isn't enough. It must actually arrive on time.
The rules vary across the country. The National Conference of State Legislatures maintains a state-by-state breakdown of ballot receipt and postmark deadlines.
Why mailing early may matter
A ProPublica investigation published on Oct. 22 found that late-ballot rejection rates doubled or tripled in some rural areas affected by changes to Postal Service operations during this year's primary elections, compared with the 2022 primaries.
The changes reduced mail pickups at certain rural post offices and routed more mail through regional processing facilities, sometimes adding time to delivery and delaying postmarks.
The Postal Service says it is taking additional precautions ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
In a statement to Hearst Television, USPS said it has begun deploying extraordinary measures, including additional deliveries and collections, special pickups and expedited local processing that can bypass normal processing steps when necessary.
The agency also pointed to its performance in previous federal elections, saying it delivered 99.9% of ballots from voters to election officials within seven days during the 2022 and 2024 election cycles.
USPS says it is confident it will successfully deliver election mail again this year.
Still, election experts say voters shouldn't assume mailing their ballots is their only option.
Amy Cohen, executive director of the National Association of State Election Directors (NASED), told Hearst Television that voters who cannot mail their ballots by the recommended date should review the alternatives available in their states.
"They need to be looking at the information available to them from their election officials to understand what their other options for return are," Cohen said.
Depending on the state, that could mean returning a ballot directly to an election office, using an authorized drop box, or voting in person.
Voters can find links to their state's official election website through NASED's voter resources page.
Your ballot arrived. Does that mean it will count?
Election officials still have to review mailed ballots to determine whether they meet the state's requirements.
A Common Cause analysis released Monday found approximately 3,700 mail ballots in North Carolina had been flagged for problems as of Oct. 24.
About two-thirds had been classified as spoiled, meaning voters needed to complete and submit replacement ballots. Others had problems that could potentially be corrected without casting an entirely new ballot.
Problems included missing witness information, signatures and improperly sealed envelopes.
Those figures do not mean 3,700 votes have been permanently rejected. Election officials notify voters of problems and provide opportunities to correct them, depending on state law.
Tim Tsujii, elections director in Forsyth County, North Carolina, told Hearst Television that as of Oct. 26, his office had spoiled 173 absentee ballots and sent replacements to affected voters. Another 24 ballots were awaiting corrections.
Tsujii said his office was contacting voters about those problems and working to resolve them.
"Typically it's because it's missing a signature. The witness signature," Tsujii said when asked about common ballot problems.
North Carolina requires absentee voters to have either two witnesses or a notary public complete the required certification.
Other states have different requirements for signatures, envelopes, identification and correcting errors.
Carol Evans, vice president of policy at Common Cause, cautioned against interpreting the North Carolina findings as evidence of widespread problems with mail voting nationally.
"We are not seeing systemic concerns with vote by mail. Vote by mail is safe and secure," Evans told Hearst Television.
She encouraged voters to follow their ballot instructions carefully and check whether election officials have received their ballots.
How to check whether your mail ballot was accepted
Many states offer online tracking systems that allow voters to check the progress of their mail ballots.
Some systems show when a ballot was mailed to the voter, when it was returned, and whether it was accepted by election officials.
"Given that we're within a week of the election, we also encourage voters that have any concerns about whether their ballot has arrived to track their ballot. Most states let you track your ballot," Evans said.
The U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC), a federal agency that provides election information and guidance, encourages voters to familiarize themselves with their state's requirements and points them to official resources for tracking ballots and understanding how problems can be corrected.
Here's how voters can put that guidance into practice:
- Visit NASED's state voter-information directory or the U.S. Election Assistance Commission's voter resources for links to official state election websites.
- Check your ballot's status. If tracking is available, look for confirmation that the ballot was received and, where reported separately, accepted.
- Act quickly if there's a problem. Contact your local election office to find out whether you can correct an error, submit a replacement ballot, or use another legally permitted voting method.
Some states allow voters to correct certain ballot problems after Election Day. Others impose earlier deadlines, and some problems require an entirely new ballot.
That's why voters should check their own state's rules rather than assume the same deadlines apply nationwide.
Evans said for additional assistance, voters can call the nonpartisan Election Protection Hotline at 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683). The hotline connects voters with trained volunteers who can help answer questions and address voting problems.
The Postal Service says dropping a ballot in a mailbox doesn't necessarily mean it will receive that day's postmark. Changes to mail transportation and processing can mean a piece of mail is postmarked after the day it was collected.
That distinction can be particularly important in states that accept ballots arriving after Election Day, provided they were postmarked by the required deadline.
USPS says voters can request a free manual postmark by bringing their completed ballot to a Postal Service retail counter.

title: Japanese manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, known for his boxing masterpiece 'Ashita no Joe,' dies at 87
text:
Japanese manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, known for his boxing masterpiece 'Ashita no Joe,' dies at 87
Legendary Japanese manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, who caused a national sensation with his boxing series "Ashita no Joe" or "Fighting for Tomorrow," a story about an orphan becoming a professional boxer, has died. He was 87.
Chiba's masterpiece series became so popular that fans even attended a mock funeral for the protagonist Joe Yabuki's rival.
Chiba died at a Tokyo hospital last Thursday, his publisher Kodansha Ltd. said Tuesday, without specifying the cause of his death.
While he depicted aspiring young athletes fighting for their life and career, Chiba was a vocal supporter of peace and freedom of expression, telling stories of his harrowing memories of war as a child in autobiographical stories and manga.
Months after he was born in Tokyo in January, 1939, his family moved to northeastern China and Chiba spent his early childhood there during Japan's occupation in the region, where his father worked at a printing factory.
At the age of six, Chiba and his family marked Japan's surrender on Aug. 15, 1945, while they were still in China. There, they faced danger and hunger in the face of anti-Japanese riots, but survived with the help of his father's Chinese translator who hid the family in an attic, where Chiba drew pictures for his three younger brothers.
The family eventually fled to China's port city of Huludao and returned to Japan in 1946.
The harrowing memories later influenced his work and activity with an anti-war theme.
Chiba debuted as a manga artist in 1956, initially drawing comic books for girls and later moving on to works for boys in the early 1960s.
In 1961, he debuted in a boys comic magazine with a baseball manga "Chikai no Makyu (The Magic Ball)," paving the way for a new genre of sports-themed manga in Japan.
Chiba's sports-themed mangas also included "Ore wa Teppei (I'm Teppei)," the story of a high school student training in the martial art of kendo, "Notari Matsutaro" about sumo wrestling, and "Ashita Tenki ni Naare (Let's hope the weather's fine tomorrow)" about a teenage golfer.

title: Risks spelled out for Anthropic investors include possible harms from runaway AI
text:
(AP) - Any time a company looks to start selling shares on Wall Street, it’s required to disclose potential risks for investors. In the case of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic, that has included the possibility that its products could threaten nothing less than humanity itself.
The risks laid out by the San Francisco company in its filing Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission included discussion of bad actors potentially using AI models to build deadly weapons or the technology itself going rogue with untold consequences.
Of the 335 pages outlining Anthropic’s finances, executive compensation, dividend policy and the like, 93 pages are devoted to “risk factors” — the things that could hurt potential shareholders’ investments. Rival SpaceX’s listed risk factors, in comparison, took up 38 out of more than 250 pages.
In selling itself to investors, Anthropic presents its own initial public offering as a step toward mitigating the risks it believes AI poses.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” write the company’s founders in a letter to prospective shareholders in the IPO filing. “Anthropic is a deeply values-driven organization, founded in large part to help the world realize AI’s benefits and avoid its dangers.”
Still, the risks are many. They range from the mundane — the possibility it won’t be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — to involvement in cyberattacks and the spread of dangerous misinformation.
Here is a look at some of the risks Anthropic details:
The technology’s rapid development
Anthropic said it’s possible its models could develop so quickly the company won’t be able to implement adequate safety measures, “which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in September that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet. The warning — and now Anthropic’s move to sell shares — comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also act on their own to carry out other, more harmful tasks.
As AI systems “become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the SEC filing said, there’s a risk that such systems could “take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.”
“Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier AI could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business,” Anthropic said.
Now that the AI models are themselves contributing to Anthropic’s own research and development, it’s possible that AI could progress “beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models,” according to the filing. This, the document said, could adversely affect Anthropic’s business.
Malicious actors could cause mayhem with the technology
The filing discussed concerns that advanced AI systems, if not developed and operated with enough safeguards and oversight, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.”
The company said it would be harmed if use by bad actors causes damage, “or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse.”
Anthropic sketched out the prospect of bad actors using AI models to build chemical weapons or authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens. In September, the company disclosed that it had blocked efforts to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapon development.
The company could run up against limits on processing power
Compute — the computing power or resources needed to build, test and improve AI models — is expensive and in high demand. Anthropic notes that if it’s unable to secure adequate compute, or if “we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers.”
Anthropic mentioned community opposition to data centers as a risk to its business. Data center development “has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources,” the filing said, adding that if regulators impose new requirements or charges as a result, its ability to do business could suffer.
In addition, the company relies on a small number of customers, including SpaceX and Microsoft, and distribution channels for a large portion of its revenue. This means that even if just one of its big customers decides to scale back — or drop the company altogether — Anthropic said it could see its prospects and finances suffer.
Mitigating the risks
In some ways, AI’s enormous risk, combined with its enormous potential, is Anthropic’s main selling point. The company has tried to position itself as a responsible AI company, and courts business customers by emphasizing safety-mindedness.
“We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology,” the filing said.
Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Research, said IPO deals have to display “very clearly” what risks people face when they invest their money in a newly public stock.
“That’s one of the things that’s great about our capital markets here domestically is the level of transparency that you must commit to, to be a publicly traded corporation on a U.S. exchange requires you to outline those risks in a very clear way, so that people understand if they want to participate by offering their hard-earned money and help finance this type of a deal,” he said.
___
AP Business Writer Bernard Condon and AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed to this story.

title: UMaine police comfort dog Bear meets the woman who donated him
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Bear, the University of Maine Police Department’s comfort K-9, met the woman who donated him Tuesday.
Bear has served as the university’s first comfort K-9 since June. The 5-month-old lab has doubled in size and has garnered thousands of Instagram followers and countless adoring fans on campus.
Bear joined the department by donation from New Hampshire author Claire Hebert-Dow. After owning a comfort dog and witnessing the power of puppy kisses, Hebert-Dow began donating comfort dogs to fire and police departments.
Two years ago, Hebert-Dow published Saving Mama, a memoir told through the perspective of her five pets.
She met Bear on Tuesday and saw the effect he has on campus.
“I’ve already seen what my own dog was able to do in the elementary school system,” Hebert-Dow said. “So whether it’s elementary school or college, everybody needs a wagging tail.”
Bear’s handler, Sgt. Jamey Dover, said having Bear has helped him connect with students and staff, both in crisis and in day-to-day interactions.
“Everything around me went from people being slightly uncomfortable or uncertain to hearing about their dogs at home or they talk to people they don’t even know about their dogs at home,” Dover said. “It’s a whole different community vibe, which is very important to our department. We want to be members of the community, not just cops on campus.”
Hebert-Dow said she has donated two other dogs to fire departments, with a third in the works.
Dover said Bear is requested somewhere on campus every day.
People can meet Bear at the department’s Halloween event Saturday in the campus police department’s parking lot from 4:30 to 9 p.m.

title: Cold Overnight. More Clouds Wednesday With Warmer Temperatures By Thursday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Clear skies and light winds will make for a cold night across the region, with some communities expecting one of the coldest nights so far this season. A warming trend midweek will then bring a big boost in temperatures ahead of Halloween, which looks seasonable and dry for trick-or-treaters.
Tuesday Night: Coldest Night So Far for Some
Skies will stay clear overnight as high pressure slides across the region and winds continue to weaken. That setup allows temperatures to drop quickly after sunset. Overnight lows will range from the upper teens to the upper 20s.
Wednesday: Brisk Start, More Afternoon Clouds
The area of high pressure will slide into the Gulf of Maine Wednesday morning, bringing a brisk but sunny start to the day. As the high slides east Wednesday afternoon, more clouds will build in. Afternoon highs will range from the upper 40s to the mid 50s.
Thursday: Big Warm-Up
A warm front will cross the region Thursday, bringing a big boost to highs. Widespread 60s are likely, with spots in southern Maine that could get close to 70 degrees. A few coastal communities will stay in the upper 50s with winds off the water.
Friday: Isolated Morning Shower, Then Partly Cloudy
A cold front Thursday night into early Friday morning will bring the chance for isolated showers, ending by mid-Friday morning. Do not expect much rainfall as most spots will be lucky to see a few hundredths of an inch. The rest of Friday will feature partly cloudy skies with highs in the 50s and 60s.
Halloween: Seasonable and Dry
Halloween will feature seasonable temperatures in the 40s and 50s and will remain dry. Trick-or-treaters heading out Saturday evening may want an extra layer or two once the sun goes down.

title: Utah authorities are connecting serial killer Ted Bundy to another 1970s homicide
text:
PARK CITY, Utah (AP) — Authorities in Utah are holding a news conference Tuesday to pin another decades-old homicide on serial killer Ted Bundy.
The Summit County sheriff and county attorney “will provide information regarding the investigation, the findings that led to this conclusion, and the decision to close the case,” the sheriff’s office said.
The victim’s name has not been released yet, though the local death of 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith in 1974 has long been listed as a cold case.
Bundy has been dead for nearly 40 years, but the tally of his confirmed victims continues to grow due to advances in DNA testing.
Bundy killed at least 30 women and girls in multiple states in the 1970s, and many more escaped or survived with injuries.
In April, Utah authorities said Bundy was responsible for the murder of Laura Ann Aime, 17, who disappeared on Halloween in 1974.
He was executed in 1989 by electric chair in Florida for the 1978 murders of two women at the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University.
Bundy gave a series of confessions in his final days, including to some crimes that were previously unknown to police. Not all of those cases have been confirmed.

VIDEO: Driver plows through police car door during traffic stop
text:
Close call: Video captures moment driver plows through police car door during traffic stop
A close call was caught on camera after a suspected drunk driver slammed into a deputy's car door as the officer attempted to exit the vehicle.
The Montgomery County Sheriff's Office in Conroe, Texas, shared video of the Oct. 24 incident on Facebook, which showed a vehicle plow through the patrol car's door at a high rate of speed and continue traveling down the road.
Authorities said they were first conducting an investigation after receiving reports of a different suspected intoxicated driver along Interstate 45. The video shared by the sheriff's office showed one person being placed into the back of a patrol vehicle.
A second deputy arrived on scene and was positioned in a marked patrol vehicle with its emergency lights activated to protect the deputy conducting the investigation, the sheriff's office said.
As the second deputy began getting out of the patrol car, the driver of a passing vehicle failed to move over or slow down, crashing into the open door of the patrol car. The driver failed to stop after the crash.
Deputies identified the vehicle that left the scene of the crash and responded to the registered address. There, they located the vehicle with damage consistent with the crash and evidence that supported the owner, 33-year-old Elizabeth Perez, as the driver.
Authorities said Perez was arrested for failure to stop and render aid, passing an emergency vehicle causing bodily injury, and DUI.
The driver of the initial traffic stop, 24-year-old Jacob Zamora, was also arrested for DUI.
Both were taken to the Montgomery County Jail.
The deputy involved in the incident was taken to the hospital and later released.
No other injuries were reported.

title: An intergenerational duo teams up to make greeting cards
text:
LANSING, Mich. (InvestigateTV) - Riley Haughey sits at her kitchen table with a tackle box of tools, drawing her newest critter with markers.
“I just really like the close up of looking at how markers go onto the paper. It kind of is like magic for me,” Riley said.
The 11-year-old fifth grader creates colorful animal drawings she calls Riley’s Critters. Each critter ends up on a greeting card.
“This is like top notch printing I feel like,” Riley said.
The printer is 85-year-old Tony Klain.
Klain has no grandchildren of his own. He became a friend of the Haughey family six years ago when they were backyard neighbors.
“He’s so kind,” said Whitney Haughey, Riley’s mother.
When the family was looking for a cost-effective way to get Riley’s Critters on greeting cards to help pay for Riley’s dance classes, Klain stepped up.
“He was like, I can do it,” Whitney said.
At his home office, Klain uploads Riley’s animal art and cleans up imperfections.
“We’ll call it Cherry the squirrel,” Klain said while working on one card.
He preserves Riley’s signature mark, a paw print in the shape of a heart, and her brush strokes.
“I don’t like to change what she’s done,” Klain said.
The work is familiar to Klain. His wife Phoebe did similar artwork.
“My wife did the same thing and so that’s kind of cool,” Klain said.
The artistic connection to Klain’s wife has helped mend his broken heart.
“Actually, when my wife died, she left a whole bunch of journals, and she did a lot of really neat drawings and stuff,” Klain said.
Klain perfected his Photoshop talent by turning his wife’s art into a collection of calendars. He pulled drawings from her journals and scanned them to match each month.
Now the 85-year-old is matching wits with an 11-year-old in a friendship built on art.
Riley gives a nod of approval when she sees the finished product.
“It looks good,” Riley said.
“Makes my day every time I do it,” Klain said.

title: Voters to weigh Trump’s record on 2024 campaign promises
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump won a second term by making many promises to voters. Nearly two years after he was sworn in, those voters can judge whether he kept them, and they will decide in days how he has done.
When Trump campaigned for president in 2024, he told voters he would turn around the U.S. economy and close America’s borders.
Trump often speaks about his record on illegal immigration on the campaign trail.
“Two years ago, we inherited the worst border in American history, and we turned it into the safest border, the best border by far in the history of our country,” Trump said at a rally in Arizona October 14.
Voters give the president high marks on closing the southern border. However, his immigration policies have been met with criticism.
Also, Trump has consistently received low approval ratings on his management of the U.S. economy, in part due to the ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs.
Trump fulfilled promises to eliminate taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security. He also frequently made another pledge during the 2024 campaign.
“We will target everything from car affordability to housing affordability to insurance costs to supply chain issues … to the price of prescription drugs,” Trump said in a campaign speech in Asheville, N.C., on August 14, 2024.
Gas prices are up 40% since Trump was sworn in. The increase is driven primarily by disruptions to global oil supplies related to the conflict in Iran.
Trump repeatedly promised “no new wars” during his 2024 presidential campaign and said he would keep the U.S. out of foreign conflicts.
The war in Iran is continuing, as is the Ukraine-Russia war. Trump promised to end the Ukraine-Russia war on his first day in office.
Trump is now promising to deal with Cuba on the way home from Iran.

title: Biddeford taps Kennebunkport leader as new city manager
text:
Biddeford announced the nomination of a new city manager Tuesday.
Laurie Smith, the town manager of Kennebunkport, will begin her three-year contract on Dec. 29.
The council will vote to confirm Smith’s appointment at its Nov. 5 meeting.
In a news release Tuesday, Mayor Liam LaFountain said he is pleased to nominate Smith, pointing to her extensive municipal experience, financial acumen and management skills.
“I look forward to working with Laurie, our staff and the City Council to address the challenges ahead and better serve our residents,” LaFountain added.
Smith has worked as Kennebunkport’s town manager since 2014. She previously served in the same role in Boothbay, Oxford, Boothbay Harbor, Wiscasset and Auburn, where she spent 10 years. She holds a bachelor’s degree in public administration from the University of Maine and resides in Kennebunk.
In Tuesday’s news release, Smith said she is honored to be joining Biddeford.
“Throughout this process, I’ve been impressed by how deeply people care about this city and its future,” she wrote. “I look forward to getting to know the community, supporting our dedicated employees and working with the mayor and City Council to turn shared priorities into meaningful progress.”
Smith will be the third manager to serve Biddeford in just over a year. She will succeed Cornell Knight, who has served as interim city manager since June.
The previous city manager, Truc Dever, resigned in April. In her resignation letter, Dever pointed to the “scope and complexity of the issues facing (the city) — many of which are long-standing and systemic” as one of the reasons for her departure.
Dever succeeded former manager James Bennett, who resigned in early 2025. Prior to his resignation, Bennett came under fire for several issues, including his handling of the proposed research pier at the University of New England. Bennett later filed a lawsuit against the city, claiming that it owed him a large amount of money; that lawsuit was settled in October 2025.
Smith said Tuesday that she believes she has the experience necessary to help the city find solutions to its problems.
“I thought I could be helpful and create some structure,” she said in a phone interview. “This council is very interested in moving forward and doing the right thing, but they need help.”
As city manager, Smith says she hopes to get Biddeford’s finances in order, create and follow good process and policy, be responsive to citizens, and have systems set in place to provide appropriate responses to issues.
While she will miss the employees and citizens of Kennebunkport, Smith said she is ready to step into her new role this December.

title: More young adults are living with their parents, according to survey
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - The high cost of living and a challenging job market are keeping more young Americans at home.
Nearly half of adults under the age of 30 now live with a parent, according to the Federal Reserve’s latest survey of household economics and decision-making.
That’s up 6 percentage points since 2022 and 12 percentage points since 2019.
The cost of housing, high mortgage rates and everyday expenses like groceries and gas are the main reasons behind the trend.
According to AAA data, U.S. diesel futures have also surged above $5 a gallon, for the first time since April 2022.
Americans are feeling a little better about the economy after consumer confidence hit a 12-year low in September.
According to the Conference Board’s latest report, the consumer confidence index jumped 7.5 points in October to 91.7.
However, confidence remains well below recent historical levels, and persistent inflation continues to squeeze household budgets.
